In this book, Bhurijana dasa has woven together the Bhagavatam’s potent verses with Srila Prabhupada’s powerful purports. He has then added many extraordinary comments from our previous acaryas, Visvanatha Cakravarti, Sridhara Swami, and Jiva Goswami.

The result is a striking tapestry, a detailed, easily readable, coherently flowing overview of the Bhagavatam’s first four cantos.

This is an absolute need for serious students of the Bhagavad philosophy.

# Unveiling His Lotus Feet

## Dedication

Desiring to evoke auspiciousness, I first offer my humble obeisances and my gratitude to Srila Prabhupada, my spiritual master:

*nаmа оm visnu-padaya krsna-presthaya bhutale srimate bhaktivedanta-svamin iti namine*  
*namas te sarasvate deve gaura-vani-pracdrine nirvisesa-sunyavadi-pascatya-desa-tarine*

**“I offer my respectful obeisances unto His Divine Grace A. C. Bhakti-vedanta Swami Prabhupada, who is very dear to Lord Krsna, having taken shelter at His lotus feet. Our respectful obeisances are unto you, О spiritual master, servant of Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Gosvami. You are kindly preaching the message of Lord Caitanyadeva and delivering the Western countries, which are filled with impersonalism and voidism.”**

My life rests fully on the gifts Srila Prabhupada has given me. I dedicate this book to him. In Bhagavatam [10.31.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/31.9) the gopis say:

*tava kathamrtam tapta-jivanam kavibhir iditam kalmasapaham*  
*sravana-mangalam srimad atatam bhuvi grinanti ye bhuri'da jandh*

**“The nectar of Your words and the descriptions of Your activities are the life and soul of those suffering in this material world. These narrations, transmitted by learned sages, eradicate one’s sinful reactions and bestow good fortune upon whoever hears them. These narrations are broadcast all over the world and are filled with spiritual power. Certainly those who spread the message of Godhead are most munificent.”**

These words glorify Srila Prabhupada and his munificence, for he has filled the world with krsna-katha, especially by translating and publishing Srimad-Bhagavatam and then inspiring its distribution. May this book, offered into Srila Prabhupada’s lotus hand, be pleasing to him.

## Introduction

Gaze at the cover of this book. In San Francisco in 1967, Srila Prabhu-pada looked at this picture of Krsna and quoted a text from Bhakti-rasdmrta-sindhu ([1.2.239](https://vedarama.com/en/books/rupa-brs1/1.2.239)): “My dear friend, if you are indeed attached to your worldly friends, do not look at the smiling face of Lord Govinda as He stands on the bank of the Yamuna at Kesighata. Casting sidelong glances, He places His flute to His lips, which seem like newly blossomed twigs. His transcendental body, bending in three places, appears very bright in the moonlight.”

Lord Brahma had also gazed at this same all-powerful and unbounded Supreme Personality of Godhead in the cowherd pastures of Vrndavana. He then described what he saw: “My dear Lord, You are the only worshipable Lord, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and therefore I offer my humble obeisances and prayers just to please You. О son of the king of the cowherds, Your transcendental body is dark blue like a new cloud, Your garment is brilliant like lightning, and the beauty of Your face is enhanced by Your gunja earrings and the peacock feather on Your head. Wearing garlands of various forest flowers and leaves, and equipped with a herding stick, a buffalo horn and a flute, You stand beautifully with a morsel of food in Your hand.”

Yet despite Krsna’s omnipresence and all-attractive beauty, He remains forever veiled before the eyes of conditioned souls. Srimati Kunti said: “O Krsna, I offer my obeisances unto You because You are the original personality and are unaffected by the qualities of the material world. You are existing both within and without everything, yet You are invisible to all. Being beyond the range of limited sense perception, You are the eternally irreproachable factor covered by the curtain of deluding energy. You are invisible to the foolish observer, exactly as an actor dressed as a player is not recognized.” (Bhag. [1.8.18-19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.18))

Krsna Himself describes the concealing curtain that veils Him as His impenetrable deluding energy, His own unconquerable potency: “This divine energy of Mine, consisting of the three modes of material nature, is difficult to overcome . . .” (Bg. [7.14](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/7.14)) And, “I am never manifest to the foolish and unintelligent. For them I am covered by My internal potency, and therefore they do not know that I am unborn and infallible.” (Bg. [7.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/7.25))

Yet Krsna can be known; may as veil can be lifted. Srila Prabhupada brought the method for doing so to the West. Indeed, he felt prepared to journey westward only when carrying with him his three-volume translation of the Bhagavatam’s First Canto. On his arrival in Boston Harbor in 1965, he wrote, “All living entities have become under the control of the illusory energy by Your will, and therefore, if You like, by Your will they can also be released from the clutches of illusion. . . . The words of Srimad-Bhagavatam are Your incarnation, and if a sober person repeatedly receives them with submissive aural reception, then he will be able to understand Your message.”

Because of the Srimad-Bhagavatam’s power to reveal Krsna, Srila Prabhupada spent his most cherished time, his early morning hours, alone, translating Srimad-Bhagavatam. He also stressed that his disciples hear, read, speak on, and distribute Srimad-Bhagavatam. His words often glorified the Bhagavatam’s potency:

**Krsna is present within the universe, within our hearts, and even within the atom, so it is not difficult to find Him. But one must know the process by which to do so. This process is very simple, and by the order of Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu we are distributing this process to everyone, without charge. The process is to chant Hare Krsna. As soon as one chants Hare Krsna, one will immediately understand Krsna. Similarly, simply by hearing or chanting the verses of Srimad-Bhagavatam, one can be purified. Whatever knowledge exists in the world is present in Srimad-Bhagavatam. It includes literature, poetry, astronomy, philosophy, religion, and love of Godhead. Srimad-Bhagavatam pramanam amalam. If one simply reads Srimad-Bhagavatam, he gains the topmost education, for if one studies Srimad-Bhagavatam he will be well versed in every subject matter. Even if one does not understand a single word of the mantras of Srimad-Bhagavatam, the vibrations themselves have such power that simply by chanting one will be purified. Srnvatdm sva'kathah krsnah punya'sravana'ldrtanah. The word punya means “pious,” sravana means “hearing,” and kirtana means “chanting.” One who chants or hears the verses of Srimad-Bhagavatam becomes pious automatically. To become pious one generally has to endeavor a great deal, but if one simply hears the verses of Srimad-Bhagavatam or Bhagavad-gita one becomes pious automatically. Therefore it is a rigid principle in every temple of our Krsna consciousness movement that there must be a daily class for hearing and chanting. Our movement is meant for training spiritual leaders, but without hearing and chanting it is impossible to become a leader. Of course, in the material world it is possible, but not in the spiritual world. Mali hand sei bija hare aropana sravana-lartana jale karaye secana. Hearing and chanting waters the seed of devotional service, which develops one’s original consciousness. (TQK, pp. 23-24)**

Clearly, Srila Prabhupada intensely desired the world to become absorbed in the Srimad-Bhagavatam and its message. Unveiling His Lotus Feet, A Detailed Overview of Cantos One-Four is a humble attempt by one insignificant soul to assist devotees in doing so.

The seed of this book was planted in the rich soil of Sri Vrnda-vana in late 1983. I had just arrived to live in this holy place, and circumstantially, I was asked to gives classes on several of the early chapters of Canto One. As I began to pore over “The Son of Drona Punished,” “Prayers by Queen Kunti and Pariksit Saved,” and “The Passing Away of Bhismadeva in the Presence of Lord Krsna,” I was stunned. 1 had read these chapters many times, but now as I studied them to discover the main points of each of Srila Prabhupada’s purports, I noted that these points could be connected. 1 discovered, as the Bhagavatam's story flowed from one pastime to the next, that the Bhagavatam’s philosophical continuum had its own flow.

This excited me, and as I sectioned each chapter into its natural cluster of texts, 1 studied each text to string together that section’s philosophical essence. I felt that I had tapped into a hidden stream of philosophical ideas, and that that flow was progressive from chapter to chapter, canto to canto. I began to see that if I entered into the stream and became purified by it, I would be carried from Krsna’s lotus feet to His smiling face, the Tenth Canto. As I studied these early First Canto chapters, I became increasingly eager to discover what the Srimad-Bhagavatam would present next. Enraptured by having tapped into the flow of this mysterious book, I felt I had glimpsed the genius of both Srila Vyasadeva and Srila Prabhupada’s presentation. This book is my attempt to present that flow, traced from Canto One to Canto Four.

A part of me wonders whether some devotees will feel that this book might distract readers from Srila Prabhupada’s own rendition of Srimad-Bhagavatam, especially since it so closely follows Srila Prabhupada’s presentation. After considering the point, however, I have concluded that Srila Prabhupada’s purity, potency, and unparalleled devotional stature makes this highly unlikely. Indeed, Srila Prabhupada himself said in 1976, while driving in a car with disciples: “My books will be the lawbooks for human society for the next ten thousand years.” May Unveiling His Lotus Feet encourage devotees to study Srila Prabhupada’s Srimad-Bhagavatam in its entirety.

My primary motive in writing Unveiling His Lotus Feet was to myself become absorbed in Srimad-Bhagavatam. I need the purification such absorption offers. Adding another personal note, in 1996 I sadly observed that although I had been attending Bhagavatam classes for almost thirty years and had read the Bhagavatam in its entirety a number of times, I still had little grasp of the continuum I mentioned. The contents of many Srimad-Bhagavatam cantos, especially Two, Three, and Four, eluded me. A burning enthusiasm to fit the pieces together as well as to improve my own preaching fueled my writing. I also desired to associate directly with Srila Prabhupada through his written word.

My first objective in presenting Unveiling His Lotus Feet as a book was to offer readers an overview that would weave together the story and the philosophy. I hope this book will assist devotees to clarify the pieces of the first four cantos and how they fit together. Unveiling His Lotus Feet also attempts to answer questions that typically arise when reading those cantos. For these reasons I assume this book will be helpful to devotees studying the first six cantos in preparation for their Bhakti'vaibhava degree.

**A Note About the Comments Included from the Acaryas**

Into the tapestry of storyline and philosophy in Unveiling His Lotus Feet, I have inserted pieces of commentaries from the Vaisnava acaryas, especially from Srila Sridhara Svami, Srila Jiva Gosvami, and Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura. As I know no Sanskrit, and no full and accurate English translations of these commentaries exist, I begged the assistance of quite a few Sanskrit scholars. Other than the comments of the acaryas presented in quotation marks, I have included paraphrases and summaries of the acaryas’ words.

Literal translations of Sanskrit commentaries are often highly technical and may require knowledge of Sanskrit to grasp. In addition, some comments, especially those included from Srila Jiva Gosvami’s Sat-Sandarbhas, speak about specific texts only peripherally, as Sri Jiva’s purpose in his own book is to establish the Gaudiya Vaisnava siddhanta, not to offer textual analysis of the Bhagavatam. In Unveiling His Lotus Feet, then, I generally offer summaries and paraphrases of portions of the commentary or Sandarbha text. I apologize to readers whose thirst for the acaryas’ words remains unquenched by this. The future appears bright, however, as the number and quality of translations from Sanskrit to English seem to be increasing.

To check the accuracy of the paraphrases, I first wrote them from the translated texts I had available. Whenever possible I checked the comments against other available translations. That scholarly and gentle-hearted soul, Gopiparanadhana Prabhu, then did a preliminary check on what I had written. The paraphrases were then checked again by a host of scholars, each taking a few commentaries. I wish to thank all the Sanskrit scholars (in alphabetical order) who kindly offered their expertise in this and other ways: Adi-purusa dasa, Matsya-avatara dasa, Radhika-Ramana dasa, and Vinode Bihari dasa.

**Four Remaining Points**

1. How the material is marked: Each “chapter” in Unveiling His Lotus Feet was written as an essay, which we have called a “Dialogue.” To avoid confusion, I have numbered the Dialogues, but readers should note that these numbers do not necessarily follow the Bhagavatam’s chapters. Rather, most of the Dialogues cover several Bhagavatam chapters. For example, Canto Three, Dialogue Four covers Chapters Thirteen through Nineteen of the Third Canto. In this way, Canto One has eight Dialogues, Canto Two has three, and Cantos Three and Four have seven each. Perhaps a reader, seeing the word “Dialogue,” will ask whether the Bhagavatam can be divided into dialogues. Yes, it can. Throughout the Bhagavatam, Srila Vyasadeva presents much of his material as a series of questions and answers, themselves dialogues, but which often become dialogues within dialogues. The narratives describing the Lord’s various incarnations and pastimes are all related through the dialogue form. Therefore, I felt this word appropriate for the presentation in Unveiling His Lotus Feet.
2. The creation: The creation is a complex topic and is described a number of times in the second and third cantos. Although these descriptions may differ in their details and terminology, I based my own presentation on Kapila Muni’s description in Canto Three, Chapter Twenty-six. Compiling an account of the universal creation was extremely difficult and time-consuming, especially the section dealing with texts [3.26.20-24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.20). Several scholarly devotees checked my attempt, and taking their comments into consideration, I adjusted my description accordingly. Undoubtedly, my description is flawed, and I request readers to forgive any mistakes they may uncover in this (and other parts) of my presentation. I wish to express my appreciation for the comments and translations of Bhanu Swami, Radha-Govinda Swami, Gopiparanadhana Prabhu, and Dravida Prabhu.
3. Anticipating the question: Is Unveiling His Lotus Feet the first in a series that will take the reader through the end of the Twelfth Canto? Only time will tell. It depends on whether Krsna awards me both the required physical and mental stamina to continue this work, and access to translations of the required Sanskrit commentaries. It also depends on whether the devotees recognize a need for further books along this line. In any case, the present book, as an independent volume, will assist readers in their study of the early cantos of Srimad-Bhagavatam.
4. Special appreciations: Years ago, in the 1980s, when I first began to study the Bhagavatam, I made it a practice to copy the sections of purports that especially struck me. 1 have included many of these selections in this book out of my own special appreciation for them, as well as a number of other sections of purports that demanded inclusion in the narrative flow. Therefore, the purport sections included are my own choices. Please don’t consider them authoritative denotations of “the most important sections” of any purports.

## CANTO ONE

## Dialogue One - Questions by the Sages

**Introducing Srimad-Bhagavatam**

## Chapter 1 - The Opening Words of Srila Vyasadeva

## Texts 1-3: Invocation

Srila Prabhupada’s Preface to the Srimad-Bhagavatam contains a powerful inspiration to begin studying the Bhagavatam from its opening text: “Srimad-Bhagavatam begins with the definition of the ultimate source. It is a bona fide commentary on the Vedanta'Sutra by the same author, Srila Vyasadeva, and gradually it develops into nine cantos up to the highest state of God realization. The only qualification one needs to study this great book of transcendental knowledge is to proceed step by step cautiously and not jump forward haphazardly as with an ordinary book. It should be gone through chapter by chapter, one after another. The reading matter is so arranged with the original Sanskrit text, its English transliteration, synonyms, translation and purports so that one is sure to become a God-realized soul at the end of finishing the first nine cantos.”

Srila Prabhupada continues: “The Tenth Canto is distinct from the first nine cantos because it deals directly with the transcendental activities of the Personality of Godhead, Sri Krsna. One will be unable to capture the effects of the Tenth Canto without going through the first nine cantos.”

After offering humble and grateful obeisances to Srila Prabhupada, let us begin our gradual journey through the Bhagavatam’s texts, chapters, and cantos, beginning with the Bhagavatam’s first verse. In this text, Vyasadeva defines and offers obeisances to the Absolute Truth, the “ultimate source” of all, Sri Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

## Text 1: Definition the Absolute Truth

Srila Vyasadeva begins the Srimad-Bhagavatam by offering his obeisances to and defining the Absolute Truth:

*оm namo bhagavate vasudevaya*  
*janmady asya yato ’nvayad itaratas carthesv abhijnah svarat*  
*tene brahma hrda ya adi-kavaye muhyanti yat surayah*  
*tejo’vari'mrdam yatha vinimayo yatra tri-sargo ’mrsa*  
*dhamna svena soda nirasta-kuhakam satyam param dhimahi*

**Перевод:**

**О my Lord, Sri Krsna, son of Vasudeva, О all-pervading Personality of Godhead, I offer my respectful obeisances unto You. I meditate upon Lord Sri Krsna because He is the Absolute Truth and the primeval cause of all causes of the creation, sustenance and destruction of the manifested universes. He is directly and indirectly conscious of all manifestations, and He is independent because there is no other cause beyond Him. It is He only who first imparted the Vedic knowledge unto the heart of Brahmaji, the original living being. By Him even the great sages and demigods are placed into illusion, as one is bewildered by the illusory representations of water seen in fire, or land seen on water. Only because of Him do the material universes, temporarily manifested by the reactions of the three modes of nature, appear factual, although they are unreal. I therefore meditate upon Him, Lord Sri Krsna, who is eternally existent in the transcendental abode, which is forever free from the illusory representations of the material world. I meditate upon Him, for He is the Absolute Truth.**

The Bhagavatam’s first three texts form a prelude to the book. The first text defines the Absolute Truth, the second describes the Bhagavatam and defines actual religion, and the third invites humanity to taste the Bhagavatam’s sweetness.

In his Introduction to the Srimad-Bhagavatam, Srila Prabhupada immediately differentiates the Absolute Truth, which it is the goal of the Bhagavatam to describe, from the common understanding of God: “The conception of God and the conception of the Absolute Truth are not on the same level. The Srimad-Bhagavatam hits on the target of the Absolute Truth. The conception of God indicates the controller, whereas the conception of the Absolute Truth indicates the summum bonum, or the ultimate source of all energies.” This first verse, then, is Srila Vyasadeva’s definition and description of the Absolute Truth— that substance from which nothing is different. That Absolute Truth is a person, the divine son of Vasudeva and Devaki known as Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Everything else, including the brahmajyoti (God’s “oneness” aspect), emanates from Him.

One can understand how Srila Prabhupada derived his translation of text 1 by examining the Sanskrit text’s word-by-word definitions and comparing them to the English translations. We have analyzed the Bhagavatam’s opening three texts by joining each Sanskrit phrase with its corresponding English phrase from Prabhupada’s translation. Then we added explanations of those phrases drawn mainly from Prabhupada’s purports. But as this analysis is quite lengthy, we have placed it, along with commentaries from two great Vaisnava acaryas, Sridhara Svami and Jiva Gosvami, at the end of this chapter. By moving this important material to later in the chapter, we hope to facilitate the reader’s progress into the body of this book while still offering the serious student an opportunity to enter more deeply into Srila Prabhupada’s presentation of the Bhagavatam’s opening texts.

## Other Discussions in Bhagavatam 1.1.1 - The Bhagavatam Comments on the Gayatri-mantra

After defining Krsna as the all-perfect, all-attractive Supreme Personality of Godhead, the Absolute Truth and the cause of all causes, Srila Prabhupada recommends that everyone surrender to Him and become a great soul, a mahatma. The topic of the twelfth paragraph of Srila Prabhupada’s purport then shifts to deal with a challenge: “Some Mayavadi scholars argue that Srimad-Bhagavatam was not compiled by Sri Vyasadeva. And some of them suggest that this book is a modem creation written by someone named Vopadeva. In order to refute such meaningless arguments, Sri Sridhara Svami points out that there is reference to the Bhagavatam in many of the oldest Puranas. This first sloka of the Bhagavatam begins with the Gayatri mantra.”

Srila Prabhupada has referred here to Srila Sridhara Svami’s comment on Bhagavatam [1.1.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.1), which says: “The Purana known as Srimad-Bhagavatam has eighteen thousand verses divided into twelve cantos, begins with Gayatri, describes the hayagriva-brahma'vidya and narrates the slaying of Vrtrasura.” In the rest of the twelfth paragraph, Srila Prabhupada supports the authenticity of the Bhagavatam.

In Paramatmasandarbha, anuccheda 105, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains how the Bhagavatam’s opening text comments on the Gayatri-mantra. He shows correlations between words in the Brahma-gayatri and words in the Bhagavatam’s first text. For example, Sri Jiva notes that orh, the initial syllable of the Brahma-gayatri, is explained in Bhagavatam [1.1.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.1) as janmady asya yatah, which indicates that the Absolute Truth, Sri Krsna, is the cause of the creation, sustenance, and destruction of the manifested universes. Similarly, the Brahma-gayatri’s words, bhur bhuvah svah, denoting the lower, middle, and upper planetary systems, are explained in the Bhagavatam’s first text as yatra tri'sargo ’mrsa, words that also refer to the material universes. The next phrase in Brahma-gayatri, describing the sun’s self-sustaining effulgence, savitur varenyam bhargah, is contained in the Bhagavatam’s word svarat. Svarat refers to the Lord’s full independence.

Jiva Gosvami then compares the Brahma-gayatri’s prayerful mood of enlightenment—“May the Lord mercifully engage our thoughts in meditation on Him”—to the words tene brahma hrda, meaning that the Lord enlightens Brahma because of Brahma’s prayerful mood. Sri Jiva also says that Vyasa’s words satyam param dhimahi—“I meditate upon the Absolute Truth”—at both the beginning and the end of the Bhagavatam ([1.1.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.1) and [12.13.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-12/13.19)), indicate that the Bhagavatam’s ultimate objective is meditation on Krsna, because He is the Absolute Truth. That the Brahma-gayatri mantra also uses the word dhimahi indicates that the goal of chanting the mantra is the same as the goal of the Bhagavatam: meditation on Krsna, the Absolute Truth.

Lord Caitanya says: “In the beginning of the Srimad-Bhagavatam there is an explanation of the Brahma-gayatri mantra. ‘The Absolute Truth, satyam param,’ indicates the relationship, and ‘we meditate \[dhimahi\] on Him’ indicates the execution of devotional service and the ultimate goal of life.” (Cc. Madhya [25.147](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/25.147))

## Two Other Meanings of Bhagavatam 1.1.1 Offered by Srila Jiva Gosvami

**FIRST: Bhagavatam 1.1.1 as Pointing to Sri Krsna’s Lilas**

The first text has unlimited meanings. Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura spoke on it in Dacca (now Bangladesh) each day for three months. Here is one other translation compiled from information in Srila Jiva Gosvami’s Krsna-sandarbha, anuccheda 82:

**janma—after taking birth; adyasya—\[the Supreme Lord\] who eternally remains in three abodes (Mathura, Dvaraka, and Gokula); yatah—when; anvayat—because of His being Nanda’s son, due to His connection or family relation. Thus He went elsewhere, to Nanda’s home, because of His filial relationship with Nanda; itaratah—to another place, i.e., the home of Nanda Maharaja; \[ca\] arthesv abhijnah—knowing His purpose (He knows why He was being carried to Vraja: to deceive Kamsa and to perform pastimes with His intimate devotees in Vraja); svarat—one who shines within His own (the Vrajavasis, the residents of Gokula).**

**\[Let us meditate on\] the original Personality, who, just after taking His birth \[in a prison house\] in Mathura, wished to go and live with His intimate devotees in Gokula \[and inspired His father to take Him to that place\].**

**tene brahma—He expanded (tene) His glory (brahma), which consists of a form of rasa that is pure truth, knowledge, and limitless bliss; hrda ya—by His own mere desire or determination; adi-kavaye—Lord Brahma; muhyanti—became bewildered (becoming helpless due to an arising of an abundance of prema; yat surayah —because (yat), i.e., for the purpose of His pastimes with the Vrajavasis.**

**He expanded by His thinking power into many cows and boys, bewildering great personalities. \[Not only was Brahma, a demigod, bewildered, but even Baladeva was bewildered for one year.\]**

**tejo—effulgence; vari—water; mrdam—earth; yatha vinimayo— exchanged, transformed; yatra—in whom (i.e., “in Krsna”); tri-sargo—the three abodes—Vrndavana, Mathura, and Dvaraka— are manifest in Sri Krsna and are (therefore); amrsa—not false, but real.**

**The Lord created pastimes in three places: Vrndavana, Mathura, and Dvaraka. His wonderful pastimes changed the inherent nature of things—the moon lost its effulgence when Krsna played His flute, and the Yamuna became solid, while rocks melted.**

**dhamna svena soda nirasta-kuhakam—all the places of Krsna’s pastimes are free from illusion; param satyam—Govinda is called Satya; dhimahi—I meditate.**

**All the places of Krsna’s pastimes are free from mdyd, illusion, because illusion cannot approach these holy abodes, or dhamas. I therefore meditate on the Supreme Lord Krsna. I therefore meditate on Him, Lord Sri Krsna, who is eternally existent in the transcendental abode, which is forever free from the illusory representations of the material world. I meditate on Him, for He is the Absolute Truth.**

**SECOND: Bhagavatam 1.1.1 as Pointing to Sri Sri Radha-Krsna’s Sweetness**

In Krsna-sandarbha, anuccheda 189, Srila Jiva Gosvami states, commenting on Bhagavatam [1.1.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.1), that the first verse of the Srimad-Bhagavatam is intended to describe not only the opulence and glory of Sri Sri Radha-Krsna but Their transcendental sweetness. The words yato ’nvayad mean “to Lord Krsna, who is attached to Srimati Radharani, His transcendental pleasure potency.” The word itaratah means “His eternal companion, Srimati Radharani.” The word yatah means “from whom,” adyasya means “the mellow of madhurya^rasa” (conjugal love), and janma means “manifestation.” Together, these words mean that Sri Sri Radha and Krsna are the transcendental abode of the science of mddhurya-rasa.

Next, the great sweetness of Their wonderful pastimes is described: carthesu means “in many pastimes,” and abhijnah means “expert.” The word svarat means “by His own self, possessing such qualities, He shines with great splendor.” Thinking that Their mercy alone was what was required to be able to describe the Divine Couple, Vyasadeva spoke the words adi-kavaye, “to me, Vyasadeva.” Thus Vyasadeva now begins to describe Their pastimes. Hrda means “through the heart,” brahma means “the spiritual words that describe Their pastimes,” and ya tene means “who in the beginning revealed this entire Purana in my heart.”

The word у ad means “about whom,” surayah, “even Ananta-sesa and those like Him,” and muhyanti, “are unable to even begin to understand or describe Her astonishing virtues and beauty.” Vyasadeva thinks, “If Srimati Radharani is not merciful to me, then even if I have Lord Madhava’s mercy, I shall not be able to understand Her pastimes, such as the one that begins with this verse (Bhag. [10.30.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/30.26)): ‘The gopis began to follow the footprints, and shortly they saw another set of footprints beside them, and immediately they became very sorry.’”

The phrase tejo-vdri'mrdam yatha vinimayah also describes Sri Sri Radha-Krsna’s pastimes. These words refer to Lord Krsna playing His flute. On hearing the sound of His flute, all inanimate objects in Vrn-davana became overwhelmed with transcendental bliss and changed their nature. The shining moon and stars (tejah) dimmed and appeared like water or earth. In the presence of the effulgence of Radha and Krsna’s toenails, the moon (and so on) became as if without radiance. Water and rivers took on the properties of fire and flowed upward. These astonishing things occurred as a result of Sri Sri Radha-Krsna’s wonderful pastimes.

In the phrase yatra tri'sargo ’mrsd, yatra may be interpreted as follows: yatra means “in Srimati Radharani.” Tri-sargah may refer to Krsna’s three potencies (Sri, Bhu, and Lila-sakti), His three abodes (Dvaraka, Mathura, and Vrndavana), or the three classes of gopis in Vrndavana (friendly, neutral, or opposed to Srimati Radharam). Mrsa means “irrelevant.” That is, all these—the Lord’s potencies, abodes, and even the gopis of Vrndavana—are insignificant compared to the transcendental opulence, qualities, and beauty of Srimati Radharani. Krsna does not need any of these three things to satisfy His transcendental desires because all His desires can be fulfilled by Srimati Radharani alone.

The word dhimahi means “I meditate on Sri Sri Radha-Krsna.” By Their power and opulence, Sri Sri Radha and Krsna remain always (soda) free (nirasta) from the illusory interference offered by Radharani’s gopi rivals. These cannot obstruct Sri Radha-Krsna’s pastimes.

The word satyam (eternal) in this verse should be understood to mean that Sri Sri Radha and Krsna are eternally situated in the highest perfection. They continuously relish transcendental bliss in Their pastimes, and this condition never changes. The word param means that the unprecedented transcendental qualities, pastimes, and other features of Sri Sri Radha-Krsna are superior to everything found anywhere else. (These superexcellent qualities and pastimes fill the entire universe with wonder. The flooding rivers of nectar of their transcendental qualities are the life of the devotees. Indeed, who would not become delighted by hearing the transcendental pastimes of Their lotus feet?)

The charming sweetness of Sri Sri Radha-Madhava is enhanced by Their exchanges of pure and playful dancing glances. That sweetness has anointed Them with the greatest skill in delighting each other with the pastimes of madhurya-rasa, and that sweetness has made Them intoxicated with the fragrance of the nectarean love They bear for each other. May that sweetness of the golden and blackish forms of Sri Sri Radha-Krsna continually overtake my thoughts.

## Text 2: The Glories of the Srimad-Bhagavatam

After offering obeisances to the Absolute Truth, Srila Vyasadeva now glorifies the Bhagavatam and defines actual religion.

*dharmah projjhita-kaitavo ’tra paramo nirmatsaranam satam*  
*vedyam vastavam atra vastu sivadam tapa-trayonmulanam snmad-bhagavate maha-muni-krte kim va parair isvarah sadyo hrdy avarudhyate ’tra krtibhih. susriisubhis tat-ksanat*

**Перевод:**

**Completely rejecting all religious activities which are materially motivated, this Bhagavata Purana propounds the highest truth, which is understandable by those devotees who are fully pure in heart. The highest truth is reality distinguished from illusion for the welfare of all. Such truth uproots the threefold miseries. This beautiful Bhagavatam, compiled by the great sage Vyasadeva \[in his maturity\], is sufficient in itself for God realization. What is the need of any other scripture? As soon as one attentively and submissively hears the message of Bhagavatam, by this culture of knowledge the Supreme Lord is established within his heart.**

Prabhupada’s purport offers advice to those wishing to achieve the full benefit of hearing the Bhagavatam: “The proper method for receiving this transcendental message is to hear it submissively. A challenging attitude cannot help one realize this transcendental message. One particular word is used herein for proper guidance. This word is susriisu. One must be anxious to hear this transcendental message. The desire to sincerely hear is the first qualification.”

Srila Prabhupada continues:

**Less fortunate persons are not at all interested in hearing this Srimad-Bhagavatam. The process is simple, but the application is difficult. Unfortunate people find enough time to hear idle social and political conversations, but when invited to attend a meeting of devotees to hear Srimad-Bhagavatam they suddenly become reluctant. Sometimes professional readers of the Bhagavatam immediately plunge into the confidential topics of the pastimes of the Supreme Lord, which they seemingly interpret as sex literature. Srimad-Bhagavatam is meant to be heard from the beginning. . . . The intelligent person, with thoughtful discretion, can be assured by the great sage Vyasadeva that he can realize the Supreme Personality directly by hearing Srimad-Bhagavatam. Without undergoing the different stages of realization set forth in the Vedas, one can be lifted immediately to the position of paramahamsa simply by agreeing to receive this message.**

Srila Sridhara Svami comments that the point of this second Bhagavatam text is to impress on readers that Srimad-Bhagavatam is the greatest scripture. He adds that Bhagavatam [1.1.2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.2) defines true religion. He asserts that those religions teaching humanity to adore the Lord simply to fulfill one’s desires, even up to the point of liberation, are cheating religions. The Srimad-Bhagavatam rejects such religions. Pra (the prefix of projjhita) emphasizes the meaning “completely rejected”; this sweeping rejection includes even the desire for salvation.

## Text 3: An Invitation to Taste the Bhagavatam’s Sweetness

*nigama-kalpa-taror galitam phalam*  
*suka-mukhad amrta-drava-samyutam*  
*pibata bhagavatam rasam alayam*  
*muhur aho rasika bhuvi bhavukah*

**Перевод:**

**О expert and thoughtful men, relish Srimad-Bhagavatam, the mature fruit of the desire tree of Vedic literatures. It emanated from the lips of Sri Sukadeva Gosvami. Therefore this fruit has become even more tasteful, although its nectarean juice was already relishable for all, including liberated souls.**

Srila Prabhupada’s purport again and again glorifies the Srimad-Bhagavatam and thereby invites readers to hear it with patience: “In this sloka it is stated that Srimad-Bhagavatam is not only a superior literature but is the ripened fruit of all Vedic literature. In other words, it is the cream of all Vedic knowledge. Considering all this, patient and submissive hearing is definitely essential. With great respect and attention, one should receive the message and lessons imparted by the Srimad-Bhagavatam.

“. . . Every living entity, beginning from Brahma, the first-born living being within the material world, down to the insignificant ant, desires to relish some sort of taste derived from sense perceptions. These sensual pleasures are technically called rasas. . . . The sum total of all these rasas is called affection or love. ... In this sloka, it is definitely stated that spiritual rasa, which is relished even in the liberated stage, can be experienced in the literature of the Srimad-Bhagavatam due to its being the ripened fruit of all Vedic knowledge. By submissively hearing this transcendental literature, one can attain the full pleasure of his heart’s desire.

“The subject matter is so presented through the lips of Srila Suka-deva Gosvami that any sincere listener that hears submissively can at once relish transcendental tastes which are distinct from the perverted tastes of the material world . . . Srimad-Bhagavatam is so carefully presented that a sincere and serious person can at once enjoy the ripened fruit of Vedic knowledge simply by drinking the nectar-ean juice through the mouth of Sukadeva Gosvami or his bona fide representative.”

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on Bhagavatam [1.1.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.3) in the Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 110: nigama-kalpa'taror galitam phalam means “O auspicious souls, learned in the mellows of love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead, please relish in your hearts the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is the sweet fruit of the desire tree of the Vedas, a tree with many branches and twigs that bear all fruits, a tree that has come to this earth from the spiritual world of Vaikuntha.”

In Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 110, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains that one will never become satiated by tasting the nectar of Srimad-Bhagavatam and that one’s desire to taste it will never diminish; therefore, even after liberation (alayam) one will continue to drink (pibata) the Bhagavatam’s nectar.

In Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 110, Srila Jiva Gosvami also notes that the word aho in this text hints that Srimad-Bhagavatam enables one to attain what is otherwise unattainable. He also explains that the Srimad-Bhagavatam is described by the word rasa because rasaikamayata'vivaksaya, it deals only with spiritual mellows and not with anything else. When one understands Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as the reservoir of rasa (raso vai sah), one becomes transcendentally blissful.

## Additional Analysis of Bhagavatam 1.1.1-3

**Text 1**

**1. om namo bhagavate vasudevaya** —“O my Lord, Sri Krsna, son of Vasudeva, О all-pervading Personality of Godhead, I offer my respectful obeisances unto You.”

Srila Prabhupada explains that “obeisances unto the Personality of Godhead, Vasudeva, directly indicate Lord Sri Krsna, who is the divine son of Vasudeva and Devaki.” Krsna is indeed the Supreme Personality of Godhead and the object of Vyasadeva’s obeisance.

Krsna Himself directly confirms that He is also known as Vasu-deva in Bhagavatam [11.16.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/16.32): “My devotees worship Me in nine different forms, among which I am the original and primary Vasudeva.” In this text, adi-murtih means “the original form, Vasudeva,” aham means “I am,” and para means “the Supreme.” Thus the Bhagavatam immediately introduces its readers to the Absolute Truth, Sri Krsna, who is so charming that His qualities and pastimes attract us to His loving service in the spiritual world.

**2. janmady asya yato** —“\[I meditate upon Lord Sri Krsna because\] He is the Absolute Truth and the primeval cause of all causes of the creation, sustenance and destruction of the manifest universes.”

Prabhupada writes: “Vasudeva, or Lord Sri Krsna, is the cause of all causes. Everything that exists emanates from the Lord.” Nothing is foreign to or separate from Him; no one can compete with Him. The Absolute Truth is the source of everything in existence. Thus the Bhagavatam’s opening text contains the same definition of the Absolute Truth (janmady asya yato) as the Vedanta-sutra. Indeed, the Garuda Purana states that the Srimad-Bhagavatam comments on the Vedanta-sutra: “The Srimad-Bhagavatam presents the meaning of the Vedanta-sutras, the full purport of the Mahabharata, the commentary on Brahma-gayatri, and the fully expanded knowledge of the Vedas.”

**3.  ’nvayad itaratas carthesv abhijnah** —“He is directly and indirectly conscious of all manifestations.”

Krsna knows everything directly and indirectly, just as one knows both directly and indirectly the sensations of one’s body. When one’s arm is pinched, he experiences the sensation directly. He may also experience the pinch indirectly by observing the pincher in action. Krsna, however, is simultaneously the substance (the arm), the subjective ex-periencer, and the objective observer. He is nondifferent from everything in existence. Srila Prabhupada writes: “Whatever happens to the body quickly becomes known to the embodied. Similarly, the creation is the body of the absolute whole. Therefore, the Absolute knows everything directly and indirectly that happens in the creation.”

**4. svarat** —“He is independent because there is no other cause beyond Him.”

Prabhupada writes: “Conditioned souls, beginning from Brahma, who engineers the entire universe, down to the insignificant ant, are all creating, but none of them are independent of the Supreme Lord.” Everything is dependent on Him.

The abilities, qualities, and even existence of everything in this world, including the most powerful of persons, Lord Brahma, depend on Lord Krsna, who exists independently. It may be raining in Delhi, but that is not an independent truth, because the existence of both rain and Delhi depend on and rest in Krsna. Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, along with His qualities and pastimes, is alone independent. He is the Absolute Truth. Everything else necessarily exists in relation to Him.

**5. tene brahma hrda ya adi-kavaye** —“It is He only who first imparted the Vedic knowledge unto the heart of Brahmaji, the original living being.”

Brahma is not the ultimate creator, as Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport: “Herein it is stated that the Supreme Lord inspired the secondary creator, Brahma, in order that Brahma could carry out his creative functions. So, the supreme intelligence behind all creations is the Absolute Godhead, Sri Krsna.”

**6-9.** **muhyanti yat surayah** —“\[By Him\] even the great sages and demigods are placed into illusion . . .” tejo'vari'mrdarh yatha—“\[as one is bewildered by\] the illusory representation of water seen in fire, or land seen on water.” vinimayo yatra tri-sargo—“Only because of Him do the material universes, temporarily manifested by the reactions of the three modes of material nature, ...” ’mrsa—“appear factual \[although they are unreal\].”

Prabhupada explains these points as follows: “This cosmic creation results from interaction of the three modes of nature, and the temporary manifestations are so created as to present an illusion of reality to the bewildered mind of the conditioned soul, who appears in so many species of life, including the higher demigods, like Brahma, Indra, Candra, and so on. In actuality, there is no reality in the manifested world. There appears to be reality, however, because of the true reality which exists in the spiritual world, where the Personality of Godhead eternally exists with His transcendental paraphernalia.”

The words tejo'vari'mrdam yatha vinimayo offer an example of illusion: a mirage. When one sees the mirage of a lake on desert sands, one perceives an image of water above the sand. There is such a thing as water, but when one perceives water over desert sands, he is seeing an illusion. Despite one’s capacity to perceive water in the desert or to mistake a rope for a snake, water, deserts, ropes, and snakes are all real. Similarly, despite one’s misperception that his true home is this world, it is a mirage based on a fact. One’s actual home—the eternal spiritual world of Vrndavana—is objectively real. It is its objective reality that lends credence to the mirage.

Under illusion’s spell, a living entity seeks eternal love and happiness in the material world. However, neither eternal love nor eternal happiness exists here. Rather, each exists as an objective reality in the spiritual world. In this world, we see only their mirages. Under illusion one imposes these desirable conceptions on the ephemeral realm of matter and thus becomes frustrated. Yet even the maya that facilitates a living entity’s illusion is not separate from the Absolute Truth. This maya, too, is one of Krsna’s energies and is fully dependent on Him. The illusory energy is so strong that even sex desire, the primary attraction in this world, appears extraordinarily important.

Sex in this world is not ultimately important; rather, it is a mirage of pleasure. Like everything, sex has its pure origin in Krsna and is purely expressed in His spiritual realm. This is explained in Srila Prabhupada’s purport: “Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura specifically deals with the original and pure sex psychology (adi-rasa), devoid of all mundane inebriety. . . . The material sex life is but a perverted reflection of the original fact. The original fact is in the Absolute Truth, and thus the Absolute Truth cannot be impersonal. It is not possible to be impersonal and contain pure sex life. Consequently, the impersonalist philosophers have given indirect impetus to the abominable mundane sex life because they have overstressed the impersonality of the ultimate truth. Consequently, man without information of the actual spiritual form of sex has accepted perverted material sex life as the all in all.”

Muhyanti yat surayah: through His maya, Krsna bewilders even the greatest demigods, Brahma and Siva, what to speak of ordinary living entities. Thus yatra tri-sargo ’mrsa: the material world appears real, even though it is not, because the spiritual world is real.

**10. dhamna svena sada** —“\[I therefore meditate upon Him, Lord Sri Krsna,\] who is eternally existent in the transcendental abode.”

Vyasadeva describes Lord Krsna’s transcendental activities in the Tenth Canto, but one must become purified by studying the nine preliminary cantos before he is able to relish the tenth. Srila Prabhupada writes: “In Bhagavad-gita, the Lord says that there is no other para-tattva (summum bonum) than Himself. Therefore, Sri Vyasadeva at once worships the para-tattva, Sri Krsna, whose transcendental activities are described in the Tenth Canto.. . . This Srimad-Bhagavatam will gradually elevate the unbiased reader to the highest perfectional stage of transcendence.”

**11. nirasta-kuhakam**—“which is forever free from the illusory representation of the material world.”

Srila Prabhupada asserts: “There appears to be reality, however, because of the true reality which exists in the spiritual world, where the Personality of Godhead eternally exists with His transcendental paraphernalia.” That realm, Krsna’s abode and the place where He performs His eternal pastimes, can be distinguished from this world by its absence of material illusion. The Srimad-Bhagavatam is meant to free its hearers from the tinge of material consciousness so that they may enter Krsna’s abode.

**12. satyam param dhimahi** —“I meditate upon Him, for He is the Absolute Truth.”

Srila Vyasadeva concludes by meditating on satyam param, the Absolute Truth, also known as Sri Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. That it is Krsna who is specifically referred to as satyam param is confirmed in the demigods’ prayers to Krsna in Devaki’s womb (garbha-stuti). In Bhagavatam [10.2.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/2.26), the word satya is used nine times to directly indicate Krsna:

*satya-vratam satya-param tri-satyam*  
*satyasya yonim nihitam ca satye*  
*satyasya satyam rta-satya-netram*  
*satyatmakam tvam saranam prapannah*

**The demigods prayed: О Lord, You never deviate from Your vow, which is always perfect because whatever You decide is perfectly correct and cannot be stopped by anyone. Being present in the three phases of cosmic manifestation—creation, maintenance and annihilation—You are the Supreme Truth. Indeed, unless one is completely truthful, one cannot achieve Your favor, which therefore cannot be achieved by hypocrites. You are the active principle, the real truth, in all the ingredients of creation, and therefore you are known as antaryami, the inner force. You are equal to everyone, and Your instructions apply for everyone, for all time. You are the beginning of all truth. Therefore, offering our obeisances, we surrender unto You. Kindly give us protection.**

In addition to the words satyam param dhimahi being included in the Bhagavatam’s first text, they are also contained in one of the Bhagavatam’s concluding texts, Bhagavatam [12.13.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-12/13.19):

**I meditate upon that pure and spotless Supreme Absolute Truth, who is free from suffering and death and who in the beginning personally revealed this incomparable torchlight of knowledge to Brahma. Brahma then spoke it to the sage Narada, who narrated it to Krsna-dvaipayana Vyasa. Srila Vyasa revealed this Bhagavatam to the greatest of sages, Sukadeva Gosvami, and Sukadeva mercifully spoke it to Maharaja Pariksit.**

**Text 2**

Srila Prabhupada’s translation mostly follows the Sanskrit text line by line.

**1. dharmah projjhita-kaitavo ’tra paramo nirmatsarandm satam**: “Completely rejecting all religious activities which are materially motivated, this Bhagavata Purana propounds the highest truth, which is understandable by those devotees who are fully pure in heart.”

The Bhagavatam’s method is described first. Dharmah projjhita-kaitavo ’tra: scriptures generally offer dharma, religiosity, which tends to be limited to teaching social propriety and how to gain wealth and satisfy material desire; beyond that, religiosity may point to liberation or enlightenment as life’s goal. In contemporary times many people are inclined to pursue these activities without scriptural or religious guidance. They neither accept nor feel they need scripture or religion. But those who become frustrated by material life and turn to religion gradually become elevated by their practice of piety. Still, all such self-centered attempts to gain pleasure, whether they are pious or impious, are not the subject of the Bhagavatam. Rather, the Bhagavatam calls these attempts, performed in the guise of religion, cheating or deception. Here, at the beginning, Srila Vyasadeva makes it clear that the Srimad-Bhagavatam rejects all materially motivated religious activities. Srila Sridhara Svami comments that the Bhagavatam completely rejects the processes of dharma (religiosity), artha (economic development), kdrna (sense gratification), and moksa (impersonal liberation) because they are not the religion of the soul.

What the Srimad-Bhagavatam has to give is far greater. In the Bhagavatam, paramah, the highest truth, is revealed, but only truly to the nirmatsaranam satam. The satam (devotees) are defined as nir-mat'saranam, completely free from envy. Being nonenvious of Krsna, a devotee achieves freedom from envy toward all living entities. The conditioned souls, either consciously or unconsciously, ask why Krsna is God; they want to be God themselves. Envy of Krsna is the origin of all other envy, and when one overcomes such invidiousness by surrendering to Krsna, all envy ends. Envy manifests as engaging in undue competition with others and in taking pleasure in others’ misfortune. Devotees overcome envy by valuing something far different from that coveted by nondevotees: they value pleasing Krsna by rendering loving devotional service.

In Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 73, Srila Jiva Gosvami says that freedom from the fallacy of impersonalist philosophy is described in the words dharmah projjhita-kaitavo ’tra; Bhagavatam [1.1.2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.2) rejects impersonal liberation, terming it kaitavo, “materially motivated.”

**2. vedyam vastavam atra vastu sivadam tapa-trayonmulanam**: “The highest truth is reality distinguished from illusion for the welfare of all. Such truth uproots the threefold miseries.”

Krsna is vastu, the ultimate substance from which everything originates. Thus Krsna is reality. Reality may be philosophically defined as “something that exists independently of all other things and from which all other things derive.” Because everything comes from the Absolute Truth, our understanding this Truth affords us an accurate perspective from which we can automatically understand everything else. What one sees as existence without connection to Krsna is illusion, maya.

The Second and Third Cantos of Srimad-Bhagavatam describe Krsna’s creation of the material world. Prior to the existence of the cosmos, Krsna’s plenary expansion, Maha-Visnu, exists. By His glance, living entities, their karma, and time are injected into the cloudlike area of the brahmajyoti known as pradhana (which also emanates from Krsna). Then by the agitation caused by the living entities, karma, and time in pradhana, the mahat-tattva evolves. Following that, the false ego, the mind, the sense objects, the demigods, and so on are all created. Everything at every step depends on the Absolute Truth, Krsna. Everything originates in Him and is maintained and ultimately destroyed by Him. Thus both the material world and the eternal, spiritual world rest on Krsna.

Understanding the Absolute Truth and one’s relationship with Him causes sivadam, auspiciousness, and tapa'trayonmulanam, the immediate annihilation of misery. If by one’s spiritual advancement one views material misery as Krsna’s mercy in his life, the miseries will bring him closer to Krsna and thereby become a source of happiness. Krsna Himself comes to this world and enacts His Vrndavana pastimes to attract one away from shadow and toward substance—away from the miserable material world and toward Vrndavana. The Bhagavatam teaches that being always Krsna conscious and awakening one’s relationship with Him is the process to remove misery. Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu taught this message by His life’s example.

Srila Sridhara Svami says about vedyam vdstavam atra vastu that in the beautiful Bhagavatam, the ultimate reality in its highest manifestation is to be known, not reality merely in terms of substance, qualities, and so on, as taught by the Vaisesika philosophers (adherents of Kanada Rsi’s atomic theory of existence) and others.

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments in Bhagavat-sandarbha, anuccheda 11, that bhagavan, the Lord’s personal feature, is not an idea imagined by theologians or philosophers. Thus in the second of the Bhagavatam’s opening texts, Srila Vyasadeva describes the Supreme Truth as sivadam and trayonmulanam. Sivadam means “He who gives transcendental bliss by means of His own potency,” and tapa'traycmmulanam means “He who uproots the threefold miseries caused by the illusory potency, maya.”

**3. srimad-bhagavate maha-muni-kite kim va parair**: “This beautiful Bhagavatam, compiled by the great sage Vyasadeva \[in his maturity\], is sufficient in itself for God realization. What is the need of any other scripture?”

That no literature other than Srimad-Bhagavatam is required for self-realization is also stated by Suta Gosvami in the Bhagavatam’s final chapter ([12.13.15](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-12/13.15)): “Srimad-Bhagavatam is declared to be the essence of all Vedanta philosophy. One who has felt satisfaction from its nectarean mellow will never be attracted to any other literature.”

Although Srila Vyasadeva compiled many holy books, his Srimad-Bhagavatam is the most powerful, for the sage wrote it after experiencing a complete revelation of the Absolute Truth. (This revelation will be discussed in the seventh chapter of the First Canto.) Therefore Vyasadeva states kim va parair isvarah: there is no need for any other literature. The Srimad-Bhagavatam bypasses other instruction and leads one directly to Krsna. Srila Prabhupada spoke this truth succinctly: ‘“What is the use of other sastra? Here is the essence of sastra given by Mahamuni Vyasadeva. Take it.’ That is final.” (Room conversation, Vrndavana, July 5, 1977)

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments in Bhagavat-sandarbha, anuccheda 94 that the cause of the Srimad-Bhagavatam’s glories is revealed in the word mahamuni: Because the Bhagavatam’s author is the crest jewel of philosophers, the Srimad-Bhagavatam is glorious.

**4. isvarah sadyo hrdy avarudhyate ’tra krtibhih susrusubhis tat-ksanat**: “As soon as one attentively and submissively hears the message of Bhagavatam, by this culture of knowledge, the Supreme Lord is established within his heart.”

Srila Jiva Gosvami continues: The sruti-sastra explains that the Srimad-Bhagavatam is the best of all scriptures. Bhagavatam [1.1.2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.2) exclaims that the Supreme Personality’s direct appearance, which is the best goal of life and the best Vedic knowledge, easily comes into one’s possession by relishing Srimad-Bhagavatam. Hearing the Srimad-Bhagavatam establishes the Lord in the living entity’s heart. Of course, Krsna is already there (Bg. [15.15](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/15.15)), but toward most living entities He remains neutral (Bg. [9.29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/9.29)). Lord Brahma (in Bhag. [3.9.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/9.12)) confirms that the Lord in the heart is unavailable to nondevotees: “You are situated in everyone’s heart as the Supersoul just to show Your causeless mercy, and You are the eternal well-wisher, but You are unavailable for the nondevotee.”

Krsna does instruct those souls who are His devotees (Bg. [9.29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/9.29)). Krtibhih susrusubhis tat-ksanat: if they eagerly hear Srimad-Bhagavatam, Krsna personally removes all obstacles to their advancement in Krsna consciousness, for He Himself purifies His devotees’ hearts (Bhag. [1.2.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.17)). The word susrusubhih. means “those who desire to hear.” As soon as one desires to hear the Bhagavatam, the Lord becomes established in one’s heart.

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments along this line in the Bhagavat-sandarbha, anuccheda 95. He writes that this text describes the super-excellent glory of the Srimad-Bhagavatam by saying: What is the need of any other scripture or the spiritual paths described in them? As soon as one attentively and submissively hears the message of Bhagavatam, the Supreme Lord is established within his heart by this culture of knowledge. Jiva Gosvami then asks a rhetorical question: Is

it not true that everyone hears Srimad-Bhagavatam? Is the Lord then actively established in everyone’s heart? Sri Jiva next indicates that the word sukrtibhih answers the question, and states that without having pious credits one will not develop the desire to hear.

**Text 3**

The translation below (Bhag. [1.1.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.3)) follows Prabhupada’s word-for-word definitions:

1. \[This Bhagavatam is the\] mature fruit of the tree of Vedic literature
2. \[and\] this nectar, which emanated from the mouth of Sukadeva Gosvami, is easy to swallow and perfect in all respects.
3. The Bhagavatam’s nectarean juice is relishable by liberated souls and souls still to achieve liberation, and
4. it is especially relishable for the expert and thoughtful souls folly conversant with the mellows of devotional love.

**1. nigama-kalpa'taror galitarh phalam**: “\[The Srimad-Bhagavatam\] is the mature fruit of the tree of the Vedic literature.”

The kalpa-taror is a desire tree, with the potency to fulfill one’s desires. The Vedic system instructs both those on the spiritual platform and those still in material consciousness. For those with material desires, the process of spiritual advancement is gradual, because an abrupt leap from material life to spiritual life is not easy. Thus the Vedas instruct one how to live in the material world with wealth, family, land, and pleasure, yet gradually become purified.

The fulfillment of material desires, however, is not the ultimate purpose of the Vedas. Rather, the Vedic mode of instruction is meant to gradually encourage spiritual advancement, the goal of the entire Vedic civilization. Thus the Vedic literature is divided into sections, each of which emphasizes appropriate practices for individuals at different levels of advancement. The eighteen Puranas, for example, are divided into three divisions for people influenced by each of the three modes of nature. One Purana may therefore appear to contradict another in its instructions and emphasis. Even after compiling the four Vedas, almost all the Puranas, the Vedanta'sutra, and the Mahabharata, Srila Vyasadeva felt dissatisfied. He realized that he had not emphasized the ultimate goal, Krsna consciousness. Only after compiling the Bhagavata Purana, Srimad-Bhagavatam, was he content.

As stated in Bhagavatam [1.1.2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.2), all other means of advancement— karma, jnana, and yoga—although scripturally justified, are rejected by Srimad-Bhagavatam. Only the process of devotional service to Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is established as the method to attain life’s ultimate goal. Why? In Kali-yuga, the present age of quarrel and hypocrisy, it is necessary to take a direct approach, for in this age no one can progress methodically through the intricate Vedic system and achieve the actual goal. The words galitam phalam mean “mature fruit.” The Bhagavatam offers only the ripe fruit of the tree of Vedic literature. One may obtain a sweet, tree-ripened mango only after lengthy and arduous endeavor. It requires that one first plant, nourish, and water the tree, protecting it from weeds, and then wait years until the tree is mature enough to produce ripe fruit. Many fruit trees reach maturity after dozens of years. But when the first sweet, juicy mangos finally ripen, he who planted the tree can finally harvest the fruit and experience pleasure. His hard work has finally achieved fruition. The tasty, ripened fruit of the tree of Vedic literature is the Srimad-Bhagavatam, and it is directly available in this age.

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on Bhagavatam [1.1.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.3) in the Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 110: nigama'kalpa'taror galitam phalam means “O auspicious souls, learned in the mellows of love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead, please relish in your hearts the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is the sweet fruit of the desire tree of the Vedas, a tree with many branches and twigs that bear all fruits, a tree that has come to this earth from the spiritual world of Vaikuntha.”

**2. suka-mukhad amrta-drava'samyutam**: “This nectar, which emanated from the mouth of Sukadeva Gosvami, is easily swallowed and perfect in all respects.”

Suka-mukhad means that the Srimad-Bhagavatam emanates from the mouth of Srila Sukadeva Gosvami. Although a suka is a parrot, this does not indicate that Sukadeva Gosvami parroted the Bhagavatam. A parrot, devoid of understanding, simply mimics words. Rather, Suka-deva’s being called a parrot implies that as the cut of a parrot’s beak sweetens a fruit, the Bhagavatam became sweeter still when presented with the depth of Sukadeva Gosvami’s realization.

Srila Vyasadeva (Sukadeva Gosvami’s father and spiritual master) had spoken the Bhagavatam to his son, and both Vyasadeva and Narada Muni (Vyasadeva’s spiritual master) were present when Sukadeva spoke the Bhagavatam to Maharaja Pariksit. These great souls experienced Sukadeva’s words as if they had never heard these teachings before. For this reason Vyasadeva says, suka-mukhad amrta'drava' samyutam: “The Bhagavatam is enriched with nectarean juice from the mouth of suka.”

The Srimad-Bhagavatam is nectar in an easily digested form (amrta' drava-samyutam). Unless one is a liberated soul, he will be unable to assimilate spiritual rasa, the mellows of relationship with Krsna, especially the mellows experienced during Krsna’s rasa dance. Attempting to understand such pastimes from the conditioned platform is like drinking ghee: it is simply too rich for us. Sukadeva Gosvami presented Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes in the Bhagavatam, but only in the Tenth Canto, after systematically presenting all the topics needed to appreciate and “digest” these pastimes. Thus the words drava-samyutam emphasize that Sukadeva did not dilute the contents but presented nectar in an easily digestible form.

**3. pibata bhagavatam rasam alayam**: “The Bhagavatam’s nectarean juice is relishable by liberated souls and souls still to achieve liberation.”

Everyone is searching for happiness. The attempt to find pleasure in matter will cease for those who read the Bhagavatam and relish its contents. When one watches a movie, he endeavors to taste rasa, the mellow of relationship with Krsna—without Krsna. Srila Bhakti-vinoda Thakura refers to this mundane rasa as “heavenly rasa.” He writes: In heavenly rasa there is only a relationship between enj oyer and enjoyed, experienced in the same four types of relationships: dasya \[servitude\], sakhya \[friendship\], vatsalya \[parenthood\], and madhurya \[conjugal mood\]. “But the object of such rasa is improper and unworthy. That is why svargiya'rasa cannot be eternal.”

The Bhagavatam, however, shifts one’s attention from oneself to Krsna, and insists that every soul has a relationship with Krsna that must be awakened. Srila Prabhupada’s purport to text 3 discusses rasa, which is “originally exchanged between the spiritual living being and the spiritual whole, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The spiritual exchange or rasa is fully exhibited in spiritual existence between living beings and the Supreme Lord.” Prabhupada explains that Krsna is the fountainhead of all rasa, and “When one associates with the Supreme Lord and exchanges one’s constitutional rasa with the Lord, then the living being is actually happy.”

How can one learn to relish rasa with Krsna? Srila Prabhupada states that this spiritual rasa is present in the Srimad-Bhagavatam, and one who hears the Bhagavatam submissively from Sukadeva Gosvami or his bona fide representative “can attain the full pleasure of his heart’s desire.”

In Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 110, Jiva Gosvami comments that one will never become satiated by tasting the nectar of the Srimad-Bhagavatam, and that one’s desire to taste it will never diminish; therefore, even after liberation (alayam) one will continue to drink (pibata) the Bhagavatam’s nectar.

That even liberated souls are attracted to Srimad-Bhagavatam is confirmed by Sukadeva Gosvami in Bhagavatam [2.1.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/1.9): “O saintly King, I was certainly situated perfectly in transcendence, yet I was still attracted by the delineation of the pastimes of the Lord, who is described by enlightened verses.”

**4. muhur aho rasika bhuvi bhavukah**: “Srimad-Bhagavatam is especially relishable for the expert and thoughtful souls fully conversant with the mellows of devotional love.”

Those souls who are bhuvi bhavukah, experienced and thoughtful, and who actually understand the nature of this world, should always (muhur) be rasika, relishers of the Bhagavatam's nectar. Sukadeva Gosvami is an ideal example of such a fortunate soul. He was liberated even before birth and had no desire to enjoy this world. Indeed, for sixteen years he refused to leave his mother’s womb for fear that he would fall under mrryd’s spell. Yet such a great soul eagerly relished the Bhagavatam by first hearing, then speaking, this great literature.

In Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 110, Jiva Gosvami comments that the word aho in this text hints that the Bhagavatam enables one to attain what is otherwise unattainable. He also explains that the Bhagavatam is described by the word rasa because rasaikamayata-vivaksaya, it deals only with spiritual mellows and not with anything else. When one understands Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, as the reservoir of rasa (raso vai sah), one becomes transcendentally blissful.

These first three texts form a prelude to the Bhagavatam. The first text defines the Absolute Truth, the second describes the Bhagavatam and defines actual religion, and the third invites humankind to taste the Bhagavatam’s sweetness.

## The Sages at Naimisaranya Inquire from Suta Gosvami\<br\> Texts 4—8: Setting the Scene

Srila Vyasadeva next begins to narrate the history of Suta Gosvami speaking Srimad-Bhagavatam to the sages at Naimisaranya: “Once, in a holy place in the forest of Naimisaranya, great sages headed by the sage Saunaka assembled to perform a great thousand-year sacrifice for the satisfaction of the Lord and His devotees.” (Bhag. [1.1.4](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.4))

In his purport to text 4, Srila Prabhupada explains the sages’ motivation: “The great sages are always anxious to do good to the people in general, and as such the sages headed by Saunaka and others assembled at this holy place of Naimisaranya with a program of performing a great and continuous chain of sacrificial ceremonies. Forgetful men do not know the right path for peace and prosperity. However, the sages know it well, and therefore for the good of all men they are always anxious to perform acts which may bring about peace in the world. They are sincere friends to all living entities, and at the risk of great personal inconvenience they are always engaged in the service of the Lord for the good of all people.”

“One day, after finishing their morning duties by burning a sacrificial fire and offering a seat of esteem to Srila Suta Gosvami, the great sages made inquiries, with great respect . . .” (Bhag. [1.1.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.5)). Suta Gosvami, son of Romaharsana Suta, was the most revered sage at Naimisaranya. He had sat on the bank of the Ganges and listened as Maharaja Pariksit heard the Srimad-Bhagavatam from Sukadeva Gosvami. Suta mentions the disciplic line from which he had heard this knowledge in Bhagavatam [12.13.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-12/12.19): “I meditate upon that pure and spotless Supreme Absolute Truth, who is free from suffering and death and who in the beginning personally revealed this incomparable torchlight of knowledge to Brahma. Brahma then spoke it to the sage Narada, who narrated it to Krsna-dvaipayana Vyasa. Srila Vyasa revealed this Bhagavatam to the greatest of sages, Sukadeva Gosvami, and Sukadeva mercifully spoke it to Maharaja Pariksit.”

Suta’s father, Romaharsana, was killed by Lord Balarama after failing to stand when Balarama entered the arena at Naimisaranya where Romaharsana was reciting the Puranas. The speaker at a sacred function is usually not required to stand when a guest arrives, but the guest in this case was Balarama, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus Romaharsana, while occupying a position reserved for the learned, acted proudly—against the spirit of true knowledge.

After killing Romaharsana with a blade of kusa grass, Balarama was willing to restore him to life, but instead the sages requested Him to bless Romaharsana’s son, Suta Gosvami, with long life and strength. Carrying Lord Balarama’s full blessings, along with the blessings of the sages at Naimisaranya, Suta was then offered great respect and the opportunity to speak the Bhagavatam.

The Bhagavatam ([1.1.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.6)) describes Suta Gosvami as anagha, sinless and free from vice, the same word used in the Bhagavad-gita to describe Arjuna. Suta Gosvami was also learned in the scriptures, as the text describes, for he had studied them under proper guidance and had also explained them. Srila Prabhupada explains the importance of properly hearing and then explaining the scriptures in his purport to text 6: “To hear and explain them is more important than reading them. One can assimilate the knowledge of the revealed scriptures only by hearing and explaining. Hearing is called sravana, and explaining is called kirtana. The two processes of sravana and kirtana are of primary importance to progressive spiritual life. Only one who has properly grasped the transcendental knowledge from the right source by submissive hearing can properly explain the subject.”

Saunaka continues: “And because you are submissive, your spiritual masters have endowed you with all the favors bestowed upon a gentle disciple. Therefore you can tell us all that you have scientifically learned from them.” (Bhag. [1.1.8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.8)) The sages, respecting Suta’s preeminence, request him to enlighten them with the knowledge he has heard from his preceptors. Now Saunaka, speaking for the sages, will \[in the remainder of this chapter\] ask Suta six questions.

## Texts 9-11: Questions One and Two

Many acaryas, including Srila Sridhara Svami, Srila Jiva Gosvami, Srila Vijayadhvaja Tirtha, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura have listed Saunaka Rsi’s six questions. Their lists sometimes differ.

Saunaka’s first inquiry: “Please .. . explain to us, in an easily understandable way, what you have ascertained to be the absolute and ultimate good \[sreyas\] for the people in general.” (Bhag. [1.1.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.9)). Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that the sages pay Suta a compliment, saying that he is fit to speak because he has studied all the sastras for years. They then ask, “What is the ultimate good for humankind?” The ultimate good for humanity is to attain love for the transcendent Lord (Bhag. [1.2.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.6)). Such love produces all happiness because Bhagavan can be pleased by such loving service.

The sages then describe the unfortunate population of the current age: “O learned one, in this iron age of Kali men have but short lives. They are quarrelsome, lazy, misguided, unlucky and, above all, always disturbed.” (Bhag. [1.1.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.10)) Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments: In this vicious age it is impossible to perform the rites and sacrifices recommended in sastra or to ascertain truth. People lack time to seek truth or to do themselves good. Thus they need preceptors.

Anxious for the population’s spiritual improvement, the sages make a second inquiry of Suta Gosvami: “There are many varieties of scriptures, and in all of them there are many prescribed duties, which can be learned only after many years of study in their various divisions. Therefore, О sage, please select the essence of all these scriptures and explain it for the good of all living beings, that by such instruction their hearts may be fully satisfied.” (Bhag. [1.1.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.11)) The sages understood that Kali-yuga had begun. They knew that the Vedic social structure would gradually crumble and that the people would become lazy, diseased, and disturbed. No one would study sastra. Concocted remedies to problems would cause still greater disasters. Thus the sages inquired about the essential recommendations of the sastra.

## Texts 12-16: Question Three

Saunaka Rsi continues (in text 12): “All blessings upon you, О Suta Gosvami. You know for what purpose the Personality of Godhead appeared in the womb of Devaki as the son of Vasudeva.” Saunaka is asking, “For what purpose did the Personality of Godhead appear?” Implied by his question is the desire to hear about Krsna and His pastimes. Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport that Saunaka’s use of the phrase bhadram te, “blessings upon you,” indicates the sages’ anxiety to hear about Krsna. Suta Gosvami will answer this question in Bhagavatam [1.2.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.34) and in the Tenth Canto.

Saunaka Rsi knows that Krsna appears by His own desire; He is not forced to appear in this world. Therefore it is difficult to under stand why the Supreme Personality of Godhead would enter the prison house of this world at all. Saunaka’s reference to Krsna as satvatdm patih, the protector of His pure devotees, reveals Krsna’s most endearing quality: He is bhakta-vatsala, the lover of His devotees.

Saunaka continues: “O Suta Gosvami, we are eager to learn about the Personality of Godhead and His incarnations.” (Bhag. [1.1.13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.13)) Here Saunaka hints at his fourth and fifth questions. He will ask them both directly, beginning in text 17, but first he will link texts 14-16 to increase the listeners’ enthusiasm. Saunaka states: “Living beings who are entangled in the complicated meshes of birth and death can be freed immediately by even unconsciously chanting the holy name of Krsna, which is feared by fear personified. О Suta, those great sages who have completely taken shelter of the lotus feet of the Lord can at once sanctify those who come in touch with them, whereas the waters of the Ganges can sanctify only after prolonged use. Who is there, desiring deliverance from the vices of the age of quarrel, who is not willing to hear the virtuous glories of the Lord?”

Srila Prabhupada increases the readers’ enthusiasm still further with his purport to text 14: “This indicates that the name of Krsna is non-different from Krsna. Therefore, the name of Krsna is as powerful as Lord Krsna Himself. There is no difference at all. Anyone, therefore, can take advantage of the holy names of Lord Sri Krsna even in the midst of greatest dangers. The transcendental name of Krsna, even though uttered unconsciously or by force of circumstances, can help one obtain freedom from the hurdle of birth and death.”

Jiva Gosvami comments on text 14 in Krsna^sandarbha, anuccheda 66. He says that because Sri Krsna is the origin of all the incarnations of Godhead, all God’s holy names actually refer to Krsna. The Visnu Purana confirms that Lord Krsna is the origin of all the holy names of God. For this reason, all the Lord’s holy names—Vasudeva, Damodara, Govinda, Kesava, and all other names of the Lord—should be understood as names of Sri Krsna. Those who chant Krsna’s holy names become free from the cycle of birth and death because even fear personified fears the Lord’s holy name.

In Bhagavatam [1.1.15](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.15) Suta Gosvami glorifies the effect of associating with pure devotees.
