However, materialistic activities cause only suffering. We suffer both while enacting the activities and attaining the results. Devotional service, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains further, brings only happiness, because both the aspiration to advance in devotional service and the perfection of our practice bring happiness. The conclusion, therefore, is that we should serve only Sri Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

Still, one may ask, What about Brahma, Visnu, and Siva? They are the creator, maintainer, and destroyer of the universe. Aren’t these powerful deities the natural recipients of devotional offerings? In Bhagavatam [1.2.23-25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.23) Suta Gosvami describes the relationship between these deities and Sri Krsna.

## Texts 23-25: The Worship of Brahma, Visnu, and Siva

“The transcendental Personality of Godhead is indirectly associated with the three modes of material nature, namely passion, goodness and ignorance, and just for the material world’s creation, maintenance and destruction He accepts the three qualitative forms of Brahma, Visnu and Siva. Of these three, all human beings can derive ultimate benefit from Visnu, the form of the quality of goodness.”(Bhag. [1.2.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.23))

Srila Sridhara Svami comments on this text: Who is that Deity whom the devotees adore? Krsna has assumed these three forms for material dealings. Of these three, only Visnu should be worshiped, for goodness, predominated by Visnu, increases knowledge.

Although persons desiring material results will tend to worship either Brahma, who is empowered by the mode of passion to create, or Siva, who is empowered by the mode of ignorance to destroy, only Lord Visnu, who is a direct expansion of Krsna and who empowers the mode of goodness for maintenance, is an appropriate object for devotional offerings. This is because only Krsna (or one of His visnu' tattva expansions) can release us from the prison of the material world. No demigod can do this. This ultimate benediction is available only from Krsna.

Suta next offers an example demonstrating the comparative value of each of the three modes of material nature, and therefore the value of worshiping their presiding deities. “Firewood is a transformation of earth, but smoke is better than the raw wood. And fire is still better, for by fire we can derive the benefits of superior knowledge \[through Vedic sacrifices\]. Similarly, passion \[rajas\] is better than ignorance \[tamos\], but goodness \[sattva\] is best because by goodness one can come to realize the Absolute Truth.” (Bhag. [1.2.24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.24))

Wood, from which fire springs, is bom of earth; smoke is bom of fire. Fire is superior to both smoke and wood because it allows us to perform Vedic sacrifices, which award knowledge. In that sense, smoke is superior to wood because smoke heralds the coming of fire and is thus closer to the goal (fire). Similarly, the mode of passion is better than the mode of ignorance, for it offers clues (in the form of the fine arts, music, philosophy, and morality) to help us realize the Absolute Truth. Passion is also active and thus produces results that may be offered to Krsna. Still, goodness is better, for through goodness we can actually realize the goal of understanding the Absolute Truth.

Commenting on Bhagavatam [1.2.24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.24), Srila Jiva Gosvami cites a number of sastras, all of which prove the superiority of Visnu and Visnu worship. He concludes that we should worship only Visnu, although no deity should be blasphemed, disdained, or reviled.

Suta Gosvami further instructs: “Previously all the great sages rendered service unto the Personality of Godhead due to His existence above the three modes of material nature. They worshiped Him to become free from material conditions and thus derive the ultimate benefit. Whoever follows such great authorities is also eligible for liberation from the material world.” (Bhag. [1.2.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.25))

In a sense, the three forms of Brahma, Visnu, and Siva are one because Krsna acts through them to create, maintain, and destroy the world. The great sages, knowing that the Lord is beyond the three modes of material nature, therefore worship Him to attain the ultimate benefit. As Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 25, “There are twelve particular agents of the Lord who know the purpose of religion, and all of them render transcendental service unto Him. Persons who desire their own good may follow these mahajanas and thus attain the supreme benefit.”

In the Paramatma-sandarbha, anuccheda 11, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains that we can truly attain liberation only when we understand that Brahma and Siva are partial expansions of the Supersoul, and then strive to find that Supersoul. Sri Jiva quotes from the Skanda Purana to demonstrate that worship of Lord Visnu awards liberation: “He binds the souls with the ropes of birth and death; He unties the ropes of birth and death that bind the souls. In this way, eternal Lord Visnu brings liberation.”

He further explains the benefit we can derive from the mode of passion, for in this mode we come closer to seeing the Supreme than when we are in ignorance. However, because passion is agitating and troublesome, the mode of passion does not allow us to see the Supreme properly. In Bhagavatam [1.2.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.25), Sri Jiva continues, goodness is compared to fire, for one in the pure and peaceful mode of goodness can directly see the Supreme. (Goodness, therefore, like fire, is the goal.)

In Bhakti-sandarbha, anuccheda 18, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains more about Bhagavatam [1.2.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.25): Great souls abandon other deities and engage in devotional service to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. When explaining why passion is superior to ignorance, he says that passion can lead to goodness but ignorance cannot. Sri Jiva explains ksemaya kalpante ye ’nu tan iha (found in text 25) to mean that those in this world who follow these sages attain auspiciousness.

## Texts 26-27: Worship of the Other Demigods

How should we regard the many other demigods? Suta Gosvami continues: “Those who are serious about liberation . . . respect all. Yet they reject the . . . forms of the demigods and worship only the all-blissful forms of Lord Visnu and His plenary portions.” (Bhag. [1.2.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.26))

Srila Prabhupada clarifies this point in his purport: “Therefore Visnu, and none else, is called mukti-pada, or the Personality of Godhead who can bestow upon us mukti, liberation. The demigods, being like other living entities in the material world, are all liquidated at the time of the annihilation of the material structure. They are themselves unable to get liberation, and what to speak of giving liberation to their devotees. The demigods can award the worshipers some temporary benefit only, and not the ultimate one. It is for this reason only that candidates for liberation deliberately reject the worship of the demigods, although they have no disrespect for any one of them.”

Why, then, do so many people direct their worship toward demigods or entities other than Lord Visnu? In Bhakti-sandarbha, anu-ccheda 19, Srila Jiva Gosvami asks this same question: Why is it seen that many worship other deities, especially Lord Siva? They do so because they have material desires. But those desiring liberation, what to speak of those whose only goal in life is devotional service to the Lord, do not worship anyone but the Supreme Personality of Godhead. According to Srila Jiva Gosvami, that is the meaning of Bhagavatam [1.2.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.26).

Suta Gosvami explains the same point in text 27: “Those who are in the modes of passion and ignorance worship the forefathers, other living beings and the demigods who are in charge of cosmic activities, for they are urged by a desire to be materially benefited with women, wealth, power and progeny.”

Although people could get the same results by worshiping Lord Narayana, the husband of the goddess of fortune, they do not choose to do so because they are impelled by the lower modes of nature. Sri Jiva explains in Bhakti-sandarbha, anuccheda 20, that the word sama-silah means that the worshipers have the same nature as the pitrs and other demigods, for these beings are also influenced by the modes of passion and ignorance.

Who then is to be worshiped? Suta Gosvami gives a clear response in the following texts.

## Texts 28-29: Vasudeva is the Actual Object of Worship

*vasudeva-para veda, vasudeva-para makhah vasudeva-para yoga, vasudeva-parah kriyah vasudeva-param jnanam, vasudeva-param tapah vasudeva-paro dharmo, vasudeva-para gatih*

**In the revealed scriptures, the ultimate object of knowledge is Sri Krsna, the Personality of Godhead. The purpose of performing sacrifice is to please Him. Yoga is for realizing Him. All fruitive activities are ultimately rewarded by Him only. He is supreme knowledge, and all severe austerities are performed to know Him. Religion \[dharma\] is rendering loving service unto Him. He is the supreme goal of life. (Bhag.** [**1.2.28—29**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.28)**)**

Vasudeva is Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Krsna equates Himself directly with Vasudeva in Bhagavad-gita [7.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/7.19): “After many births and deaths \[bahfinam janmanam ante\], he who is actually in knowledge surrenders unto Me \[jnanavan mam prapadyate\] knowing Me to be the cause of all causes \[vasudevah\] and all that is \[sarvam iti\]. Such a great soul is very rare \[sa mahatma su-durlabhah\].”

Prabhupada has already emphatically and conclusively stated in his purport to Bhagavatam [1.2.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.27): “One should work hard and worship the Supreme Lord by the fruits of one’s hard labor for existence, and that should be the motto of life.” And in his purport to Bhagavatam [1.2.28-29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.28) he writes: “In the Bhagavad-gita it is said that those who are mahatmas, or those whose minds have been so broadened as to be engaged in the service of Lord Krsna, are under the influence of the internal potency, and the effect is that such broadminded living beings are constantly engaged in the service of the Lord without deviation. That should be the aim of life. And that is the verdict of all the Vedic literatures.”

In Bhakti-sandarbha, anuccheda 21, Srila Jiva Gosvami comments that the Vedic scriptures conclude that only Lord Visnu should be worshiped, and that these texts (Bhag. [1.2.28-29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.28)) confirm this truth. Commenting on the same texts, Srila Sridhara Svami states that understanding Vasudeva is the purpose of the Vedas. If someone asks, “Don’t the Vedas describe various yajnas?" he assures us that these texts state that because all Vedic methods actually aim at Vasudeva, all sacrifices are performed to please Him. Anticipating the question “Don’t the yoga-sastras describe only yogic activities, beginning with sitting postures and breath control?” Sridhara Svami states that yogic activities are employed in the attempt to attain Vasudeva. Anticipating that someone may ask, “Don’t the jnana-sastras describe transcendental knowledge?” this text asserts that Lord Vasudeva is the highest transcendental knowledge. What was said of knowledge may also be said of austerity. In answer to the question “Don’t the dharma-sastras describe pious activities, charity, and vows, activities by which one attains Svargaloka and other heavenly realms?” this text insists that these results ultimately depend on Lord Vasudeva. The word gatih (goal), derived from the verb gam (to go), refers to the attainment of heavenly planets. Reaching that goal depends on Lord Vasudeva, because the heavenly planets are manifest from a tiny portion of His transcendental bliss.

## Text 30-34: Vasudeva, Krsna, Manifests the Material Worlds in His Three Visnu Features (Purusa-avataras)

**The Answer to Question Four (from Bhagavatam 1.1.17) as Understood by Srila Jiva Gosvami**

In Bhagavatam [1.1.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.17) Saunaka Rsi asked about the Lord’s pastimes in His various incarnations. If that question is taken as an expression of the Naimisaranya sages’ desire to hear about Krsna’s many incarnations, as Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains it, then the answer to that request will appear in the next chapter, Chapter Three, and throughout the rest of the Bhagavatam. However, Srila Jiva Gosvami has analyzed Saunaka Rsi’s question differently. He states that it specifically refers to the Lord’s creation pastimes. Therefore, he explains, Suta Gosvami responds in Bhagavatam [1.2.30-33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.30):

**In the beginning of the material creation, that Absolute Personality of Godhead \[Vasudeva\], in His transcendental position, created the energies of cause and effect by His own internal energy. After creating the material substance, the Lord \[Vasudeva\] expands Himself and enters into it. And although He is within the material modes of nature and appears to be one of the created beings, He is always fully enlightened in His transcendental position. The Lord, as Supersoul, pervades all things, just as fire permeates wood, and so He appears to be of many varieties, though He is the absolute one without a second. The Supersoul enters into the bodies of the created beings who are influenced by the modes of material nature and causes them to enjoy the effects of these modes by the subtle mind.**

If we heard Saunaka Rsi’s question according to Jiva’s perspective, Saunaka has asked to hear how Krsna creates and maintains the material world through His three purusa-avatdras, Maha-Visnu, Garbho-dakasayi Visnu, and Ksirodakasayi Visnu. These topics are outlined in Bhagavatam [1.2.30-33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.30) and discussed extensively in the Second and Third Cantos.

Srila Suta Gosvami will later make it clear that Krsna is the original Bhagavan (Bhag. [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28)). He has already made it clear that Bhagavan is also known as Vasudeva (Bhag. [1.2.28-29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.28)) and that understanding Him is the ultimate goal of the Vedas. Now Suta explains that the same Vasudeva acts as Visnu (Bhag. [1.2.30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.30)), the source of the material worlds. Krsna, Bhagavan, Vasudeva, and Visnu are nondif-ferent. Always aloof from His material energy, Krsna, as Visnu, creates the universes through His energies and expansions.

Clearly Visnu, although a person, is extraordinary. Desires to enjoy matter neither attract nor entangle Him any more than activities in a prison cell attract a king to become a prisoner. The king may visit the prison at his will, but he becomes neither a prisoner nor subject to prison law.

Whether Krsna is creating universes or acting in a way that resembles the activities of ordinary living entities, His activities are always transcendental. This understanding is foundational to comprehending Krsna’s Vrndavana pastimes. Hearing that universes come from Visnu’s pores (Bs. [5.48](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bs/48)) makes it clear that Krsna, who is the source of unlimited Visnus, is extraordinary; He is God. But maintaining this concept about Krsna is more difficult, for the Tenth Canto will describe how Krsna wrestles with His cowherd boyfriends and dances with the cowherd girls in the middle of the night. Those who lack knowledge and realization are certain to become bewildered.

That same Lord Vasudeva, through His expansions and energies, and who in His ultimate feature is Sri Krsna, creates the material realm. Although seemingly in contact with material nature, the Lord always remains transcendental to it. In his comment on Bhagavatam [1.2.30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.30), Srila Sridhara Svami notes that someone may object: “Don’t Vedic scriptures describe the creation, maintenance, and control of the material universes? Why then do you state that the Vedas describe only Krsna, Lord Vasudeva (who is neither involved in universal creation, maintenance, or control)?” In answer, the Bhagavatam presents these four texts, Bhagavatam [1.2.30-33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.30).

In Bhakti-sandarbha, anuccheda 22, commenting on Bhagavatam [1.2.30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.30), Srila Jiva Gosvami explains that the word idam (this) refers to the entirety of Lord Vasudeva’s material creation. “This” begins with the mahat-tattva and extends to the demigod Brahma. The Lord’s activities that begin with His entrance into the material universe will be described in the texts that follow text 30.

During creation, Vasudeva, as Karanodakasayi Visnu, enters each universe and is then called Garbhodakasayi Visnu. He remains transcendental, despite the fact that He appears to be in matter. When He then enters the heart of each living entity and into all matter, He is known as Ksirodakasayi Visnu. Again He remains transcendental.

Srila Prabhupada comments in his purport to text 32 on how we should perceive Lord Ksirodakasayi Visnu: “Lord Vasudeva, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, by one of His plenary parts expands Himself all over the material world, and His existence can be perceived even within the atomic energy. Matter, antimatter, proton, neutron, etc., are all different effects of the Paramatma feature of the Lord. As from wood, fire can be manifested, or as butter can be churned out of milk, so also the presence of the Lord as Paramatma can be felt by the process of legitimate hearing and chanting of the transcendental subjects which are especially treated in the Vedic literatures like the Upanisads and Vedanta. Srimad-Bhagavatam is the bona fide explanation of these Vedic literatures. The Lord can be realized through the aural reception of the transcendental message, and that is the only way to experience the transcendental subject. As fire is kindled from wood by another fire, the divine consciousness of man can similarly be kindled by another divine grace. His Divine Grace the spiritual master can kindle the spiritual fire from the woodlike living entity by imparting proper spiritual messages injected through the receptive ear. Therefore one is required to approach the proper spiritual master with receptive ears only, and thus divine existence is gradually realized. The difference between animality and humanity lies in this process only. A human being can hear properly, whereas an animal cannot.”

As the Supersoul, Vasudeva enters everything in each universe. Generally, the conditioned living entity’s mind is filled with desires. Based on those desires, the Supersoul is inspired to reciprocate with the conditioned living entity. He connects the soul with His own external energy (maya) so that the soul can experience matter. However, if a living entity desires his connection with Krsna’s energy changed to one of service in the spiritual world, the Supersoul inspires that living entity differently.

Srila Prabhupada’s purport to Bhagavatam [1.2.33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.33) emphasizes this point: “The Lord as Paramatma helps the living being to get material happiness because the living being is helpless in all respects in obtaining what he desires. He proposes, and the Lord disposes. In another sense, the living beings are parts and parcels of the Lord. They are therefore one with the Lord. In the Bhagavad-gita the living beings in all varieties of bodies have been claimed by the Lord as His sons. The sufferings and enjoyments of the sons are indirectly the sufferings and enjoyments of the father. Still the father is not in any way affected directly by the suffering and enjoyment of the sons. He is so kind that He constantly remains with the living being as Paramatma and always tries to convert the living being towards the real happiness.”

**Bhagavatam 1.2.34: The Answer to Question Three (from Bhagavatam 1.1.12)**

In the final text of this chapter, Bhagavatam [1.2.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.34), Srila Suta Gosvami answers Saunaka Rsi’s third question (asked in Bhag. [1.1.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.12)): Why does Sri Krsna descend? Suta Gosvami replies: “Assuming the roles of incarnations, He performs pastimes to reclaim those in the mode of pure goodness.” Thus Sri Krsna comes to attract souls to His eternal abode.

Srila Prabhupada comments on text 34 as follows: “Sometimes He incarnates Himself or empowers a suitable living being to act for Him, but in either case the purpose is the same: the Lord wants the suffering living being to go back home, back to Godhead. The happiness which the living beings are hankering for is not to be found within any comer of the innumerable universes and material planets. The eternal happiness which the living being wants is obtainable in the kingdom of God, but the forgetful living beings under the influence of the material modes have no information of the kingdom of God. The Lord, therefore, comes to propagate the message of the kingdom of God, either personally as an incarnation or through His bona fide representative as the good son of God. Such incarnations or sons of God are not making propaganda for going back to Godhead only within the human society. Their work is also going on in all types of societies, amongst demigods and those other than human beings.”

Srila Sridhara Svami’s commentary on Bhagavatam [1.2.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.34) explains that the specific purpose of the Krsna avatara is mentioned in Kunti’s prayers. In Bhagavatam [1.8.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.35), Queen Kunti states, “. . . You appeared to rejuvenate the devotional service of hearing, remembering, worshiping and so on in order that the conditioned souls suffering from material pangs might take advantage and gain liberation.”

Prabhupada writes: “The Lord . . . out of His causeless mercy, because He is more merciful to the suffering living beings than they can expect, appears before them and renovates the principles of devotional service comprised of hearing, chanting, remembering, serving, worshiping, praying, cooperating and surrendering unto Him. Adoption of all the above-mentioned items, or any one of them, can help a conditioned soul get out of the tangle of nescience and thus become liberated from all material sufferings created by the living being illusioned by the external energy. This particular type of mercy is bestowed upon the living being by the Lord in the form of Lord Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu.” (Bhag. [1.8.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.35), purport)

Another reference to confirm that Krsna personally comes to the material world to reclaim souls is found in Bhagavatam [10.8.49](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/8.49): “Drona and Dhara said: Please permit us to be bom on the planet earth so that after our appearance, the Supreme Lord, the Personality of Godhead, the supreme controller and master of all planets, will also appear and spread devotional service, the ultimate goal of life, so that those bom in this material world may very easily be delivered from the miserable condition of materialistic life by accepting this devotional service.”

Srila Prabhupada’s purport to this text explains: “Foolish persons do not know how risky life is here if one does not follow the instructions of Krsna. The Krsna consciousness movement, therefore, has been started so that by practicing Krsna consciousness one can avoid the risky life of this material existence. There is no question of accepting or not accepting Krsna consciousness. It is not optional; it is compulsory. If we do not take to Krsna consciousness, our life is very risky. Everything is explained in Bhagavad-gita. Therefore, to learn how to become free from the miserable condition of material existence, Bhagavad-gita As It Is is the preliminary study. Then, if one understands Bhagavad-gita, one can proceed to Srimad-Bhagavatam, and if one advances further, one may study Caitanya'Caritdmrta. We are therefore presenting these invaluable books to the whole world so that people may study them and be happy, being delivered from miserable conditional life.”

## Dialogue Three - Krsna Is the Source Of All Incarnations

## A Review of Bhagavatam 1.2.28-34

In text [1.2.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.11), the one Absolute Truth (jnanam advayam) was categorized according to an ascending order of realization as Brahman, Paramatma, and Bhagavan. In texts 28 and 29, Suta Gosvami explained that it is Bhagavan, Vasudeva Krsna, who is to be known by the Vedas. In text 31 he stated: “After creating the material substance, the Lord \[Vasudeva\] expands Himself and enters into it.” Suta Gosvami then explained how in the form of Lord Visnu, the Lord expands into all things (Bhag. [1.2.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.32)) and into the hearts of all living beings (Bhag. [1.2.33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.33)), and enters each universe to perform pastimes as the lila-avatdras (Bhag. [1.2.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.34)).

Now in the third chapter of the First Canto, Suta Gosvami will describe in more detail Visnu’s forms for creating the universe—the purusa-avataras (Bhag. [1.3.1-5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.1)). Then he will describe the Lord’s many entries into the universe as the lila-avataras (Bhag. [1.3.6-27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.6)). These descriptions will inspire Suta to proclaim Krsna the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the original Narayana, the supreme Lord Vasudeva, and the ultimate source of the purusa- and lila-avataras (Bhag. [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28)).

## Chapter 3 - Krsna Is the Source Of All Incarnations

## Texts 1-5: Describing in Further Detail the Three Purusa-avataras

Chapter Three opens with Srila Suta Gosvami describing in more detail Lord Visnu’s role in the universe’s creation:

*jagrhe paurusam rupath*  
*bhagavan mahad-adibhih*  
*sambhutam sodasa-kalam*  
*adau loka-sisrksayd*

**Suta said: In the beginning of the creation, the Lord first expanded Himself in the universal form of the purusa incarnation and manifested all the ingredients for the material creation. And thus at first there was the creation of the sixteen principles of material action. This was for the purpose of creating the material universe. (Bhag.** [**1.3.1**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.1)**)**

The above text explains that Bhagavan, who has previously been described as Vasudeva, accepted (jagrhe) the form of the purusa incarnation (paurusam rupam) to create the material universes (loka-sisrksaya). Srila Prabhupada writes about the relationship between Vasudeva (Krsna) and the three purusa-avatdras (Karanodakasayi Visnu, Garbhodakasayi Visnu, and Ksirodakasayi Visnu) in his purport to text 1: “The Bhagavad-gita states that the Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna maintains these material universes by extending His plenary expansions. So this purusa form is the confirmation of the same principle. The original Personality of Godhead Vasudeva, or Lord Krsna, who is famous as the son of King Vasudeva or King Nanda, is full with all opulences, all potencies, all fame, all beauty, all knowledge and all renunciation. Part of His opulences are manifested as impersonal Brahman, and part of His opulences are manifested as Paramatma. This purusa feature of the same Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna is the original Paramatma manifestation of the Lord. There are three purusa features in the material creation, and this form, who is known as the Karanodakasayi Visnu, is the first of the three. The others are known as the Garbhodakasayi Visnu and the Ksirodakasayi Visnu, which we shall know one after another. The innumerable universes are generated from the skin holes of this Karanodakasayi Visnu, and in each one of the universes the Lord enters as Garbhodakasayi Visnu. . . . All these universes are collectively produced by the Karanodakasayi Visnu, called also the Maha-Visnu, who simply throws His glance to impregnate the material sky.”

Sri Jiva Gosvami explains (Krsna-sandarbha, anuccheda 1): Suta Gosvami anticipated a question from Saunaka and the sages: “Formerly you said that although the Absolute Truth is one, it manifests in three features. What are the qualities of these three features of Brahman, Paramatma, and Bhagavan?” Therefore, Suta spoke Bhagavatam [1.3.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.1).

In texts 3 and 4 Suta Gosvami describes the Paramatma feature of the Absolute Truth by describing the second purusa-avatara, Garbhodakasayi Visnu: “It is believed that all the universal planetary systems are situated on the extensive body of the purusa, but He has nothing to do with the created material ingredients. His body is eternally in spiritual existence par excellence. The devotees, with their perfect eyes, see the transcendental form of the purusa who has thousands of legs, thighs, arms and faces—all extraordinary. In that body there are thousands of heads, ears, eyes and noses. They are decorated with thousands of helmets and glowing earrings and are adorned with garlands.” Srila Prabhupada writes: “This Garbhodakasayi Visnu is glorified in the Vedas in the hymns of Garbha-stuti, which begin with the description of the Lord as having thousands of heads, etc. The Garbhodakasayi Visnu is the Lord of the universe, and although He appears to be lying within the universe, He is always transcendental.” (Bhag. [1.3.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.5), purport)

The third purusa-avatara, Ksirodakasayi Visnu, is described next: “This form \[the second manifestation of the purusa\] is the source and indestructible seed of multifarious incarnations within the universe. From the particles and portions of this form, different living entities, like demigods, men and others, are created.” (Bhag. [1.3.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.5)) Srila Prabhupada explains Ksirodakasayi Visnu’s position: “The Visnu who is the plenary portion of the Garbhodakasayi Visnu is the Supersoul of the universal life, and He is known as the maintainer of the universe, or Ksirodakasayi Visnu. So the three features of the original purusa are thus understood. And all the incarnations within the universe are emanations from this Ksirodakasayi Visnu.”

Srila Prabhupada explained that the lila-avataras appear through Ksirodakasayi Visnu, although the text states that Garbhodakasayi Visnu is the source of all incarnations. It is to be understood that because Garbhodakasayi Visnu is the source of Ksirodakasayi Visnu, Garbhodakasayi Visnu can also be glorified as the source of all incarnations.

## Texts 6-27: Naming and Describing Twenty-two Avataras—Answering the Fourth and Fifth Questions

Suta Gosvami will now list the Illa and other incarnations of the Lord one after another. He begins with the four Kumaras, who underwent austerities to realize the Absolute Truth. The next incarnation mentioned is Varahadeva, the Lord’s boar incarnation, then the powerful sage Narada Muni. Suta Gosvami next names Nara-Narayana Rsi, Lord Kapiladeva, Dattatreya Muni, Yajna, King Rsabha, Prthu Maharaja, Matsyadeva (the fish incarnation), Kurma-avatara (the tortoise), Dhanvantari, Mohini-murti (the Lord’s form as a beautiful woman), Nrsimhadeva (the half-lion, half-man incarnation), the dwarf brahmana Vamanadeva, Parasurama, Vyasadeva, King Rama, Lord Balarama, Lord Krsna, Buddha, and Kalki. In Krsna-sandarbha, anuccheda 25, Srila Jiva Gosvami offers a quotation from the Visnu Dharma Purana that states that the Lord is known as Triyuga; that is, He appears in every age but Kali. It is interesting to note that in this list of incarnations, the word “Bhagavan” is used only in texts referring to Krsna and Balarama. One after another, Srila Suta Gosvami has listed the incarnations that spring from the “indestructible seed” of the purusa^avatara, Ksirodakasayi Visnu.

Suta continues: “O brahmanas, the incarnations of the Lord are innumerable, like rivulets flowing from inexhaustible sources of water.” (Bhag. [1.3.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.26)) Jiva Gosvami mentions in anuccheda 26 of Krsna-sandarbha that Suta spoke this text to indicate the Lord’s innumerable other incarnations, none of which he described. Included in that list are Hayagriva, Hari, Prsnigarbha, Vibhu, Satyasena, Vai-kuntha, Ajita, Sarvabhauma, Visvaksena, Dharmasetu, Sudhama, Yogesvara, Brhadbhanu, Sukla, and many others. Jiva then explains that the words hareh sattva-nidher denote Hari as the treasure house of potencies for the manifestation of the innumerable incarnations.

Text 27: “All the rsis, Manus, demigods and descendants of Manu, who are especially powerful, are plenary portions or portions of the plenary portions of the Lord. This also includes the Prajapatis.” Of these avataras, as Prabhupada writes in his purport, “Those who are comparatively less powerful are called vibhiiti, and those who are comparatively more powerful are called dvesa incarnations.” Suta Gosvami gives a brief description of each incarnation he has named, but before describing them in more detail he wants to clarify that Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is the origin of all the incarnations.

## Texts 28: Krsna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead

*ete camsa-kalah pumsah*  
*krsnas tu bhagavan svayam*  
*indrari-vyakularh lokam*  
*mrdayanti yuge yuge*

**All of the above-mentioned incarnations are either plenary portions or portions of the plenary portions of the Lord, but Lord Sri Krsna is the original Personality of Godhead. All of them appear on planets whenever there is a disturbance created by the atheists. The Lord incarnates to protect the theists.**

Srila Prabhupada’s word-for-word translation for the first half of this text follows:

ete—all these; ca—and; arhsa—plenary portions; kaldh.—portions of the plenary portions; pumsah—of the Supreme; krsnah—Lord Krsna; tu—but; bhagavan—the Personality of Godhead; svayam— in person.

Ete, “all these,” refers to all the incarnations Suta has just mentioned. Ca, “and,” adds to the list all those he has not mentioned. Some of those incarnations are arhsa, plenary portions (fully powerful expansions of the Supreme Lord), and some are kaldh, expanded portions of the plenary portions (who are relatively less powerful). In addition, there are other varieties of incarnations, such as saktyavesa-avatdras, gundvatdras, and yuga-avatdras. All these incarnations, Suta Gosvami explains, come from the pumsah, the purusa-avatara form of the Supreme (pumsah means “person,” as does purusa) mentioned in text 1: jagrhe paurusam ruparh, bhagavan mahad'ddibhih. Bhagavan had expanded and accepted the form of the first purusa-avatdra, which was His plenary portion. Later, that first purusa-avatara expanded into a second purusa-avatara, the second into a third. The third purusa' avatdra, Ksirodakasayi Visnu, is the pumsah, the Supreme Person who is the source of all the incarnations now being mentioned by Suta Gosvami.

After stating that all incarnations named and unnamed come from the purusa-avatara, Srila Suta Gosvami changes the text’s topic with the words krsnas tu. By using the word tu, “but,” Seta Gosvami clearly distinguishes Krsna from the amsa'kalah, the “plenary portions and parts of the plenary portions” of the purusa-avataras. Tu is а strong word; it denotes a change of category, as in the sentence, “All the men in the room are important, but that man is the president.” As the word “but” denotes that the president is in a different category than the other important men, Suta Gosvami uses tu to show that Krsna is in a different category from the incarnations. He is bhaga' van svayam, the Supreme Personality of Godhead in person (svayam means “in person”) and the origin of everything. Even though Krsna is included among the incarnations listed earlier, He is nevertheless the source of all the others. Because Balarama is Lord Krsna’s constant and intimate companion, He should be accepted as a direct expansion of Lord Krsna rather than an expansion of the purusa-avatar as.

The second half of the text, indrari-vyakulam lokam, mrdayanti yuge yuge, explains the incarnations’ general function. As described in Bhagavad-gita ([4.7-8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/4.7)), these incarnations stop the disturbances of atheists and protect theists. Srila Prabhupada writes: “In this particular stanza Lord Sri Krsna, the Personality of Godhead, is distinguished from other incarnations.... According to Srila Jiva Gosvami’s statement, in accordance with authoritative sources, Lord Krsna is the source of all other incarnations. It is not that Lord Krsna has any source of incarnation. All the symptoms of the Supreme Truth in full are present in the person of Lord Sri Krsna, and in the Bhagavad-gita the Lord emphatically declares that there is no truth greater than or equal to Himself. In this stanza the word svayam is particularly mentioned to confirm that Lord Krsna has no other source than Himself. Although in other places the incarnations are described as bhagavdn because of their specific functions, nowhere are they declared to be the Supreme Personality. In this stanza the word svayam signifies the supremacy as the summum bonum.” (Bhag. [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28), purport)

In his Sat'Sandarbha, especially in Krsna-sandarbha, Jiva Gosvami describes the preeminence of this text in establishing Krsna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the source even of Lord Narayana. In his purport to this text, Prabhupada has concisely presented the essence of those arguments. In Krsna-sandarbha, anuccheda 28, Jiva Gosvami explains Bhagavatam [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28) in detail, and in anuccheda 29 he points to that text as a paribhasa-sutra of the Bhagavatam, a text explaining the book’s essence. Jiva Gosvami begins by expressing a doubt often raised by the opposition: “You have presented a single quotation to demonstrate that Krsna is the original source of all incarnations of Godhead. This single quotation, however, contradicts many other quotations that describe Krsna as an expansion of the Personality of Godhead and not the source of all incarnations. This single statement teaching that Krsna is the source of all arhsas contradicts and opposes the many statements that assert that Krsna is indeed an amsa.”

Jiva Gosvami then declares that Bhagavatam [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28) is a paribhasa-sutra and that the remainder of the Bhagavatam must be understood through this text. A paribhasa-sutra regulates something that is not otherwise regulated; it creates a rule or restriction where no rule or restriction previously existed. It is thus a rule of interpretation and provides the key by which one may understand the purport of a series of apparently unrelated facts and arguments. A book’s paribhasa-sutra acts as a lens through which the entire book can be seen. It dictates how all succeeding points in the book should be interpreted.

It is especially necessary to present a paribhasa-sutra in a lengthy Sanskrit book, because Sanskrit literature at times uses indirect statements even to assert important points. Krsna Himself (Bhag. [11.21.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/21.35)) confirms His appreciation for indirect statements of truth that may contain many meanings: “The Vedas, divided into three divisions, ultimately reveal the living entity as pure spirit soul. The Vedic seers and mantras, however, deal in esoteric terms, and I also am pleased by such confidential descriptions.”

Thus in a lengthy Sanskrit work containing many indirect meanings, the author’s true and consistent intention can be understood through the book’s paribhdsa-siitras. The entire book’s meaning can then be understood by applying these sutras. Without them, we may see only unrelated stories and inconsistent philosophy.

Jiva Gosvami then raises two additional arguments that oppose the acceptance of Bhagavatam [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28) as the Bhagavatam’s paribhasa-sutra. First, he questions the idea that Krsna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead as Bhagavatam [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28) states, when many of the texts within the Bhagavatam itself seem to oppose that conclusion. Secondly, the idea stated in Bhagavatam [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28) is opposed to many statements

in Vedic literature. Citing references from Srila Sridhara Svami, the original authority on understanding the Bhagavatam, however, Srila Jiva Gosvami comments that Sridhara Svami accepts Bhagavatam [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28) as one of the Bhagavatam’s paribhasa-sutras. Then he cites references from the Bhagavatam itself that concur with krsnas tu bhagavdn svayam and shows how texts that seem opposed to this conclusion can be understood favorably through the lens of this important verse.

In Krsna-sandarbha, anuccheda 39-42, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains that in his commentaries Sridhara Svami continuously uses the conclusion—krsnas tu bhagavdn svayam—presented by Suta Gosvami in this text. In anuccheda 74, this scripture is named Bhagavatam because it explains Sri Krsna as the original Personality of Godhead (svayam bhagavan). It is not that the Bhagavatam contains only a few isolated descriptions of Sri Krsna. Rather, almost half the book (including parts of Cantos One and Three) is dedicated to descriptions of Krsna. Even though the Bhagavatam deals almost exclusively with the theme of Krsna, it is neither boring nor tedious; rather, it is wonderful.

For this reason also it may be said that the essence of the Bhagavatam can be found in the ete camsa-kalah pumsah verse. Sri Jiva concludes anuccheda 75 by comparing the Bhagavatam’s texts to an army and krsnas tu bhagavdn svayam to the monarch who is the general of that army. “In this way,” Srila Jiva Gosvami writes, “I have described the army of Srimad-Bhagavatam and its commander.”

In anuccheda 74 Srila Jiva Gosvami shows that statements in the Bhagavatam that appear opposed to the conclusion of [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28) actually support it. He then names other Bhagavatam texts—Bhagavatam [9.24.55](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-9/24.55) and Bhagavatam [10.1.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/1.23)—as subordinate and supportive generals that work under the jurisdiction of the supreme commander. In anuccheda 75-82 he offers more quotations from the Bhagavatam along with quotations from other Vedic literature, all showing that Krsna is the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus the sastric and logical arguments presented by Sri Jiva Gosvami in his Sat-sandarbhas establishes Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu’s conclusion: Krsna is the Absolute Truth, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. We can also understand from Sri Jiva’s powerful presentation that after accepting that the Vedic literature reveals the Absolute Truth, many statements from that literature, especially from Srimad-Bhagavatam, directly point to Krsna as the fullest expression of the Absolute Truth.

Still, one must acknowledge that it is possible to interpret Vedic statements in various ways, and thus it is theoretically possible to use the same statements to draw a different conclusion. But to do this successfully a presenter must not only prove his claim through supporting Vedic texts, he must reinterpret the many Vedic texts that do indicate that Krsna is the Absolute Truth. These texts must either support his conclusion or at least not oppose it. However, while some indirect Vedic statements leave room for interpretation, the many direct statements on this point do not. One who tries to make a strong presentation opposing the conclusion of ete camsa'kalah pumsah will find the going hard. Because Gaudiya Vaisnavas can provide a consistent and convincing presentation, we must conclude that Krsna is the Absolute Truth as they have proposed. Thus Jiva’s powerful presentation removes opposing opinions and convincingly establishes the conclusion.

In the Caitanya-caritamrta, Adi [2.30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/2.30), Srila Krsnadasa Kaviraja cites Bhagavatam [10.14.14](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/14.14) to prove that Krsna, not even Narayana, is the original Supreme Personality of Godhead:

*narayanas tvam na hi sarva-dehinam*  
*atmasy adhisakhila-loka-saksi*  
*narayano ’ngam nara-bhu-jalayandt*  
*tac capi satyam na tavaiva maya*

**О Lord of lords, You are the seer of all creation. You are indeed everyone’s dearest life. Are You not, therefore, my father, Narayana? Narayana refers to one whose abode is in the water bom from Nara \[Garbhodakasayi Visnu\], and that Narayana is Your plenary portion. All Your plenary portions are transcendental. They are absolute and are not creations of maya.**

To further substantiate his proof, Srila Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami then cites (in Cc. Adi [2.63](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/2.63)) Bhagavatam [1.2.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.11):

*vadanti tat tattva-vidas*  
*tattvam yaj jnanam advayam*  
*brahmeti paramatmeti*  
*bhagavan iti sabdyate*

**Learned transcendentalists who know the Absolute Truth say that it is nondual knowledge and is called impersonal Brahman, the localized Paramatma and the Personality of Godhead.**

While explaining this text, Srila Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami notes that the Absolute Truth, that “nondual knowledge” (jnanam advayam), is perceived in three ways, as Brahman, Paramatma, and Bhagavan, “the Personality of Godhead.” He next (in Cc. Adi [2.67](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/2.67)) quotes ete camsa-kalah. pumsah, krsnas tu bhagavdn svayam to show that Krsna is not an avatdra of Lord Narayana. Arguing from a grammatical standpoint in Adi [2.73-90](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/2.73), he shows that Bhagavatam [1.3.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.28) cannot signify Krsna as an incarnation of Narayana but can only denote Krsna alone as the original Supreme Personality of Godhead. To comment on the first text of the Tenth Canto, Srila Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami then offers a verse (Cc. Adi [2.95](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/2.95)) written by Sridhara Svami: “The Tenth Canto of Srimad-Bhagavatam reveals the tenth object, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is the shelter of all surrendered souls. He is known as Sri Krsna, and He is the ultimate source of all the universes. Let me offer my obeisances unto Him.”

## Text 29: The Phala-sruti—the Fruit of Hearing

Suta Gosvami now offers readers the blessing of a phalaAruti, a gift offered for their patient and devoted hearing of what has just been recited: “Whoever carefully recites the mysterious appearances of the Lord, with devotion in the morning and in the evening, gets relief from all miseries of life.” (Bhag. [1.3.29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.29)) Krsna’s appearance is mysterious, for although He is unborn He nevertheless takes birth. Only those who penetrate the topic by devotional service can truly understand. Bhagavad-gita ([4.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/4.9)) states that knowing these mysteries in truth liberates us from future birth and death. Clearly, the Lord’s birth and activities are transcendental; otherwise, how could reciting them offer us liberation? Although Krsna’s activities often resemble those of humans, they are nevertheless transcendental and are therefore mysterious.

We have now heard that Krsna is the fountainhead of all incarnations, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and the ultimate realization of the bhagavata^tattva that Suta Gosvami described previously in Bhagavatam [1.2.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.11). Krsna is jnanam advayam and is realized as Brahman, Paramatma, and Bhagavan. Suta will now briefly describe the other two tattvas—Brahman and Paramatma—but before doing so will answer three questions: What is the virat-rupa’s position in relation to Krsna? Is the virat-rupa an incarnation of Krsna situated in matter? And does Krsna, therefore, as the virat-rupa, possess a material form?

## Texts 30-39: Progressing from Matter Upward to Brahman, Paramatma, and Finally Bhagavan

## Texts 30-31: A Start—Seeing Spirit in Matter

Suta Gosvami says that the Lord is fully spiritual and possesses no material form. The conception of the virdprupa—that act of perceiving the Lord’s form in matter—is simply presented to materialistic persons to help them bridge the gap between matter and spirit. Because they can see nothing but matter, they are taught to connect everything to the Supreme Lord’s form. The concept of the universal form is meant to help them take the ultimate step of accepting Krsna’s eternal, spiritual form. Srila Prabhupada writes: “The conception of the Lord known as the visva-гuра or the virdprupa is particularly not mentioned along with the various incarnations of the Lord because all the incarnations of the Lord mentioned above are transcendental and there is not a tinge of materialism in their bodies. There is no difference between the body and self as there is in the conditioned soul. The virat-rupa is conceived for those who are just neophyte worshipers.” (Bhag. [1.3.30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.30), purport)

It is interesting to note the final lines in Prabhupada’s purport: “The conclusion is that the material conception of the body of the Lord as virdt is imaginary. Both the Lord and the living beings are living spirits and have original spiritual bodies.” In these lines, Srila Prabhupada compares a living entity’s identification with his material body with imagining that Krsna has a material body. Srila Prabhupada thus states that either form of thinking is imaginary, a product of illusion. Suta offers an example: “Clouds and dust are carried by the air, but less intelligent persons say that the sky is cloudy and the air is dirty. Similarly, they also implant material bodily conceptions on the spirit self.” (Bhag. [1.3.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.31)) Despite appearances and common speech, clouds and sky remain forever separate, just as dirt and air or water and earth never really mix. However, we may speak as if they do as a convenience or when speaking with those with less ability to conceptualize.

Similarly, as Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 31, “Those who want to see the Lord with their present material eyes or . . . senses are advised to meditate on the gigantic external feature called the virdprupa. For instance, when a particular gentleman goes in his car, which can be seen very easily, we identify the car with the man in the car. When the President goes out in his particular car, we say, ‘There is the President.’ For the time being we identify the car with the President. Similarly, less intelligent men who want to see God immediately without necessary qualification are shown first the gigantic material cosmos as the form of the Lord, although the Lord is within and without.”

## Texts 32-34: Seeing All As Spirit

Suta now describes the next step in spiritual understanding: materialist to spiritual impersonalist. “Beyond this gross conception of form is another, subtle conception of form which is without formal shape and is unseen, unheard and unmanifest. The living being has his form beyond this subtlety, otherwise he could not have repeated births.” (Bhag. [1.3.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.32)) Embedded in this text are two additional concepts that underlie the beginning of spiritual life. First, a learned soul sees everything not only in terms of gross matter; he sees beyond the ever-shifting material varieties to the one, all-pervading, eternal, nondual, spiritual substance. This realization is called Brahman in Bhagavatam [1.2.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.11) and is one of the three levels of realization of the jnanam advayam, the nondual truth. In a parallel point, Suta Gosvami explains that beyond the gross material body with which a living entity identifies is something subtle, eternal, and spiritual. The text asks: If we were not eternal, how could we take birth in one body after another?Suta next explains that by following a process of self-realization we can break our identification with gross and subtle bodies and see both our true self and the Lord. He adds: “If the illusory energy subsides and the living entity becomes fully enriched with knowledge by the grace of the Lord, then he becomes at once enlightened with self-realization and thus becomes situated in his own glory.” (Bhag. [1.3.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.34)) In Krsna-sandarbha, anuccheda 1, Jiva comments that of the three features of the Absolute Truth mentioned in Bhagavatam [1.2.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.11), text 33 of this chapter describes the Lord’s Brahman feature. The purports to texts 34 and 33 (presented respectively) are potent and sweet:

**The external energy, which now bewilders the living being into continuation of birth and death, is turned into internal potency by the will of the Lord to lead the living being to eternal life.**

**When a living being is thus graced by the Lord, he is placed in his proper constitutional position to enjoy eternal spiritual life.**

**This perfect stage of self-realization is attained not by artificial means, but under the lotus feet of the Lord, who is always transcendental. In the Bhagavad-gita the Lord says that He is present in everyone’s heart, and from Him only all knowledge, remembrance or forgetfulness take place. When the living being desires to be an enjoyer of material energy (illusory phenomena), the Lord covers the living being in the mystery of forgetfulness, and thus the living being misinterprets the gross body and subtle mind to be his own self. And by culture of transcendental knowledge, when the living being prays to the Lord for deliverance from the clutches of forgetfulness, the Lord, by His causeless mercy, removes the living being’s illusory curtain, and thus he realizes his own self. He then engages himself in the service of the Lord in his eternal constitutional position, becoming liberated from the conditioned life. All this is executed by the Lord either through His external potency or directly by the internal potency.**

The Lord’s external energy, His maya, which facilitates our illusion, can also carry us closer to Krsna. When Maharaja Pariksit insulted Samika Rsi, the king immediately repented. Nevertheless, the sage’s son cursed him to die in seven days. The king responded “sadhu”; he accepted the adverse situation as “well and good.” Maharaja Pariksit, an exalted Vaisnava, remained ever receptive to Krsna’s desire. Through his example, Maharaja Pariksit instructs us how to respond to the external energy so that it will bring us closer to Krsna. When one responds properly, the external energy acts as Krsna’s internal energy.

Another example of the Vaisnava response to the material energy is Vidura’s reaction to Duryodhana’s insults. The Bhagavatam tells us that Vidura perceived Krsna’s mercy through the insults (Bhag. [3.1.16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/1.16)). Duryodhana was certainly acting under Krsna’s external illusory energy, but through Duryodhana’s actions the internal energy nevertheless pulled Vidura closer to Krsna. Srila Prabhupada writes: “A pure devotee of the Lord is never perturbed by an awkward position created by the external energy of the Lord.... Vidura could see that Duryodhana, under the influence of maya, the external energy, was making progress on the path toward his own ruination. He therefore considered the acts of the external energy to be supreme, yet he also saw how the internal energy of the Lord helped him in that particular situation. A devotee is always in a renounced temperament because the worldly attractions can never satisfy him.” (Bhag. [3.1.16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/1.16), purport)

These examples illustrate how Krsna’s devotees, by their devotional attitudes, may change Krsna’s maya from material to spiritual. Only devotees can be peaceful, for they alone see the movements of the material world as assisting them in their quest for spiritual realization.

In his comment on Bhagavatam [1.3.33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.33) in Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 3, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains that a person learns the truth about the gross and subtle bodies through self-realization. What kind of truth does the soul learn? It learns that “both the gross and subtle bodies have nothing to do with the self.” When one understands this lesson, one sees the Supreme directly. When he understands that identifying with the gross and subtle bodies is illusion, and when he then sees the Supreme Lord directly, he attains liberation, even though he may remain in the material world.

## Texts 35-39: Knowing Paramatma and Bhagavan

Suta Gosvami carries his current progression upward toward realization of Paramatma as an expansion of Bhagavan: “Thus learned men describe the births and activities of the unborn and inactive, which is undiscoverable even in the Vedic literatures. He is the Lord of the heart. The Lord, whose activities are always spotless, is the master of the six senses and is fully omnipotent with six opulences. He creates the manifested universes, maintains them and annihilates them without being in the least affected. He is within every living being and is always independent.” (Bhag. [1.3.35-36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.35)) Although the Lord as Supersoul creates this world, He remains unaffected by it. This shows yet another difference between the Lord and the living entities. Krsna is the creator, the living entities the created. Krsna is forever free from illusion; the living entities can become covered by it. When the living entities do become free from illusion (Bhag. [1.3.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.34)), do they suddenly become the Supersoul, the creator? Do they suddenly lose their individuality and become devoid of qualities, even if the Supersoul is neither impersonal nor devoid of characteristics? No. More sensibly, as Srila Prabhupada states in his purport to text 34: “When a living being is thus graced by the Lord, he is placed in his proper constitutional position to enjoy eternal spiritual life.”

In Chapter Two as well as in the first five texts of Chapter Three, Suta Gosvami has described the Supersoul and His activities. In Bhagavatam [1.2.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.31) he has explained that the Supersoul is an expansion of Vasudeva, who is Bhagavan. Here in texts 35 and 36 Suta summarizes the Supersoul’s position. The Supersoul expands into the heart of every living entity. Srila Prabhupada points out: “. . . He is called the amoghadilah, which indicates that there is nothing lamentable in His creation. Those who create disturbance in His creation are themselves disturbed.” (Bhag. [1.3.36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.36), purport) The Supersoul is always aloof from the creation, ever pure, and always neutral despite the fact that He appears to be in contact with the world of matter.

Jiva Gosvami states (Bhagavat-sandarbha, anuccheda 46) that text 35 may be understood by studying it with texts 33 and 34. Text 33 explains that one may become free from the ignorance of identifying with the gross and subtle bodies by gaining full spiritual knowledge. This will allow one to see the Lord. Text 34 explains that when the illusory energy subsides, one’s own spiritual form becomes manifest. Finally, text 35 says that learned men who take pleasure in the Supreme Self describe the births and activities of the Supersoul, the Lord in the heart. Thus when material misconceptions subside, the transcendental treasure of directly perceiving the Lord’s birth and activities becomes manifest. Then we can understand that the Lord’s forms and pastimes are filled with spiritual bliss.

Srila Jiva explains text 35 in more detail: The phrase akartur aja-nasya, “the Lord has neither birth nor activities,” should be understood to mean that the Lord has no material birth or activities. His birth and activities are completely spiritual and are different from their material counterparts. The phrase veda'guhyani, “undiscoverable even in the Vedas,” is explained in the following prayers by Akriira (Bhag. [10.48.23-24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/48.23), as paraphrased in Krsna book):

**To consider Your Lordship one of us, conditioned by the material nature, is a mistake due to our imperfect knowledge. When people deviate from the original knowledge of the Vedas, they try to identify the ordinary living entities with Your Lordship, who has appeared on this earth in Your original form in order to reestablish the real knowledge that the living entities are neither one with nor equal to the Supreme God. My dear Lord, You are always situated in uncontaminated goodness (suddha'Sattva). Your appearance is necessary to reestablish actual Vedic knowledge, as opposed to the atheistic philosophy that tries to establish that God and the living entities are one and the same. My dear Lord Krsna, this time You have appeared in the home of Vasudeva as his son, along with Your plenary expansion, Sri Balarama. Your mission is to kill all the atheistic royal families and destroy their huge military strength. You have advented Yourself to minimize the burden of the world, and to fulfill this mission, You have glorified the dynasty of Yadu by appearing as one of its members. (Chapter 48, p. 453)**

Srila Sridhara Svami comments as follows: Someone may say that the Lord’s pastimes are actually manifestations of material illusion and that they only appear to be spiritual under the influence of devotion to the Lord, just as a glittering oyster shell may sometimes be mistaken for silver. This is not a fact. The Supreme Lord’s pastimes are spiritual. They are not the ordinary activities of conditioned souls, but are the Supreme Godhead’s sport.

Suta Gosvami continues: “The foolish with a poor fund of knowledge cannot know the transcendental nature of the forms, names and activities of the Lord, who is playing like an actor in a drama. Nor can they express such things, neither in their speculations nor in their words.” (Bhag. [1.3.37](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.37)) Does this mean that no one can know Krsna? Is He completely unknowable? Suta Gosvami explains that Krsna is knowable, but only by those who render Him unreserved and uninterrupted service. Only they “can know the creator of the universe in His full glory, power and transcendence.” (Bhag. [1.3.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.38))

Krsna’s devotees can know Him because Krsna gives them His mercy. Krsna personally awards them the knowledge by which they can come to Him (Bg. [10.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/10.10)). He does this because the spontaneous affection with which they serve attracts Him to them. This is the secret of entering the kingdom of God. Great souls inquire about the birth and activities of He who has neither birth nor activities. Krsna creates everything, possesses everything, is within everything, and is fully independent. Because He is like an actor in a drama, few people know His actual identity. Thus Suta has again presented, albeit briefly, the pinnacle of realization of the Absolute Truth: He is Bhagavan Sri Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

Srila Prabhupada again emphasizes how we can realize Krsna: “Such favorable servitors are devotees of the Lord, and by the grace of the Lord they can enter into the mysterious region of transcendence by the mercy of the Lord.” (Bhag. [1.3.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.38), purport)

Inquiring about the Absolute Truth is the purpose of human life. Suta Gosvami congratulates Saunaka Rsi and the sages of Naimisaranya for having asked such spiritually provocative questions. By text 38, Suta Gosvami has already answered five out of their six questions. He says: “Only by making such inquiries in this world can one be successful and perfectly cognizant, for such inquiries invoke transcendental ecstatic love unto the Personality of Godhead, who is the proprietor of all the universes, and guarantee cent-percent immunity from the dreadful repetition of birth and death.”

Suta glorifies the sages’ questions because they give rise to his speaking the Bhagavatam, which has so much spiritual potency. Why is the Bhagavatam potent? This will be addressed in the next section of texts.

## Texts 40—44: Glorification of Srimad-Bhagavatam— Suta Gosvami Answers Question Six

Suta Gosvami states: “This Srimad-Bhagavatam is the literary incarnation of God, and it is compiled by Srila Vyasadeva, the incarnation of God. It is meant for the ultimate good of all people, and it is all-successful, all-blissful and all-perfect.” (Bhag. [1.3.40](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.40)) The Bhagavatam is Krsna! We may benefit by associating with the book bhagavata by hearing it from the pure person bhagavata—he who is “of Krsna” and whose life is fully dedicated to His service. Srila Prabhupada’s purport to this verse is powerful:

Lord Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu declared that Srimad-Bhagavatam is the spotless sound representation of all Vedic knowledge and history. There are selected histories of great devotees who are in direct contact with the Personality of Godhead. Srimad-Bhagavatam is the literary incarnation of Lord Sri Krsna and is therefore non-different from Him. Srimad-Bhagavatam should be worshiped as respectfully as we worship the Lord. Thereby we can derive the ultimate blessings of the Lord through its careful and patient study. As God is all light, all bliss and all perfection, so also is Srimad-Bhagavatam. We can have all the transcendental light of the Supreme Brahman, Sri Krsna, from the recitation of the Srimod-Bhagavatam, provided it is received through the medium of the transparent spiritual master. Lord Caitanya’s private secretary Srila Svariipa Damodara Gosvami advised all intending visitors who came to see the Lord at Puri to make a study of the Bhagavatam from the person Bhagavatam. Person Bhagavatam is the self-realized bona fide spiritual master, and through him only can one understand the lessons of Bhagavatam in order to receive the desired result. One can derive from the study of the Bhagavatam all benefits that are possible to be derived from the personal presence of the Lord. It carries with it all the transcendental blessings of Lord Sri Krsna that we can expect from His personal contact.

Suta Gosvami then describes the disciplic succession through which he has himself heard the Bhagavatam: “Sri Vyasadeva delivered it to his son, who is the most respected among the self-realized, after extracting the cream of all Vedic literatures and histories of the universe. Sukadeva Gosvami, the son of Vyasadeva, in his turn delivered the Bhagavatam to the great Emperor Pariksit, who sat surrounded by sages on the bank of the Ganges, awaiting death without taking food or drink.” (Bhag. [1.3.41-42](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.41))

In his purport to text 41, Srila Prabhupada reveals the Bhagavatam’s glories: “It is compared to the cream of the milk. Vedic literature is like the milk ocean of knowledge. Cream or butter is the most palatable essence of milk, and so also is Srimad-Bhagavatam, for it contains all palatable, instructive and authentic versions of different activities of the Lord and His devotees. ... In the Bhagavad-gita the Lord says that the purpose of all the Vedas is to know Him (Lord Krsna), and Srimad-Bhagavatam is Lord Sri Krsna Himself in the form of recorded knowledge. Therefore, it is the cream of all the Vedas, and it contains all historical facts of all times in relation with Sri Krsna. It is factually the essence of all histories.”

Srila Prabhupada also comments on the Bhagavatam’s potency to deliver one from the jaws of death: “At the critical hour of death one must recite the name of Govinda. This is the recommendation of all great transcendentalists. Sukadeva Gosvami had long ago stated the same truth, that at the end one must remember Narayana. That is the essence of all spiritual activities. In pursuance of this eternal truth, Srimad-Bhagavatam was heard by Emperor Pariksit, and it was recited by the able Sukadeva Gosvami. And both the speaker and the receiver of the messages of Bhagavatam were duly delivered by the same medium.” (Bhag. [1.3.42](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.42), purport)

Then before telling how he himself heard the Bhagavatam, Suta Gosvami describes its glories and thus answers Saunaka’s sixth and final question: “Since Sri Krsna, the Absolute Truth, the master of all mystic powers, has departed for His own abode, please tell us to whom the religious principles have now gone for shelter.” (Bhag. [1.1.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/1.23))

Suta’s reply is direct:

*krsne sva-dhamopagate dharma-jnanadibhih saha*  
*kalau nasta-drsam esa puranarko ’dhunoditah*

**This Bhagavata Purana is as brilliant as the sun, and it has arisen just after the departure of Lord Krsna to His own abode, accompanied by religion, knowledge, etc. Persons who have lost their vision due to the dense darkness of ignorance in the age of Kali shall get light from this Purana. (Bhag.** [**1.3.43**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.43)**)**

Srila Prabhupada is just as direct: “In the Kali-yuga the population is just a royal edition of the animals. They have nothing to do with spiritual knowledge or godly religious life. They are so blind that they cannot see anything beyond the jurisdiction of the subtle mind, intelligence or ego, but they are very much proud of their advancement in knowledge, science and material prosperity. They can risk their lives to become a dog or hog just after leaving the present body, for they have completely lost sight of the ultimate aim of life. The Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna appeared before us just a little prior to the beginning of Kali-yuga, and He returned to His eternal home practically at the commencement of Kali-yuga. While He was present, He exhibited everything by His different activities. He spoke the Bhagavad-gita specifically and eradicated all pretentious principles of religiosity. And prior to His departure from this material world, He empowered Sri Vyasadeva through Narada to compile the messages of the Srimad-Bhagavatam, and thus both the Bhagavad-gita and the Srimod-Bhagavatom are like torchbearers for the blind people of this age. In other words, if men in this age of Kali want to see the real light of life, they must take to these two books only, and their aim of life will be fulfilled. Bhagavad-gita is the preliminary study of the Bhagavatam. And Srimad-Bhagavatam is the summum bonum of life, Lord Sri Krsna personified. We must therefore accept Srimad-Bhagavatam as the direct representation of Lord Krsna. One who can see Srimad-Bhagavatam can see also Lord Sri Krsna in person. They are identical.”

Suta now completes his description of the disciplic succession in which the Bhagavatam was spoken by telling how he himself heard this great literature: “O learned brahmanas, when Sukadeva Gosvami recited Bhagavatam there \[in the presence of Emperor Pariksit\], I heard him with rapt attention, and thus, by his mercy, I learned the Bhagavatam from that great and powerful sage. Now I shall try to make you hear the very same thing as I learned it from him and as I have realized it.” (Bhag. [1.3.44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.44))

He then speaks the final text of the First Canto’s third chapter. The beginning of Srila Prabhupada’s purport strongly informs us from whom we should hear the Bhagavatam: “One can certainly see directly the presence of Lord Sri Krsna in the pages of Bhagavatam if one has heard it from a self-realized great soul like Sukadeva Gosvami. One cannot, however, learn Bhagavatam from a bogus hired reciter whose aim of life is to earn some money out of such recitation and employ the earning in sex indulgence. No one can learn Srimad-Bhagavatam who is associated with persons engaged in sex life. That is the secret of learning Bhagavatam. Nor can one learn Bhagavatam from one who interprets the text by his mundane scholarship. One has to learn Bhagavatam from the representative of Sukadeva Gosvami, and no one else, if one at all wants to see Lord Sri Krsna in the pages. That is the process, and there is no alternative. Suta Gosvami is a bona fide representative of Sukadeva Gosvami because he wants to present the message which he received from the great learned brahmana. Sukadeva Gosvami presented Bhagavatam as he heard it from his great father, and so also Suta Gosvami is presenting Bhagavatam as he had heard it from Sukadeva Gosvami.”

Srila Prabhupada continues to guide one in how to hear the Bhagavatam: “Simple hearing is not all; one must realize the text with proper attention. The word nivista means that Suta Gosvami drank the juice of Bhagavatam through his ears. That is the real process of receiving Bhagavatam. One should hear with rapt attention from the real person, and then he can at once realize the presence of Lord Krsna in every page. The secret of knowing Bhagavatam is mentioned here. No one can give rapt attention who is not pure in mind. No one can be pure in mind who is not pure in action. No one can be pure in action who is not pure in eating, sleeping, fearing and mating. But somehow or other if someone hears with rapt attention from the right person, at the very beginning one can assuredly see Lord Sri Krsna in person in the pages of Bhagavatam.”

One can see Krsna directly in the Bhagavatam if one hears it from a self-realized soul. Krsna is by nature merciful. Even if one is neither qualified nor pure in mind or action, if one hears the Bhagavatam from the right person, he may still “see” Krsna in the book’s pages. Srila Prabhupada is the “somehow or other” factor for millions of devotees. His spreading of hari'nama chanting around the world and his translation of and inspiration to study Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam have afforded him the honor of being Krsna’s unparalleled servant. By his potency, he extended the Bhagavatam’s mercy even to the fallen and disqualified. His forceful insistence that people accept this mercy created piety even in the impious. Prabhupada’s deeds prove that Krsna does award His pure devotees license to freely dispense His mercy.

The first three chapters of this canto are deep, for they present the essence of Srimad-Bhagavatam. They define the Absolute Truth, describe the various levels of realizing that Absolute, clarify the purpose of performing our prescribed work, summarize the stages through which bhakti progresses, describe the Lord’s incarnations, and authoritatively and powerfully present Krsna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, proving Him to be the ultimate realization of the Absolute Truth. The third chapter names the means of progress: one must hear Srimad-Bhagavatam, which is both Krsna Himself and His abode during this darkest age. Chapters Four through Seven will describe how the Srimad-Bhagavatam came to be recorded.

## Dialogue Four - Narada Muni Instructs Vyasadeva

## Chapter 4 - The Appearance of Sri Narada

## Texts 1-13: Saunaka Inquires from Suta Gosvami

Saunaka Rsi’s eagerness to hear the Bhagavatam has increased. He has heard Suta Gosvami answer questions from the sages at Naimisaranya as well as Suta’s glorification of the Bhagavatam as being as “brilliant as the sun” because it bestows knowledge on those trapped in the darkness of Kali-yuga (Bhag. [1.3.43](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/3.43)). Saunaka now recognizes that krsna-katha is the medicine to cure the ills of Kali-yuga. He probes deeper, asking Suta about the Bhagavatam’s history.

Saunaka asks why the great sage Vyasadeva, who had already compiled a vast amount of Vedic literature (including the Vedanta-sutra, literally “the conclusion of Vedic knowledge”), became inspired to compile yet another huge work. Why did Sukadeva, who was already liberated from bodily identification, desire to study the resultant texts? Sukadeva was so renounced that when he went door to door to beg alms he would stay at a householder’s home for no more than thirty minutes—the length of time it took for the householder to milk his cow. Why did that strictly detached soul spend seven days—twenty-four hours each day—with Maharaja Pariksit, who was not only a householder but a king? How did others recognize Sukadeva as an exalted soul, qualified to speak to Maharaja Pariksit on the deepest subjects? After all, Sukadeva’s realization had taken him beyond matter, and he had approached the riverbank after roaming the countryside as a dishevelled madman. Aside from that, why had Maharaja Pariksit, a powerful devotee-king and the shelter of countless citizens, renounced his throne to sit on the bank of the Ganges, fasting and awaiting death?

## Texts 14-33: Suta Gosvami Retells Srila Vyasadeva’s Accomplishments in Having Compiled the Vast Vedic Literature

In his reply, Suta Gosvami describes the great sage Vyasadeva meditating alone at Badarikasrama, high in the Himalayas, on the bank of the Sarasvati River. In his meditation, Vyasadeva glimpsed a troubled future: Kali-yuga, the confused age of quarrel and deviation from Vedic principles, was to set in. Everything would then begin to deteriorate. As the ignorance and materialism of this dark age increased, the population’s life span, intelligence, and memory would dwindle. Society would crumble as more and more people became victims of envy, deceit, anxiety, and strife. Nothing in Kali-yuga would engender people’s faith. Families, nations, and religious institutions would offer no security, and placing faith in them would give uncertain fruits.

In Kali-yuga, goodness vanishes and ignorance and passion dominate. People become impatient, greedy, and angry. Vyasadeva understood that the purifying sacrifices he had previously prescribed in the Vedas would now prove impossible to perform. The coming of Kali-yuga would require him to simplify and reorganize the Vedic prescriptions and, especially, to record them. Vyasadeva thus divided the one Veda, the Yajur Veda, into four: Yajur, Rg, Sama, and Atharva. He then added the Puranas and Itihasas (histories containing the pastimes of the Lord’s various incarnations) as the fifth Veda, and entrusted each Veda to a learned scholar for development. Paila Rsi became the professor of the Rg Veda, Jaimini of the Sama Veda, and Vaisampayana of the Yajur Veda. Ahgira Muni was offered custody of the Atharva Veda, and the Puranas and histories were consigned to Romaharsana Suta, Suta Gosvami’s father. In turn, these powerful sages entrusted their disciples and successive followers with these many branches of Vedic knowledge.

Next Vyasadeva consolidated all the Vedic philosophical principles into the Vedanta-sutra. Then he wrote the Mahabharata to give those who lacked piety or philosophical inclination the opportunity to achieve the goal of life.
