While the Mahabharata is filled with exciting historical tales and political intrigue, it nevertheless summarizes the Vedas because it contains the Bhagavad-gita.

Still, at the end of all this work, Vyasadeva was dissatisfied. He felt incomplete despite having followed the Vedas perfectly and being pure in heart. Ultimately, Krsna had planted these feelings of despondency in Vyasadeva’s heart to set the stage for him to write Srimad-Bhagavatam. Nevertheless, it was reasonable for him to ask himself: Why am I dissatisfied despite my strenuous work on the physical, emotional, and intellectual level? Narada Muni will later answer this question on the deepest level, but Srila Prabhupada hints at this ultimate question in his purport to text 30: “Undoubtedly Srila Vyasadeva was complete in all the details of Vedic achievements. Purification of the living being submerged in matter is made possible by the prescribed activities in the Vedas, but the ultimate achievement is different. Unless it is attained, the living being, even though fully equipped, cannot be situated in the transcendentally normal stage. Srila Vyasadeva appeared to have lost the clue and therefore felt dissatisfaction.” Perhaps, Vyasadeva thought, my dissatisfaction exists because “I did not specifically point out the devotional service of the Lord, which is dear both to perfect beings and to the infallible Lord.” (Bhag. [1.4.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/4.31))Srila Prabhupada highlights Vyasadeva’s problem in his purports to texts 31 and 32, assuring us that it is the same essential problem each soul in the material world faces: alienation. Naturally, all souls trapped in matter feel dissatisfied, lonely, and empty because all of them are separated from Krsna. Activities performed in the material realm—from shopping to intoxication, from humanitarianism to nationalism—are simply the conditioned soul’s attempt to relieve that emptiness. But none of these activities go to the heart of the matter and therefore none of them can negate the emptiness. The only thing that can relieve the conditioned souls of their sense of alienation is the reestablishment of their constitutional loving relationship with Krsna. No activity—even writing spiritual masterpieces, as Srila Vyasadeva’s example shows—can replace alienation with a lasting sense of completeness. Nothing short of devotedly serving and glorifying Krsna can deeply satisfy the soul. Here are some selections from purports to texts 31 and 32:

**The dissatisfaction which was being felt by Srila Vyasadeva is expressed herein in his own words. This was felt for the normal condition of the living being in the devotional service of the Lord. Unless one is fixed in the normal condition of service, neither the Lord nor the living being can become fully satisfied. (Bhag.** [**1.4.31**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/4.31)**, purport)**

**Although Vyasadeva was an empowered divinity, he still felt dissatisfaction because in none of his works were the transcendental activities of the Lord properly explained. The inspiration was infused by Sri Krsna directly in the heart of Vyasadeva, and thus he felt the vacuum as explained above. It is definitely expressed herewith that without the transcendental loving service of the Lord, everything is void; but in the transcendental service of the Lord, everything is tangible without any separate attempt at fruitive work or empiric philosophical speculation. (Bhag.** [**1.4.32**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/4.32)**, purport)**

As Vyasa sat considering his defects, his guru Narada Muni arrived at his cottage. Vyasa rose immediately and respectfully greeted and worshiped the great, auspicious sage.

## Chapter 5 - Narada’s Instructions on Srimad-Bhagavatam for Vyasadeva

## Texts 1-7: Narada Inquires about Vyasa’s Despondency, and Vyasa Replies

After being welcomed and seated, Narada smiled. He knew the cause of Vyasa’s disappointment, and his first words hinted at the solution: “Are you satisfied by identifying with the body or the mind as objects of self-realization?” (Bhag. [1.5.2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.2)) Narada continued: Your Vedic studies have been full, and the work that proceeded from them has been extremely successful. You have even produced the wonderful Mahabharata, which explains the entire Vedas. You have fully delineated the subject of impersonal Brahman as well as the knowledge we can derive from it. Why, then, should you be despondent, “thinking that you are undone, my dear prabhu?”

In his Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 1 commentary on text 4, Jiva Gosvami writes that mere Brahman realization, as Vyasadeva had achieved and described in his books, cannot satisfy the soul. The soul’s true need is love, priti. Direct perception of Bhagavan, who appears as Paramatma and in many other forms, is the highest kind of liberation. In that highest liberation the most exalted spiritual activities are known by names like bhakti, devotional service, and priti, spiritual love. Spiritual love is considered the highest of all spiritual sentiments. Priti eradicates all suffering. Without priti, it is not possible to attain the highest stage of spiritual life. Priti is not dependent on anything else. To the extent that we have priti we are fortunate. Priti is present as we make progress toward liberation; it is also present when we have attained liberation. That is the correct understanding. The form of the Supreme Personality of Godhead is full of transcendental bliss. Transcendental bliss is the abode of priti. Priti is most important in the experience of transcendental bliss. Therefore a spirit soul should always try to attain priti. Priti is the greatest need, the highest goal, of all spirit souls.

Srila Vyasadeva begins his reply to Narada’s pointed inquiries: “All you have said about me is perfectly correct. Despite all this, I am not pacified. I therefore question you about the root cause of my dissatisfaction, for you are a man of unlimited knowledge due to your being the offspring of one \[Brahma\] who is self-born \[without mundane father and mother\]. . . . Like the sun, Your Goodness can travel everywhere in the three worlds, and like the air you can penetrate the internal region of everyone. As such, you are as good as the all-pervasive Supersoul. Please, therefore, find out the deficiency in me, despite my being absorbed in transcendence under disciplinary regulations and vows.” (Bhag. [1.5.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.5), [7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.7))

Srila Prabhupada concisely defines the root of despondency in his purport to text 5: “In the material world everyone is engrossed with the idea of identifying the body or the mind with the self. As such, all knowledge disseminated in the material world is related either with the body or with the mind, and that is the root cause of all despondencies. This is not always detected, even though one may be the greatest erudite scholar in materialistic knowledge. It is good, therefore, to approach a personality like Narada to solve the root cause of all despondencies.”

## Texts 8-22: Narada Reveals to Vyasa the Importance of Describing Krsna’s Pastimes

Narada is straightforward: “You have not actually broadcast the sublime and spotless glories of the Personality of Godhead. That philosophy which does not satisfy the transcendental senses of the Lord is considered worthless. Although, great sage, you have very broadly described the four principles beginning with religious performances, you have not described the glories of the Supreme Personality, Vasudeva.” (Bhag. [1.5.8-9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.8))

Srila Prabhupada’s powerful purport to text 9 clarifies Narada’s observations:

**The prompt diagnosis of Sri Narada is at once declared. The root cause of the despondency of Vyasadeva was his deliberate avoidance of glorifying the Lord in his various editions of the Puranas. He has certainly, as a matter of course, given descriptions of the glories of the Lord (Sri Krsna), but not as many as given to religiosity, economic development, sense gratification and salvation. These four items are by far inferior to engagement in the devotional service of the Lord. Sri Vyasadeva, as the authorized scholar, knew very well this difference. And still instead of giving more importance to the better type of engagement, namely, devotional service to the Lord, he had more or less improperly used his valuable time, and thus he was despondent. . . . Narada \[thus\] recommended to Vyasadeva that he (Vyasadeva) should now eagerly and repeatedly describe the path of devotional service. This would cure him from gross despondency.**

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on this verse that even knowledge of our etemality is useless if it is knowledge devoid of the Lord’s glories. In Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 18, he explains: Sri Narada spoke these words to Vyasadeva because he knew that the descriptions of the Supreme Lord’s glories would awaken love for Him (tat' priti'Utbodhanam). And in his Bhagavat-sandarbha, anuccheda 80, he mentions two reasons why the Bhagavatam was manifest: to show that mere knowledge of Brahman is insufficient to satisfy the soul, and that the Supreme Personality of Godhead can be seen directly only through loving devotional service. These reasons are explained in six verses: Bhagavatam 1.5.4, 7, 8, 12, 37, and 38.

Sridhara Svami discusses similar points in his commentary on text 12: Naiskarmyam means both “spiritual realization” and “freedom from fruitive work.” Niranjanam means “free from designations.” This kind of knowledge of self-realization does not look well if it is devoid of love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead. While acting and attaining the results of action, this kind of knowledge is full of pain (abhadram). The word ca (“and”) here means that this description applies to both fruitive and nonfruitive work. If work is not offered to the Supreme Lord, how can it be auspicious (sobhate)? It is inauspicious both because it has no relation to the Supreme and because it does not purify the heart.

Narada has leveled strong criticism at Vyasa’s previous literary accomplishments. Why? Did Vyasadeva not glorify Krsna in at least some of the Puranas? Does any literature that fails to glorify the Lord have merit? Is imperfectly composed literature that does describe the Lord valuable? Narada continues: “Those words which do not describe the glories of the Lord, who alone can sanctify the atmosphere of the whole universe, are considered by saintly persons to be like unto a place of pilgrimage for crows. Since the all-perfect persons are inhabitants of the transcendental abode, they do not derive any pleasure there. On the other hand, that literature which is full of descriptions of the transcendental glories of the name, fame, forms, pastimes, etc., of the unlimited Supreme Lord is a different creation, full of transcendental words directed toward bringing about a revolution in the impious lives of this world’s misdirected civilization. Such transcendental literatures, even though imperfectly composed, are heard, sung and accepted by purified men who are thoroughly honest.” (Bhag. [1.5.10-11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.10))

After rejecting materialistic literature, however skillfully composed, Narada continues to define what is valuable: devotional service. Everything else is condemned. This includes fruitive work (the goal of the karma-kanda sections of the Vedas) and knowledge of matter and spirit devoid of devotion (the goal of the jnana'kanda sections). Srila Prabhupada comments on text 12: “Not only ordinary literatures devoid of the transcendental glorification of the Lord are condemned, but also Vedic literatures and speculation on the subject of impersonal Brahman when they are devoid of devotional service. When speculation on the impersonal Brahman is condemned on the above ground, then what to speak of ordinary fruitive work, which is not meant to fulfill the aim of devotional service.” In his commentary on the same text, Sridhara Svami states: Rituals without devotion are useless. Srila Jiva Gosvami adds: Spiritual knowledge (jndna) is less valuable than devotion to the Lord, what to speak of the value of karma (fruitive work).

What should Vyasa do? If everything he had previously written was incomplete or insufficient, what should he write now? Noting Vyasadeva’s unparalleled qualification as a transcendental author— “your vision is completely perfect. Your good fame is spotless. You are firm in vow and situated in truthfulness”—Narada adds the positive substance to his instructions: Please think of the Lord’s pastimes in trance in order to help people become liberated from material bondage. Srila Prabhupada’s purport to this text (13) stresses the urgent need for spiritual literature in today’s world:

**There are thousands and thousands of literary men all over the world, and they have created many, many thousands of literary works for the information of the people in general for thousands and thousands of years. Unfortunately none of them have brought peace and tranquillity on the earth. This is due to a spiritual vacuum in those literatures; therefore the Vedic literatures, especially the Bhagavad-gita and the Srimad-Bhagavatam, are specifically recommended to suffering humanity to bring about the desired effect of liberation from the pangs of material civilization, which is eating the vital part of human energy. The Bhagavad-gita is the spoken message of the Lord Himself recorded by Vyasadeva, and the Srimad-Bhagavatam is the transcendental narration of the activities of the same Lord Krsna, which alone can satisfy the hankering desires of the living being for eternal peace and liberation from miseries. Srimad-Bhagavatam, therefore, is meant for all the living beings all over the universe for total liberation from all kinds of material bondage. Such transcendental narrations of the pastimes of the Lord can be described only by liberated souls like Vyasadeva and his bona fide representatives who are completely merged in the transcendental loving service of the Lord. Only to such devotees do the pastimes of the Lord and their transcendental nature become automatically manifest by dint of devotional service.**

Narada continues: In your writing you must describe everything in relation to the Lord and His service. Other descriptions will only agitate the readers’ minds, reacting with and increasing their sense desires. Thus the people will become trapped in matter. Your other writings have only authorized your readers’ proclivities for material pleasure and allowed them to call these proclivities “religious.” This was not your intention, but it is the result. Now thinking themselves sheltered by your instructions, they will hardly care for prohibitions and will act irresponsibly, misusing their lives. Please, therefore, describe the Supreme Lord’s transcendental activities and guide those who remain materially attached toward spiritual realization.

In his purport to text 15, Srila Prabhupada continues Narada’s assessment: “A patient suffering from a particular type of malady is almost always inclined to accept eatables which are forbidden for him. The expert physician does not make any compromise with the patient by allowing him to take partially what he should not at all take.”

As we analyze the various positions of living entities trapped in matter, we may try to assess the dangers of following the bhakti path. For example, what happens to those who are materially attached but somehow become inspired to renounce everything and practice devotional service? What if they later fall down? Have they lost everything? After all, they have renounced material life and failed in spiritual life.

Actually, their losses are only apparent; they lose nothing, because relentless time would have soon crushed or stolen all they imagined they possessed anyway. However, even incomplete spiritual progress is never destroyed; it is always protected. Narada comments in text 16: “The Supreme Lord is unlimited. Only a very expert personality, retired from the activities of material happiness, deserves to under stand this knowledge of spiritual values. Therefore those who are not so well situated, due to material attachment, should be shown the ways of transcendental realization, by Your Goodness, through descriptions of the transcendental activities of the Supreme Lord.” He adds: “One who has forsaken his material occupations to engage in the devotional service of the Lord may sometimes fall down while in an immature stage, yet there is no danger of his being unsuccessful. On the other hand, a nondevotee, though fully engaged in occupational duties, does not gain anything.” (Bhag. [1.5.16-17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.16))

Krsna safeguards the spiritual assets of His devotees. Bharata, Citra-ketu, and Ajamila prove Krsna’s promise to protect His devotees’ advancement. A devotee never serves in vain. In his purport to text 17, Prabhupada emphasizes the value of even seemingly unsuccessful attempts at devotion: “\[SJometimes . . . one surrenders ... by some temporary sentiment, and in the long run, due to so many other reasons, he falls down from the path of service by undesirable association. . . . But in spite of all this, the stress is given here to surrendering unto the lotus feet of the Lord, even if there is a chance of falling down, because even though one falls down from the prescribed duties of devotional service, he will never forget the lotus feet of the Lord. Once engaged in the devotional service of the Lord, one will continue the service in all circumstances. In the Bhagavad-gita it is said that even a small quantity of devotional service can save one from the most dangerous position.”

Narada continues to minimize the value of materialistic life: The intelligent endeavor only for that which is eternal and cannot be obtained in the world of matter. Why work for material happiness? Material happiness comes according to our karma, automatically, just as we experience distress. Then he again emphasizes the power of devotional service: “Even though a devotee of Lord Krsna sometimes falls down somehow or other, he certainly does not undergo material existence like others \[fruitive workers, etc.\] because a person who has once relished the taste of the lotus feet of the Lord can do nothing but remember that ecstasy again and again.” (Bhag. [1.5.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.19))

In his purport to this text, Srila Prabhupada compares the suffering of a devotee who has fallen from the path to that of a materialist: “\[E\]ven though he falls down, a devotee is never to be considered the same as a fallen karmi. A karmi suffers the results of his own fruitive reactions, whereas a devotee is reformed by chastisement directed by the Lord Himself.” An orphan’s suffering and the suffering of a beloved child are not the same. Orphans may be poor because no one cares for them, but beloved children, although impoverished like an orphan, live always under the vigilance of a capable father.

Narada next asserts that everyone is related to Krsna, even those who have forgotten Him, and the incompleteness and alienation each conditioned living entity feels is thus an illusion. He explains that Krsna, as the Paramatma, manifests and maintains the material creation, and then the material creation enters into Him at annihilation. Indeed, the Personality of Godhead is Himself the cosmos, although He is nevertheless aloof from it. Still, the illusioned living entities in this world perceive themselves as separate from the Lord. The reality, however, is that nothing—neither dull matter nor the illusioned living entity—is separate from Krsna.

The wise have concluded that virtuous deeds—sacrifice, charity, austerity, and study, all of which are recommended in the Vedas— are not meant to award pious enjoyment but to gradually lead one to the Lord and His service. Narada states that the gradual method Vyasadeva has delineated is unsatisfactory because it encourages the readers’ tendency to seek self-centered pleasure. The only thing that can help them reestablish their relationship with God is krsna-katha. Pious deeds will not be enough to break theit attraction to mundane enjoyment. Although people were meant to understand that all Vedic teachings culminate in devotional service to Krsna, few people would actually understand that and would instead chase a mixed perfection through karma and jnana.

Narada has now explained to Vyasadeva the ultimate position of devotional service and how his previous endeavors did not emphasize that conclusion. What does Narada expect him to do? Narada instructs him to use his advanced knowledge to establish the Lord’s glories: “Your Goodness has perfect vision. You yourself can know the Supersoul Personality of Godhead because you are present as the plenary portion of the Lord. Although you are birthless, you have appeared on this earth for the well-being of all people. Please, therefore, describe the transcendental pastimes of the Supreme Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna more vividly.” (Bhag. [1.5.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.21)) These descriptions will help the misguided souls accept the Lord’s supremacy and agree to serve Him. This was the order for Vyasa to write Srimad-Bhagavatam.

## Texts 23-31: Narada Tells of his Life

To show the influence of a surcharged devotional environment, Narada describes how such an atmosphere affected his own life. Previous to his birth as the son of a maidservant, Narada Muni was a Gandharva named Upabarhana. Cursed, Upabarhana took birth in an impoverished family and received no education. He did not know his father and lived the life of a servant. Nevertheless, due to powerful spiritual association, he blossomed spiritually and became the immortal sage Narada.

While still young, Narada served a group of Vaisnava brahmanas, bhakti'Vedantas, as they followed their Caturmasya vows at the inn where his mother worked. Although the sages were impartial by nature (tulya-darsanah), Narada’s qualities impelled them to bless him. He was self-controlled, sober, and possessed the sweet spirit of sevd. Once, with their permission, he ate the holy remnants of their food, destroying his sins. By serving these great souls and hearing them describe Krsna’s activities, he became purified; he found himself deeply attracted to their nature. Gradually he developed the same spiritual attraction and taste for Krsna consciousness that the; possessed.

Prabhupada glorifies the efficacy of association with pure devotees in his purport to text 25: “There are many things which hinder one from entering devotional service. But by the association of pure devotees all these obstacles are removed. The neophyte devotee becomes practically enriched with the transcendental qualities of the pure devotee, which means attraction for the Personality of Godhead’s name, fame, qualities, pastimes, etc. Infection of the qualities of the pure devotee means to imbibe the taste of pure devotion always in the transcendental activities of the Personality of Godhead. This transcendental taste at once makes all material things distasteful.”

The real value of Vaisnava association is that it gives us the opportunity to hear krsna'kathd. This hearing about Krsna can transform one into a devotee. Srila Prabhupada explains: “The whole idea is that simply by hearing about the Lord’s pastimes one can become one of the associates of the Lord. . . . One can attain to the highest perfection of life simply by attentive hearing of the transcendental pastimes of the Lord from the right sources, as Sri Narada heard them from the pure devotees (bhakti-vedantas) in his previous life. This process of hearing in the association of the devotees is especially recommended in this age of quarrel (Kali).” (Bhag. [1.5.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.26), purport)

Narada catalogues the effects of krsna-katha on his life: “\[T\]hus listening attentively, my taste for hearing of the Personality of Godhead increased at every step.... as soon as 1 got a taste for the Personality of Godhead, my attention to hear of the Lord was unflinching. And as my taste developed, I could realize that it was only in my ignorance that I had accepted gross and subtle coverings, for both the Lord and I are transcendental. ... As the flow of my devotional service began, the coverings of the modes of passion and ignorance vanished. I was very much attached to those sages. I was gentle in behavior, and all my sins were eradicated in their service. In my heart I had strong faith in them. I had subjugated the senses, and I was strictly following them with body and mind.” (Bhag. [1.5.26-29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.26))

Srila Prabhupada emphasizes that the qualities Narada developed are essential for full advancement: “These are the necessary qualifications of a prospective candidate who can expect to be elevated to the position of a pure unadulterated devotee. Such a candidate must always seek the association of pure devotees. One should not be misled by a pseudodevotee. He himself must be plain and gentle to receive the instructions of such a pure devotee. A pure devotee is a completely surrendered soul unto the Personality of Godhead. He knows the Personality of Godhead as the supreme proprietor and all others as His servitors. And by the association of pure devotees only, one can get rid of all sins accumulated by mundane association. A neophyte devotee must faithfully serve the pure devotee, and he should be very much obedient and strictly follow the instructions. These are the signs of a devotee who is determined to achieve success even in the existing duration of life.” (Bhag. [1.5.29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.29), purport)

Narada concludes: “As they were leaving, those bhakti-vedantas, who are very kind to poor-hearted souls, instructed me in that most confidential subject which is instructed by the Personality of Godhead Himself. By that confidential knowledge, I could understand clearly the influence of the energy of Lord Sri Krsna, the creator, maintainer and annihilator of everything. By knowing that, one can return to Him and personally meet Him.” (Bhag. [1.5.30-31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.30)) In his commentary on text 30, Srila Jiva Gosvami states: By confidential knowledge, Narada was referring to the catuh-sloki \[Bhag. [2.9.33-36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/9.33)\]. This knowledge is far above impersonal knowledge. Narada wished Vyasadeva to emphasize these same sacred truths in his own writing.

## Texts 32-40: Narada Advises Vyasa to Reveal in his Writing the Principle of Hearing about the Almighty Lord and Working for Him

Narada knew what a powerful effect using Krsna’s material energy in Krsna’s service (yena gacchanti tat-padam) has on the consciousness and said: “It is decided by the learned that the best remedial measure for removing all troubles and miseries is to dedicate one’s activities to the service of the Supreme Lord Personality of Godhead \[Sri Krsna\].” (Bhag. [1.5.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.32)) As self-centered actions cause suffering and bondage, Narada emphasizes that actions intended to give Krsna pleasure purify one, lead one toward liberation, and end one’s suffering. In his purport to text 32 Srila Prabhupada suggests that constant hearing about Krsna is the best spiritual process. He also hints, however, at how one may work effectively for Krsna: “The best thing is, after all, to get relief from all material activities and engage oneself completely in hearing the transcendental pastimes of the Lord. But in case of the absence of such an opportunity, one should try to engage in the service of the Lord everything for which one has specific attraction, and that is the way of peace and prosperity.” By dedicating everything to the Lord’s service, one becomes spiritually advanced instead of materially entrapped. That which would have enslaved one instead awards him freedom. Narada illustrates this principle with a medical example: “O good soul, does not a thing, applied therapeutically, cure a disease which was caused by that very same thing?” (Bhag. [1.5.33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.33))

Do not renounce work simply because it causes suffering and bondage. Rather, renounce the spirit of self-centered enjoyment. Then work for Krsna. Prabhupada’s purport to text 33 further emphasizes this:

**An expert physician treats his patient with a therapeutic diet. For example, milk preparations sometimes cause disorder of the bowels, but the very same milk converted into curd and mixed with some other remedial ingredients cures such disorders. Similarly, the threefold miseries of material existence cannot be mitigated simply by material activities. Such activities have to be spiritualized, just as by fire iron is made red-hot, and thereby the action of fire begins. Similarly, the material conception of a thing is at once changed as soon as it is put into the service of the Lord. That is the secret of spiritual success. We should not try to lord it over the material nature, nor should we reject material things. The best way to make the best use of a bad bargain is to use everything in relation with the supreme spiritual being.**

Narada explains that by dedicating one’s activities to Krsna’s service and working for His pleasure, the activities that would have caused bondage free him and automatically award him knowledge.

In addition, Narada continues, it is natural for those who work with Krsna’s pleasure at the center of their activities to chant and remember Krsna’s names, glories, and qualities. Let us therefore chant and remember the glories of Lord Krsna and His expansions.

Srila Sridhara Svami explains that chanting and remembering the Lord’s name and glories cause one to develop devotion for the Lord, and Srila Jiva Gosvami states that while working for Krsna’s pleasure, devotees naturally chant His name and remember Him due to their affection for Him.

Narada Muni continues: Those who actually know the Lord worship Him and associate with Him through His transcendental sound form (mantra-murtim). By following this system, Narada was gradually awarded the confidential knowledge of the Lord that is taught in the Vedas. Then he received spiritual opulence (including all eight mystic powers) and ultimately the Lord’s intimate loving service.

Speaking from practical experience about the best spiritual process, Narada requests Vyasa: “Please, therefore, describe the almighty Lord’s activities which you have learned by your vast knowledge of the Vedas, for that will satisfy the hankerings of great learned men and at the same time mitigate the miseries of the masses of common people who are always suffering from material pangs. Indeed, there is no other way to get out of such miseries.” (Bhag. [1.5.40](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.40)) Srila Prabhupada’s final words in this chapter point out the universality of the Bhagavatam’s message: “Sri Naradaji advised Vyasadeva to describe the glories of the Lord just to do good to all . . . classes of men, both good and bad. Srimad-Bhagavatam is therefore not meant for any particular class of men or sect. It is for the sincere soul who actually wants his own welfare and peace of mind.”

## Chapter 6 - Conversation Between Narada and Vyasadeva

## Texts 1-19: Vyasadeva Inquires into Narada’s Life, and Narada Speaks of the Lord’s Appearance Before Him

Vyasadeva was eager to hear more about Narada’s life because he wanted to follow Narada’s example and attain perfection himself. He asks: What did you do after the great sages departed? How did you pass your life after initiation? How did you quit your body and attain your present form as the great sage Narada? How are you now able to remember your previous life, for the events of that life occurred during another day of Brahma?

Narada replies: When the great sages left, I wanted to accompany them, but because my mother had no one else to care for her I was bound by her affection. Then one night when I was only five years old, my poor mother went out to milk a cow and was bitten on the leg by a serpent. “I took this as the special mercy of the Lord, who always desires benediction for His devotees, and so thinking, I started for the north.” (Bhag. [1.6.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.10))

Narada Muni had wished to leave home after hearing the bhakti' vedantas’ instructive words, but he awaited Krsna’s arrangement. He was a responsible young boy, bound by both his duty to his mother and her dependence on him. Then disaster struck for this five-year-old: his mother died suddenly. But Narada was so spiritually advanced that he understood his misfortune as a sign of Krsna’s mercy. Srila Prabhupada’s short purports to texts 9 and 10 show how to view calamity as God’s grace: “That is the way of dragging a sincere soul nearer to God. The poor boy was being looked after only by his affectionate mother, and yet the mother was taken from the world by the supreme will in order to put him completely at the mercy of the Lord.” And: “Confidential devotees of the Lord see in every step a benedictory direction of the Lord. What is considered to be an odd or difficult moment in the mundane sense is accepted as special mercy of the Lord. Mundane prosperity is a kind of material fever, and by the grace of the Lord the temperature of this material fever is gradually diminished, and spiritual health is obtained step by step. Mundane people misunderstand it.” (Bhag. [1.6.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.9), [10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.10), purports respectively)

Young, alone, and walking unknown lands, Narada wandered through cities, towns, villages, farms, mines, agricultural fields, valleys, hills, gardens, lakes, rivers, and dangerous jungles. Thus he experienced good and bad, fortune and disaster. Such wandering without external shelter increases one’s dependence on Krsna because it tests and strengthens one’s faith. One begins to realize fearlessness. True dependence on Krsna is a great challenge, and one necessarily faces this challenge when he travels as a dependent sannyasi. Srila Prabhupada’s purport to text 13 explains the value of a sannyasis traveling: “It is the duty of a mendicant (parivrajakacarya) to experience all varieties of God’s creation by traveling alone through all forests, hills, towns, villages, etc., to gain faith in God and strength of mind as well as to enlighten the inhabitants with the message of God. A sannyasi is duty-bound to take all these risks without fear, and the most typical sannydsi of the present age is Lord Caitanya, who traveled in the same manner through the central Indian jungles, enlightening even the tigers, bears, snakes, deer, elephants and many other jungle animals. In this age of Kali, sannyasa is forbidden for ordinary men. ... In this age, devotional service of hearing and repeating the holy glories of the Lord is strongly recommended, and one who takes the vow of renunciation of family life need not imitate the parivrajakacarya like Narada or Lord Caitanya, but may sit down at some holy place and devote his whole time and energy to hear and repeatedly chant the holy scriptures left by the great acaryas like the six Gosvamis of Vrndavana.”

Once, while traveling, Narada felt physically and mentally exhausted. Hungry and thirsty, he bathed in a lake formed by a river and drank some of its water to relieve his fatigue. Then in the uninhabited forest on the river’s bank, Narada sat in the shade of a pippala tree and meditated on the Supersoul in his heart. As soon as he focused on the Lord’s lotus feet, Narada’s mind transformed and he experienced transcendental love. Tears of ecstasy rolled down his cheeks as Sri Krsna appeared on the lotus of his heart.

Narada offers us a glimpse of his ecstatic experience: “At that time, being exceedingly overpowered by feelings of happiness, every part of my body became separately enlivened. Being absorbed in an ocean of ecstasy, I could not see both myself and the Lord.” (Bhag.[1.6.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.17)) Seeing the Lord’s form fully satisfied Narada. As each of his senses focused on the Lord in the heart, each sense seemed to become fully awake. In his full absorption he was unable to experience the Lord as separate from himself.

Then suddenly the Lord disappeared. Narada now became perturbed. Shocked almost to madness he leapt up in an attempt to again view the Lord. As Prabhupada states in his purport to text 18: “What we desire life after life was obtained by Narada Muni, and losing sight of Him again was certainly a great shock for him.” With great eagerness Narada again tried to meditate on the Lord in his heart, but despite his efforts, Narada tells Vyasa, “I could not see Him any more, and thus dissatisfied, I was very much aggrieved.” (Bhag. [1.6.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.19))

The Lord is independent. He awards a devotee the ability to see Him when He chooses. In his purport to text 19 Srila Prabhupada describes the Lord’s independence: “There is no mechanical process to see the form of the Lord. It completely depends on the causeless mercy of the Lord. We cannot demand the Lord to be present before our vision, just as we cannot demand the sun to rise whenever we like. The sun rises out of his own accord; so also the Lord is pleased to be present out of His causeless mercy. One should simply await the opportune moment and go on discharging his prescribed duty in devotional service of the Lord. . . . When He pleases, being satisfied with the sincere attempt of devotional service depending completely on the mercy of the Lord, then He may be seen out of His own accord.”

## Texts 20-27: The Lord Instructs Narada, and Narada Follows These Instructions Until his Death

Narada’s glimpse of the Lord inflamed his Krsna consciousness. Narada further describes: “Seeing my attempts in that lonely place, the Personality of Godhead, who is transcendental to all mundane description, spoke to me with gravity and pleasing words, just to mitigate my grief. ‘O Narada, I regret that during this lifetime you will not be able to see Me anymore. Those who are incomplete in service and who are not completely free from all material taints can hardly see Me.”’ (Bhag. [1.6.20-21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.20))

This is shocking. Narada was already so pure! What material dirt could be covering his heart? Srila Prabhupada hints that Narada was still covered by goodness, the “balanced mode of nature,” and then points to the cure: “To search the audience of God in a lonely forest is considered to be in the mode of goodness. One can go out into the forest to attain spiritual perfection, but that does not mean that one can see the Lord personally there. One must be completely freed from all material attachment and be situated on the plane of transcendence, which alone will help the devotee get in personal touch with the Personality of Godhead.... In his present life, which is completely freed from all material hankerings, Sri Narada Muni does not go into the forest, although he can turn every place into Vaikuntha by his presence only. He travels from one planet to another to convert men, gods, Kinnaras, Gandharvas, rsis, munis and all others to become devotees of the Lord. ... A pure devotee of the Lord, therefore, follows in the footsteps of the great devotees like Narada and Prahlada and engages his whole time in glorifying the Lord by the process of kirtana. Such a preaching process is transcendental to all material qualities.” (Bhag. [1.6.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.21), purport)

Krsna tells Narada: “O virtuous one, you have only once seen My person, and this is just to increase your desire for Me, because the more you hanker for Me, the more you will be freed from all material desires.” (Bhag. [1.6.22](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.22))

“The more a person is engaged in the transcendental loving service of the Lord,” Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to text 22, “the more he acquires a hankering for it. That is the transcendental nature of godly service. Material service has satiation, whereas spiritual service of the Lord has neither satiation nor end. One can go on increasing his hankering for the loving transcendental service of the Lord, and yet he will not find satiation or end. By intense service of the Lord, one can experience the presence of the Lord transcendentally. Therefore seeing the Lord means being engaged in His service because His service and His person are identical.”

Krsna states: “By service of the Absolute Truth, even for a few days, a devotee attains firm and fixed intelligence in Me. Consequently he goes on to become My associate in the transcendental world after giving up the present deplorable material worlds.” (Bhag. [1.6.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.23)) Even after the annihilation of the universe, by the Lord’s mercy Narada’s remembrance of the Lord would remain forever unchecked. By serving Him in increasingly full remembrance of Him, Narada’s devotional service would reach full maturity, allowing him to enter the Lord’s association.

When the unseen Lord stopped speaking, Narada bowed his head in gratitude. Now aware that he could associate with the Lord through constant devotional service, Narada continuously chanted the Lord’s holy name. “Thus I began chanting the holy name and fame of the Lord by repeated recitation, ignoring all the formalities of the material world. Such chanting and remembering of the transcendental pastimes of the Lord are benedictory. So doing, I traveled all over the earth, fully satisfied, humble and unenvious.” (Bhag. [1.6.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.26)) Narada, Srila Jiva Gosvami states, being satisfied (tustamanah), without any other desires (sprha-antara-sunyah), without pride (vimadah), and without envy (vimatsarah), only awaited the time (kalam) when the Lord would award him His mercy. Srila Prabhupada classifies such a life as “sincere,” a life one should emulate:

**The life of a sincere devotee of the Lord is thus explained in a nutshell by Narada Muni by his personal example. Such a devotee, after his initiation by the Lord or His bona fide representative, takes very seriously chanting of the glories of the Lord and traveling all over the world so that others may also hear the glories of the Lord. Such devotees have no desire for material gain. They are conducted by one single desire: to go back to Godhead. This awaits them in due course on quitting the material body. Because they have the highest aim of life, going back to Godhead, they are never envious of anyone, nor are they proud of being eligible to go back to Godhead. Their only business is to chant and remember the holy name, fame and pastimes of the Lord and, according to personal capacity, to distribute the message for others’ welfare without motive of material gain. (Bhag.** [**1.6.26**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.26)**, purport)**

Narada continues: “And so ... in due course of time I, who was fully absorbed in thinking of Krsna and who therefore had no attachments, being completely freed from all material taints, met with death, as lightning and illumination occur simultaneously.” (Bhag. [1.6.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.27))    Srila Sridhara Svami writes that death, at his leisure, suddenly appeared before Narada. Prabhupada describes an exalted devotee’s death in his purport: “\[I\]n due course of time, when a pure devotee is completely prepared, all of a sudden the change of body occurs which is commonly called death. And for the pure devotee such a change takes place exactly like lightning, and illumination follows simultaneously. That is to say a devotee simultaneously changes his material body and develops a spiritual body by the will of the Supreme.”

## Texts 28—38: Narada’s Full Perfection

In his transcendental body—free from the afflictions of karma and the modes of nature, and surcharged by eternity, bliss, and knowledge—Narada eventually entered Lord Narayana’s body through His breathing when the Lord lay down at the end of the millennium. When Brahma awoke by the Lord’s will after millions of years, Narada and the other sages were created from the Lord’s transcendental body. Since then, Narada explains, by the Lord’s causeless and unparalleled grace he has been traveling without restriction through both matter and spirit, remaining fixed in the Lord’s devotional service, “constantly singing the transcendental message of the glories of the Lord, vibrating this instrument called a vtna, which is charged with transcendental sound and which was given to me by Lord Krsna.” As he sings, the “Supreme Lord Sri Krsna, whose glories and activities are pleasing to hear, at once appears on the seat of my heart, as if called for, as soon as I begin to chant His holy activities.” (Bhag. [1.6.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.32), [33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.33))

Concluding his instructions to Vyasadeva on the literature Vyasa should now write, Narada reiterates his personal realization: “It is personally experienced by me that those who are always full of cares and anxieties due to desiring contact of the senses with their objects can cross the ocean of nescience on a most suitable boat—the constant chanting of the transcendental activities of the Personality of Godhead.” (Bhag. [1.6.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.34))

In his purport to this text Prabhupada offers guidance on how one can activate this principle in his life. He explains that no one can remain silent, and that one needs objects on which to base one’s thought and speech. Generally, however, materialistic persons choose objects in maya’s realm. Such objects cannot offer ultimate satisfaction. “So Narada Muni, by his personal experience, says that satisfaction for such frustrated beings engaged in sense gratification is to chant always the activities of the Lord. The point is that the subject matter only should be changed. No one can check the thinking activities of a living being, nor the feeling, willing or working processes. But if one wants actual happiness, one must change the subject matter only. . . . The almighty Personality of Godhead, by His causeless mercy, descends on the earth and manifests activities almost on the line of the worldly men, but at the same time extraordinarily, because He is almighty. He does so for the benefit of all conditioned souls so that they can turn their attention to transcendence. By doing so, the conditioned soul will gradually be promoted to the transcendental position and easily cross the ocean of nescience, the source of all miseries. This is stated from personal experience by such an authority as Sri Narada Muni. And we can have the same experience also if we begin to follow in the footsteps of the great sage, the dearmost devotee of the Lord.”

This process, concludes Narada, is superior to all others: Even if one is able to restrain his senses by yoga and thus become relieved from desire and lust, the soul will nevertheless remain dissatisfied, for the soul’s actual satisfaction can blossom only through his devotional service to the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

The narration of Narada’s birth and activities enlightened Vyasa-deva, and he now knew how to remove the dissatisfaction from his heart. Seeing this, Narada, vibrating his vina, departed. In his commentary on text 35, Srila Sridhara Svami writes that a little service to Krsna pacifies the soul. What can be said of the effect of describing His glories?

Srila Prabhupada’s purport to text 37 speaks of the freedom devotional service offers: “We can just imagine the extent and unlimitedness of \[Narada’s\] freedom, which is as good as that of the Supreme Lord. There is no reason or obligation for his traveling, and no one can stop him from his free movement. Similarly, the transcendental system of devotional service is also free. It may or may not develop in a particular person even after he undergoes all the detailed formulas. Similarly, the association of the devotee is also free. One may be fortunate to have it, or one may not have it even after thousands of endeavors. Therefore, in all spheres of devotional service, freedom is the main pivot. Without freedom there is no execution of devotional service. The freedom surrendered to the Lord does not mean that the devotee becomes dependent in every respect. To surrender unto the Lord through the transparent medium of the spiritual master is to attain complete freedom of life.”

Suta Gosvami completes his discussion about Narada Muni’s conversation with Vyasadeva by praising Narada before the sages at Naimisaranya: “All glory and success to Srila Narada Muni because he glorifies the activities of the Personality of Godhead, and so doing he himself takes pleasure and also enlivens all the distressed souls of the universe.” (Bhag. [1.6.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/6.38)) Srila Sridhara Svami comments that one owes praise to the fortunate person who chants the Supreme Lord’s glories.

## Chapter 7 - The Son of Drona Punished

## Texts 1-7: Srila Vyasadeva’s Meditation and Samadhi

Saunaka Rsi now inquires about Srila Vyasadeva’s activities after Narada’s departure. Suta Gosvami’s reply describes Vyasadeva’s asrama on the western bank of the Sarasvati River. There, surrounded by badari trees, Vyasa performed acamana, then concentrated his mind as his spiritual master had directed. What meditation technique did Vyasadeva use? “\[H\]e fixed his mind, perfectly engaging it by linking it in devotional service \[bhakti-yoga\] without any tinge of materialism, and thus he saw the Absolute Personality of Godhead along with His external energy, which was under full control.” (Bhag. [1.7.4](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.4))

Vyasadeva thus perfectly realized the Absolute Truth. He saw the Lord (who was clearly a person \[purusam рйгпат\] and not impersonal); His energies, including His internal, external, and marginal energies; and His incarnations. These realizations manifest through Vyasa’s meditation, executed with loving devotion and a pure heart, free from “any tinge of materialism.” Thus Vyasadeva saw that the Absolute Truth, as Srila Prabhupada’s purport to text 4 explains, can be fully realized only through bhakti-yoga. In addition, that Vyasadeva saw the Lord “along with His external energy, which was under full control,” shows that the Lord Himself can never fall under the control of illusion as the Mayavadis claim. That the Lord’s maya-sakti is subordinate and inferior to the Lord—and can therefore never control Him—will be confirmed in Bhagavatam [2.7.47](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/7.47), where it is stated, mayaparaity abhimukhe ca vilaj-jamdna: maya, “the Lord’s illusory energy, flees from His presence due to shame.” In his purport to Bhagavatam [1.7.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.5), Srila Prabhupada emphasizes maya’s inferiority: “It is clear, however, from the present statement of Bhagavatam that the same external energy is situated in the inferior position before the Personality of Godhead, or the perfect being. The perfect being, or the Lord, cannot be approached even by the illusory energy, who can only work on the living entities. Therefore it is sheer imagination that the Supreme Lord is illusioned by the illusory energy and thus becomes a living being.”

Although the Lord’s external energy is under His control and therefore unable to bewilder Him, it can fully bewilder an insignificant part and parcel of the Lord, the jiva, as Vyasadeva next envisions and Suta Gosvami explains. “Due to this external energy, the livingentity, although transcendental to the three modes of material nature, thinks of himself as a material product and thus undergoes the reactions of material miseries.” (Bhag. [1.7.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.5))

Vyasadeva’s realizations continue, and he sees the world as it has been created by the Lord’s mayd'Sakti, His external, illusory energy. The words yaya sammohitah indicate that it is the external energy and not the Lord that deludes and imprisons the living entity. Thus the living entity, who is constitutionally eternal and transcendental, suffers from the delusion of thinking himself material. Srila Prabhupada explains why the Lord allows His external energy (which is fully under His control) to bewilder His parts and parcels. Prabhupada also points out the path of freedom:

**The present conditional state is due to the influence of the external energy, which means that the illusory energy takes the initiative while the Supreme Lord is aloof. The Lord does not desire that a living being be illusioned by external energy. The external energy is aware of this fact, but still she accepts a thankless task of keeping the forgotten soul under illusion by her bewildering influence. The Lord does not interfere with the task of the illusory energy because such performances of the illusory energy are also necessary for reformation of the conditioned soul. An affectionate father does not like his children to be chastised by another agent, yet he puts his disobedient children under the custody of a severe man just to bring them to order. But the all-affectionate Almighty Father at the same time desires relief for the conditioned soul, relief from the clutches of the illusory energy. The king puts the disobedient citizens within the walls of the jail, but sometimes the king, desiring the prisoners’ relief, personally goes there and pleads for reformation, and on his doing so the prisoners are set free. Similarly, the Supreme Lord descends from His kingdom upon the kingdom of illusory energy and personally gives relief in the form of the Bhagavad-gita, wherein He personally suggests that although the ways of illusory energy are very stiff to overcome, one who surrenders unto the lotus feet of the Lord is set free by the order of the Supreme. This surrendering process is the remedial measure for getting relief from the bewildering ways of the illusory energy. The surrendering process is completed by the influence of association. The Lord has suggested, therefore, that by the influence of the speeches of saintly persons who have actually realized the Supreme, men are engaged in His transcendental loving service. The conditioned soul gets a taste for hearing about the Lord, and by such hearing only he is gradually elevated to the platform of respect, devotion and attachment for the Lord. The whole thing is completed by the surrendering process. (Bhag.** [**1.7.5**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.5)**, purport)**

How can our illusory identification with matter be removed? How will Vyasa be able to help free the suffering jivas from maya’s control and thus from misery? “The material miseries of the living entity, which are superfluous to him, can be directly mitigated by the linking process of devotional service. But the mass of people do not know this, and therefore the learned Vyasadeva compiled this Vedic literature, which is in relation to the Supreme Truth.” (Bhag. [1.7.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.6))

Srila Prabhupada’s purport summarizes Vyasadeva’s revelation. It also includes a description of the living entities’ predicament as well as the means of their deliverance: “\[Vyasadeva\] specifically observed the unwanted miseries of the conditioned souls, who are bewildered by the external energy. And at last he saw the remedial measure for the conditioned souls, namely, the process of devotional service. It is a great transcendental science and begins with the process of hearing and chanting the name, fame, glory, etc., of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”

Although Srila Prabhupada emphasizes hearing and chanting, he nevertheless makes clear the essence of the process: “Revival of the dormant affection or love of Godhead does not depend on the mechanical system of hearing and chanting, but it solely and wholly depends on the causeless mercy of the Lord. When the Lord is fully satisfied with the sincere efforts of the devotee, He may endow him with His loving transcendental service. But even with the prescribed forms of hearing and chanting, there is at once mitigation of the superfluous and unwanted miseries of material existence.”

What will result if we hear the Bhagavatam Vyasadeva will write?

“Simply by giving aural reception to this Vedic literature, the feeling for loving devotional service to Lord Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, sprouts up at once to extinguish the fire of lamentation, illusion and fearfulness.” (Bhag. [1.7.7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.7))

Commenting on this text, Srila Sridhara Svami states that not only does hearing the Bhagavatam destroy inauspiciousness, “it generates devotion to Lord Krsna.” When we hear about the Bhagavatam’s potency we understand why Srila Prabhupada so much emphasized its translation, publication, distribution, and reading in the lives of his disciples. His purport to text 7 adds emphasis to the point about the importance of hearing: “Simply by hearing the message of Srimad-Bhagavatam one gets attachment for the Supreme Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna, and as soon as this is effected the symptoms of the material diseases disappear. . . . Loving devotional service to the Lord begins with hearing about the Lord. There is no difference between the Lord and the subject matter heard about Him. The Lord is absolute in all respects, and thus there is no difference between Him and the subject matter heard about Him. Therefore, hearing about Him means immediate contact with Him by the process of vibration of the transcendental sound. And the transcendental sound is so effective that it acts at once by removing all material affections mentioned above. . . . The conclusion is that simply by hearing the Vedic literature Srimad-Bhagavatam, one can have direct connection with the Supreme Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna, and thereby one can attain the highest perfection of life by transcending worldly miseries, illusion and fearfulness. These are practical tests for one who has actually given a submissive hearing to the readings of the Srimad-Bhagavatam.”

## Texts 8—11: Vyasa Teaches the Bhagavatam to his Son, Sukadeva

After compiling the Vedas and summarizing their conclusions in the Vedanta-sutra, Srila Vyasadeva experienced his revelation about the Absolute Truth and then wrote and revised the Bhagavatam. He then taught the Bhagavatam to Sukadeva Gosvami, who was an extraordinary personality. Srila Prabhupada describes Sukadeva’s birth in his purport to Srimad-Bhagavatam [9.21.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/21.25):

**Sukadeva Gosvami, the son of Vyasadeva, is described in great detail in the Brahma'vaivarta Purana. There it is said that Vyasadeva maintained the daughter of Jabali as his wife and that after they performed penances together for many years, he placed his seed in her womb. The child remained in the womb of his mother for twelve years, and when the father asked the son to come out, the son replied that he would not come out unless he were completely liberated from the influence of maya. Vyasadeva then assured the child that he would not be influenced by maya, but the child did not believe his father, for the father was still attached to his wife and children. Vyasadeva then went to Dvaraka and informed the Personality of Godhead about his problem, and the Personality of Godhead, at Vyasadeva’s request, went to Vyasadeva’s cottage, where He assured the child in the womb that he would not be influenced by maya. Thus assured, the child came out, but he immediately went away as a parivrajakacarya. When the father, very much aggrieved, began to follow his saintly boy, Sukadeva Gosvami, the boy created a duplicate Sukadeva, who later entered family life. Therefore, the suka'kanyd, or daughter of Sukadeva, mentioned in this verse \[Bhag.** [**9.21.25**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-9/21.25)**\] is the daughter of the duplicate or imitation Sukadeva. The original Sukadeva was a lifelong brahmacari.**

Saunaka Rsi was surprised to hear that Sukadeva, who was already self-satisfied and fixed in the Absolute had nevertheless studied Bhagavatam. “So why did he take the trouble to undergo the study of such a vast literature?” (Bhag. [1.7.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.9)) Indeed, although Vyasadeva had wanted his son to hear the Bhagavatam, Sukadeva left home immediately after birth without performing any purificatory or reformatory ceremonies. “\[H\]is father, Vyasadeva, fearing separation from him, cried out, ‘O my son!’ Indeed, only the trees, which were absorbed in the same feelings of separation, echoed in response to the begrieved father.” (Bhag. [1.2.2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.2))

Later, as described in the Devi Bhagavata, Vyasadeva sent Sukadeva two exquisite Bhagavatam verses (Bhag. [3.2.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/2.23) and Bhag. [10.21.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/21.5)) through messengers. These verses respectively describe Krsna’s compassion and beauty, and they so captivated Sukadeva’s mind that he returned home, enticed by a desire to hear the Bhagavatam his father had composed.

Suta’s explanation of why the already self-realized Sukadeva studied the Srimad-Bhagavatam forms the famous atmarama-sloka ([1.7.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.10)): “All different varieties of atmaramas \[those who take pleasure in atma, or spirit self\], especially those established on the path of selfrealization, though freed from all kinds of material bondage, desire to render unalloyed devotional service unto the Personality of Godhead. This means that the Lord possesses transcendental qualities and therefore can attract everyone, including liberated souls.” Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu presented eighteen meanings of this text to Sarvabhauma Bhattacarya, Jagannatha Puri’s great scholar (Cc. Madhya-lila, Chapter Six). After hearing Mahaprabhu’s explanations, Sarvabhauma was struck with wonder and understood that Mahaprabhu was the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Later, Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu spoke extensive additional meanings of the text to Sanatana Gosvami (Cc. Madhya-lila, Chapter Twenty-four). But the essence of the verse is that even those who are already self-satisfied, having realized themselves as souls and been situated in the etemality of their existence, become attracted to Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, because the Lord’s fully spiritual form, qualities, and pastimes are all-attractive.

Srila Prabhupada summarizes Sukadeva’s attraction for the Bhagavatam—and Krsna—as follows: “By His personal features and transcendental attributes, the Lord attracts fill psychological activities of a pure devotee. Such is the attractive power of Lord Krsna. The attraction is so powerful that a pure devotee never hankers for any one of the four principles of religion. These are the attractive features of the transcendental attributes of the Lord.... So by interpreting each and every word of this sloka, one can see unlimited numbers of transcendental qualities of Lord Krsna that attract the mind of a pure devotee.” (Bhag. [1.7.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.10), purport)

Sukadeva, who was transcendentally powerful, became dear to the devotees after he became a Vaisnava. This great soul heard Srimad-Bhagavatam from its author, his father, and later spoke it to Maharaja Pariksit. Srila Sridhara Svami comments (on text 11): Let Sukadeva become a devotee! What was the necessity for him to learn the vast scripture? He did so because He was attracted to hari-katha. Thus after his study of the Bhagavatam, Suka became visnujarui'priya, beloved of the devotees of the Lord.

It is interesting to note Srila Prabhupada’s statement that Vyasadeva “impressed” on Sukadeva only a “synopsis of the Bhagavatam so that the child could be made attached to the transcendental activities of the Lord.” Prabhupada continues speaking about the source of Sukadeva’s continued Bhagavatam education: “After his birth, the child was still more educated in the subject of the Bhagavatam by recitation of the actual poems.”

Although Sukadeva was already a realized impersonalist, he followed a progression to becoming a Vaisnava. Prabhupada describes his elevation to devotional service. By the “mercy of Vyasadeva, Srila Sukadeva Gosvami was able to grasp the \[Bhagavatam’s\] import. The transcendental qualities of the Lord are so attractive that Srila Sukadeva Gosvami became detached from being completely absorbed in impersonal Brahman and positively took up the personal activity of the Lord.” (Bhag. [1.7.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.11), purport)

By text 11, Srila Suta Gosvami has completed his response to Saunaka Rsi’s first questions, asked at the beginning of the First Canto’s fourth chapter: Why did the great sage Vyasadeva, who had already compiled a vast amount of Vedic literature, become inspired to compile yet another huge work? And why did Sukadeva, who was already transcendental—liberated from bodily identification—desire to study the Bhagavatam?

## Dialogue Five - Krsna and His Devotees

## Chapter 7 (Continued) - The Son of Drona Punished

## Texts 12—40: Arjuna Captures Asvatthama

In text 9 of Chapter Four, Saunaka Rsi inquired from Suta Gosvami about Maharaja Pariksit’s birth and life because that story would lead to the retelling of how the Bhagavatam came to be spoken. Suta Gosvami’s words are always vaksye krsna-kathodayam—words that give rise to speaking krsna-katha (Bhag. [1.7.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.12)). Suta begins his story at the point of disaster, just after the Battle of Kuruksetra.

Krsna shows His kindness by displaying His pastimes, the most attractive of which are in Sri Vrndavana-dhama. Prabhupada offers the process by which we attain the purity and maturity to enter the spirit of those activities, which are recited in the Tenth Canto, in his purport to text 12: “Srimad-Bhagavatam is thus recommended by Lord Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu as the spotless Purana. There is a class of less intelligent devotees of the Bhagavata Purana who desire to relish at once the activities of the Lord narrated in the Tenth Canto without first understanding the primary cantos. They are under the false impression that the other cantos are not concerned with Krsna, and thus more foolishly than intelligently they take to the reading of the Tenth Canto. These readers are specifically told herein that the other cantos of the Bhagavatam are as important as the Tenth Canto. No one should try to go into the matters of the Tenth Canto without having thoroughly understood the purport of the other nine cantos.”

For the first time in this narration of the Bhagavatam we will see Krsna in action. We have heard His glories spoken since the first verse, where He was defined as satyam param, the Absolute Truth. We have also heard about the potency of performing devotional service: we immediately acquire causeless knowledge and material detachment (Bhag. [1.2.7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.7)). And we have heard that He is supremely attractive: even atmaramas become attracted to hearing of Him (Bhag. [1.7.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.10)). Now Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the all-attractive Absolute Truth, will be introduced personally. How does He make His first appearance? He is serving His devotee, Arjuna, as His chariot driver. This next section of the Bhagavatam (Canto One, Chapters Seven through Eleven) will offer us an intimate glimpse of Krsna interacting with His dear devotees—the most intimate glimpse we will have before the Tenth Canto pastimes.

From the thirteenth verse on, Chapter Seven offers a brief background of the bloody conclusion of the Kuruksetra war. Asvatthama, an opponent of the Pandavas during the battle and the son of Dronacarya, their martial teacher, has just murdered their five young sons in their sleep. Draupadi is grief-stricken. To pacify her, Arjuna, the great hero of the battle, vows revenge, promising to deliver to her Asvatthama’s head to her. Arjuna then arms himself and mounts his chariot in pursuit of Asvatthama. Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, takes the reins.

Arjuna is furious, and this terrifies Asvatthama. As Asvatthama flees, he notes that his horses are becoming fatigued and he begins to despair for his life. He concludes that he has no choice but to slay Arjuna if he does not wish to be slain by him, so he unleashes his ultimate weapon, the infallible brahmastra. In doing so, Asvatthama breaks the rules of combat; he should not have released a weapon he could not withdraw.

In his pursuit, Arjuna perceives a fierce glare spreading toward him from all directions. Realizing that his life is in danger, he calls to his chariot driver, Lord Krsna:

*krsna krsna maha-baho bhaktanam abhayankara*

**О my Lord Sri Krsna, You are the almighty Personality of Godhead. There is no limit to Your different energies. Therefore only You are competent to instill fearlessness in the hearts of Your devotees. (Bhag.** [**1.7.22**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.22)**)**

Fear and its accompanying need to defend are the core principles governing the material world. Every living entity is afraid; everyone lacks security. Why is it that only Krsna can instill fearlessness? Arjuna continues:

*tvam adyah purusah saksad*  
*isvarah prakrteh parah*  
*mayam vyudasya cic-chaktya*  
*kaivalya sthita-atmani*

**You are the original Personality of Godhead who expands Himself all over the creations and is transcendental to material energy. You have cast away the effects of the material energy by dint of Your spiritual potency. You are always situated in eternal bliss and transcendental knowledge. (Bhag.** [**1.7.23**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.23)**)**

Krsna is more powerful than illusion. He is the ultimate cause of all and resides eternally and fully in the spiritual realm, Goloka Vrndavana. His descent to the material world is not actually a descent, for as Arjuna explains in text 23, Krsna is forever spiritually situated in pure knowledge and bliss (kaivalye), having thrown aside (vyudasya.) the material energy (mayam) by dint of His internal potency (cit-sakti). Arjuna’s fear is the fear suffered by the everyman caught in illusion’s grip; all of us are continuously threatened by the fire of suffering. His words point to the cooling shelter of Krsna’s protection: “. . . You descend as an incarnation to remove the burden of the world and to benefit Your friends, especially those who are Your exclusive devotees and are rapt in meditation upon You.” (Bhag. [1.7.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.25))

In his comment on this text, Srila Sridhara Svami, speaking in the first person on the Lord’s behalf, states, “Isn’t it that removing the burden of the earth happens just by My wish?” He thus notes that Lord Krsna does not need to personally appear in this world to remove the earth’s burden, for He can do that simply by wishing it to be done. The actual reason for the Lord’s appearance is given in this verse: “You descend to benefit Your friends, especially those who are Your exclusive devotees and are rapt in meditation upon You.”

Srila Jiva Gosvami (Bhagavat-sandarbha, anuccheda 47) comments on this verse as follows: О Lord, just as You have formerly appeared as the purusa-avatdras and other incarnations, You have now appeared (tathdyam avatarah) in Your original form as Sri Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. You have appeared to remove the burden of the earth planet (bhuvo bhara-jihirsayd), who is Your great devotee, and to enable Your devotees to constantly relish the happiness of worshiping and meditating on You (anudhyanaya).

Jiva Gosvami then poses a question: Krsna must take birth in the material world to give happiness to His devotees; He cannot avoid coming. Does this conflict with His independence? Jiva Gosvami replies that it does not. Krsna is not forced to do anything; He is free and independent, a fact described in the Narayana'Samhitd: “The independent Personality of Godhead is foil of all transcendental bliss. How is it possible to say that He needs anything or is forced to do anything? It is not possible.”

Jiva Gosvami continues: As for His appearing in this world to give happiness to the pure devotees (ananya-bhdvdndm), that does not detract from His independence. He comes because He is merciful to His devotees. He is free from all faults, and because lack of mercy is a fault, He is also free from all mercilessness. Free from that fault, He is very merciful to His pure devotees, and He voluntarily appears before them to give them transcendental happiness. One may say that His supreme independence and His mercy contradict one another and that His mercy detracts somewhat from His independence. Actually He is both independent and merciful. Both qualities exist in the Lord even though they may sometimes contradict one another. The Kurma Purana explains the mutually contradictory qualities of the Lord by simply stating that the Supreme Personality of Godhead possesses such mutually contradictory qualities.

Asvatthama’s brahmastra is approaching. Fearing its power, Arjuna has urgently sought the shelter of his friend Krsna. Arjuna faces an impossible situation because the brahmastra is unstoppable and never fails to find its target. Krsna replies immediately, and it is interesting to note that the first words He speaks in the Bhagavatam are not philosophical but practical instructions to save His friend and devotee from destruction.

“O Arjuna, only another brahmastra can counteract this weapon. Since you are expert in the military science, subdue this weapon’s glare with the power of your own weapon.” (Bhag. [1.7.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.28)) Arjuna follows Krsna’s advice without hesitation and unleashes his own brahmastra. When the rays of the two brahmastras combine and form a great circle of fire, Arjuna expertly retracts both weapons.

But now Arjuna is even angrier, and his eyes blaze like coppery balls of fire. He subdues Asvatthama and binds him with ropes like an animal. Krsna looks on with His lotus eyes and demands that Arjuna not show him mercy, “for he has killed innocent boys in their sleep.” (Bhag. [1.7.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.35)) He has acted irreligiously and should be killed for his own well-being. Otherwise, how will he escape the horrendous reactions due him for his heinous deed? You have soothed Draupadi’s grief by vowing to bring her this killer’s head. “Kill him immediately.”

This is how Krsna’s prodding examined Arjuna’s understanding of duty and religion. Arjuna, however, wants to spare Asvatthama. Although he knows that Asvatthama is both degraded and unworthy, he is his teacher’s son. Srila Prabhupada discusses Krsna’s examination of Arjuna in his purport to text 40: “Lord Sri Krsna encouraged Arjuna outwardly just to test Arjuna’s sense of duty. It is not that Arjuna was incomplete in the sense of his duty, nor was Lord Sri Krsna unaware of Arjuna’s sense of duty. But Lord Sri Krsna put to test many of His pure devotees just to magnify the sense of duty. The gopis were put to such tests as well. Prahlada Maharaja also was put to such a test. All pure devotees come out successful in the respective tests by the Lord.”

Arjuna does not act immediately but returns to the Pandavas’ camp with Asvatthama captured and bound.

## Texts 41-58: The Punishment of Asvatthama

At the camp, Draupadi is suddenly presented not with Asvatthama’s head but with Asvatthama himself, bound and silent. Despite his heinous actions, however, she listens to her own tender heart; instead of crying for his head, she offers him respect, asking Arjuna to release him: You learned the military sciences by his father’s mercy. Is it proper to cause his respected mother to cry for his death as I now cry for the death of my sons? Let us not offend and enrage the families of the spiritually advanced and bring further grief on ourselves.

Yudhisthira supported Draupadi’s merciful words. “Nakula and Sahadeva and also Satyaki, Arjuna, the Personality of Godhead Lord Sri Krsna, son of Devaki, and the ladies and others all unanimously agreed with the King.” (Bhag. [1.7.50](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.50)) Bhima, however, did not. He cried: Kill this culprit who has murdered sleeping children!

As Bhima rushed forward to kill Asvatthama, however, Draupadi obstructed him. To keep them apart, Krsna displayed four arms. Smiling, He instructed Arjuna with these equivocal words: “A friend of a brahmana is not to be killed, but if he is an aggressor he must be killed. All these rulings are in the scriptures, and you should act accordingly. You have to fulfill your promise to your wife, and you must also act to the satisfaction of Bhimasena and Me.” (Bhag. [1.7.53-54](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.53))

Arjuna understood Krsna’s intention; he took his sword and cut off both Asvatthama’s hair and the jewel adorning his topknot. Although it is usually impossible to carry out contradictory orders, by Krsna’s mercy Arjuna understood what action to take to reconcile the situation: insulting Asvatthama by cutting off his hair and jewel humiliated him and was thus a kind of death. At the same time, it spared his life. His jewel and pride gone, and because of his heinous actions, Asvatthama lost his bodily luster and strength, and the Pandavas drove him from their camp.

Countless family members and friends then began their lament for the millions killed in the fratricidal war. The Pandavas, overwhelmed with grief, performed the funeral rites for their young sons and other relatives who had died during the Battle of Kuruksetra.

## Chapter 8 - Prayers by Queen Kunti And Pariksit Saved

## Texts 1-16: Krsna Again Saves His Devotees

Krsna had saved Arjuna, His devotee and friend, from Asvatthama’s brahmastra. Then He artfully reconciled the Pandavas’ family struggle as they tried to settle Asvatthama’s fate. After the funeral rites had been performed, Krsna and the grieving members of the Kuru dynasty went to bathe in the Yamuna, while the many sages in the entourage attempted to pacify those who were mourning. Thus the Bhagavatam reveals Krsna’s sweet exchanges with His devotees. While reciprocating with Krsna, the devotees reveal their minds to Him through their prayers and we are able to witness this. Their devotional mentalities, expressed through both their lotuslike mouths and their deeds, instruct us on our own journey back to Godhead.

Later, after a suitable time had passed, Krsna inspired Maharaja Yudhisthira to perform three asvamedha-yajhas (horse sacrifices) to increase his fame and piety. Finally, after seeing Yudhisthira installed as emperor of the world, Lord Krsna, Satyaki, and Uddhava prepared to mount their chariots and leave Hastinapura for Krsna’s capital city of Dvaraka. Just as Krsna seated Himself on His chariot, however, Uttara, the young pregnant wife of Arjuna’s son Abhimanyu, ran to Him for shelter. Uttara called out (text 9):

*pahi pahi maha-yogin*  
*deva-deva jagat'pate*  
*nanyam tvad abhayampasye*
