*yatra mrtyhuh parasparam*

**О Lord of lords, Lord of the universe! You are the greatest of mystics. Please protect me, for there is no one else who can save me from the clutches of death in this world of duality.**

Other than Krsna, Srila Sridhara Svami notes in his commentary on text 8, no one is devoid of fear. In her terror, Uttara, Krsna’s devotee, now took shelter of her Lord just as Arjuna had done earlier. Why was she afraid? “O my Lord, You are all-powerful. A fiery iron arrow is coming towards me fast. My Lord, let it burn me personally, if You so desire, but please do not let it burn and abort my embryo. Please do me this favor, my Lord.” (Bhag. [1.8.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.10)) After having been shamed and driven from the Pandava camp, Asvatthama had sought revenge and unleashed two more brahmastras. This time he had targeted the five Pandavas as well as the youngest member of their dynasty, the future Pandava emperor still lying unborn in Uttara’s womb.

Sometimes one wonders how after everything Asvatthama had suffered he still had the power to send brahmastras, but one should note that although he had lost both his power and his effulgence, neither his knowledge nor his memory were affected. Obviously, neither was his hatred for the Pandavas. Ultimately, Asvatthama’s shooting these additional brahmastras, as well as the fact that he was later given the benediction to become one of the seven great sages in the next manvantara, indicate that everything that took place after the Kuruksetra war was Krsna’s pastime. Krsna’s pastimes proceed only according to His desire and simply for His pleasure, and participants in those pastimes are suitably empowered to play their respective roles.

Krsna heard Uttara’s words patiently but immediately understood Asvatthama’s intentions. Srila Sridhara Svami comments on texts 11 and 13 that because of Arjuna’s insult, Asvatthama had retaliated by releasing a brahmastra that would kill every remaining member of the Pandava dynasty. As no weapon can counteract the brahmastra, Krsna, considering the approaching calamity, invoked His Sudarsana cakra to protect His devotees, even as the Pandavas were taking up their weapons. The irresistible power of Krsna’s cakra neutralized the brahmastra.

As Krsna was protecting the five Pandavas, He who is the Supersoul in the heart of everyone simultaneously used His personal energy to cover Uttara’s embryo and shield King Pandu’s unborn descendant. The helpless child was conscious in the womb, and he felt the burning heat of the brahmastra. Then he saw his protector: Someone had come to save him! He observed the Lord as “only thumb high, but He was all transcendental. He had a very beautiful, blackish, infallible body, and He wore a dress of lightning yellow and a helmet of blazing gold. . . . The Lord was enriched with four hands, earrings of molten gold and eyes blood red with fury. As He loitered about, His club constantly encircled Him like a shooting star. The Lord was thus engaged in vanquishing the radiation of the brahmastra, just as the sun evaporates a drop of dew. He was observed by the child, who thought about who He was.” (Bhag. [1.12.8-10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/12.8))

Srila Prabhupada describes the Lord’s presence in Uttara’s womb as follows: “He became visible to His devotee Maharaja Pariksit even in that awkward position (in the womb of his mother) in a shape just suitable for his vision. The Lord can become bigger than thousands of universes and can become smaller than an atom at the same time. Merciful as He is, He becomes just suitable to the vision of the limited living being. He is unlimited. He is not limited by any measurement of our calculation. He can become bigger than what we can think of, and He can become smaller than what we can conceive. But in all circumstances He is the same all-powerful Lord. There is no difference between the thumblike Visnu in the womb of Uttara and the full-fledged Narayana in the Vaikuntha-dhama, the kingdom of Godhead.” (Bhag. [1.12.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/12.9), purport)

Srimad-Bhagavatam [3.3.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/3.17) also speaks of how Krsna protected Maharaja Pariksit: “The embryo of Puru’s descendant begotten by the great hero Abhimanyu in the womb of Uttara, his wife, was burnt by the weapon of the son of Drona, but later he was again protected by the Lord.” Srila Prabhupada comments: “The embryonic body of Pariksit which was in formation after Uttara’s pregnancy by Abhimanyu, the great hero, was burned by the brahmastra of Asvatthama, but a second body was given by the Lord within the womb, and thus the descendant of Puru was saved. This incident is the direct proof that the body and the living entity, the spiritual spark, are different.”

And: “The particular living entity who was selected to be the descendant of Maharaja Puru, or the Pandavas, was not an ordinary living entity, and by the superior will of the Lord he was destined to be the successor to Maharaja Yudhisthira. Therefore, when Asvatthama destroyed the embryo of Maharaja Pariksit, the Lord, by His own internal potency, entered into the womb of Uttara by His plenary portion just to give audience to the would-be Maharaja Pariksit, who was in great danger. By His appearance within the womb, the Lord encouraged the child and gave him complete protection in a new body by His omnipotency. By His power of omnipresence He was present both inside and outside of Uttara and other members of the Pandava family.”

For Krsna to stop the unstoppable brahmastra or to replace Maharaja Pariksit’s body is as difficult as it is for the sun to evaporate a drop of morning dew. Such deeds are not astounding for the Lord. Indeed, Suta Gosvami concludes this section by commenting to the sages of Naimisaranya: “O brahmanas, do not think this to be especially wonderful in the activities of the mysterious and infallible Personality of Godhead. By His own transcendental energy, He maintains and annihilates all material things, although He Himself is unborn.” (Bhag. [1.8.16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.16))

## Texts 17-36: Kuntidevi Begins to Offer Prayers

The crisis over, Krsna again prepared to start for Dvaraka. Before He could leave, one of His great devotees, Srimati Kuntidevi, expressed her distress. She had observed how Krsna had simultaneously protected the Pandavas from the outside and Maharaja Pariksit from the inside. Kunti was astonished by Krsna’s power, and she understood that He was the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Aside from that, His imminent departure caused her overwhelming pain. She who is described as supremely chaste (sati) in her devotion to Krsna began to express her devotion in heartfelt prayers: О Krsna, I offer my obeisances unto You. You are the original personality, the Supersoul, the controller, and are beyond the material world. You are present everywhere—within and without everything—but nevertheless You remain invisible to all. You sit on this chariot, remaining simultaneously inside and outside everything, yet no one can actually know You. I saw You protect the Pandavas with Your cakra, and I know that as the Supersoul, You entered Uttara’s womb to protect her embryo. You now sit directly before me on a chariot. Are You still within everything? Are You localized? All-pervading? Both?

It is easy to understand why Kuntidevi would make this inquiry. If we take a paper and tear it to pieces, then scatter the scraps throughout a room, the original wholeness of the paper no longer exists. Being both localized and all-pervading seems contradictory. Can someone be present in a specific place and present everywhere concurrently? And if this were possible—that Krsna is a person both localized and all-pervading—how can one who is both present everywhere and all powerful remain unrecognized? After all, Krsna, who is Kuntidevi’s nephew, is standing before Kunti in humanlike form engaging in humanlike activities despite the fact that He is unlimitedly powerful and the all-pervading Lord.

Kuntidevi then answers her own question: Just as one cannot recognize an actor when he is in costume, so Krsna remains beyond the limit of common people’s perception because the curtain of His deluding energy covers their eyes. Conditioned souls are so fully covered by illusion that they remain unable to see Krsna.

Kuntidevi states, however: You kindly appear in this world to further enlighten those souls who are already advanced, those already able to distinguish between matter and spirit. You come to give bhakti to such exalted souls. But what about people like me? How will we women, who are not great philosophers, know You? Thus Kunti teaches us the proper mentality required when approaching Krsna. One must feel humility. Material strength, beauty, intelligence, and assorted other good qualities remain insufficient assets when one tries to know the Lord. Srila Prabhupada is encouraging in his purport to text 20: “The Lord is so kind that He does not show special favor only to one who is a great philosopher. He knows the sincerity of purpose.”

In Bhagavat-sandarbha, anuccheda 10, Sri Jiva Gosvami comments on Krsna’s descent as mentioned in text 20: Why does the Supreme Personality of Godhead come (srayate) to this world? He comes so that embodied souls (saririnam) may learn to fix their thoughts on His lotus feet and, most importantly, so the devotees may taste the happiness of devotional service.

Kuntidevi’s next prayer, which names Krsna in relationship to many of His beloved devotees, offers hope to women—and everyone else—by hinting at the answer to her question. Kuntidevi prays: “Let me therefore offer my respectful obeisances unto the Lord, who has become the son of Vasudeva, the pleasure of Devaki, the boy of Nanda and the other cowherd men of Vrndavana, and the enlivener of the cows and the senses.” (Bhag. [1.8.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.21)) Krsna’s devotees are especially dear to Him. Indeed, His most intimate names are those that indicate His dealings with His devotees. When Krsna is called by one of those names, He remembers Himself in relation to the particular devotee connected with that name and His heart melts. Thus devotees pray to Krsna by those names to evoke compassion from His already softened heart. Because of His quality as bhakta'Vatsala, the lover of His devotees, He may be known by His own grace.

Kuntidevi’s next prayer compares the Lord to a lotus, mentioning His lotuslike abdomen, garland of lotus flowers, glance that is as cool as a lotus, and lotus-marked feet. Srila Jiva Gosvami indicates Krsna’s capacity to bring happiness and remove miseries in one compound word (sukha'pradatva'tapa'haritva'rupam): In his own purport, Srila Prabhupada assures us that although one may not be qualified to see the Lord, he can see Him in His deity form (arca-vigraha) in the temple.

Kuntidevi continues: You, dear Krsna, appear in this world untouched by anything. Just as the waxy coating on a lotus leaf protects it from the water in which it sits, so You are not truly of this world. Still, You have protected the lives of Your devotees, the Pandavas, again and again.

The Mahabharata depicts Krsna protecting and saving the Pandavas continuously. Now we see that His protection has extended beyond the Battle of Kuruksetra and the establishment of Yudhisthira on the throne to emergencies with deadly brahmastras.

With Yudhisthira securely in power, Kuntidevi, now the Queen Mother, is nevertheless afraid that Krsna will leave them. Thus she illuminates a deeper relationship with Krsna than “God, the remover of the devotees’ dangers.” Instead she points to the higher realization in which exalted devotees desire not protection and an anxiety-free life in this world bereft of Krsna’s association, but even a life of trial if such trials keep them in Krsna’s association. Kunti prays: “I wish that all those calamities would happen again and again so that we could see You again and again, for seeing You means that we will no longer see repeated births and deaths.” (Bhag. [1.8.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.25))

In his purport to this text, Srila Prabhupada underscores how one gains from life’s inevitable calamities:

**For a pious person, if there is some calamity there is no other alternative than to take shelter of the lotus feet of the Lord. Constantly remembering the lotus feet of the Lord means preparing for liberation from birth and death. Therefore, even though there are so-called calamities, they are welcome because they give us an opportunity to remember the Lord, which means liberation. . . . This material world is certified by the Lord in the Bhagavad-gita as a dangerous place full of calamities. Less intelligent persons prepare plans to adjust to those calamities without knowing that the nature of this place is itself full of calamities. They have no information of the abode of the Lord, which is full of bliss and without trace of calamity. The duty of the sane person, therefore, is to be undisturbed by worldly calamities, which are sure to happen in all circumstances. Suffering all sorts of unavoid-able misfortunes, one should make progress in spiritual realization because that is the mission of human life.**

Material life means dissatisfaction. It centers on the attempt to avoid calamities, but one is nevertheless forced to face the most inevitable calamity, death. Life’s real challenge is to transform difficulties into sources of freedom—to sever material attachment and seek Krsna’s shelter. True devotees hold on more tightly to Krsna with every difficulty.

How wonderful Krsna’s actual association must be! His association dims the value of peace, pales the worth of material security, and nullifies what most people consider the goal: life without anxiety. Hearing Kuntidevi’s words should spark one’s desire to attain Krsna’s association by becoming His devotee.How can one approach the lotuslike Lord? Kuntidevi’s affectionate words describe the price of approaching Him: “My Lord, Your Lordship can easily be approached, but only by those who are materially exhausted. One who is on the path of \[material\] progress, trying to improve himself with respectable parentage, great opulence, high education and bodily beauty, cannot approach You with sincere feeling.” (Bhag. [1.8.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.26)) Kuntidevi uses the words tvam актсапа-gocaram to describe that state of full dependence on Krsna wherein one values nothing in the material realm. In a lecture on this verse given in Mayapur in October 1974, Srila Prabhupada spoke of two kinds of devotees who display full dependence on Krsna (akincana):

**Gaura-kisora dasa Babaji always remained niskincana. And his disciple, Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati, he also remained niskincana although he possessed so many temples, because nothing was for his personal enjoyment, but all was for Krsna. . . Gaura-kisora dasa Babaji was sitting by the side of a municipal lavatory. Because so many people will come for darsana and asirvada \[blessings\], he did not like it. He did not like to be disturbed by these asirvada. People usually desire materialistic blessings and will not take any spiritual instruction. They are thinking that “Here is a saintly person and he’ll bless me. I now have one thousand. I’ll take ten thousand.” That’s all. Therefore they come. Therefore it is botheration. ... So Maharaja Mahindranandi had organized one sankirtana festival. He came to Gaura-kisora dasa Babaji Maharaja to invite him. After many requests, Gaura-kisora dasa Babaji Maharaja said, “Maharaja, you have got many tenants. Why you are trying to make me your tenant? You are a rich man, and as your tenants carry out your order, so you also want me.” Maharaja Mahindranandi replied, “No, sir, no. You are my lord. Whatever you say, I shall carry out.” “Will you carry out?” “Why not?” So he said, “Don’t go home. Sit down here. Chant Hare Krsna.” He fled. You see? He was humorous also, Gaura-kisora dasa Babaji. \[He\] said that “If you are so obedient, then I ask you, ‘Don’t go home. Better give up your dress and chant Hare Krsna here.’” He was akincana.**

**But Ramananda Raya was a grhastha, very opulent, and a governor. He is also akincana because everything was for Jagan-natha. This is the distinction. On one side, Rupa Gosvami, a renunciant, and on the other side, Ramananda Raya. And Ramananda Raya is the most confidential devotee of Caitanya Mahaprabhu, although he’s a grhastha, because he is akincana, as akincana as Riipa Gosvami. So we have to become akincana. Then we shall realize Krsna. Therefore it is said akincana-gocaram: “You are understandable only by a person who does not possess so-called material opulence.” We should always remember that whatever we are trying for in the material world, it is all for Krsna. Nothing is for us.**

In his purport to text 26, Srila Prabhupada also explains that those who feel sheltered by their material assets—their birth in a prestigious family or nation, their wealth, their academic learning, or their personal beauty—are “incapable of uttering the holy name of the Lord by addressing Him feelingly, ‘O Govinda, О Krsna.’” Srila Prabhupada continues: “It is said in the sastras that by once uttering the holy name of the Lord, the sinner gets rid of a quantity of sins that he is unable to commit. Such is the power of uttering the holy name of the Lord. There is not the least exaggeration in this statement. Actually the Lord’s holy name has such powerful potency. But there is a quality to such utterances also. It depends on the quality of feeling. A helpless man can feelingly utter the holy name of the Lord, whereas a man who utters the same holy name in great material satisfaction cannot be so sincere.” (Bhag. [1.8.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.26), purport)

Yet it must again be said that matter used fully in Krsna’s service does not cause a devotee to stumble. A devotee, like a bank teller, must pass on all that comes through his hands. Poverty does not exactly help one make spiritual advancement, but selfish attempts to prosper materially will certainly hinder one’s progress.

Kuntidevi continues, again offering her obeisances to Krsna, the property of the akincana, who is above the modes of material nature, and who is satisfied, gentle, and the master of all monists (brahmano hi pratistaham—the origin of that which the monists or impersonal-ists realize as Supreme): “My Lord, I consider Your Lordship to be eternal time, the supreme controller, without beginning and end, the all-pervasive one. In distributing Your mercy, You are equal to everyone. The dissensions between living beings are due to social intercourse.” (Bhag. [1.8.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.28))

Krsna’s being samam carantam sarvatra (equal to all) means that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, being equal to and merciful toward all His parts and parcels, descends by His free will to evoke surrender, which makes a soul receptive to His mercy.

Kuntidevi: Your activities, although transcendental, so parallel those of humans that they mislead those who view them into thinking of You as an ordinary man. How can one easily understand how You, who exist eternally and are unborn, nevertheless take birth among animals, men, sages, and aquatics? “Verily this is bewildering.” (Bhag. [1.8.30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.30))

After all, how can God descend as a hog (Varaha) or fish (Matsya)? How can the Supreme, Rama, be banished? How can He who is unborn take birth in a prison cell? How can the Pandavas, Krsna’s dear friends, undergo continuous tribulations? How can God steal butter and feed it to monkeys? One acts, motivated by the desire to achieve something, but Krsna lacks nothing. He possesses supreme self-satisfaction. Why then does He act? He is not impelled by anything outside Himself, as no such thing exists. Why does He even descend to this world? Jiva Gosvami concludes that the Lord’s pastimes are inconceivable.

Yet still more bewildering than the unborn’s taking birth, Kunti states, is how the omnipresent, omniscient, omnipotent Lord becomes a plaything in His devotees’ hands simply to increase their ecstasy. “My dear Krsna, Yasoda took up a rope to bind You when You committed an offense, and Your perturbed eyes overflooded with tears, which washed the mascara from Your eyes. And You were afraid, though fear personified is afraid of You. This sight is bewildering to me.” (Bhag. [1.8.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.31)) This verse speaks the most sublime truth: Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is conquered by love.

Kuntidevi further describes Krsna’s mysterious birth and activities by citing others’ thoughts: Have You appeared in this world to increase the fame of the Yadavas, the dynasty of devotees in which You took birth? Or. as others say, did You descend in response to Vasudeva and Devaki’s prayers for a son? Did You come to vanquish the envious or diminish the demoniac elements present on this overburdened earth? Or did You appear in this world to enact wonderful pastimes that would offer release to those suffering the pain of material life? “O Krsna, those who continuously hear, chant and repeat Your transcendental activities, or take pleasure in others’ doing so, certainly see Your lotus feet, which alone can stop the repetition of birth and death.” (Bhag. [1.8.36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.36))

Srila Prabhupada emphasizes the potency of hearing properly about Krsna: “\[Ejven though the Lord may be present before our eyes, it is not possible to see Him unless we have the necessary vision. This necessary qualification is developed by the process of devotional service only, beginning with hearing about the Lord from the right sources. The Bhagavad-gita is one of the popular literatures which are generally heard, chanted, repeated, etc., by the people in general, but in spite of such hearing, etc., sometimes it is experienced that the performer of such devotional service does not see the Lord eye to eye. The reason is that the first item, sravana, is very important. If hearing is from the right sources, it acts very quickly. Generally people hear from unauthorized persons. . . . Therefore, first one should select a competent and bona fide speaker and then hear from him. . . . There are different transcendental activities of the Lord, and each and every one of them is competent to bestow the desired result, provided the hearing process is perfect.” (Bhag. [1.8.36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.36), purport)

## Texts 37-43: Kuntidevi Concludes by Expressing Her Fear—and Her Actual Desire

After glorifying Lord Krsna for being unperceivable to anyone other than His devotees, for adventing Himself in this world, and for enacting wonderful humanlike pastimes, Kuntidevi now expresses her deepest fear: the Lord, after guiding the Pandavas through innumerable difficulties will soon depart. “Are you leaving us today, though we are completely dependent on Your mercy and have no one else to protect us, now when all kings are at enmity with us?” (Bhag. [1.8.37](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.37)) In his purport, Srila Prabhupada tenderly expresses Kuntidevi’s mood and purpose as he turns the point into a lesson for all: “For \[the Pandavas\] separation from the Lord was just like the separation of a fish from water. Srimati Kuntidevi, therefore, felt such separation like a thunderbolt, and the whole prayer of the Queen is to try to persuade the Lord to stay with them. After the Battle of Kuru-ksetra, although the inimical kings were killed, their sons and grandsons were still there to deal with the Pandavas. It is not only the Pandavas who were put into the condition of enmity, but all of us are always in such a condition, and the best way of living is to become completely dependent on the will of the Lord and thereby overcome all difficulties of material existence.”

From the affection in Kuntidevi’s heart come further words of attachment and dependence: Superficially, my dear Krsna, we Pandavas now possess everything, for we rule the entire kingdom. But without the imprints of Your lotus footprints decorating our kingdom, this kingdom has as much value as a body after the soul’s departure. Our kingdom flourishes only due to Your continued merciful glances.

Krsna’s imminent departure from Hastinapura for Dvaraka, where the Vrsnis await Him, gives rise to conflicting emotions for Kuntidevi. Srila Prabhupada’s purport reveals her dilemma: “The Pandavas are her own sons, and the Vrsnis are the members of her paternal family. Krsna was equally related to both the families. Both the families required the Lord’s help because both were dependent devotees of the Lord. Srimati Kuntidevi wished Sri Krsna to remain with her sons the Pandavas, but by His doing so her paternal house would be bereft of the benefit. All these partialities troubled the mind of Kunti, and therefore she desired to cut off the affectionate tie.” (Bhag. [1.8.41](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.41), purport)

She prays: “Please, therefore, sever my tie of affection for my kinsmen, the Pandavas and the Vrsnis. ... as the Ganges forever flows to the sea without hindrance, let my attraction be constantly drawn unto You without being diverted to anyone else.” (Bhag. [1.8.41-42](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.41))Jiva Gosvami comments in Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 115: Queen Kunti thinks, “If Lord Krsna departs from Hastinapura, that will be inauspicious for the Pandavas, and if He does not depart from Hastinapura and return to Dvaraka, that will be inauspicious for the Vrsnis.” Her heart thus agitated by competing affections for these two sides of her family, Queen Kunti herein prays that the affection she bears for her kinsmen be destroyed. The truth is that when she sees how the two sides of her family dearly love Lord Krsna, her own love for Lord Krsna increases. Therefore, on the pretext of saying, “Please destroy my affection for my kinsmen,” Queen Kunti is really praying, “Please do not leave the association of either of the two sides of my family.” Prabhupada further clarifies Kunti’s desire in his purport to text 42:

**Srimati Kunti wanted to serve the Lord without diversion, and that was her prayer. This unalloyed devotion is the ultimate goal of life. . . . Srimati Kuntidevi wanted that perfection and prayed for it from the Lord.**

**Her affection for the Pandavas and the Vrsnis is not out of the range of devotional service because the service of the Lord and the service of the devotees are identical. Sometimes service to the devotee is more valuable than service to the Lord. But here the affection of Kuntidevi for the Pandavas and the Vrsnis was due to family relation. This tie of affection in terms of material relation is the relation of maya because the relations of the body or the mind are due to the influence of the external energy. Relations of the soul, established in relation with the Supreme Soul, are factual relations. When Kuntidevi wanted to cut off the family relation, she meant to cut off the relation of the skin. The skin relation is the cause of material bondage, but the relation of the soul is the cause of freedom.**

Kuntidevi concludes: “. . . You descend to relieve the distresses of the cows, the brahmanas and the devotees. You possess all mystic powers, and You are the preceptor of the entire universe. You are the almighty God, and I offer You my respectful obeisances.” (Bhag. [1.8.43](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.43))

## Texts 44-52: Krsna Accepts Kuntidevi’s Prayers and Hears the Distressed Words of Yudhisthira Maharaja

Krsna smiled enchantingly as He accepted Kuntidevi’s glorification and statement of dependence, because she had offered them with devotion. “No amount of chosen words is sufficient to enumerate the Lord’s glory,” Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to text 44, “and yet He is satisfied by such prayers as the father is satisfied even by the broken linguistic attempts of the growing child.”

As Krsna again prepared to depart, Yudhisthira lovingly implored the Lord to stay a few days longer. Srila Prabhupada’s short comment, in his purport to text 45, on Krsna’s acquiescence to Yudhisthira’s affection is worth noting, because it encapsulates the theme of chapters Seven through Eleven: “No one could make Lord Krsna stay at Hastinapura when He decided to start for Dvaraka, but the simple request of King Yudhisthira that the Lord remain there for a few days more was immediately effective. This signifies that the power of King Yudhisthira was loving affection, which the Lord could not deny. The almighty God is thus conquered only by loving service and nothing else. He is fully independent in all His dealings, but He voluntarily accepts obligations by the loving affection of His pure devotees.”

Yudhisthira was feeling great anxiety; he was overwhelmed by the amount of blood shed during the Battle of Kuruksetra simply to enthrone him. After the battle, Krsna had encouraged Yudhisthira to perform three asvamedha'yajnas to increase the auspiciousness of his rule, but Yudhisthira still had to live with the fact that millions had died to place him on the throne. Boys, brahmanas, well-wishers, friends, parents, preceptors, brothers, and innocent citizens had been killed. Neither Vyasadeva nor Krsna nor the weight of scriptural or historical evidence could remove Yudhisthira’s sense of guilt, misery, or fear. Yudhisthira lamented: “O my lot! I am the most sinful man! Just see my heart, which is full of ignorance! This body, which is ultimately meant for others, has killed many, many phalanxes of men. I have killed many boys, brahmanas, well-wishers, friends, parents, preceptors and brothers. Though I live millions of years, I will not be relieved from the hell that awaits me for all these sins. ... As it is not possible to filter muddy water through mud, or purify a wine-stained pot with wine, it is not possible to counteract the killing of men by sacrificing animals.” (Bhag. [1.8.48-49](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.48), [52](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.52))

Yudhisthira Maharaja has properly stated how one becomes entangled in karma and must suffer for his misdeeds. Srila Prabhupada addresses this problem and gives its solution in his purport to text 51:

**In war either the husband or the brother or even the father or sons go to fight. And when they are killed, a fresh enmity is created, and thus a chain of actions and reactions increases which is not possible to be counteracted even by thousands of asvamedha-yajnas. The way of work (karma) is like that. It creates one action and another reaction simultaneously and thus increases the chain of material activities, binding the performer in material bondage. In the Bhagavad-gita (**[**9.27-28**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/9.27)**) the remedy is suggested that such actions and reactions of the path of work can be checked only when work is done on behalf of the Supreme Lord. The Battle of Kuruksetra was actually fought by the will of the Supreme Lord Sri Krsna, as it is evident from His version, and only by His will was Yudhisthira placed on the throne of Hastinapura. Therefore, factually no sin whatsoever touched the Pandavas, who were only the order carriers of the Lord. For others, who declare war out of personal interest, the whole responsibility lies on them.**

Prior to the battle, Arjuna foresaw unlimited destruction and refused to fight. Now that the battle was over, Yudhisthira could declare that he had actually seen this carnage. Because the battle had been fought to enthrone him, he feared that all the resulting sinful reactions would rest on him. Amazingly, Krsna Himself was unable to remove Yudhisthira’s doubts, although He had successfully removed Arjuna’s doubts by speaking Bhagavad-gita. Why was Krsna unsuccessful? Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to text 46:

**As Supersoul of King Yudhisthira, He did not allow the King to be convinced by the words of Vyasa and others, including Himself, because He desired that the King hear instructions from the dying Bhismadeva, who was another great devotee of the Lord. The Lord wanted that at the last stage of his material existence the great warrior Bhismadeva see Him personally and see his beloved grandchildren, King Yudhisthira, etc., now situated on the throne, and thus pass away very peacefully. . . . Besides this, the Lord also desired that King Yudhisthira be pacified by the words of Bhismadeva so that the world could see that Bhismadeva excelled all in knowledge, including the Lord Himself.**

Additionally, Srila Jiva Gosvami comments elsewhere on the same text that Vyasa and other sages knew that Yudhisthira could not be pacified because they were aware that Krsna had a plan He wished to fulfill. Still, they tried to console Yudhisthira, because that too was Krsna’s desire. Krsna had a plan. For His own wonderful reasons— which express so much affection for His devotees—Krsna wanted Yudhisthira Maharaja to question Bhismadeva, Yudhisthira’s grandfather and the great hero of Kuruksetra, who was now close to death.

## Chapter 9 - The Passing Away of Bhismadeva in the Presence of Lord Krsna

## Texts 1-24: Krsna and the Pandavas Approach the Dying Bhismadeva, who Offers Guidance to Yudhisthira Maharaja

In his youth, Bhisma had received the benediction that he would die only by his own will. Now, his body pierced with arrows from the Kuruksetra war, Bhisma was waiting for the sun to move into the northern hemisphere so that he could leave this world.

As he waited, Bhismadeva, the beloved grandfather of the Kuru dynasty, was surrounded by dozens of holy sages, including Vyasadeva and Sukadeva Gosvami. During that time, Krsna, Yudhisthira Maharaja, and the other Pandavas were traveling in an opulent procession to Kuruksetra to hear Bhismadeva’s final instructions.

On their arrival, Krsna and the Pandavas bowed to the stricken hero. They then sat before Bhisma and accepted his sweet and heartfelt welcoming words. Bhismadeva worshiped Sri Krsna, knowing that the Lord of his heart had mercifully come to be present at his death. The sons of Pandu sat nearby, overcome by their affection for their dying grandfather. Bhisma, crying tears of love as he looked at the Pandavas, said: “Oh, what terrible sufferings and what terrible injustices you good souls suffer for being the sons of religion personified. You did not deserve to remain alive under those tribulations, yet you were protected by the brahmanas, God and religion.” (Bhag. [1.9.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.12))

Bhisma, who knew all about the injustices the Pandavas had suffered, consoled the grieving Yudhisthira. In his purport to text 12, Srila Prabhupada reveals the heart behind Bhismadeva’s words:

**Maharaja Yudhisthira was disturbed due to the great massacre in the Battle of Kuruksetra. Bhismadeva could understand this, and therefore he spoke first of the terrible sufferings of Maharaja Yudhisthira. He was put into difficulty by injustice only, and the Battle of Kuruksetra was fought just to counteract this injustice. Therefore, he should not regret the great massacre. He wanted to point out particularly that they were always protected by the brahmanas, the Lord and religious principles. As long as they were protected by these three important items, there was no cause of disappointment. Thus Bhismadeva encouraged Maharaja Yudhisthira to dissipate his despondency. As long as a person is fully in cooperation with the wishes of the Lord, guided by the bona fide brahmanas and Vaisnavas and strictly following religious principles, one has no cause for despondency, however trying the circumstances of life. Bhismadeva, as one of the authorities in the line, wanted to impress this point upon the Pandavas.**

Yet one is still left with two questions: How can such misfortune befall Krsna’s devotees? And how should one who has experienced misfortune proceed in his activities? Bhismadeva offers a prescription for assimilating and dealing with circumstances that bring grief (and yes, such circumstances may befall even Krsna’s devotees): “In my opinion, this is all due to inevitable time, under whose control everyone in every planet is carried, just as the clouds are carried by the wind.” (Bhag. [1.9.14](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.14)) Although you (Yudhisthira) are the personification of righteousness and religion and were in the presence of your great warrior brothers, you suffered catastrophe after catastrophe. (Such calamities occurred even in Lord Krsna’s presence!) “. . . I maintain, therefore, that all this is within the plan of the Lord. Accepting the inconceivable plan of the Lord, you must follow it. You are now the appointed administrative head, and, my lord, you should now take care of those subjects who are now rendered helpless.” (Bhag. [1.9.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.17))

Bhismadeva instructed Yudhisthira to accept all that had happened as Krsna’s arrangement, understanding that he could not know the reasons behind the Lord’s plans. He should simply perform his royal duty and protect his citizens.Srila Prabhupada’s purports to texts 14-17 speak directly to a devotee’s vision of misfortune. Here is a sampling:

**Everything, therefore, is controlled by the supreme kola, a forceful representative of the Lord within the material world. . . . Everyone has to bear the actions and reactions of time as long as one is within the conditions of the material world. (Bhag.** [**1.9.14**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.14)**, purport)**

**Despite the power of pious acts, the power of personalities, the power of expert management and the power of weapons under the direct supervision of Lord Krsna, the Pandavas suffered so many practical reverses, which can only be explained as due to the influence of kala, inevitable time. Kola is identical with the Lord Himself, and therefore the influence of kola indicates the inexplicable wish of the Lord Himself. There is nothing to be lamented when a matter is beyond the control of any human being. (Bhag.** [**1.9.15**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.15)**, purport)**

**Bhisma wanted to impress upon Maharaja Yudhisthira that since time immemorial no one, including such demigods as Siva and Brahma, could ascertain the real plan of the Lord. So what can we understand about it? It is useless also to inquire about it. Even the exhaustive philosophical inquiries of sages cannot ascertain the plan of the Lord. The best policy is simply to abide by the orders of the Lord without argument. (Bhag.** [**1.9.16**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.16)**, purport)**

**The popular saying is that a housewife teaches the daughter-in-law by teaching the daughter. Similarly, the Lord teaches the world by teaching the devotee. (Bhag.** [**1.9.17**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.17)**, purport)**

Bhismadeva continued: Although you consider yourself sinful and unfortunate, He whom you have accepted as your cousin, dear friend, and intimate counselor is actually Sri Krsna, the supreme enjoyer, the highest authority, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Who in this world, therefore, is more fortunate than you?

In his purport to text 19, Srila Prabhupada states, quite amazingly: “Tribulations imposed upon the devotees by the Lord constitute an-other exchange of transcendental bhava \[affection\] between the Lord and the devotees. The Lord says ‘I put My devotee into difficulty, and thus the devotee becomes more purified in exchanging transcendental bhava with Me.’”

Difficult circumstances beyond one’s control occur in everyone’s life, even in the lives of devotees. Why? Bhagavatam [1.8.4](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/8.4) states that while discussing this question with Yudhisthira, Krsna and the munis cited “the stringent laws of the Almighty and their reactions upon living beings.” Ultimately, however, it is Krsna who is the Almighty Lord—even when He cites universal laws. One must ultimately accept everything that happens, Bhismadeva concludes, as Krsna’s will.

But why would Krsna sanction suffering for His great devotees? Srila Prabhupada once attributed such suffering simply to the nature of the material world: “Because this is the material world, even Krsna’s mother was put into suffering. Devaki was so advanced that she became the mother of Krsna, but still she was put into difficulties by her own brother, Kamsa. That is the nature of this material world.” (Teachings of Queen Kunti, p. 31) He has also said that Krsna, the Almighty Lord, has a plan and that everything and everyone in the universe is serving that plan. Devotees should therefore not expect lives free from turmoil and trouble. Haridasa Thakura was caned in twenty-two marketplaces. Jesus Christ was crucified, as were many of his followers. Yet devotees, even through extreme tribulations, can remain free from anxiety by accepting that Krsna is the Supreme Controller. Such consciousness is most wonderful.

It is also said that although the world moves by Krsna’s desire, even He is at times surprised by its workings. Is that possible? Can God not know something? If he does know everything, can He enjoy a surprise or an interesting turn of events? If not, He is lacking something. If He doesn’t know everything, is He God? Very mysterious.

What stops one from becoming distraught in this world is unshakeable faith in Krsna as one’s personal shelter. A devotee remains always confident of Krsna’s affection, nourishment, and guardianship. Indeed, as Srila Jiva Gosvami notes in Bhakti-sandarbha, anuchedda 236, the act of accepting Krsna as one’s personal shelter is synonymous with saranagati, surrender. Thus a devotee cultivates confidence in the promise Krsna made Arjuna: kaunteya pratijanihi na me bhak~ tah pranasyati—“O son of Kunti, declare it boldly that My devotee never perishes.” Such confidence is needed if one wishes to go back to Godhead; those with this consciousness inherit the kingdom of God.

Srila Prabhupada takes us to the heart of this issue, which is also at the essence of surrender to Krsna in pure devotion, in his purports to texts 22 and 24: “Having unflinching faith in the Supreme Lord as one’s protector, friend and master is the natural condition of eternal life. A living entity is so made by the will of the Almighty that he is most happy when placing himself in a condition of absolute dependence. The opposite tendency is the cause of falldown. . . . One must draw towards the Lord in all circumstances.” (Bhag. [1.9.22](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.22), purport)

“A pure devotee is never very anxious to go back to the kingdom of God. He entirely depends on the good will of the Lord. He is equally satisfied even if the Lord desires him to go to hell. The only desire that a pure devotee entertains is that he may always be in rapt attention with thinking of the lotus feet of the Lord, regardless. Bhismadeva wanted this much only: that his mind be absorbed in thinking of the Lord and that he pass away thus. That is the highest ambition of a pure devotee.” (Bhag. [1.9.24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.24), purport)

Ultimately, as Bhagavatam 10.14-8 indicates, we are tiny, insignificant, and helpless; we are also in Krsna’s hands and fully dependent on Him. We may legitimately accept everything as His kindness. This consciousness situates a devotee in the spiritual world.

Bhismadeva continues: Being in everyone’s heart, Sri Krsna is equally kind to all, yet He has graciously come before me as I end my life, for I am His unflinching servitor. This Krsna, who appears in the mind of a devotee fixed in devotion, releases that devotee from material bondage at the time of death. “May my Lord, who is four-handed and whose beautifully decorated lotus face, with eyes as red as the rising sun, is smiling, kindly await me at that moment when I quit this material body.” (Bhag. [1.9.24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.24))

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on texts 18 and 20-22 in Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 95, where Bhismadeva explains Krsna’s affectionate dealings with His devotees: The word sauhrdat in text 20 means “because of love.” This verse means, “Out of love you thought Him your maternal cousin, affectionate friend, well-wisher, and chariot driver, but in truth He is the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” Here someone

may protest: “As He is the Supersoul present in every living being, the Supreme Lord sees everyone equally (sama-drsah), and because everything that exists is His potency, the Supreme Lord is not different from anything (advayasya). The Supreme Lord, therefore, cannot be thinking, ‘I am the maternal cousin of such and such person.’” How can the faultless Supreme Lord think He is someone’s maternal cousin? He cannot be bewildered (mati'Vaisamyam) into thinking in that way. To answer this protest, Bhismadeva speaks texts 21 and 22: Even though He cannot be anyone’s maternal cousin, still (tathapi), О king (bhupa), please see how the Supreme Lord is merciful to His unalloyed devotees (ekanta-bhaktesu). He is so strongly controlled by His devotees’ pure devotion that He indeed thinks He is their friend or kinsman.

## Texts 25-49: Bhisma Offers Yudhisthira Instructions on Ruling the Kingdom and then Meditates on the Lord Before Leaving his Body

Yudhisthira Maharaja accepted Bhismadeva’s instructions. He knew he must rule the kingdom because it was the Lord’s desire. He then inquired from Bhisma about the essential principles of rulership. By Bhismadeva’s offering cogent instructions to Yudhisthira while in the most awkward of conditions—on his deathbed made of arrows piercing his body—Krsna further glorifies Bhisma, His devotee. In response to Yudhisthira’s inquiry, Bhisma first delineated the duties of those in each of the four occupational varnas and the four social asramas, explaining how those who were materially attached or detached should be trained. Citing historical references, he described the duties of women, devotees, and kings, as well as various forms of charity. As Bhismadeva continued revealing knowledge required for rulership, the sun moved to the northern hemisphere. This was the auspicious time he had chosen for his death.

One can learn from Bhismadeva’s example. As one nears death, one should withdraw consciousness from everything but direct thought of Krsna. Bhisma had been discussing subjects in pursuance of Krsna’s desire, yet he withdrew his mind from these worldly topics at the moment of death. That great warrior-devotee now fixed his mind and wide-open eyes on Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who stood before him, four-handed and dressed in glittering yellow garments.

Thus Bhisma was immediately relieved from all material inauspiciousness and the pain of his arrow wounds. His mind focused, he glorified all-attractive Sri Krsna: Let Krsna, who drove the chariot of His intimate friend Arjuna, whose body resembles the bluish color of a tamala tree, be the object of my attraction. Let me not desire any fruitive results.

Bhisma, the chivalrous warrior, centered his consciousness on the feature of the Lord that most attracted him: Sri Partha-sarathi, the Supreme Person driving His devotee’s chariot, fighting him (Bhisma) on the battlefield. He envisioned Krsna’s form, coated in dust raised by the horses’ hooves, His face wet with perspiration, and His transcendental body decorated with wounds caused by Bhisma’s own sharp arrows.

Commenting on text 34 in Bhagavat-sandarbha, anuccheda 58, Jiva Gosvami states that because the transcendental body of Lord Krsna can never be harmed, this pastime should be understood as a specific illusion arranged by the Lord. Srila Prabhupada supports this commentary in his purports to texts 34 and 38: “It appears that Bhismadeva is repenting the actions he committed against the person of the Lord. But factually the Lord’s body was not at all pained, due to His transcendental existence. His body is not matter. Both He Himself and His body are complete spiritual identity. Spirit is never pierced, burnt, dried, moistened, etc. This is vividly explained in the Bhagavad-gita.” (Bhag. [1.9.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.34), purport) And in his purport to text 38, he writes:

**Bhismadeva played the part of a valiant warrior, and he purposely pierced the body of the Lord so that to the common eyes it appeared that the Lord was wounded, but factually all this was to bewilder the nondevotees. The all-spiritual body cannot be wounded, and a devotee cannot become the enemy of the Lord. Had it been so, Bhismadeva would not have desired to have the very same Lord as the ultimate destination of his life. Had Bhismadeva been an enemy of the Lord, Lord Krsna could have annihilated him without even moving. There was no need to come before Bhismadeva with blood and wounds. But He did so because the warrior devotee wanted to see the transcendental beauty of the Lord decorated with wounds created by a pure devotee. This is the way of exchanging transcendental rasa, or relations between the Lord and the servitor. By such dealings both the Lord and the devotee become glorified in their respective positions.**

The purport to text 34 also includes a paraphrase of Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s commentary on how the Lord accepts His devotee’s offerings in a spirit of love, even if those offerings are sharp arrows shot in combat:

**Sri Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, a great acarya and devotee in the humor of conjugal love with the Lord, remarks very sali-ently in this regard. He says that the wounds created on the body of the Lord by the sharpened arrows of Bhismadeva were as pleasing to the Lord as the biting of a fiancee who bites the Lord’s body directed by a strong sense of sex desire. Such biting by the opposite sex is never taken as a sign of enmity, even if there is a wound on the body. Therefore, the fighting as an exchange of transcendental pleasure between the Lord and His pure devotee, Sri Bhismadeva, was not at all mundane. . . . The Lord enjoyed the wounds created by His great devotee Bhismadeva, and because Bhismadeva is a devotee in the chivalrous relation, he fixes up his mind on Krsna in that wounded condition.**

Bhismadeva further remembered Krsna’s driving Arjuna’s chariot on the battlefield, His removal of Arjuna’s ignorance by speaking Bhagavad-gita, and His merciful glance that diminished the life span of the opposite party. Bhisma then focused on Krsna’s behavior on the battlefield, especially the deed most dear to him: the Lord dismounting the chariot and rushing angrily toward him with a broken chariot wheel raised as a weapon. The word caladguh, “trampling the earth,” is used in text 37 to describe Krsna’s hurried and angry steps toward Bhismadeva. Srila Sridhara Svami explains in his commentary that while performing His humanlike pastimes, Krsna allowed the weight of the entire universe to rest in His body. Thus the earth trembled as He walked. Srila Jiva Gosvami comments that because Krsna was in such a hurry, His steps moved the earth.Srila Prabhupada told of the events leading up to this pastime during a Bhagavad-gita lecture in New York in 1966:

**I will give you one example how Krsna sometimes breaks His promise. It is very nice story. Krsna, when He joined Arjuna before the Battle of Kuruksetra, promised, “Because the fight is between brothers, and because both of you are My relatives, it is not My duty to join one party and not to join another. But because Duryodhana has decided to take My soldiers, not Me, so I shall join you, Arjuna. But I shall not fight. I may take some work which may assist you.” So Arjuna offered, “Whatever work You like, You can take.” So He said, “All right, I shall drive your chariot.” So Krsna’s promise was to not fight.**

**But once, on the battlefield, Arjuna was in danger while fighting Bhisma, the greatest fighter, although a very old man. Duryodhana had incited Bhisma in the midst of the war: “The Pandavas, on the other side, are your pet grandsons; you are not fighting folly.” That was the complaint of Duryodhana. So in order to encourage him, Bhisma said to Duryodhana, “All right, tomorrow I shall finish all these five brothers. And I have got now special arrows for killing these five chivalrous brothers.**

**So Duryodhana was very intelligent. “Please give me these five arrows for the night. I shall deliver them to you tomorrow morning.” “All right,” said Bhisma, “take them.”**

**But Krsna understood. He knows everything—past, present, and future. Krsna knew that “Bhisma has now promised to kill all the Pandavas.” So He asked Arjuna—this is also politics—that “You go to Duryodhana. Do you remember that Duryodhana once vowed, ‘Arjuna, whenever you want something, I shall give you’? Now, at this time, remind Duryodhana of his words. He has five arrows for killing you. You ask for them and bring them to Me.”**

**That evening, after the day’s fight, the warriors acted as friends. So Arjuna went to the camp of Duryodhana and was well received. “Well, Arjuna, come on. What do you want? Come on, sit down. Do you want anything from me? If you want, I can stop this fight. I can return to you the kingdom if this is your wish.”**

**Arjuna said, “No, I have not come to you for begging my kingdom. The fighting will go on. But do you remember your promise to me?” Duryodhana replied, “Yes, I know. Whatever you want, I offer you.” “Now,” said Arjuna, “I want those five arrows.” Duryodhana at once delivered the arrows, knowing Krsna was behind Arjuna’s request.**

**When Bhisma heard of Arjuna’s begging those five arrows, he thought, “Krsna is very cunning also. He will save His devotee. So He has done this. All right, Krsna has broken my promise, and tomorrow I will make Krsna break His promise to not fight. If Krsna does not break His promise, then His friend Arjuna will be killed. I will fight in such a way.”**

**So in the battle that day, Bhisma fought so powerfully that Arjuna was almost killed. His chariot was tom into pieces and Arjuna fell down. And then Krsna took up one of the wheels of the chariot and rushed before Bhisma: “Now, Bhisma, you stop this fighting; otherwise I will kill you.” Bhisma at once gave up his arrows and offered, “All right, kill me.”**

**Bhisma had promised, “I shall kill Arjuna tomorrow,” and Krsna had also promised not to fight. So just to save these two devotees, Arjuna and Bhisma, He rushed to Bhisma to kill him. Krsna thought that “Either I shall break My promise to not fight or you shall kill Arjuna. So better that I break My promise.” In this way, sometimes, to protect His devotee, Krsna sometimes breaks His own promise.**

Thus Bhismadeva fondly remembered Krsna, the shawl covering His shoulders dropping to the ground, the chariot wheel upraised as He angrily charged him for having threatened Arjuna. Srila Prabhupada describes the scene in his purport to text 38: “The astounding feature of suck dealings is that a devotee can please the Lord by playing the part of an enemy. The Lord, being absolute, can accept service from His pure devotee even in the garb of an enemy. ... By such dealings both the Lord and the devotee become glorified in their respective positions. The Lord was so angry that Arjuna checked Him when He was moving towards Bhismadeva, but in spite of Arjuna’s checking, He proceeded towards Bhismadeva as a lover goes to a lover, without caring for hindrances. Apparently His determination was to kill Bhismadeva, but factually it was to please him as a great devotee of the Lord.”

As Bhismadeva thought of the Lord’s beauty while He was driving Arjuna’s chariot, he realized his own good fortune. He came to consider himself more fortunate than Arjuna, because while Krsna was driving Arjuna’s chariot, Arjuna could see the Lord only from behind whereas Bhisma was facing the Lord and could see His full form, covered with dust and decorated with wounds, standing on Arjuna’s chariot, a whip in His right hand and a bridle rope in His left.

After remembering Krsna as Partha-sarathi, Bhisma then fixed his mind on those whose serving mood is topmost and to whom Krsna remains indebted. Desiring their blessings before leaving his body, Bhisma remembered the Vraja gopis.

His mind then moved to Krsna’s being worshiped during Yudhisthira’s rajasuya sacrifice. Remembering these pastimes, Bhisma recognized Krsna’s position as the all-pervading Supreme Personality of Godhead. Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on Bhismadeva’s meditation on Krsna’s all-pervasiveness in Bhagavat-sandarbha, anuccheda 43: Now I can meditate with full concentration (samadhi'gato ’smi) on that one Lord, Sri Krsna, now present before me (tarn imam), and whom I have described in my previous prayers. The Supreme Lord is present in the hearts of all conditioned souls (sarira-bhajam hrdi hrdi) in His form as the Supersoul, yet I now see Him everywhere in His unequaled, two-armed form of Sri Krsna.

As Bhisma lovingly focused his mind on Krsna, his breathing stopped. Everyone present became as silent as birds at the end of day. Then drums rolled in his honor and flowers fell from the sky. All were overtaken by grief. That person who had protected Yudhisthira since his childhood, who had been his well-wisher until the final moments of his life, no longer graced this world.

Srila Prabhupada describes the mixture of emotion and philosophical understanding that confront one after the death of a great soul: “. . . Bhismadeva was always a sincerely sympathetic well-wisher, grandfather, friend and philosopher to Maharaja Yudhisthira, even up to the last moment of his life . . . Maharaja Yudhisthira was quite aware of all these good wishes of Bhismadeva, and therefore he must have been feeling the great separation. He was sorry for the separation of a great soul, and not for the material body which Bhismadeva relinquished.” (Bhag. [1.9.46](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.46), purport)

Yudhisthira Maharaja and Lord Krsna then returned to Hastina-pura, and Yudhisthira assumed his royal duties, governing according to the principles Bhismadeva had taught him.

## Chapter 10 - Departure of Lord Krsna for Dvaraka

## Texts 1-20: Krsna Departs for Dvaraka

Saunaka Rsi next inquired about Yudhisthira’s reign. Suta Gosvami replied that Krsna was pleased to install Yudhisthira on the throne, thus restoring to power the Kuru dynasty, issuing from Pandu.

For his part, Yudhisthira, guided by Bhisma’s words and assisted by his younger brothers, ruled his kingdom dutifully and effectively. Clouds showered water, milk was abundant, and no one in the kingdom was disturbed by agony, disease, heat, or cold. With Yudhisthira Maharaja established on the throne and Maharaja Pariksit, the kingdom’s heir, safe, the Supreme Lord, Sri Krsna, was satisfied.

During the first few months of Yudhisthira Maharaja’s reign, Krsna remained in Hastinapura to please His relatives. Finally, the Lord requested the king’s permission to depart for Dvaraka. Fainting in fear of separation from Krsna, their hearts melting in affection, the residents of Hastinapura stared at the Lord with unblinking eyes. In his purport to Bhagavatam [1.10.9-10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/10.9), Srila Prabhupada describes in appealing words separation from Krsna:

**Lord Sri Krsna is so attractive for the living beings, especially for the devotees, that it is impossible for them to tolerate separation. The conditioned soul under the spell of illusory energy forgets the Lord; otherwise, he cannot. The feeling of such separation cannot be described, but it can simply be imagined by devotees only. After His separation from Vrndavana and the innocent rural cowherd boys, girls, ladies and others, they all felt shock throughout their lives, and the separation of Radharani, the most beloved cowherd girl, is beyond expression. Once they met at Kuruksetra during a solar eclipse, and the feeling which was expressed by them is heartrending. There is, of course, a difference in the qualities of the transcendental devotees of the Lord, but none of them who have ever contacted the Lord by direct communion or otherwise can leave Him for a moment. That is the attitude of the pure devotee.**

Thus the Bhagavatam helps one remember Him whom one has forgotten. It awakens in one a longing—as well as teaches one the method—to reestablish his relationship with God. When love for Krsna blossoms in one’s heart, a moment apart from Him will seem an eternity.

In text 11, Suta points out that one who has understood Krsna in the association of pure devotees and has freed himself from materialistic association is attracted to hearing Krsna’s glories constantly. Such a person’s attraction will increase, and, as Prabhupada states in his purport, “will go on progressively without stoppage, like fire in gunpowder.” If such attraction to Krsna expands in one’s heart after only slight association with Krsna through His devotees, who can estimate the intensity of the feelings of the Pandavas at the prospect of separation from Him? The Pandavas had associated intimately with Krsna, had seen Him face to face, touched Him, and spoken, dined, and rested with Him. As Krsna prepared to leave for Dvaraka, the Pandavas could do nothing but stare at Him with unblinking eyes. Indeed, Sridhara Svami defines vicelus tatra tatra (“moved hither and thither”) in text 13 as “following Krsna everywhere.”

After speaking enthusiastically about the Pandavas’ attraction for Krsna, Suta Gosvami continues his description of the Lord’s departure from Hastinapura, saying that drums were sounded to honor the Lord. Wishing to see Krsna as He departed, the ladies of the royal family stood shyly on the palace roof and showered flower petals on Him, their glances full of affection.

Srila Prabhupada describes their selfless mood and provides us with an important instruction: “There were hundreds of ladies in the palace of Hastinapura. All of them were affectionate to Krsna. All of them were relatives also. When they saw that Krsna was going away from the palace for His native place, they were very anxious for Him, and as usual tears began to roll down their cheeks. They thought, at the same time, that tears at that moment might be a cause of misfortune for Krsna; therefore they wanted to check them. This was very difficult for them because the tears could not be checked. Therefore, they smeared their tears in their eyes, and their hearts throbbed. Therefore ladies who were the wives and daughters-in-law of those who died in the battlefield never came in direct contact with Krsna. But all of them heard of Him and His great activities, and thus they thought of Him, talked of Him, His name, fame, etc., and became affectionate also, like those who were in direct contact. Therefore directly or indirectly anyone who thinks of Krsna, talks of Krsna or worships Krsna becomes attached to Him. Because Krsna is absolute, there is no difference between His name, form, quality, etc. Our intimate relation with Krsna can be confidentially revived by our talking of, hearing of, or remembering Him. It is so done due to spiritual potency.” (Bhag. [1.10.14](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/10.14), purport)

As Krsna’s departure became imminent, Arjuna held a jeweled and embroidered umbrella over Krsna’s head, intimate members of the Kuru dynasty fanned Him, and the ladies waited on the roofs of the houses, eulogizing Him with words sweeter than Vedic hymns.

## Texts 21-36: The Prayers of the Ladies of Hastinapura, and Krsna Departs

The ladies saw Krsna proceeding from the city and glorified Him as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the all-powerful Lord who existed before the creation and into whom, as His plenary part Lord Visnu, all living beings merge at the time of annihilation. By His potency the living entities are again manifest and placed under the guidance of material nature when the universe is again created. All this takes place by His will, the ladies state, which overrides each living entity’s attempt for happiness in the world of matter. “Here is the same Supreme Personality of Godhead whose transcendental form is experienced by the great devotees who are completely cleansed of material consciousness by dint of rigid devotional service and full control of life and the senses.” (Bhag. [1.10.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/10.23))

Srila Sridhara Svami comments that the Lord is not easily seen. The process of seeing the Lord and advancing in devotional service is to fully engage all the senses in the Lord’s service. This is the only way to control and purify the senses. While one is becoming purified, the Lord personally protects him.

The ladies continue: О dear friends, Sri Krsna’s intimate pastimes are described by His great devotees in confidential scriptures. Although we now see Him before us, He is nevertheless the aloof and unaffected creator, maintainer, and annihilator of the entire material world.

Answering the question, Why has the Supreme Lord appeared in the world? the ladies reply: He descends wonderfully in His transcendental form to protect His devotees, establish righteous rulers, and vanquish the anarchy and viciousness caused by irreligious maladministrators. After all, the cosmic creation is His property and the living entities, being His parts and parcels, are His children. The Lord’s natural duty is to sustain them.

The ladies’ attention then turns to the supreme fortune of the Yadu dynasty and the land of Mathura, for in that dynasty and on that land the Lord took birth and wandered during His childhood. The ladies say that Dvaraka City, to which the Lord was heading, is more glorious than heaven because those living in Dvaraka have attained the fortune of seeing Krsna while receiving the favor of His glances and sweet smiles. They add: This fortune we are now losing.

Srila Prabhupada extols the potency of holy lands like Dvaraka where Krsna performed His pastimes: “Any person engaged in the devotional service of the Lord is recommended to live in one of the above-mentioned three places, namely Dvaraka, Mathura or Vrndavana. Because devotional service in these three places is magnified, those who go there to follow the principles in terms of instructions imparted in the revealed scriptures surely achieve the same result as obtained during the presence of Lord Sri Krsna. His abode and He Himself are identical, and a pure devotee under the guidance of another experienced devotee can obtain all the results, even at present.” (Bhag. [1.10.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/10.27), purport)

The ladies continue: Just imagine the pious acts Krsna’s wives must have performed. They now wait for Him in Dvaraka and have attained the fortune of kissing the Lord’s lips, the contemplation of which would cause the Vraja gopis to faint.

To appreciate these intimate loving exchanges between the Lord and His most qualified devotees, which so closely resemble their reflection—the dealings between men and women in this world—one must understand Krsna’s position as the all-powerful Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus the ladies of Hastinapura opened their prayers by detailing Krsna’s potency in creating, maintaining, and annihilating the universe. If one knows Krsna’s identity, he will not mistake Krsna’s intimate dealings in transcendental love for the lust expressed in the material realm. Had Krsna’s dealings been mundane, Srila Prabhupada reminds us in his purport to text 28, “a liberated soul like Sukadeva would not have taken the trouble to relish them, nor would Lord Sri

Caitanya Mahaprabhu have been inclined to participate in those subjects after renouncing worldly life.” These hints in the ladies’ prayers prepare one for what one may relish in the Tenth Canto, providing he has been purified by what he has heard in the first nine cantos.

The ladies’ final two prayers (Bhag. [1.10.29-30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/10.29)) describe the Lord’s unparalleled, supramundane potency by further glorifying the fortune of Krsna’s 16,108 wives, every one of whom had her own palace. The Lord lived with each wife in each palace simultaneously by expanding Himself into 16,108 plenary portions. Later in the Bhagavatam, the great saint Narada Muni will become amazed after personally witnessing the Lord’s dealings with His queens in Dvaraka. At that time, after seeing that the Lord had expanded Himself and was individually relating with thousands of queens in thousands of palaces, Narada Muni tells the Lord, “Now we understand Your mystic potencies, which are difficult to comprehend, even for great mystics, О Supreme Soul, master of all mystic power. Only by serving Your feet have I been able to perceive Your powers.” (Bhag. [10.69.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/69.38))

Lord Krsna heard the ladies’ words and accepted them with a smile. After glancing at them, He departed from the city. Maharaja Yudhisthira, his brothers, and four divisions of soldiers escorted Lord Krsna for a considerable distance. Out of His love for Yudhisthira, Krsna accepted this gesture of affection. Prabhupada explains the sweetness of these loving exchanges in his purport to text 32: “If required, Lord Krsna Himself was sufficient to defend Himself from the attack of others who counted the Lord as their enemy, but still He accepted all the arrangements made by Yudhisthira because He could not disobey the King, who was His elder cousin. The Lord plays the part of a subordinate in His transcendental sporting, and thus sometimes He puts Himself in the care of Yasodamata for His protection in His so-called helplessness of childhood. That is the transcendental Illa, or pastime of the Lord. The basic principle for all transcendental exchanges between the Lord and His devotees is exhibited to enjoy a transcendental bliss for which there is no comparison ...”

The Pandavas did not cease to accompany Krsna as He journeyed from Hastinapura, for whenever they considered separation from Him they became overwhelmed by emotion. After some time, however, Krsna persuaded them to return home, and He and His other dear associates continued their journey alone. Crossing different lands (Srila Jiva Gosvami mentions in his commentary on texts 34 and 35 that Krsna passed through the land known as Surasena so He could visit Vrndavana), rivers, and deserts, heading ever westward, the Lord and His entourage at last reached Dvaraka.

## Chapter 11 - Lord Krsna’s Entrance into Dvaraka

## Texts 1-29: Krsna Enters Beautiful Dvaraka City, Greets the Citizens, and Meets His Father and Mother

As ecstatic tears of forlorn separation were pouring from the eyes of Krsna’s Hastinapura devotees, the ecstatic dejection of Dvaraka’s citizens was soon to be lifted. On approaching Dvaraka, Krsna sounded His pure white conchshell, which appeared reddened by the touch of His transcendental lips. As long as Lord Krsna had been away in Kuruksetra and Hastinapura, everyone in Dvaraka had been absorbed in remembering Him. When the residents heard His conchshell, however, they quickly ran toward Him, longing to again be in His presence.

Srila Prabhupada describes the spiritual significance of “the redness of the white conchshell due to the lip-touch of the Lord” in his purport to Bhagavatam [1.11.2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.2): “The Lord is all spirit, and matter is ignorance of this spiritual existence. Factually there is nothing like matter in spiritual enlightenment, and this spiritual enlightenment takes place at once by the contact of the Supreme Lord Sri Krsna. The Lord is present in every particle of all existence, and He can manifest His presence in anyone. By ardent love and devotional service to the Lord, or in other words by spiritual contact with the Lord, everything becomes spiritually reddened like the conchshell in the grip of the Lord.”

Exalted spiritual persons view everything as Krsna’s and use everything in Krsna’s service. For a devotee, therefore, visvam рйгпа sukh-dyate, the whole world is filled with pleasure. As soon as a soul folly contacts Krsna, the world takes on a spiritual existence. Thus Dvaraka’s citizens appeared before the Lord, offering Him valuable presentations along with affectionate words: You are supremely worshipable. Time cannot influence You. You are everything to us—mother, well-wisher, Lord, father, spiritual master, and worshipable Deity. Our success has come from following in Your footsteps. Please continue to bless us. Our fortune is that we can again see Your transcendental, auspicious form.

Commenting on texts 4 and 5, Srila Jiva Gosvami notes that praising Krsna produces devotion. It is natural, he writes, that those who pray for Krsna’s love should get it, for He whose nature is full of happiness feels love for His devotees. In Bhakti-sandarbha, anuccheda 143, he also explains that the Supreme Personality of Godhead is always satisfied with even the smallest offerings, even though He is always happy in Himself. Sri Jiva cites Bhagavatam [1.11.4-5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.4) to show that the citizens’ gifts were saturated with priti, their extraordinary happiness and love in seeing Him again, and that these emotions gave the Lord pleasure.

Seeing Krsna—something natural for every resident of Dvaraka— is natural for each individual soul. As Srila Prabhupada states in his purport to text 8: “The inhabitants of Dvaraka, because of their being pure devotees without any tinge of the material contamination of fruit-ive activities and empiric philosophical speculation, can see Him face to face by the grace of the Lord. This is the original state of the living entities and can be attained by reviving our natural and constitutional state of life, which is discovered by devotional service only.”

Dvaraka’s residents continued: Your absence seemed as if a million years. О infallible one, at that time our eyes became useless, as if bereft of the sun. We were unable to see Your attractive face while You were away. How can we exist without Your presence?

By entering Dvaraka and acknowledging with His glance those greeting Him, Krsna removed the citizens’ misery. Now in Krsna’s presence, the citizens returned to their natural, blissful consciousness. As Krsna entered further into His capital city, He saw its lushness, its auspicious decorations, painted gates, arches, flags, and festoons. Unbroken fruit, sugarcane, full water pots, candles, and fragrant incense had been placed outside each home. Hearing of His arrival, Krsna’s relatives rushed toward Him to offer their respects amid a clamor of bugles, conchshells, and Vedic hymns. Each citizen contributed to the joyous reception according to his or her capacity, and Krsna sweetly reciprocated with each citizen, friend, or relative. All praised and glorified Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, their Lord, appreciating the opportunity to see Him as the greatest of festivals.

Desiring to experience the ecstasy of greeting Krsna, conditioned souls caught beneath the cloud of illusion may also taste a sweet drop of this joyous ocean by visiting Him in His temples, especially during celebrations such as Janmastami and Jhulana-yatra, wherein He accepts worship as the deity. Whether one is qualified or unqualified, good or bad, if one approaches Krsna and sincerely offers Him whatever he or she is capable of offering, Krsna will reciprocate with auspicious benedictions, the most beneficial of which will be a deepening of one’s desire to serve Him. Unless one becomes attracted to festivals in the temple, one’s mind will remain bound by attraction to material festivals. As Srila Prabhupada describes in his purport to text 25, one can continuously see Krsna, chant His holy names, and become increasingly attracted to Him with “no satiation”: “His body is the source of everything that be, the reservoir of all beauties beyond our experience. No one, therefore, is satiated by seeing the transcendental body of the Lord because there are always manifestations of newer and newer beauties. The transcendental name, form, qualities, entourage, etc., are all spiritual manifestations, and there is no satiation in chanting the holy name of the Lord, there is no satiation in discussing the qualities of the Lord, and there is no limitation of the entourage of the Lord. He is the source of all and is limitless.”

Krsna proceeded through the streets of Dvaraka toward his parents’ palace. Flower petals offered by devotees fell at His lotus feet, and His yellow garments shone like lightning. Krsna’s moonlike face appeared as a vessel meant for those hankering to taste full beauty, and His lotus feet offered refuge to pure devotees who sing and speak only of Him. Prabhupada explains Krsna’s attractiveness in his purport to text 26:

**The pure devotees are always hankering after the lotus feet of the Lord. The lotus has a kind of honey which is transcendentally relished by the devotees. They are like the bees who are always after the honey. Srila Riipa Gosvami, the great devotee acarya of the Gaudiya-Vaisnava-sampradaya, has sung a song about this lotus honey, comparing himself to the bee: “O my Lord Krsna, I beg to offer my prayers unto You. My mind is like the bee, and it is after some honey. Kindly, therefore, give my bee-mind a place at Your lotus feet, which are the resources for all transcendental honey. I know that even big demigods like Brahma do not see the rays of the nails of Your lotus feet, even though they are engaged in deep meditation for years together. Still, О infallible one, my ambition is such, for You are very merciful to Your surrendered devotees.**

О Madhava, I know also that I have no genuine devotion for the service of Your lotus feet, but because Your Lordship is inconceivably powerful, You can do what is impossible to be done. Your lotus feet can deride even the nectar of the heavenly kingdom, and therefore I am very much attracted by them. О supreme eternal, please, therefore, let my mind be fixed at Your lotus feet so that eternally I may be able to relish the taste of Your transcendental service.” The devotees are satisfied with being placed at the lotus feet of the Lord and have no ambition to see His all-beautiful face or aspire for the protection of the strong arms of the Lord. They are humble by nature, and the Lord is always leaning towards such humble devotees.

Upon entering Vasudeva’s palace, Krsna was embraced by Devaki as well as by his stepmothers, who were all equally affectionate toward Him. Krsna reciprocated their affection by placing His head at their feet. His mothers then placed Krsna on their laps and moistened the Lord with their warm tears.

## Texts 30-39: Krsna Is Greeted by His Queens As He Enters His Palaces

In Chapter Ten, texts 28—30, the ladies on the roofs of Hastinapura spoke of the fortune of Krsna’s queens. Now at the end of Chapter Eleven we glimpse Krsna’s dealings with those queens. After leaving His father’s home, Krsna expanded Himself into 16,108 forms and simultaneously entered each of His palaces to meet His wives. Upon seeing Him, each queen rose from her seat, rejoicing, and shyly covered her face.
