According to Srila Sridhara Svami (commenting on text 31), the word asanasayat (“seated in meditation”) implies that although the queens were sitting, their anxiety to embrace their transcendental husband forced them to immediately stand. They could not bear the least delay, and they mentally and physically tried to see Him. Yet due to shyness, they looked at their husband with sidelong glances, thus expressing both eagerness and bashfulness.

Who but Krsna can simultaneously meet more than 16,000 wives in 16,000 palaces? It is essential that we keep Krsna’s extraordinariness in mind, for His actions resemble the dealings between ordinary humans. Yet despite that resemblance, He always remains the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the unequaled eternal Lord, the possessor of unlimited potency, the one who attracts the hearts and minds of all living entities. Srila Prabhupada writes that one should not doubt Krsna’s deeds. After all, He is God: “One should not, therefore, become astonished to learn that the Lord married so many wives. On the contrary, one should affirm that even if the Lord marries sixteen thousand million wives, He is not completely manifesting His unlimited and inexhaustible potency. He married only 16,000 wives and entered in each and every one of the different palaces just to impress in the history of the human beings on the surface of the earth that the Lord is never equal to or less than any human being, however powerful he may be. No one, therefore, is either equal to or greater than the Lord. The Lord is always great in all respects. ‘God is great’ is eternal truth.” (Bhag. [1.11.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.31), purport)

Upon seeing Krsna, the queens remained shy yet completely attracted to Him. Experiencing the conflicting pull of these emotions, they therefore “first embraced the Lord in the innermost recesses of their hearts. Then they embraced Him visually, and then they sent their sons to embrace Him \[which is equal to personal embracing\]. But . . . though they tried to restrain their feelings, they inadvertently shed tears.” (Bhag. [1.11.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.32)) What woman—even the restless goddess of fortune—could remain detached from Krsna for even a moment? Who, having taken shelter of the Lord once, could leave His company?

Krsna had returned to His palaces pacified, because the Kuruksetra war had completed the mission for which He had descended to earth. “He Himself was not a party in the fight. He simply created hostility between the powerful administrators, and they fought amongst themselves. He was like the wind which causes friction between bamboos and so sparks a fire.” (Bhag. [1.11.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.34)) Thus Krsna had relieved the earth’s demoniac burden.

Srila Prabhupada reveals the application of Krsna’s indomitable will on contemporary politics: “The fire in the forest takes place automatically by the force of the air, and similarly the hostility between different groups of politicians takes place by the unseen design of the Lord. The unwanted administrators, puffed up by false power and military strength, thus become engaged in fighting amongst themselves over ideological conflicts and so exhaust themselves of all powers. The history of the world reflects this factual will of the Lord, and it will continue to be enacted until the living beings are attached to the service of the Lord.” (Bhag. [1.11.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.34), purport)

Out of His causeless mercy, the Supreme Personality of Godhead Krsna appears in this world through His own potency and enjoys Himself among the most qualified women, His queens, as if He were engaging in ordinary, mundane, limited affairs. He reciprocates love ecstatically with His servitors, wives, friends, and parents to attract souls fruitlessly seeking pleasure in self-centered relationships that inevitably end in disappointment and sadness. His wives, whom He treats as queens, as well as all others with whom Krsna exchanged loving service, are not ordinary souls from this world. Rather, as Srila Prabhupada points out in his purport to text 35, they may appear to be mundane women, “but factually they are all transcendental liberated souls, perfect manifestations of internal energy.”

After hearing of Krsna’s exchanges with His queens—or friends, parents, or lovers, all fully described in the Tenth Canto—one may naturally wonder what impels Krsna to seek pleasure in exchanges of affection. In this world, a person’s motivation to act is impelled by personal shortcomings. If one did not need anything, one would not need to act, because action is meant to obtain what one lacks. Could Krsna lack something and therefore, like the conditioned souls, marry, steal, cry in childhood, or dance in a forest at night with other men’s wives? Counting the grains of sand on earth would be easier than attempting to assess Krsna’s psychology by examining one’s own.

Srila Jiva Gosvami helps our understanding in his comment on text 35 (Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 135): The Supreme Lord may sometimes seem to be lusty in His dealings with His consorts. However, what seems to be lust on His part is actually the purest love. This is seen in the following explanation of Srimad-Bhagavatam [1.11.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.35): sa esa nara'loke ’sminn, avattrnah sva-mdyayal reme stri'ratna'kutastho, bhaga-van prakrto yatha: “That Supreme Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna, out of His causeless mercy, appeared on this planet by His internal potency and enjoyed Himself among competent women as if He were engaging in mundane affairs.” The Lord does not enjoy pastimes with His queens because of the lust that is so well-known in the material world. Here the word ratna indicates that these women who associate with the Lord are very qualified. It indicates that they have great love for Him. Although the Lord’s pastimes with these women are different from anything in the material world, they superficially seem like the activities of the material world. This is described here by the words prdkrto yatha. Thus although the Lord’s pastimes may seem to be like ordinary activities, the idea that He is impelled by lust is refuted here.

Suta Gosvami continues his description of Krsna’s dealings with His queens in the next four texts (36-39). These texts penetrate and reveal the transcendental dynamics of Krsna’s pastimes. Suta uses these texts to conclude his description of the supramundane exhibitions of Lord Krsna’s intimate dealings with His beloved devotees, a topic we have been hearing about in chapters Seven through Eleven of the First Canto. “Although the queens’ beautiful smiles and furtive glances were all spotless and exciting, and although they could conquer Cupid himself by making him give up his bow in frustration, and although even the tolerant Siva could fall victim to them, still, despite all their magical feats and attractions, they could not agitate the senses of the Lord.” (Bhag. [1.11.36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.36)) In this world, loving dealings between men and women reign supreme, yet the Lord was unmoved by His queens’ attempts to entice Him.

Although the queens were unable to attract the Lord by their femininity, they did attract Him. Srila Prabhupada describes what attracts Krsna in his purport to text 36: “The queens could not satisfy the Lord by their feminine attractiveness, but they satisfied Him by their sincere affection and service. Only by unalloyed transcendental loving service could they satisfy the Lord, and the Lord was pleased to treat them as wives in reciprocation. Thus being satisfied by their unalloyed service only, the Lord reciprocated the service just like a devout husband. Otherwise He had no business becoming the husband of so many wives. He is the husband of everyone, but to one who accepts Him as such, He reciprocates.”

Suta Gosvami continues his explanation of Krsna’s intimate pastimes: The common materialistic conditioned souls speculate that the Lord is one of them. Out of their ignorance, they think that the Lord is affected by matter although He is unattached. He is the independent, all-powerful supreme controller, beyond matter, ignorance, and all shortcomings. All His actions are within the realm of bliss, full knowledge, and eternity. His true position defies the viewpoint from which we view ourselves and others.

Srila Prabhupada points out how ludicrous it is to use materialistic standards to criticize Krsna’s pastimes as unbefitting God: “When the Lord is found to act like an ordinary person in matrimonial bondage, they consider Him to be like one of them, without considering that the Lord can at once marry sixteen thousand wives or more. Due to a poor fund of knowledge they accept one side of the picture while disbelieving the other. This means that due to ignorance only they always think of Lord Krsna as like themselves and make their own conclusions, which are absurd and unauthentic from the version of the Snmad-Bhagavatam.” (Bhag. [1.11.37](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.37), purport)

Suta has thus far stated that Krsna’s acceptance of many thousands of queens was to reciprocate the specific pure desire of each of them to serve Him. No material desire or attachment can tinge the Lord; He is the independent Supreme Personality of Godhead, the controller of everything. His actions are always fully divine. As the ultimate source of all, He is all-powerful.

Neither He nor His devotees—those who have taken full shelter of Him—are influenced by matter. Srila Prabhupada describes the position of the Lord’s exalted devotees: “Even His learned devotees are not affected by the influence of the material modes. The great six Gosvamis of Vrndavana all came from greatly rich and aristocratic families, but when they adopted the life of mendicants at Vrndavana, superficially they appeared to be in wretched conditions of life, but factually they were the richest of all in spiritual values. Such maha-bhagavatas, or first-grade devotees, although moving amongst men, are not contaminated by honor or insult, hunger or satisfaction, sleep or wakefulness, which are all resultant actions of the three modes of material nature. Similarly, some of them are engaged in worldly dealings, yet are unaffected. Unless these neutralities of life are there, one cannot be considered situated in transcendence. The Divinity and His associates are on the same transcendental plane, and their glories are always sanctified by the action of yogamaya, or the internal potency of the Lord.” (Bhag. [1.11.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/11.38), purport)

Jiva comments (Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 138): The words yatha buddhis tad'dsraya (text 38) mean “the Lord’s consciousness is not like the consciousness of the conditioned souls who have taken shelter of the material nature.” These words may also be interpreted to mean “the great devotees who have taken shelter of the Lord have a consciousness like the Lord’s.” Thus even though they reside in the material world, they are not influenced by the modes of material nature.

The final verse of this section ends with a gift from Suta Gosvami, an esoteric truth woven into all of Krsna’s pastimes with His most intimate devotees: As Krsna’s queens exchanged loving sentiments with Krsna as their husband, they remained unaware of His position—ironically similar to the unawareness of atheists—as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Srila Prabhupada’s purport to the final text of this chapter (text 39) clarifies this truth further: “The Lord exchanges transcendental relations in five ways, as proprietor, master, friend, son and lover, and in each of these pastimes He plays fully by the potency of yogamaya, the internal potency. He plays exactly like an equal friend with the cowherd boys or even with friends like Arjuna. He plays exactly like a son in the presence of Yasodamata, He plays exactly like a lover in the presence of the cowherd damsels, and He plays exactly like a husband in the presence of the queens of Dvaraka. Such devotees of the Lord never think of the Lord as the Supreme, but think of Him exactly as a common friend, a pet son, or a lover or husband very much dear to heart and soul. That is the relation between the Lord and His transcendental devotees. . . . When the Lord descends, He does so along with His entourage to display a complete picture of the transcendental world, where pure love and devotion for the Lord prevail without any mundane tinge of lording it over the creation of the Lord. . . . The wives of Lord Krsna were made to forget the immeasurable glories of the Lord by the internal potency so that there might not be any flaw of exchange, and they took it for granted that the Lord was a henpecked husband, always following them in lonely places. . . . But since the dealings of the Lord with His wives are based on pure transcendental love and devotion, the wives are all on the transcendental plane without contamination.”

## Dialogue Six - Krsna’s Associates End Their Earthly Pastimes

## Chapter 13 - Dhrtarastra Quits Home

## Texts 1-17: Vidura Returns from Pilgrimage

Among his other questions at the beginning of Canto One, Chapter Four, Saunaka Rsi asked Suta Gosvami to speak about Maharaja Pariksit’s birth and activities (Bhag. [1.4.9-12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/4.9)). Suta began his answer in Chapter Twelve by describing Maharaja Pariksit’s birth. Later, in chapters Sixteen and Seventeen, Suta will describe Maharaja Pariksit’s activities. In chapters Eighteen and Nineteen, Suta Gosvami will describe the cursing of the great king, which is the immediate reason he heard the Bhagavatam from the sage Sukadeva Gosvami.

Before relating Maharaja Pariksit’s activities, beginning with his birth in Chapter Twelve, we will discuss chapters Thirteen through Fifteen, which tell of occurrences immediately after Krsna ended His pastimes in this world. Because these pastimes led to Maharaja Pariksit’s enthronement, they are part of the historical background leading up to Sukadeva Gosvami’s speaking the Bhagavatam. Srila Sridhara Svami comments on Bhagavatam [1.13.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.1) that unless both Vidura’s and Arjuna’s returns to Hastinapura are described along with how the Pandavas left their kingdom, it will not be clear how Pariksit became king and thus chastised Kali.

Just before the Battle of Kuruksetra, as we will learn in Canto Three, Chapter One, Vidura quit his palace-home after Duryodhana insulted him. While on pilgrimage, Vidura eventually heard of Lord Krsna’s departure from this world. The news devastated him. Soon after, he met the great devotee Uddhava, who had been in the Lord’s presence at the end and had, along with Maitreya Muni, heard His instructions just prior to His departure. Later, following Uddhava’s advice, Vidura took shelter of Maitreya and learned from him the science of Krsna consciousness (described in cantos Three and Four). When his questions were answered and Maitreya’s instructions complete, Vidura returned to Hastinapura. Canto One, Chapter Thirteen opens with Vidura’s dramatic reentry into his former home, now the Pandavas’ capital, after thirty years of pilgrimage. His mission? To save his aged brother Dhrtarastra from wasting the final days of his life mired in the opulence and illusions of a royal palace.

On seeing Vidura enter the palace, all the royal residents, including Maharaja Yudhisthira, hurried to greet him with delight. They had not seen Vidura for so many years that they had no longer been sure he was alive. For the Pandavas, Vidura’s return felt like regaining consciousness; Srila Sridhara Svami particularly describes Yudhisthira’s animation when he again met Vidura.

Vidura and the royalty of Hastinapura exchanged obeisances and, crying with affection, embraced one another. Yudhisthira Maharaja excitedly seated Vidura and offered him a meal. They treated him as a holy man, an advanced sadhu, not as an old friend or relative.

After allowing him time to rest, Yudhisthira inquired: “My uncle, do you remember how you always protected us, along with our mother, from all sorts of calamities? Your partiality, like the wings of a bird, saved us from poisoning and arson.” (Bhag. [1.13.8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.8)) Yudhisthira continued: You traveled for years. How did you maintain yourself? Which holy places did you visit? Actually, you yourself are a holy place, for you always carry the Supreme Lord in your heart. Wherever you stay, therefore, becomes a place of pilgrimage.

Srila Prabhupada’s striking purport to Bhagavatam [1.13.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.10) describes a sadhu's holiness: “The Personality of Godhead is omnipresent by His diverse potencies everywhere, just as the power of electricity is distributed everywhere within space. Similarly, the Lord’s omnipresence is perceived and manifested by His unalloyed devotees like Vidura, just as electricity is manifested in an electric bulb. A pure devotee like Vidura always feels the presence of the Lord everywhere. He sees everything in the potency of the Lord and the Lord in everything.... If anyone visits a holy place, he must search out the pure devotees residing in such holy places, take lessons from them, try to apply such instructions in practical life and thus gradually prepare oneself for the ultimate salvation, going back to Godhead.... The pure devotees hear from the authorities and chant, sing and write of the glories of the Lord. Mahamuni Vyasadeva heard from Narada, and then he chanted in writing; Sukadeva Gosvami studied from his father, and he described it to Pariksit; that is the way of Srimad-Bhagavatam.”

Yudhisthira Maharaja inquired further: In your travels, did you visit Dvaraka, Krsna’s home? Did you meet with His devotees, the residents of Dvaraka? Are they all well? Vidura replied to Yudhisthira’s earnest questions and gradually described everything he had experienced. Yet he neglected to reveal the news that Lord Krsna and the Yadu dynasty had departed from the world. Vidura felt compassion for the Pandavas and was unable to tolerate seeing them distressed. Thus he neglected to disclose this unbearable news.

Srila Prabhupada more fully explains Vidura’s mentality in his purport to text 13: “According to Niti'Sastra (civic laws) one should not speak an unpalatable truth to cause distress to others. Distress comes upon us in its own way by the laws of nature, so one should not aggravate it by propaganda. For a compassionate soul like Vidura, especially in his dealings with the beloved Pandavas, it was almost impossible to disclose an unpalatable piece of news like the annihilation of the Yadu dynasty. Therefore he purposely refrained from it.” Later, however, despite Vidura’s reticence, Yudhisthira Maharaja discovered for himself the details of the Lord’s departure.

Unlike Vidura, we tend to enjoy gossip, especially if it includes news of someone else’s difficulties. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura laments, para'duhkha sukhadtaro: “Others’ misery is a source of great delight for me.” If one refuses to propagate bad news, will others learn of it anyway? Miraculously, they will. One does not need to disseminate bad news; it will become disseminated on its own.

While living in the palace, Vidura noted that the Kuru kingdom was flourishing due to Yudhisthira’s piety. He also saw that Yudhisthira felt secure knowing that his grandson Pariksit was a competent heir to the Kuru throne. Nevertheless, Vidura knew that “insurmountable, eternal time imperceptibly overcomes those who are too much attached to family affairs and are always engrossed in their thought.” (Bhag. [1.13.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.17))

## Texts 18-28: Vidura Preaches Strongly to Dhrtarastra

Old, blind Dhrtarastra was well cared for, peaceful in old age, and surrounded by royal luxury. As comfortable as life was for him, however, Vidura knew that time’s insurmountable action would imperceptibly crush him. Then Dhrtarastra would die, his comfort destroyed by the ravages of death and his human life wasted without having developed spiritual knowledge. In his old age, Dhrtarastra felt himself dependent on his nephew Yudhisthira’s graciousness without understanding that he was actually dependent on Lord Krsna for his maintenance.

Vidura preached to Dhrtarastra in the presence of Maharaja Yudhisthira and other family members, hoping to break through Dhrta-rastra’s illusory sense of security. His compassion did not take the form of coddling a disheartened Dhrtarastra, whose one hundred sons had died at Kuruksetra. Rather, he said: “My dear King, please get out of here immediately. Do not delay. Just see how fear has overtaken you.” (Bhag. [1.13.18](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.18))

Everyone’s life duration is measured. In his purport, Srila Prabhupada amplifies Vidura’s words: “Cruel death cares for no one, be he Dhrtarastra or even Maharaja Yudhisthira; therefore spiritual instruction, as was given to old Dhrtarastra, was equally applicable to younger Maharaja Yudhisthira. As a matter of fact, everyone in the royal palace, including the King and his brothers and mother, was raptly attending the lectures. But it was known to Vidura that his instructions were especially meant for Dhrtarastra, who was too materialistic.” Srila Sridhara Svami states, in his comment on text 19, that no remedy exists in this world to counteract the effects of time.

Vidura addressed Dhrtarastra as “king”; this was another sarcastic cut from the sadhu’s sword. Dhrtarastra had always desired to be king, but his congenital blindness disallowed him from ascending the throne. Yet for many years Dhrtarastra had engaged in political intrigue against Yudhisthira and the Pandavas to fulfill his ambitions. Vidura wished to shatter Dhrtarastra’s current illusion of well-being. Thus he addressed him as “king” although he was in no way the king.

Vidura continued: This frightful situation cannot be remedied by any person in this material world. My lord, it is the Supreme Person as eternal time who has approached us all. Whoever is under the influence of eternal time must surrender his life, what to speak of his wealth, honor, children, land, and home. Nothing can check the cruel hands of death. Your position is precarious! Your father and your sons have already died. Your own body has been overtaken by invalidity, and you are now hard of hearing. Your memory has shortened, your teeth are loose, and you live as a dependent in another’s home. Still you wish to prolong your life more and more. Protect yourself by your own actions and by the Lord’s grace. Do not delay. Death awaits you nearby.

Vidura then cut even deeper: “Alas, how powerful are the hopes of a living being to continue his life. Verily, you are living just like a household dog and are eating remnants of food given by Bhima. There is no need to live a degraded life and subsist on the charity of those whom you tried to kill by arson and poisoning. You also insulted one of their wives and usurped their kingdom and wealth. Despite your unwillingness to die and your desire to live even at the cost of honor and prestige, your miserly body will certainly dwindle and deteriorate like an old garment.” (Bhag. [1.13.23-25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.23))

Vidura is speaking from compassion in an attempt to awaken Dhrtarastra from illusioned slumber: Time crushes all—our bodies, the mountains, the oceans. Как) ’smi loka^ksaya^krt pravrddho, lokan sama-hartum iha pravrttah: “Time I am,” Krsna says in Bhagavad-gita ([11.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/11.32)), “the great destroyer of the worlds, and I have come here to destroy all people.” Awakening to time’s devastating effect fills the heart with fear.

To combat this dread, Dhrtarastra had decided to dream of security —his kingship, family, and Yudhisthira’s dependable goodness. Vidura continued to wield the surgeon’s knife skillfully, using insults and prodding Dhrtarastra’s false dependence and attachment to his comfortable palace life. Vidura knew that all of this would ultimately lead to both material and spiritual death. Vidura said: Among the Pandavas is Bhima, who has killed each of your one hundred sons during the Battle of Kuruksetra, and here you are acting as if you are Bhima’s household dog, accepting whatever comfort and scraps of food he offers. Why accept humiliation in the form of charity from those against whom you’ve plotted and tried to kill? Open your eyes! Prepare for death, for it awaits you!

How should Dhrtarastra prepare? Vidura prescribes: Use what remains of your human life to associate with the Lord’s pure devotees. Thus you will awaken your transcendental sense of devotion, service, and surrender to the Lord. Become dhira. Free yourself from all obligations. Then go to a remote place to quit your material body, for it has become useless.

Vidura wanted Dhrtarastra to understand the inherent falsity and misery of this world. He told him that he should depend on no one in this world. Rather, he should leave home and depend fully on the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who resides in the heart. In his purport to text 27, Srila Prabhupada defines perfection as full dependence upon Krsna:

**Real perfection of the path of liberation is attained when one is prac~ ticed to depend fully on the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who lives in everyone’s heart as Paramatma. One may live in the darkest jungle alone out of home, but a steadfast devotee knows very well that he is not alone. The Supreme Personality of Godhead is with him, and He can protect His sincere devotee in any awkward circumstance. One should therefore practice devotional service at home, hearing and chanting the holy name, quality, form, pastimes, entourage, etc., in association with pure devotees, and this practice will help one awaken God consciousness in proportion to one’s sincerity of purpose.... One who desires material benefit by such devotional activities can never depend on the Supreme Personality of Godhead, although He sits in everyone’s heart. Nor does the Lord give any direction to persons who worship Him for material gain. Such materialistic devotees may be blessed by the Lord with material benefits, but they cannot reach the stage of the first-class human being.**

In his comment on text 26, Sridhara Svami explains that this verse defines a dhira, a wise man. One is wise when he tolerantly suffers in this world while attaining a spiritual result.

In his purports to texts 25-28, Prabhupada differentiates between a krpana, a dhira, a sannyasi, and a narottama. A. krpana is a miserly man who fails to use his valuable human birth for spiritual advancement. Rather, he uses his life to pursue only the temporary. A dhira is one who is undisturbed even in the presence of something disturbing. A dhira is able to renounce family relationships for spiritual advancement and become a sannyasi. Sannyasis may be of two kinds: those who have renounced family relationships and accepted the renounced order out of frustration with material life, and those who are narottama, first-class human beings, and who are sincere, pure devotees practiced in depending fully on the Supreme Lord Sri Krsna.

Srila Prabhupada summarizes Vidura’s instructions to Dhrtarastra in his purport to text 28: “To become narottama, or a first-class human being depending completely on the Supreme Lord Sri Krsna, is not possible for any ordinary man. It is stated in Bhagavad-gita ([7.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/7.28)) that a person who is completely relieved of all taints of sinful acts can alone depend on the Supreme Lord Sri Krsna, the Personality of Godhead. Dhrtarastra was advised by Vidura at least to become a dhira in the beginning if it were impossible for him to become a sannyasi or a narottama. Persistently endeavoring on the line of self-realization helps a person to rise to the conditions of a narottama from the stage of a dhira.”

Vidura now spoke privately to Dhrtarastra: “Please, therefore, leave for the North immediately, without letting your relatives know, for soon that time will approach which will diminish the good qualities of men.” (Bhag. [1.13.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.28)) Vidura knew that Kali-yuga was approaching rapidly. In Kali-yuga, passion amid madness would prevail. Animallike men would term as progress their foolish plans, even as one plan after another ended in disaster.

Television, videos, computers, corruption, polluted water and food, debt, sensuality, violence, manipulative advertisements, insanity, abortion, anxiety, cruelty, intoxication, speculative money-making, corrupt authority, dreadful disease, fear—all would contaminate the world. Still, people would think civilization was advancing. Vidura therefore advised Dhrtarastra to act quickly, for the spiritual impetus that he was creating by his words would soon fade before Kali’s charge. Kali-yuga’s influence would spread and degrade everyone, even Dhrtarastra, to the lowest standard.

## Texts 29-37: Dhrtarastra Leaves Home

Vidura’s potent words convinced Dhrtarastra. With resolute determination, he immediately broke the strong network of his family entanglement, which was filled with frustration, economics, opulence, and politics, to walk the path of perfection. In his purport to text 29, Prabhupada likens the way Vidura influenced Dhrtarastra to how his own Guru Maharaja influenced him: “Lord Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu, the great preacher of the principles of Srimad-Bhagavatam, has stressed the importance of association with sadhus, pure devotees of the Lord. He said that even by a moment’s association with a pure devotee, one can achieve all perfection. We are not ashamed to admit that this fact was experienced in our practical life. Were we not favored by His Divine Grace Srimad Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Gosvami Maharaja, by our first meeting for a few minutes only, it would have been impossible for us to accept this mighty task of describing Srimad-Bhagavatam in English. Without seeing him at that opportune moment, we could have become a very great business magnate, but never would we have been able to walk the path of liberation and be engaged in the factual service of the Lord under instructions of His Divine Grace. And here is another practical example by the action of Vidura’s association with Dhrtarastra.”

Without telling anyone, Vidura, Dhrtarastra, and the gentle and chaste Gandhari left the palace and headed for the harshness of the Himalayan slopes, “which are the delight of those who have accepted the staff of the renounced order like fighters who have accepted a good lashing from the enemy.” (Bhag. [1.13.30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.30))

The next morning, Yudhisthira, ignorant of Dhrtarastra’s departure, entered Dhrtarastra’s palace rooms to offer his respects, but his uncles and aunt were gone. He turned anxiously to Dhrtarastra’s secretary, Safijaya: “Where is our uncle, who is old and blind? Where is my well-wisher, uncle Vidura, and mother Gandhari, who is very afflicted due to all her sons’ demise? My uncle Dhrtarastra was also very mortified due to the death of all his sons and grandsons. Undoubtedly I am very ungrateful.” (Bhag. [1.13.32-33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.32)) Yudhisthira no longer remembered Dhrtarastra’s aggression toward his family. Instead, he thought of how Dhrtarastra had cared for him and his young brothers when they had become orphans. He was also aware that his uncle and aunt were still grieving the loss of their one hundred sons killed by Bhima during the Battle of Kuruksetra. As the leader of the opposing army, Yudhisthira felt personally responsible for their deaths. Now pious Yudhisthira, focused only on his own faults, saw his own ingratitude. He feared that his actions and his uncle and aunt’s grief might have driven them to suddenly decide to end their lives by drowning themselves in the Ganges.

Despite Yudhisthira Maharaja’s regrets, he was faultless. In his purport to text 33, Srila Prabhupada, pointing to Maharaja Yudhisthira’s astonishing goodness, instructs us how to improve our own behavior: “As a pious man, Maharaja Yudhisthira took into account all his unavoidable misdeeds, and he never thought of the misdeeds of his uncle and company. Dhrtarastra had suffered the effects of his own misdeeds by the will of the Lord, but Maharaja Yudhisthira was thinking only of his own unavoidable misdeeds. That is the nature of a good man and devotee of the Lord. A devotee never finds fault with others, but tries to find his own and thus rectify them as far as possible.”

Yudhisthira asked Sanjaya what had happened to Dhrtarastra and Gandhari because Sanjaya had assisted the blind Dhrtarastra for so many years, but Sanjaya was too distressed by Dhrtarastra’s absence to respond. He was aware of Dhrtarastra’s grief at the loss of his sons, but was unaware, as Srila Prabhupada notes in his purport to text 35, that Vidura had awakened Dhrtarastra’s “inner vision” and that he had “therefore. . . left home in enthusiastic cheerfulness for a better life after departure from the dark well of home.” Prabhupada adds: “Unless one is convinced of a better life after renunciation of the present life, one cannot stick to the renounced order of life simply by artificial dress or staying out of the home.”

Gradually Sanjaya composed himself. Wiping tears from his eyes, he told Yudhisthira: Although I was constantly with Dhrtarastra as his personal assistant, and although he would do nothing without consulting me, he nevertheless disclosed nothing of his plan to leave home. “. .. I have no information of the determination of your two uncles and Gandhari. О King, I have been cheated by those great souls.” (Bhag. [1.13.37](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.37))

Prabhupada speaks of this “cheating” in his purport: “That great souls cheat others may be astonishing to know, but it is a fact that great souls cheat others for a great cause. It is said that Lord Krsna also advised Yudhisthira to tell a lie before Dronacarya, and it was also for a great cause. The Lord wanted it, and therefore it was a great cause. Satisfaction of the Lord is the criterion of one who is bona fide, and the highest perfection of life is to satisfy the Lord by one’s occupational duty. That is the verdict of Gita \[[18.46](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/18.46)\] and Bhagavatam \[[1.2.13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.13)\].”

## Texts 38-50: Sri Narada Muni Arrives to Preach to Yudhisthira

Much illusion may exist in a relationship where one person depends on another. Both the dependent and the one on whom he is depending generally remain unconscious that it is Krsna who is actually the maintainer.

Dhrtarastra had thought himself fully dependent on Maharaja Yudhisthira, the other Pandavas, and Sanjaya. Vidura came to Hastinapura specifically to crack that illusion. But Yudhisthira also suffered from illusion in that he considered himself Dhrtarastra’s maintainer. Of these two illusions—the illusion of the dependent and the illusion of the maintainer—the illusion of the maintainer is stronger. The common saying is correct: “The father is more attached to the son than the son to the father.” Now it was Yudhisthira’s turn to have his illusion removed.

As Yudhisthira and Sanjaya were lamenting, everyone present began to hear the vibrating strings of a vina along with the sweet sound of Krsna’s transcendental names. Suddenly the great saint Narada Muni arrived. Maharaja Yudhisthira and his brothers stood up to offer respects. Yudhisthira Maharaja exclaimed: О godly personality, I do not know where my two uncles have gone. Nor can I find my ascetic aunt, who is grief-stricken with the loss of her sons.

Narada Muni’s philosophical reply pointed Yudhisthira toward the ultimate maintainer: Do not lament for anyone, because everyone is under the control of the Supreme Lord. It is He only who brings souls together and disperses them. All people attain their fate—either suffering or enjoyment—due to their karma, the reactions to their past deeds.

Srila Prabhupada clarifies one’s dependence on the law of karma in his purport to text 41: “Ordinarily one cannot change the course of one’s due happiness and distress by plan. Everyone has to accept them as they come under the subtle arrangement of kola, or invincible time. There is no use trying to counteract them. The best thing is, therefore, that one should endeavor to achieve salvation, and this prerogative is given only to man because of his developed condition of mental activities and intelligence.” Srila Sridhara Svami mentions that Narada Muni wanted to rescue Yudhisthira Maharaja from grief by telling him of Dhrtarastra’s fate, but he first wished to preach to Yudhisthira about the identity of the actual controller.

Sri Narada Muni continued: No one can avoid the Lord’s control. One may willingly follow His commands or unwillingly submit, forced to accept reactions due to noncompliance. In either case, either willingly or unwillingly, one must necessarily submit to Him, for the Lord is the supreme controller. One should simply act dutifully, for other actions and attempts will entangle one in the illusion of this world. “As a player sets up and disperses his playthings according to his own sweet will, so the supreme will of the Lord brings men together and separates them.” (Bhag. [1.13.43](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.43)) Thus as Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport, “We must know for certain that the particular position in which we are now set up is an arrangement of the supreme will in terms of our own acts in the past.” Srila Prabhupada adds, “\[TJhe Lord is the supreme will.” Narada assured Yudhisthira that the pain he felt at Dhrtarastra’s separation was “due only to illusory affection and nothing more.” (Bhag. [1.13.44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.44)) The soul is eternal and the body ephemeral. What, then, is worthy of lamentation? “Therefore give up your anxiety due to ignorance of the self. You are now thinking of how they, who are helpless poor creatures, will exist without you.” (Bhag. [1.13.45](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.45)) It is the Lord, not Yudhisthira, who is bhiita'bhrt, the protector of all living beings. Considering that every material body is made of and fully controlled by time, karma, and the three modes of material nature, Narada states, how “then can it, being already in the jaws of the serpent, protect others?” (Bhag. [1.13.46](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.46))

One can protect others only to the degree that one can control both others and the environment. Narada Muni told Yudhisthira that he himself was completely controlled, trapped in the jaws of the serpent of time. How, then, could he protect Dhrtarastra or anyone else? Narada continued: You may fear that your uncle, alone and away from your protection, may be eaten by some animal. Even if that happens, it is not worthy of lamentation. The law of nature states, “Those who are devoid of hands are prey for those who have hands; those devoid of legs are prey for the four-legged. The weak are the subsistence of the strong, and the general rule holds that one living being is food for another.” (Bhag. [1.13.47](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.47)) No one escapes this struggle for existence.

Nor should Yudhisthira worry about his uncle and aunt’s sustenance, for as Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 47, they could live on vegetables in the jungles as the Supreme Lord’s prasadam and thus realize the path of salvation. Birds and beasts are all supplied their food. Dhrtarastra would also be fed. On the other hand, even if he were to become food for a tiger, why should Yudhisthira grieve? Nature’s law states that every embodied being must die.

Narada Muni preached “hard” philosophy to force detachment to appear in Yudhisthira’s heart. He wanted him to remember that ultimately Krsna is the only protector. Others, if Krsna permits, may protect one to some degree, but who but Krsna can protect one from death? Who can protect someone if Krsna has not sanctioned it? If one is not habituated to focusing on Krsna as one’s protector, he will develop the tendency to depend on “fallible soldiers,” and thus his position will be precarious.

At the same time, one should be dutiful. If one’s duty is to protect others, he should protect them. If it is one’s duty to accept protection, he should act accordingly. But whether protector or protected, one should focus his mind on Krsna, knowing that ultimately Krsna and no other is one’s shelter. Narada Muni therefore states: Rather than lamenting the fate of Dhrtarastra and Gandhari, you yourself “should look to the Supreme Lord only. . . • That Supreme Personality of Godhead, Lord Sri Krsna, in the guise of all-devouring time \[kola-гйра\] has now descended on earth to eliminate the envious from the world.” (Bhag. [1.13.48-49](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.48))

How does one look—either toward or away—from someone who is all-pervading? Srila Sridhara Svami comments on text 49: Look to the Lord? But where is He now? He is in Dvaraka. He has assumed the form of destroyer, but His real form is bliss. Srila Prabhupada states: “For the devotees His factual form is disclosed, and for the nondevotees He appears like kala'rupa, which is \[His\] causal form. This causal form of the Lord is not at all pleasing to the asuras, and therefore they think of the Lord as formless in order to feel secure that they will not be vanquished by the Lord.” (Bhag. [1.13.49](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.49), purport)

What does Prabhupada mean by “causal form”? Through Krsna’s kala'ritpa, His energy of time, the world is forced to accept change. As stated in Sri Visnu Purana ([1.9.44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/vp/1.9.44)), “Seconds, minutes, hours, and all other units of time are all manifested from the potency of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” Like a great stirring rod in a pot, Krsna’s time energy moves everyone through their karma. Time may

elevate us one moment and smash us on the rocks of our fate the next. Today we are rich, and tomorrow poverty may overwhelm us. We may experience condemnation now and praise later. Time is unstoppable, and it forces us to change. For nondevotees, time ultimately means death. Devotees, however, experience time as Krsna carrying them toward Him; they may also experience time as Yudhisthira did: as beautiful Krsna who is present in Dvaraka. Krsna is all-destroying time, but He is also the sac-cid-ananda Lord who performs blissful pastimes with His relatives and citizens in the palaces at Dvaraka.

Narada Muni continued: “The Lord has already performed His duties to help the demigods, and He is awaiting the rest. You Pandavas may wait as long as the Lord is here on earth.” (Bhag. [1.13.50](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.50)) Narada Muni is hinting at Krsna’s disappearance, but like Vidura he does not directly disclose the fact that Krsna has already departed. Rather, as Srila Prabhupada points out in his purport to text 50, Narada only “indirectly gave a hint to the King and his brothers to wait till the incident happened and the Lord departed.”

Narada’s preaching about illusion, continuously shifting matter, the eternal nature of the soul, and the soul’s natural dependence on and subservience to the Lord is summarized and concluded in Srila Prabhupada’s purport to text 48: “There is ... a regular current from the Lord Himself, from within and without, by which to rectify the fallen condition of the living being. From within He corrects the desiring living beings as localized Paramatma, and from without He corrects by His manifestations, the spiritual master and the revealed scriptures. One should look unto the Lord; one should not be disturbed by the so-called manifestations of happiness or distress, but he should try to cooperate with the Lord in His outward activities for correcting the fallen souls. By His order only, one should become a spiritual master and cooperate with the Lord. One should not become a spiritual master for one’s personal benefit, for some material gain or as an avenue of business or occupation for earning livelihood. Bona fide spiritual masters who look unto the Supreme Lord to cooperate with Him are actually qualitatively one with the Lord, and the forgetful ones are perverted reflections only. Yudhisthira Maharaja is advised by Narada, therefore, not to be disturbed by the affairs of so-called happiness and distress, but to look only unto the Lord to execute the mission for which the Lord has descended. That was his prime duty.”

## Texts 51-60: Narada Muni Now Reveals to Yudhisthira that Dhrtarastra Will Meet a Glorious Death

After speaking to Maharaja Yudhisthira philosophy that should direct his actions, Narada describes what will soon happen to Dhrtarastra and Gandhari. “O King, your uncle Dhrtarastra, his brother Vidura and his wife Gandhari have gone to the southern side of the Himalaya Mountains, where there are shelters of the great sages.” (Bhag. [1.13.51](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.51)) He is now bathing three times daily, beginning to practice astahga'yoga, and performing fire sacrifices. He eats nothing and drinks only water. All these austerities help him control his mind and senses and free himself from familial affection and the contamination of the three modes of material nature. Gradually, by purifying his consciousness, Dhrtarastra will suspend the action of his senses and cross beyond all hindrances to liberation and spiritual perfection. “O King, he will quit his body, most probably on the fifth day from today. And his body will turn to ashes.” (Bhag. [1.13.57](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.57)) There is no need nor time for you go and try to bring him back.

Nor was Yudhisthira needed to assist Gandhari. “While outside observing her husband, who will burn in the fire of mystic power along with his thatched cottage, his chaste wife will enter the fire with rapt attention.” (Bhag. [1.13.58](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.58)) And Vidura? “Vidura, being affected with delight and grief, will then leave that place of sacred pilgrimage.” (Bhag. [1.13.59](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.59))

Srila Prabhupada explains Vidura’s thoughts on observing his brother’s marvelous departure as a liberated yogi; “Of course it was only due to Vidura that his brother attained the desirable goal of life. Vidura was therefore glad to learn about it. But he was sorry that he could not make his brother turn into a pure devotee. This was not done by Vidura because of Dhrtarastra’s being inimical to the Pandavas, who were all devotees of the Lord. An offense at the feet of a Vaisnava is more dangerous than an offense at the lotus feet of the Lord. Vidura was certainly very liberal to bestow mercy upon his brother Dhrtarastra, whose past life was very materialistic. But ultimately the result of such mercy certainly depended on the will of the Supreme Lord in the present life; therefore Dhrtarastra attained liberation only, and after many such liberated states of life one can attain to the stage of devotional service.” (Bhag. [1.13.59](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.59), purport)

On the one hand, one has philosophy, and on the other, natural sentiment. Even Vidura, who had preached so powerfully to his brother and the others, felt both joy and sorrow on Dhrtarastra’s death. Srila Prabhupada continues: “Vidura was certainly very mortified by the death of his brother and sister-in-law, and the only remedy to mitigate such lamentation was to go out to pilgrimage. Thus Maharaja Yudhisthira had no chance to call back Vidura, his surviving uncle.”

“Having spoken thus, the great sage Narada, along with his vina, ascended into outer space. Yudhisthira kept his instruction in his heart and so was able to get rid of all lamentations.’’ (Bhag. [1.13.60](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.60))

## Chapter 14 - The Disappearance of Lord Krsna

## Texts 1-21: Arjuna Fails to Return from Dvaraka on Schedule and Inauspicious Omens Manifest

Suta Gosvami tells the sages of Naimisaranya that months earlier Arjuna had gone to Dvaraka to see Sri Krsna, his dearmost friend, and others. Arjuna also wished to learn from the Lord of His future activities. But Arjuna had not returned. Maharaja Yudhisthira then began to observe fearful omens that filled him with anxiety for both Arjuna and the residents of Dvaraka. He waited for news. Yudhisthira wondered: As nothing inauspicious can occur in Krsna’s presence, could the Lord have disappeared from this world?

Krsna’s pastimes resemble the activities of human beings, and it is therefore difficult to understand that they are divine. Of course, even His humanlike activities are quite unhumanlike and extraordinary. For example, as a young boy, Krsna herded cows and played with His friends, but He also killed one demon after another and lifted a hill with the little finger of His left hand. Krsna also married. Anyone can marry, but when Krsna married, He married more than 16,000 queens and lived simultaneously with each queen, each situated in her own palace. When Krsna danced with young girls in the moonlight, He expanded and placed Himself between each pair of dancing partners. Actually, all of Krsna’s activities are intimate exchanges with His beloved devotees and are enacted to satisfy their desires. Although He is self-satisfied, Krsna married so many wives to reciprocate the love of those particular devotees—to cause His beloved devotee-queens to swim in an ocean of ecstasy.

Of all of Krsna’s pastimes, His disappearance may be the most difficult to understand. After all, how can God die? Krsna’s “death” indicates a continuance of His pastimes in another place. Like the sun, He sets in one field while rising in another. Krsna’s “death,” therefore, is not death as it is understood in the material world. Rather, it is a departure— a word that indicates His arrival in a different universe. Lord Brahma’s words in Bhagavatam [11.6.21-27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/6.21) and Sri Krsna’s in [11.6.28-31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/6.28) describe Krsna’s disappearance after the completion of His mission (detailed in Bhagavad-gita [4.7-8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/4.7)). Brahma speaks these words after the Battle of Kuruksetra but prior to the deaths of the members of the Yadu dynasty. He and other demigods had approached the Lord in Dvaraka. They first offered prayers. Brahma then said:

My dear Lord, previously we requested You to remove the burden of the earth. О unlimited Personality of Godhead, that request has certainly been fulfilled. . . . You have reestablished the principles of religion among pious men . . . You have also distributed Your glories all over the world, and thus the whole world can be purified by hearing about You. Descending into the dynasty of King Yadu, You have manifested Your unique transcendental form, and for the benefit of the entire universe You have executed magnanimous transcendental activities. My dear Lord, those pious and saintly persons who in the age of Kali hear about Your transcendental activities and also glorify them will easily cross over the darkness of the age. О Supreme Personality of Godhead, О my Lord, You have descended into the Yadu dynasty, and thus You have spent one hundred twenty-five autumns with Your devotees. My dear Lord, there is nothing remaining at this time for Your Lordship to do on behalf of the demigods. You have already withdrawn Your dynasty by the curse of the brahmanas. О Lord, You are the basis of everything, and if You so desire, kindly return now to Your own abode in the spiritual world. At the same time, we humbly beg that You always protect us. We are Your humble servants, and on Your behalf we are managing the universal situation. We, along with our planets and followers, require Your constant protection.

The Supreme Lord replied: О Brahma, “I understand your prayers and request. Having removed the burden of the earth, I have executed everything required on your behalf. That very Yadava dynasty in which I appeared became greatly magnified in opulence, especially in their physical strength and courage, to the extent that they threatened to devour the whole world. Therefore I have stopped them, just as the shore holds back the great ocean. If I were to leave this world without withdrawing the overly-proud members of the Yadu dynasty, the whole world would be destroyed by the deluge of their unlimited expansion. Now due to the brahmana’s curse, the annihilation of My family has already begun. О sinless Brahma, when this annihilation is finished and I am en route to Vaikuntha, 1 will pay a small visit to your abode.”

After the destruction of the Yadu dynasty, the Lord Himself departed, His mission complete. “As soon as Lord Sri Krsna left the earth, Truth, Religion, Faithfulness, Glory and Beauty immediately followed Him.” (Bhag. [11.31.7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/31.7)) Then Kali-yuga began its onslaught of quarrel and inauspiciousness. Yudhisthira had already begun to notice seasonal irregularities as well as an increase in greed, anger, and deceit among his citizens. Foul means of earning a livelihood were becoming standard. Cheating abounded, and friendships and family relationships seemed to suffer from perpetual misunderstandings. Dealings between husbands and wives were becoming fraught with strain and quarrel.

Yudhisthira speaks to Bhimasena (Bhag. [1.14.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/14.6)): I sent Arjuna to Dvaraka, but seven months have passed since his departure. Has the time Narada Muni foretold already arrived? Has the Lord ended His pastimes on earth? Just see how the planetary configurations forebode danger. Notice how the left side of my body quivers and my heart palpitates. The she-jackal cries at the rising sun while vomiting fire. Dogs fearlessly bark at me, cows pass on my left, and asses walk around me. My horses look like they are weeping. Listen! Owls shriek and violent winds blow dust everywhere. Butter no longer ignites fire, and the calves no longer suck the teats of cows but stand with tears in their eyes. Bulls no longer take pleasure in the pasturing ground. Even the Deities in the temples appear to be crying. Are They about to leave? Everything seems stripped of its beauty. What calamities await us? What is this extraordinary time? What will happen next? The great fear in Yudhisthira’s heart thus escaped through his mouth and entered Bhimasena’s ears. “I think that all these earthly disturbances indicate some greater loss to the good fortune of the world. The world was fortunate to have been marked with the footprints of the lotus feet of the Lord. These signs indicate that this will no longer be.” (Bhag. [1.14.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/14.21))

In his purport to text 8, Prabhupada discusses Yudhisthira’s lamentation and Sri Krsna’s departure from this world: “When Maharaja Yudhisthira was lamenting the possibility of \[Krsna’s\] disappearance, it was just in pursuance of a custom of lamenting the disappearance of a great friend, but factually the Lord never quits His transcendental body, as is misconceived by less intelligent persons. Such less intelligent persons have been condemned by the Lord Himself in Bhagavad-gita, and they are known as the mudhas. That the Lord left His body means that He left again His plenary portions in the respective dhamas (transcendental abodes), as He left His virdt-гйра in the material world.”

Kali-yuga, with its accompanying omens, terrors, and miseries, had begun. Prabhupada comments on Kali’s arrival in his purport to Bhagavatam [1.15.36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.36): “The age of Kali ensued just after the Battle of Kuruksetra, but it could not exert its influence because of the presence of the Lord. The Lord, however, left this earthly planet in His own transcendental body, and as soon as He left, the symptoms of Kali-yuga, as were envisioned by Maharaja Yudhisthira prior to Arjuna’s arrival from Dvaraka, began to manifest, and Maharaja Yudhisthira rightly conjectured on the departure of the Lord from the earth.”

To remove Kali’s disastrous effects, one may heed Srila Prabhupada’s purport to Bhagavatam [1.14.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/14.3): “Ignorance is the cause for all these anomalies in human society, and to remove this ignorance, especially in this age of degradation, the powerful sun is there to distribute light in the shape of Srimad-Bhagavatam.”

## Texts 22-44: Arjuna Returns and Yudhisthira Inquires from Him

Just then Arjuna returned to Hastinapura. He bowed at Yudhisthira’s feet but kept his head lowered. Tears glided from his lotus eyes and ran down his cheeks. Yudhisthira saw that Arjuna, his bold and powerful warrior brother, looked pale and anxious. Remembering again the indications Narada had given him, Yudhisthira questioned Arjuna about the well-being of the residents of Dvaraka: How are our relatives? Are they passing their days in happiness? Is our respectable grandfather Surasena in a happy mood? Are Vasudeva, his younger brothers, and his seven wives well? How is Balarama, the Personality of Godhead and the protector of devotees? Are Pradyumna, the great general of the Vrsni family, and Aniruddha, the plenary expansion of the Personality of Godhead, faring well? And the sons and companions of Lord Krsna— are they doing well? Do they, who are all eternally bound in friendship with us, remember our welfare?

Srila Prabhupada speaks of Lord Balarama, Krsna’s older brother and first expansion, in his purport to text 29: “Amongst various names of the relatives, the name of Rama or Balarama, eldest brother of Lord Krsna, is added with the words ‘the Personality of Godhead’ because Lord Balarama is the immediate expansion of visnu'tattva as prakasa' vigraha of Lord Krsna. ... Sri Rama, or Balarama, is the protector of the devotees of the Lord. Baladeva acts as the spiritual master of all devotees, and by His causeless mercy the fallen souls are delivered. Sri Baladeva appeared as Sri Nityananda Prabhu during the advent of Lord Caitanya, and the great Lord Nityananda Prabhu exhibited His causeless mercy by delivering a pair of extremely fallen souls, namely Jagai and Madhai. Therefore it is particularly mentioned herein that Balarama is the protector of the devotees of the Lord. By His divine grace only one can approach the Supreme Lord Sri Krsna, and thus Sri Balarama is the mercy incarnation of the Lord, manifested as the spiritual master, the savior of the pure devotees.”

Yudhisthira Maharaja asked about Krsna’s eternal Dvaraka companions and associates such as Srutadeva, Uddhava, Nanda, Sunanda, and others. In his purport to text 33 Srila Prabhupada contrasts these eternally liberated associates of Krsna, who have descended with the Lord to participate with Him in His pastimes, with the conditioned jivas caught in the material world: “The jiva-tattvas are infinitesimal potential particles of the Lord, and therefore they require the protection of the Lord at all times. And to the eternal servitors of the Lord, the Lord is pleased to give all protection at all times. The liberated souls never, therefore, think themselves as free as the Lord or as powerful as the Lord, but they always seek the protection of the Lord in all circumstances, both in the material world and in the spiritual world. This dependence of the liberated soul is constitutional, for the liberated souls are like sparks of a fire that are able to exhibit the glow of fire along with the fire and not independently. Independently the glow of the sparks is extinguished, although the quality of fire or the glowing is there. Thus those who give up the protection of the Lord and become so-called lords themselves, out of spiritual ignorance, come back again to this material world, even after prolonged tapasya of the severest type. That is the verdict of all Vedic literature.”

Yudhisthira Maharaja continued his inquiry by asking directly about Lord Krsna, who eternally resides in Dvaraka. “Is Lord Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who gives pleasure to the cows, the senses and the brahmanas, who is very affectionate towards His devotees, enjoying the pious assembly at Dvaraka Puri surrounded by friends? The original Personality of Godhead, the enjoyer, and Balarama, the primeval Lord Ananta, are staying in the ocean of the Yadu dynasty for the welfare, protection and general progress of the entire universe. And the members of the Yadu dynasty, being protected by the arms of the Lord, are enjoying life like the residents of the spiritual sky.” Krsna’s queens enjoy pleasures meant for the wives of the king of heaven simply because they offer comfort to the Lord’s lotus feet. “The great heroes of the Yadu dynasty, being protected by the arms of Lord Sri Krsna, always remain fearless in every respect.” (Bhag. [1.14.34-36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/14.34), [38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/14.38))

Prabhupada comments on text 34: “Since the Lord is all-perfect in Himself, there could not be any question of His welfare, and Maharaja Yudhisthira refrained from asking this question.” In a different mood and for a different purpose, Srila Sridhara Svami mentions that text 34, as well as the other texts cited above (35-38), are statements not questions, but appended to each is the heart of Yudhisthira’s inquiry: “Is Govinda well?”

Srila Prabhupada also comments in his purport to text 38 on the fearlessness of the members of the Yadu dynasty: “A forgetful, conditioned soul is fearful. But a liberated soul is never fearful, just as a small child completely dependent on the mercy of his father is never fearful of anyone. Fearfulness is a sort of illusion for the living being when he is in slumber and forgetting his eternal relation with the Lord. Since the living being is never to die by his constitution, as stated in Bhagavad-gita (2.20), then what is the cause of fearfulness? A person may be fearful of a tiger in a dream, but another man who is awake by his side sees no tiger there. The tiger is a myth for both of them, namely the person dreaming and the person awake, because actually there is no tiger; but the man forgetful of his awakened life is fearful, whereas the man who has not forgotten his position is not at all fearful. Thus the members of the Yadu dynasty were fully awake in their service to the Lord, and therefore there was no tiger for them to be afraid of at any time. Even if there were a real tiger, the Lord was there to protect them.”

Srila Prabhupada’s short purport to text 39 reveals the thoughts behind Yudhisthira Maharaja’s next questions about Arjuna’s forlorn appearance: “From all angles of vision, the Maharaja inquired from Arjuna about the welfare of Dvaraka, but he concluded at last that as long as Lord Sri Krsna Himself was there, nothing inauspicious could happen. But at the same time, Arjuna appeared to be bereft of his bodily luster, and thus the King inquired of his personal welfare and asked so many vital questions.”

It’s interesting that Yudhisthira’s questions all point to faults in performing a ksatriya’s duty, any of which might have caused Arjuna’s sense of dejection, for he possessed the character of an exalted ksat-riya. Thus Yudhisthira inquired further: My dear brother Arjuna, what has happened to you? Is your health all right? Your bodily luster appears diminished. Have you been disrespected during your long stay in Dvaraka? Has someone threatened you? Have you found yourself unable to give charity to a deserving person? Were you unable to keep your promise? Have brahmanas, children, cows, women, and the diseased approached you for shelter but you were unable to protect them? Have you mistreated women? Have you been defeated by an equal or someone inferior to you? Have you not fed those worthy of being fed or committed some unpardonable mistake?

Finally, on the basis of Narada Muni’s indication and being unable to see any other cause for Arjuna’s distress, Yudhisthira asked frankly: Or, my dear brother, are you “feeling empty for all time because you might have lost your most intimate friend, Lord Krsna? О my brother Arjuna, I can think of no other reason for your becoming so dejected.” (Bhag. [1.14.44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/14.44))

## Chapter 15 - The Pandavas Retire Timely

## Texts 1-26: Arjuna Reveals the Loss of his Dearmost Friend And Remembers their Intimate Dealings

Suta Gosvami relates how Arjuna’s lotuslike heart dried up and his bodily luster diminished even further after he heard Yudhisthira Maharaja’s questions. His throat was constricted with grief, and he was unable to utter a word in reply. Krsna’s celebrated friend was grief-stricken in his separation from the Lord, who had acted as his well-wisher, benefactor, intimate cousin, and chariot driver. Remembering Krsna and distressed by the Lord’s absence, Arjuna felt his affection for Krsna overflow. In his comment on texts 3-4, Srila Sridhara Svami describes that Arjuna’s eyes filled with tears and he was wiping away with his palm those that had already fallen. His voice was indistinct because his throat was so constricted. He began to sob and could not speak.

Finally, although overwhelmed and breathing heavily, Arjuna said: “O King! The Supreme Personality of Godhead Hari, who treated me exactly like an intimate friend, has left me alone. Thus my astounding power, which astonished even the demigods, is no longer with me. I have just lost Him whose separation for a moment would render all the universes unfavorable and void, like bodies without life.” (Bhag. [1.15.5-6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.5))

It is clear that because Arjuna (in text 5) refers to Krsna as Hari, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, he was aware of His power and opulence. Arjuna’s lamentation, therefore, was not due to thinking a calamity had befallen his dearmost friend; it was caused by his ecstatic love for Krsna. Srila Prabhupada writes: “Factually for a living being there is no one dearer than the Lord.” (Bhag. [1.15.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.6), purport) In the purport to text 5, Srila Prabhupada’s comment on Arjuna’s loss of his power is directed toward every soul: “The power and energy which were bestowed upon Arjuna were required for fulfillment of the mission of the Lord, but when His mission was fulfilled, the emergency powers were withdrawn from Arjuna because the astounding powers of Arjuna, which were astonishing even to the denizens of heaven, were no longer required, and they were not meant for going back home, back to Godhead. If endowment of powers and withdrawal of powers by the Lord are possible even for a great devotee like Arjuna, or even the demigods in heaven, then what to speak of the ordinary living beings who are but figs compared to such great souls. The lesson is, therefore, that no one should be puffed up for his powers borrowed from the Lord. The sane man should rather feel obliged to the Lord for such benefactions and must utilize such power for the service of the Lord. Such power can be withdrawn at any time by the Lord, so the best use of such power and opulence is to engage them in the service of the Lord.”

Although one’s own empowerment—one’s abilities, strengths, and possessions—may be insignificant compared to that of Arjuna, it too is only temporarily. Would it be legitimate for one to become proud if, for a few hours, he were to be driven around town in a wealthy man’s plush car? Whatever drop from Krsna’s unlimited ocean of opulence He may bestow on us is never truly our own. Everything can vanish in a moment. In addition, whatever grace one does obtain —even for the flicker of a moment—should not be squandered on selfish, petty acts. Rather, one should be determined to use everything Krsna has kindly offered—for as long as one possesses it—in His service.

Arjuna, powerless and stricken by separation from Krsna, the life of the universe, then remembers his intimate exchanges with the Lord one after another. He first remembers how Krsna helped the Pandavas obtain Draupadi, their wife. Then he remembers how Krsna empowered him to conquer even exalted demigods and enjoy heavenly delights (Arjuna defeated Indradeva, the powerful king of heaven, to offer protection to Maya Danava). He remembers how Krsna continuously cared for the Pandavas and empowered them to overcome their extremely powerful enemies (Bhima was able to kill Jarasandha). Krsna avenged insults directed at the Pandavas (He ended the lives of those who had loosened Draupadi’s hair), saved them from unsolvable intrigues (He satisfied Durvasa Muni, who would have cursed them), and caused the demigods to become pleased with them (Arjuna was even able to satisfied Lord Siva in battle). By Krsna’s mercy, Arjuna was even able to give shelter to the demigods (Indra took shelter of Arjuna’s power to kill a demon). Again and again, Krsna offered Arjuna and his brothers protection and even saved Arjuna’s life during the Battle of Kuruksetra.

О King! Arjuna cries, “His jokings and frank talks were pleasing and beautifully decorated with smiles. His addresses unto me as ‘O son of Prtha, О friend, О son of the Kuru dynasty,’ and all such heartiness are now remembered by me, and thus I am overwhelmed.” (Bhag. [1.15.18](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.18)) I joked, lived, slept, and sat with Krsna, the all-powerful Supreme Personality of Godhead. Sometimes when He exaggerated His heroic deeds among friends, I would tease Him by saying, “My friend, You are very truthful.” Exactly as a true friend excuses his true friend or a father excuses his son, He would tolerate my minimizing Him. And now in His absence, I who have conquered both demigods and countless powerful heroes have been humiliated. As the Lord ordered me, 1 was escorting His wives from Dvaraka to Hastinapura. Along the way I was attacked and defeated by a group of cowherd men. With Lord Krsna absent, the power of my Gandiva bow, arrows, chariot, and horses has vanished.

Arjuna then tells Yudhisthira the fate of the friends and relatives about whom he has inquired: “All of them were cursed by the brahmanas, and as a result they all became intoxicated with wine made of putrefied rice and fought among themselves with sticks, not even recognizing one another. Now all but four or five of them are dead and gone.... О King, as in the ocean the bigger and stronger aquatics swallow up the smaller and weaker ones, so also the Supreme Personality of Godhead, to lighten the burden of the earth, has en-gaged the stronger Yadu to kill the weaker, and the bigger Yadu to kill the smaller.” (Bhag. [1.15.22-23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.22), [25-26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.25))

After the disappearance of Balarama and the members of the Yadu dynasty, but before Lord Krsna Himself left the world, Lord Krsna’s chariot driver Daruka met the Lord at Prabhasa-ksetra. The Lord directed him (Bhag. 11.30.46-49) to return to Dvaraka and inform the people there of the “deaths” of Krsna, Balarama, and the Yadus. He asked Daruka to deliver the following message: “You and your relatives should not remain in Dvaraka, the capital of the Yadus, for once I have abandoned that city it will be inundated by the ocean. You should all take your own families, together with My parents, and under Arjuna’s protection go to Indraprastha \[Hastinapura\].” Daruka followed Krsna’s instructions and returned to Dvaraka to deliver the news of the destruction of their dynasty to the remaining Yadus. Of those that remained alive, most traveled to Prabhasa-ksetra and in great lamentation, ended their lives.

Before Dvaraka was inundated by the sea, as per Krsna’s instruction, Arjuna escaped with the final group of surviving Yadus—the women, children, old men, and Krsna’s remaining queens—and accompanied them to Hastinapura. As they traveled, cowherd men attacked and abducted those Arjuna was guarding.

Krsna and His associates had just departed from the world, and Arjuna was already bereaved. Now the great warrior, after being defeated and humiliated by a group of cowherd men, felt powerless, ruined, and hopeless. Through His devotee Arjuna, who was devastated in his defeat, Krsna will teach all of us. Arjuna’s words in Bhagavatam [1.15.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.21) compare his loss of power and failure, despite his using weapons that previously brought only victory, to “offering clarified butter on ashes, accumulating money with a magic wand or sowing seeds on barren land.” All the ingredients for success may seem present—the ghee, the seeds, the fire—but despite one’s best attempt, either no result or a negative, disastrous result may occur. Krsna’s first lesson is about humility, and Srila Prabhupada begins his purport to this text with that point: “As we have discussed more than once, one should not be puffed up by borrowed plumes. All energies and powers are derived from the supreme source, Lord Krsna, and they act as long as He desires and cease to function as soon as He withdraws. All electrical energies are received from the powerhouse, and as soon as the powerhouse stops supplying energy, the bulbs are of no use. In a moment’s time such energies can be generated or withdrawn by the supreme will of the Lord.”

Srila Prabhupada then issues a grave warning to contemporary society, which tends toward pride in its technological accomplishments: “Material civilization without the blessing of the Lord is child’s play only. As long as the parents allow the child to play, it is all right. As soon as the parents withdraw, the child has to stop. Human civilization and all activities thereof must be dovetailed with the supreme blessing of the Lord, and without this blessing all advancement of human civilization is like decoration on a dead body.”

Turning now from our own lessons in life to still deeper truths, Srila Prabhupada explains the esoteric reason behind an impossible occurrence: Krsna’s own queens were abducted from Arjuna’s care. Prabhupada quotes Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura: In the Visnu Purana and Brahma Purana “it is said that once the fair denizens of heaven pleased Astavakra Muni by their service and were blessed by the muni to have the Supreme Lord as their husband. Astavakra Muni was curved in eight joints of his body, and thus he used to move in a peculiar curved manner. The daughters of the demigods could not check their laughter upon seeing the movements of the muni, and the muni, being angry at them, cursed them that they would be kidnapped by rogues, even if they would get the Lord as their husband. Later on, the girls again satisfied the muni by their prayers, and the muni blessed them that they would regain their husband even after being robbed by the rogues. So, in order to keep the words of the great muni, the Lord Himself kidnapped His wives from the protection of Arjuna, otherwise they would have at once vanished from the scene as soon as they were touched by the rogues. Besides that, some of the gopis who prayed to become wives of the Lord returned to their respective positions after their desire was fulfilled. After the departure of Lord Krsna, He wanted all His entourage back to Godhead, and they were called back under different conditions only.” (Bhag. [1.15.20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.20), purport)

Thus after the Lord’s departure, through one means or another, Krsna’s eternal associates all returned to the spiritual world.

## Texts 27-31: Arjuna Remembers Krsna’s Instructions

Arjuna has been remembering his intimate friendship with Krsna and how Krsna helped him in every way. Indeed, all that Arjuna and the Pandavas possessed was due to Krsna’s mercy. As he laments Krsna’s departure from this world, Arjuna experiences incredibly bittersweet separation from his dearest friend, Lord Krsna, who is everything to him. Within the depths of Arjuna’s ecstatic despair, he remembers the words the Lord spoke to him when he was illusioned prior to the fight at Kuruksetra. “Now I am attracted to those instructions imparted to me by the Personality of Godhead \[Govinda\] because they are impregnated with instructions for relieving the burning heart in all circumstances of time and space.” (Bhag. [1.15.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.27))

Due to piety, a soul may be able to possess or accomplish something in this world, but at some point (at least at death, but usually before), and according to one’s karma, Krsna kindly arranges a disaster. At that time, one lands on his face, with his nose in the ashes of life. Only a child dreams that such things won’t happen to him. Life is lived naturally in cycles of ups and downs. By Krsna’s grace, nature’s law dictates that disasters must occur, and thus every person experiences such events and their corresponding emotions. In modem civilization, divorce is a common example of such a disaster. One or both partners may feel wounded and broken for years. As a result, children, jobs, money, and friends may be lost. In their despondency, people have accidents, fight, and turn to intoxication. Sadly, some never rise again. To those, life may not seem worth living.Persons in difficulty tend to respond in one of two ways: either they ascend to hopeful dreaming of a rosier future—perhaps one that includes travel, a new partner, new possessions, or a new job—or they descend into intoxication or depression. In his purport to text 27, Srila Prabhupada describes an alternative when one has given up hope and fallen into despair: one can take shelter of Krsna’s words, the Bhagavadgita, “in all critical times”:

**Herein Arjuna refers to the instruction of the Bhagavad-gita, which was imparted to him by the Lord on the Battlefield of Kuruksetra. The Lord left behind Him the instructions of the Bhagavad-gita not for the benefit of Arjuna alone, but also for all time and in all lands. The Bhagavad-gita, being spoken by the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is the essence of all Vedic wisdom.. . . The problem which arose in the heart of Arjuna on the Battlefield of Kuruksetra was solved by the teachings of the Bhagavad-gita. Again, after the departure of the Lord from the vision of earthly people, when Arjuna was face to face with being vanquished in his acquired power and prominence, he wanted again to remember the great teachings of the Bhagavad-gita just to teach all concerned that the Bhagavad-gita can be consulted in all critical times, not only for solace from all kinds of mental agonies, but also for the way out of great entanglements which may embarrass one in some critical hour.**

**The merciful Lord left behind Him the great teachings of the Bhagavad-gita so that one can take the instructions of the Lord even when He is not visible to material eyesight. Material senses cannot have any estimation of the Supreme Lord, but by His inconceivable power the Lord can incarnate Himself to the sense perception of the conditioned souls in a suitable manner through the agency of matter, which is also another form of the Lord’s manifested energy. Thus the Bhagavad-gita, or any authentic scriptural sound representation of the Lord, is also the incarnation of the Lord.
