There is no difference between the sound representation of the Lord and the Lord Himself. One can derive the same benefit from the Bhagavad-gita as Arjuna did in the personal presence of the Lord. . . . The Bhagavad-gita is therefore meant for terminating all different types of miseries, and Arjuna took shelter of this great knowledge, which had been imparted to him during the Kuruksetra battle.**

Arjuna’s specific distress—his separation from Krsna—was actually spiritual and the cause of his ecstatic emotions. Arjuna’s solution to his “problem” points us both to the root of our own problem and to its solution.

Arjuna had also become overwhelmed directly after Krsna’s disappearance, while Arjuna was still in the Dvaraka area just prior to his return to Hastinapura. At that time, as he did later in Hastinapura, he took shelter of Krsna’s words. Bhagavatam [11.31.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/31.21) describes: “Arjuna felt great distress over separation from Lord Krsna, his dearmost friend. But he consoled himself by remembering the transcendental words the Lord had sung to him.” According to Srila Sridhara Svami, Arjuna remembered such verses from the Gita as ndham prakasah sarvasya, yoga' maya-samdvrtah/ mudho ’yam nabhijandti, loko mam ajam avyayam: “I am never manifest to the foolish and unintelligent. For them I am covered by My eternal creative potency (yoga'maya), and so the deluded world knows Me not, who am unborn and infallible.” (Bg. [7.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/7.25)) Srila Jiva Gosvami states that Arjuna remembered the verse mam evaisyasi satyam te, pratijane priyo ’si me: “You will come to Me without fail. I promise you this because you are My very dear friend.” (Bg. [18.65](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/18.65)) He thus became convinced by Krsna’s promise that he would regain His dear friend’s association.

Suta Gosvami’s description of Arjuna in texts 28 and 29 offers both inspiration and instruction: “Thus being deeply absorbed in thinking of the instructions of the Lord, which were imparted in the great intimacy of friendship, and in thinking of His lotus feet, Arjuna’s mind became pacified and free from all material contamination. Arjuna’s constant remembrance of the lotus feet of Lord Sri Krsna rapidly increased his devotion, and as a result all the trash in his thoughts subsided.”

In his purports to these texts, Srila Prabhupada informs us that both Arjuna’s separation from Krsna and his remembrance of His instructions brought Arjuna bliss. For the conditioned soul, meditating deeply on Krsna’s instructions will remove all “trash”-like problems in the heart: “The Lord is like the sun; the sun’s appearance means immediate dissipation of darkness, or ignorance, and the Lord’s appearance within the mind of the devotee can at once drive away the miserable material effects. Lord Caitanya has therefore recommended constant chanting of the name of the Lord for protection from all contamination of the material world.” (Bhag. [1.15.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.28), purport) And, “Material desires in the mind are the trash of material contamination. . . . They accumulate due to our reactions to material desires, but when we get in touch with the transcendental Lord in His variegated energies by devotional service, the naked forms of all material desires become manifest, and the intelligence of the living being is pacified in its true color. As soon as Arjuna turned his attention towards the instructions of the Lord, as they are inculcated in the Bhagavad-gita, his true color of eternal association with the Lord became manifest, and thus he felt freed from all material contaminations.” (Bhag. [1.15.29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.29), purport)

Srila Sridhara Svami mentions that these two verses indicate that Arjuna’s disturbed mind was settled by his devotion to Krsna. Bhaktisandarbha, anuccheda 236, indicates that dependence on Krsna is the essence of devotional life. Indeed, both Vidura and Narada Muni taught this to Dhrtarastra and Yudhisthira Maharaja respectively in Chapter Thirteen. Naturally, after reading their powerful words, one may wish to depend fully on Krsna and become a devotee. Early in Chapter Fifteen, Arjuna remembered incident after incident of Krsna’s sweet reciprocation with His great devotees the Pandavas. This further inspires us to depend on Krsna and become His devotee.

But now we read that Krsna has left Arjuna’s presence and Arjuna is bereft! Perhaps one feels a blossoming desire to advance suddenly wilt, thinking that he too may be abandoned by Krsna. What should he do? He should do as Arjuna did: Arjuna remembered Krsna’s words, the Bhagavad-gita, and thus again experienced his Lord’s presence. That Krsna was present in His instructions and that Arjuna was able to remember them, enriched with his feelings of separation, carried Arjuna directly into Krsna’s association again.

In his Krsna book (Chapter 35), Srila Prabhupada explains the importance and potency of remembering Krsna in separation: “To acquire this strong feeling of separation is the teaching of Lord Caitanya and His direct disciplic succession of Gosvamis. When we are not in physical contact with Krsna, we can associate with Him like the gopis, through feelings of separation. Krsna’s transcendental form, qualities, pastimes and entourage are all identical with Him. There are nine different kinds of devotional service. Devotional service to Krsna in feelings of separation elevates the devotee to the highest perfectional level, to the level of the gopis.... Those who are in the disciplic succession of the Madhva-Gaudiya-sampradaya should always feel separation from Krsna, worship His transcendental form and discuss His transcendental teachings, His pastimes, His qualities and His entourage. That will enrich the devotees to the highest devotional perfection. Feeling constant separation while engaged in the service of the Lord is the perfection of Krsna consciousness.”

Jiva Gosvami comments on Bhagavatam [1.15.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.28) (Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 52) that the word santd means that Arjuna became peaceful at heart. He was free of all suffering. It was as if Lord Krsna was again present before his eyes. Vimald means that his mind became free from all material contamination. In that same anuccheda, Jiva Gosvami also comments on text 31, which he says describes Arjuna’s attainment of success: brahma'sampattya means “because of having directly seen the Supreme Personality of Godhead, whose form is like that of a human being.” Sanchinrui'dvaita'samsayah means that because he had directly seen the Supreme Lord, his doubt that the Lord was appearing only in his mind and not in person was destroyed. Because he had attained the Supreme Lord’s association, he did not take birth again at the time of his death.

Thus by remembering the wonderful words the Lord had spoken to him, Arjuna was able to associate with the Lord directly and was thus reinstated in his natural, transcendental position. His sense of duality was cut, and he was freed from the bindings of material nature and the entanglement of birth and death. Arjuna, as Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to Bhagavad-gita ([4.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/4.5)), was Krsna’s eternal associate. His being cast into forgetfulness prior to the speaking of Bhagavad' gita was purposeful; it was meant to aid our own return to Krsna’s shelter. Actually, however, no separation can truly exist between Krsna and us, for we are tiny jiva souls, His parts and parcels, eternally connected to Him as His servants. Disconnection from Krsna is impossible. Yet by maya’s influence, we are deluded into accepting the duality of a separated existence. This delusion results in our experiencing endless varieties of misery. Srila Prabhupada’s powerful purport to Bhagavatam [1.15.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.31) further directs how, like Arjuna, we too can remove illusion and always remain with Krsna:

**As soon as Arjuna took up the instructions of the Bhagavad-gita, expert as he was, he could at once eradicate the material conception of Lord Krsna, his eternal friend. He could realize that the Lord was still present before him by His instruction, by His form, by His pastimes, by His qualities and everything else related to Him. He could realize that Lord Krsna, his friend, was still present before him by His transcendental presence in different nondual energies, and there was no question of attainment of the association of the Lord by another change of body under the influence of time and space. By attainment of absolute knowledge, one can be in association with the Lord constantly, even in this present life, simply by hearing, chanting, thinking of and worshiping the Supreme Lord. One can see Him, one can feel His presence even in this present life simply by understanding the advaya'jndna Lord, or the Absolute Lord, through the process of devotional service, which begins with hearing about Him. Lord Caitanya says that simply by chanting the holy name of the Lord one can at once wash off the dust on the mirror of pure consciousness, and as soon as the dust is removed, one is at once freed from all material conditions.**

## Texts 32-51: The Pandavas Retire and Return to the Spiritual World

After hearing and deliberating on Arjuna’s words, Yudhisthira remembered the hint Narada Muni had given (Bhag. [1.13.50](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/13.50)) that he and the Pandavas should remain in this world only as long as the Lord was present performing His pastimes. Now having heard from Arjuna that Lord Krsna and the Yadu dynasty had returned to the spiritual realm, Yudhisthira and Kuntidevi decided to go back to Godhead. Yudhisthira thus turned his mind to the Lord’s instructions, the Bhagavad-gita, and deliberated on Krsna’s divine appearance, activities, and disappearance.

In his purport to Bhagavatam [1.15.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.32), Srila Prabhupada likens Krsna’s “birth” and “death” to the sun’s rising and setting in a specific location. “Therefore, in the Bhagavad-gita it is stated that anyone who factually understands the transcendental appearance and disappearance of the Lord by His inconceivable energy becomes liberated from the laws of birth and death and is placed in the eternal spiritual sky where the Vaikuntha planets are. There such liberated persons can eternally live without the pangs of birth, death, old age and disease. In the spiritual sky the Lord and those who are eternally engaged in the transcendental loving service of the Lord are all eternally young because there is no old age and disease and there is no death. Because there is no death there is no birth. It is concluded, therefore, that simply by understanding the Lord’s appearance and disappearance in truth, one can attain the perfectional stage of eternal life.”

Suta Gosvami assures the sages at Naimisaranya in texts 34 and 35 that Krsna’s disappearance, as well as the disappearance of the Yadu dynasty, is extraordinary and not at all like the experience of death in this world. He thus compares Krsna’s leaving His body to the acts of “a magician, \[who\] relinquishes one body to accept different ones, like the fish incarnation and others.” (Bhag. [1.15.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.35)) Srila Prabhupada explains Suta’s comparison in his purport to text 35: “The Lord is described as amrta, or deathless, because He has no material body. Under the circumstances, the Lord’s dying or quitting His body is like the jugglery of a magician. The magician shows by his tricks that he is cut to pieces, burnt to ashes or made unconscious by hypnotic influences, but all are false shows only. Factually the magician himself is neither burnt to ashes nor cut to pieces, nor is he dead or unconscious at any stage of his magical demonstration. Similarly, the Lord has His eternal forms of unlimited variety, of which the fish incarnation, as was exhibited within this universe, is also one. Because there are innumerable universes, somewhere or other the fish incarnation must be manifesting His pastimes without cessation. In this verse, the particular word dhatte (‘eternally accepted,’ and not the word dhitva, ‘accepted for the occasion’) is used. The idea is that the Lord does not create the fish incarnation; He eternally has such a form, and the appearance and disappearance of such an incarnation serves particular purposes.”

From Jiva Gosvami’s comment on this section of the Bhagavatam in his Krsna-sandarbha, anuccheda 106, one gleans the understanding that these verses do not show that the Supreme Lord accepts the form of Krsna and then abandons it at a certain point. The words tanu, тира, and kalevara used in texts 34 and 35 do not mean only body but may also mean condition, nature, or mental conception. Lord Krsna descended to relieve the burden of the earth and to protect the demigods and devotees. When these purposes were accomplished, the Lord gave up the desire (mental conception) to relieve the earth and protect the pious. In the same anuccheda, Jiva explains that the Personality of Godhead manifests His form in this world and then makes His form disappear from this world. It is not that He rejects His form or that it ceases to exist. That the Lord’s form is eternal, although staying in the material world for a certain time, is confirmed by the following verse (Bhag. [1.15.36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.36)): “The Personality of Godhead, Lord Krsna, left this earthly planet in His selfsame form.”In his commentary on Srimad-Bhagavatam [11.31.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/31.11), Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura further expands the comparison between Krsna’s leaving this world and a magician’s activities:

**In front of a great king, a magician approaches a stack of valuable garments, jewels, coins and so forth, all placed there by the king. Taking a jeweled necklace, the magician tells the king, “Now I am taking this necklace, and you can’t have it,” and he makes the necklace disappear. “Now I’m taking this gold coin, and you can’t have it,” he says, and makes the gold coin disappear. Next, challenging the king in the same way, the magician makes 7,000 horses disappear. Then the magician creates the illusion that the king’s children, grandchildren, brothers and other family members have attacked each other and that nearly all are dead from the violent quarrel. The king hears the magician speaking and at the same time observes these things taking place before him as he sits in the great assembly hall.**

**Then the magician says, “O King, I no longer wish to live. Just as I have studied magic, so also, by the mercy of the lotus feet of my guru, 1 have learned the mystic meditation of yoga. One is supposed to give up one’s body while meditating in a holy place, and since you have performed so many pious activities, you are a holy place yourself. Therefore I shall now give up my body.”**

**Thus speaking, the magician sits down in the proper yoga posture, fixes himself in pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana and samadhi and becomes silent. A moment later, a fire generated from his trance blazes forth out of his body and bums it to ashes. Then all the wives of the magician, distraught with lamentation, enter into that fire.**

**Three or four days later, after the magician has returned to his own province, he sends one of his daughters to the king. The daughter tells him, “O King, I have just come to your palace, bringing along with me, invisibly, all your sons, grandsons and brothers in good health—along with all the jewels and other items given by you. Please, therefore, give me whatever you consider fitting remuneration for the wisdom of the magic that has been exhibited before you.” In this way, even by ordinary magic one can simulate birth and death.**

Srila Jiva Gosvami’s commentary on Bhagavatam [11.31.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/31.11) explains that the so-called fight among the members of the Yadu dynasty was actually a display of the Lord’s pastime potency, since Lord Krsna’s personal associates are never subject to ordinary birth and death like conditioned souls.

Srila Prabhupada’s purport to Bhagavatam [1.15.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.34) further explains the departure of Krsna’s associates from this world, specifically the members of the Yadu dynasty: “Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura suggests that the rsis like Saunaka and others who were hearing Srimad-Bhagavatam from Suta Gosvami at Naimisaranya were not happy to hear about the Yadus’ dying in the madness of intoxication. To give them relief from this mental agony, Suta Gosvami assured them that the Lord caused the members of the Yadu dynasty to relinquish their bodies by which they had to take away the burden of the world. The Lord and His eternal associates appeared on earth to help the administrative demigods in eradicating the burden of the world. He therefore called for some of the confidential demigods to appear in the Yadu family and serve Him in His great mission. After the mission was fulfilled, the demigods, by the will of the Lord, relinquished their corporeal bodies by fighting among themselves in the madness of intoxication.”

Having philosophically explained Lord Krsna’s departure from this world, Suta Gosvami remarks that Kali—both the personality and the age—then manifests fully. Thus Kali-yuga began with a mission to create inauspiciousness for those deprived of true knowledge. Having already noted the increase in “avarice, falsehood, cheating and violence throughout the capital, state, home and among individuals ... \[Yudhisthira\] wisely prepared himself to leave home, and he dressed accordingly.” (Bhag. [1.15.37](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.37)) Before leaving, he enthroned his qualified grandson, Pariksit Maharaja, as emperor, and “Vajra, the son of Aniruddha \[grandson of Lord Krsna\], at Mathura as the King of Surasena.” (Bhag. [1.15.39](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.39)) He then performed a sacrifice to enable him to successfully quit household life. Afterward, free from the bodily concept of life, Yudhisthira Maharaja at once relinquished the accoutrements of kingship—the garments, belt, and ornaments of the royal order—and became completely disinterested and unattached. No longer did he think of himself as a world emperor or even the head of the Kuru dynasty. Through meditation, he merged each element with the source element from which it had come and finally merged his self, fully considering it as nonmaterial, with Brahman.

Srila Jiva Gosvami’s comments on text 42 describe that things composed of matter, such as the physical elements, the mind, and the false ego, are unfit to become merged in the soul. These were merged into their source. Then the pure soul, free from all material contamination, was offered to the Supreme Soul, Sri Krsna.

In his purport to text 42, Srila Prabhupada offers some practical hints on how to apply Maharaja Yudhisthira’s ideal example: “When one is thus inclined to become an associate of the Supreme Lord, the Personality of Godhead, in one of the innumerable planets of the spiritual sky, especially in Goloka Vrndavana, one has to think always that he is different from the material energy; he has nothing to do with it, and he has to realize himself as pure spirit, Brahman, qualitatively equal with the Supreme Brahman (Paramesvara). . . . One must not only think that he is Brahman, but must act like Brahman. One who only thinks himself Brahman is an impersonalist. And one who acts like Brahman is the pure devotee.”

“After that, Maharaja Yudhisthira dressed himself in torn clothing, gave up eating all solid foods, voluntarily became dumb and let his hair hang loose. All this combined to make him look like an urchin or madman with no occupation. He did not depend on his brothers for anything. And, just like a deaf man, he heard nothing. He then started towards the north, treading the path accepted by his forefathers and great men, to devote himself completely to the thought of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. And he lived in that way wherever he went.” (Bhag. [1.15.43-44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.43)) Yudhisthira’s brothers also noted the irreligious symptoms of Kali and, observing Yudhisthira’s example, decided to follow in his footsteps. They too rightly concluded “that the lotus feet of the Lord Sri Krsna are the supreme goal of all. Therefore they meditated upon His feet without interruption.” (Bhag. [1.15.46](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.46)) Thus all the Pandavas, by their “pure consciousness due to constant devotional remembrance . . . attained the spiritual sky, which is ruled over by the Supreme Narayana, Lord Krsna. This is attained only by those who meditate upon the one Supreme Lord without deviation. This abode of the Lord Sri Krsna, known as Goloka Vrndavana, cannot be attained by persons who are absorbed in the material conception of life. But the Pandavas, being completely washed of all material contamination, attained that abode in their very same bodies.” (Bhag. [1.15.47-48](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.47))

Srila Prabhupada comments in his purport to text 47—48 that “there is no doubt at all that one can attain the supreme spiritual planet, Goloka Vrndavana, without change of body . . .” Srila Jiva Gosvami explains (Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 271) that the word atmana means “in their very same bodies.” This was possible because their bodies were not material (virajena). The word hi (certainly) is used here to dispel any doubt that it is not possible.

Vidura, absorbed in thoughts of Lord Krsna while on pilgrimage, left his body at Prabhasa.

“Draupadi also saw that her husbands, without caring for her, were leaving home. She knew well about Lord Vasudeva, Krsna, the Personality of Godhead. Both she and Subhadra became absorbed in thoughts of Krsna and attained the same results as their husbands.” (Bhag. [1.15.50](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.50)) Srila Prabhupada’s famous purport to this text is powerful:

**When flying an airplane, one cannot take care of other planes. Everyone has to take care of his own plane, and if there is any danger, no other plane can help another in that condition. Similarly, at the end of life, when one has to go back home, back to Godhead, everyone has to take care of himself without help rendered by another. The help is, however, offered on the ground before flying in space. Similarly, the spiritual master, the father, the mother, the relatives, the husband and others can all render help during one’s lifetime, but while crossing the sea one has to take care of himself and utilize the instructions formerly received. Draupadi had five husbands, and no one asked Draupadi to come; Draupadi had to take care of herself without waiting for her great husbands. And because she was already trained, she at once took to concentration upon the lotus feet of Lord Vasudeva, Krsna, the Personality of Godhead. The wives also got the same result as their husbands, in the same manner; that is to say, without changing their bodies they reached the destination of Godhead.**

Suta Gosvami’s final words in this chapter are a benediction: “The subject of the departure of the sons of Pandu for the ultimate goal of life, back to Godhead, is fully auspicious and is perfectly pure. Therefore anyone who hears this narration with devotional faith certainly gains the devotional service of the Lord, the highest perfection of life.” (Bhag. [1.15.51](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.51))

## Dialogue Seven - Maharaja Pariksit’s Birth and Activities

## Chapter 12 - Birth of Emperor Pariksit

The previous chapters (Seven through Eleven) described Krsna’s wonderful dealings with His devotees and (Thirteen through Fifteen) the Pandavas’ great love for Krsna. We have come to know that Arjuna was so spiritually elevated that he was able to directly associate with Krsna simply by remembering His instructions. We also know that eventually, each of the Pandavas returned to the spiritual world, fixed in constant remembrance of the Lord. Attaining such an exalted level of consciousness is the goal of life, but how to attain it? A compassionate and socially-minded devotee inquires about systematically organizing society to assist the population in advancing toward love of Krsna. To accomplish this on a societal level, Krsna Himself has devised the varnasrama system, which requires a qualified ruler to maintain it. Therefore the Bhagavatam will now describe the qualities and activities of an ideal Vaisnava king, Maharaja Pariksit.

The eighth chapter of the First Canto described Krsna’s protection of Maharaja Pariksit, at that time still in his mother’s womb. Years later, as mentioned in Bhagavatam [1.15.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/15.38), Yudhisthira Maharaja crowned his grandson Pariksit emperor just before Yudhisthira and his brothers retired to the Himalaya Mountains to begin their journey back to Godhead. Before narrating Pariksit Maharaja’s activities (contained in chapters Sixteen and Seventeen of the First Canto), the Bhagavatam will first tell of his birth and the predictions made about his life. Thus in addition to describing Maharaja Pariksit’s characteristics—and therefore the characteristics of an ideal king—Suta Gosvami will also reply to another of Saunaka Rsi’s questions: “It is said that Maharaja Pariksit is a great first-class devotee of the Lord and that his birth and activities are all wonderful. Please tell us about him.” (Bhag. [1.4.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/4.9)) This will all be described in Chapter Twelve.

## Texts 1-11: Inquiring and Speaking About Maharaja Pariksit

The sages of Naimisaranya, headed by Saunaka Rsi, again asked Suta Gosvami about Maharaja Pariksit, whom Krsna had saved from Asvatthama’s brahmastra. Prabhupada’s first purport in Chapter Twelve sets the scene: “The sages assembled in the forest of Naimisaranya inquired from Suta Gosvami about the birth of Maharaja Pariksit, but in the course of the narration other topics like the release of the brahmastra by the son of Drona, his punishment by Arjuna, Queen Kuntidevi’s prayers, the Pandavas’ visit to the place where Bhismadeva was lying, his prayers and thereafter the Lord’s departure for Dvaraka were discussed. His arrival at Dvaraka and residing with the sixteen thousand queens, etc., were narrated. The sages were absorbed in hearing such descriptions, but now they wanted to turn to the original topic, and thus the inquiry was made by Saunaka Rsi. So the subject of the release of the brahmastra weapon by Asvatthama is renewed.”

Saunaka begins: Please tell us about the birth and death of the greatly intelligent devotee Maharaja Pariksit. What was his destination after dying? Suta first describes the pure Krsna consciousness with which Maharaja Pariksit’s grandfather, Yudhisthira Maharaja, ruled his kingdom. Although the greatness of Yudhisthira’s opulence enchanted even the denizens of heaven, “because he was absorbed in the service of the Lord, nothing could satisfy him except the Lord’s service.” (Bhag. [1.12.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/12.6)) Srila Prabhupada reveals Yudhisthira’s mood while governing: “A father is always a father because he always has

the good of the son at heart. The father wants every one of his sons to become a better man than himself. Therefore, a king like Maharaja Yudhisthira, who was the personality of goodness, wanted everyone under his administration, especially human beings who have better developed consciousness, to become devotees of Lord Krsna so that everyone can become free from the trifles of material existence. His motto of administration was all good for the citizens, for as personified goodness he knew perfectly well what is actually good for them.” (Bhag. [1.12.4](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/12.4), purport)

During Maharaja Yudhisthira’s ideal reign, Maharaja Pariksit was saved while still in Uttara’s womb. At that time he saw the allpervading Lord, who to save His devotee could appear in any place or form He chose. Thus He stood in His four-armed form wearing a helmet of blazing gold. His eyes were red with anger, and He was whirling His mace to protect His devotee. The impression of that vision of the Lord remained with him, and when he was bom he was named Pariksit, “observer-examiner.” From birth he observed and examined everyone he met in his attempt to again find Krsna, his protector.

In his purport to text 30, Srila Prabhupada stresses the importance of providing children with favorable Krsna conscious impressions: “Maharaja Pariksit, fortunate as he was, got the impression of the Lord even in the womb of his mother, and thus his contemplation on the Lord was constantly with him. Once the impression of the transcendental form of the Lord is fixed in one’s mind, one can never forget Him in any circumstance. Child Pariksit, after coming out of the womb, was in the habit of examining everyone to see whether he was the same personality whom he first saw in the womb. But no one could be equal to or more attractive than the Lord, and therefore he never accepted anyone. But the Lord was constantly with him by such examination, and thus Maharaja Pariksit was always engaged in the devotional service of the Lord by remembrance.” Prabhupada adds:

**Srila Jiva Gosvami remarks in this connection that every child, if given an impression of the Lord from his very childhood, certainly becomes a great devotee of the Lord like Maharaja Pariksit. One may not be as fortunate as Maharaja Pariksit to have the opportunity to see the Lord in the womb of his mother, but even if he is not so fortunate, he can be made so if the parents of the child desire him to be so. There is a practical example in my personal life in this connection. My father was a pure devotee of the Lord, and when I was only four or five years old, my father gave me a couple of forms of Radha and Krsna. In a playful manner, I used to worship these Deities along with my sister, and I used to imitate the performances of a neighboring temple of Radha-Govinda. By constantly visiting this neighboring temple and copying the ceremonies in connection with my own Deities of play, I developed a natural affinity for the Lord. My father used to observe all the ceremonies befitting my position. Later on, these activities were suspended due to my association in the schools and colleges, and I became completely out of practice. But in my youthful days, when I met my spiritual master, Sri Srimad Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Gosvami Maharaja, again I revived my old habit, and the same playful Deities became my worshipful Deities in proper regulation. This was followed up until I left the family connection, and I am pleased that my generous father gave the first impression which was developed later into regulative devotional service by His Divine Grace.**

## Texts 12-29: The Brahmanas’ Predictions After Maharaja Pariksit’s Birth

At the time of an auspicious astrological alignment, Maharaja Pariksit, heir to Pandu’s throne, took birth. Maharaja Yudhisthira immediately called for learned brahmana priests to recite Vedic hymns and perform the newborn boy’s purificatory birth ceremony. The emperor, satisfied by the birth of a qualified successor, offered to the brah' manas profuse quantities of charity in the form of gold, land, villages, elephants, horses, and food grains. The brafimanas were in turn satisfied by this charity, and they confirmed that the king’s grandson would be a suitable descendant of the ruling dynasty. They assured the emperor that the all-powerful Lord had personally restored this boy, although he had been doomed by Asvatthama’s irresistible weapon.

Therefore, they said, he would be known as Visnurata, one protected by the Personality of Godhead. “O most fortunate one, there is no doubt that this child will become a first-class devotee and will be qualified with all good qualities.” (Bhag. [1.12.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/12.17))

In his purport to text 16, Srila Prabhupada describes why Krsna protected Pariksit Maharaja: “The child Pariksit was saved by the all-powerful and all-pervasive Visnu (Lord Krsna) for two reasons. The first reason is that the child in the womb of his mother was spotless due to his being a pure devotee of the Lord. The second reason is that the child was the only surviving male descendant of Puru, the pious forefather of the virtuous King Yudhisthira. The Lord wants to continue the line of pious kings to rule over the earth as His representatives for the actual progress of a peaceful and prosperous life.”

Yudhisthira inquired of the brahmanas about the newborn’s qualities: Will he become as saintly, famous, and glorious a king as those who appeared previously in this great royal dynasty? The brahmanas then described Pariksit’s future qualities. By hearing about Maharaja Pariksit’s spotless character and power to rule, the deficiency of most contemporary elected and appointed leaders becomes apparent. Society longs for powerful leaders of spotless character like Maharaja Pariksit. Srila Prabhupada lays bare the basic flaw in democracy in his purport to text 18: “In the modem setup of the democratic states, the people themselves are fallen to the qualities of the siidras or less, and the government is run by their representative, who is ignorant of the scriptural mode of administrative education. Thus the whole atmosphere is surcharged with sudra qualities, manifested by lust and avarice. Such administrators quarrel every day among themselves. The cabinet of ministers changes often due to party and group selfishness. Everyone wants to exploit the state resources till he dies. No one retires from political life unless forced to do so. How can such low-grade men do good to the people? The result is corruption, intrigue and hypocrisy. They should leam from the Srimad-Bhagavatam how ideal the administrators must be before they can be given charge of different posts.”

In response to Yudhisthira’s inquiry, the brahmanas compared the child to the dynasty’s previous glorious kings: Maharaja Pariksit will maintain those bom in his kingdom as King Iksvaku maintained his citizens. He will be as true to his promise as Lord Rama, the Personality of Godhead, was to his. He will be as generous with charity as King Sibi, and will expand his family’s fame as did Bharata, the son of Maharaja Dusyanta. His bowmanship will rival Arjuna’s. He will be as irresisti-ble as fire and as unsurpassable as the ocean. His ability to offer shelter will be like the Himalaya Mountains. He will be as forbearing as the earth and as strong as a lion. Srila Prabhupada mentions: “One is compared to the lion when one is very strong in chasing an enemy. One should be a lamb at home and a lion in the chase. The lion never fails in the chase of an animal; similarly, the head of the state should never fail in chasing an enemy.” (Bhag. [1.12.22](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/12.22), purport) Pariksit’s equanimity will be like Yudhisthira’s and his munificence like Siva’s. He will follow in the footsteps of Sri Krsna and, by constantly associating with the Lord through remembrance, will take on His qualities. He will be as magnanimous as Maharaja Rantideva, as religious as Maharaja Yayati, as patient as Bali Maharaja, and as devotionally staunch as Prahlada Maharaja. He will follow old and experienced men. He will father sagelike kings and, for the sake of peace, will chastise all opponents of religion.

In his purport to text 26, Srila Prabhupada describes the target of Maharaja Pariksit’s chastisements, and in so doing presents a challenge to modem administrators: “Maharaja Pariksit wanted to kill the personified Kali, who was attempting to kill a cow, the emblem of peace and religion. The symptoms of Kali are (1) wine, (2) women, (3) gambling and (4) slaughterhouses. Wise rulers of all states should take lessons from Maharaja Pariksit in how to maintain peace and morality by subduing the upstarts and quarrelsome people who indulge in wine, illicit connection with women, gambling and meat-eating supplied by regularly maintained slaughterhouses. In this age of Kali, regular license is issued for maintaining all of these different departments of quarrel. So how can they expect peace and morality in the state? The state fathers, therefore, must follow the principles of becoming wiser by devotion to the Lord, by chastising the breaker of discipline and by uprooting the symptoms of quarrel, as mentioned above. If we want blazing fire, we must use dry fuel. Blazing fire and moist fuel go ill together. Peace and morality can prosper only by the principles of Maharaja Pariksit and his followers.”

The brahmanas then addressed the future king’s death: “After hearing about his death, which will be caused by the bite of a snakebird sent by a son of a brahmana, he will get himself freed from all material attachment and surrender unto the Personality of Godhead, taking shelter of Him. After inquiring about proper self-knowledge from the son of Vyasadeva, who will be a great philosopher, he will renounce all material attachment and achieve a life of fearlessness.” (Bhag. [1.12.27-28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/12.27)) Maharaja Yudhisthira and Pariksit’s other guardians were thus informed of the circumstances by which this child would later die. That his life would be cut short by a premature death made Pariksit appear unfortunate, yet because he would have notice of his death, Pariksit would be able to turn this misfortune into the greatest fortune. Srila Prabhupada explains how to use misfortune for positive spiritual gain: one should practice hearing and chanting. “Out of the nine different transcendental means of devotional service to the Lord prescribed in the Bhagavatam, either all of them, or some of them or even one of them are equally beneficial if properly discharged. Maharaja Pariksit and Sukadeva Gosvami were serious performers of the first two important items, namely the process of chanting and the process of hearing, and therefore both of them were successful in their laudable attempt. Transcendental realization is attained by such serious hearing and chanting and not otherwise.... The process is simple, but only the sincere party can achieve the desired result.” (Bhag. [1.12.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/12.3))

It is interesting to remember that Krsna protected Maharaja Pariksit while he was still in his mother’s womb but did not appear to protect him from the brahmana boy’s curse. Srila Prabhupada responds to this point in his purport to text 27: “Devotional service to the Lord, while existing in the material world, is a way to practice one’s transcendental relation with the Lord. . . . Since he was always protected by the Lord, he could have avoided the effect of such a curse by the grace of the Lord, but he did not take such undue advantage for nothing. Rather, he made the best use of a bad bargain. For seven days continuously he heard Srimad-Bhagavatam from the right source, and thus he got shelter at the lotus feet of the Lord by that opportunity.”

Maharaja Pariksit accepted the curse as the Lord’s mercy. He thus effectively took advantage of that mercy—making “the best use of a bad bargain”—and used the opportunity the curse provided to attain Krsna’s lotus feet by hearing Srimad-Bhagavatam from Sukadeva Gosvami. In this way, Maharaja Pariksit conquered all his fears. In his purport to text 28, Srila Prabhupada explains how to conquer fear: “In this material existence \[we\] are always fearful. This fearfulness is called anxiety. Everyone in the material life, in all species and varieties of life, is full of anxieties, either by breaking or without breaking the laws of nature. Liberation, or mukti, means getting relief from these constant anxieties. This is possible only when the anxiety is changed to the devotional service of the Lord. Srimad-Bhagavata gives us the chance to change the quality of anxiety from matter to spirit.”

After completing their predictions, the brahmanas completed the birth ceremonies, accepted Maharaja Yudhisthira’s generous gifts of gold, land, villages, grains, and cows, and returned to their homes.

## Texts 30-36: Maharaja Yudhisthira Performs a Sacrifice

As the moon in its waxing fortnight develops day after day, so the exalted qualities of the future king developed. Pariksit was bom just after the Kuruksetra war. Because of his participation in the war, Yudhisthira Maharaja desired to purify himself from sin by performing an asvamedha-yajna, the horse sacrifice mentioned in Vedic literature. Requiring funds for these elaborate ceremonies, the Pandava brothers headed north to collect the gold discarded by Maharaja Marutta when he had performed a sacrifice in days of yore. Yudhisthira Maharaja asked his cousin Krsna to supervise the sacrifice, and Krsna arranged that it be performed by qualified brahmanas. Thus Yudhisthira managed to satisfy the lord of all sacrifices, Sri Krsna.

Although at times the procedures recommended for the performance of a sacrifice may differ, the purpose behind the sacrifice remains the same: to please Krsna. Krsna Himself orders the performance of Vedic sacrifices like the horse sacrifice; therefore He is pleased when the priests perform it carefully and correctly. In his purport to text 34, Srila Prabhupada describes the need for sacrifice: “Let any man of any place or community, caste or creed be engaged in any sort of occupational duty, but he must agree to perform sacrifices as it is recommended in the scriptures for the particular place, time and person. In the Vedic literatures it is recommended that in Kali-yuga people engage in glorifying the Lord by chanting the holy name of Krsna (kirtandd eva krsnasya mukta-sangah param vrajet) without offense. By doing so one can be freed from all sins and thus can attain the highest perfection of life by returning home, back to Godhead.”

After the horse sacrifice was completed, Lord Krsna stayed in Hastinapura for a few months with Yudhisthira and His relatives. Then, accompanied by Arjuna and other members of the Yadu dynasty, Sri Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, headed back to Dvaraka.

## Chapter 16 - How Pariksit Received the Age of Kali

The thirteenth chapter of the First Canto described Vidura’s return to the palace at Hastinapura after years of pilgrimage. With Vidura’s guidance and help, blind Dhrtarastra and his wife Gandhari left the comforts of palace life to advance toward the ultimate spiritual destination. Chapter Fourteen described how Yudhisthira began to observe inauspicious omens, which ignited in him the fear that Krsna had left the world. As the King expressed his fear to Bhima, a dejected Arjuna returned to Hastinapura from Dvaraka. Yudhisthira inquired from Arjuna about their friends and relatives in Dvaraka, and Arjuna’s reply, related in Chapter Fifteen, admitted that Sri Krsna had indeed left the world along with almost all the members of the Yadu dynasty. Yudhisthira then enthroned Pariksit Maharaja and renounced the world. His brothers, Kuntidevi, Draupadi, and Subhadra followed.

## Texts 1-9: Suta Gosvami Speaks of Maharaja Pariksit’s Life, and Saunaka Rsi Asks to Hear More about Maharaja Pariksit’s Chastisement of Kali

Maharaja Pariksit, now the king, used his glorious qualities to rule under the guidance of the brahmanas and sastra. He too performed three horse sacrifices on the bank of the Ganges. Once, Suta Gosvami explains, as the king toured his kingdom, he came across Kali, the master of the age of quarrel, hypocrisy, and discontent, disguised as a king and striking the legs of a cow and a bull. “The King at once caught hold of him to deal sufficient punishment.” (Bhag. [1.16.4](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.4))

The age of Kali began just after the Battle of Kuruksetra, but its effects had been checked because Lord Krsna was still present. Now with the Lord gone, Kali immediately exerted his influence. In his purport to text 4, Srila Prabhupada explains a prime step in Kali’s systematic plan: “The age of Kali means mismanagement and quarrel. And the root cause of all mismanagement and quarrel is that worthless men with the modes of lower-class men, who have no higher ambition in life, come to the helm of the state management. Such men at the post of a king are sure to first hurt the cow and the brahminical culture, thereby pushing all society towards hell. Maharaja Pariksit, trained as he was, got the scent of this root cause of all quarrel in the world. Thus he wanted to stop it in the very beginning.”

Knowing this, Saunaka Rsi and the sages of Naimisaranya were shocked. “Please describe all these incidents if they relate to th topics of Lord Krsna.” (Bhag. [1.16.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.5)) The sages were amazed that someone would beat mother cow, the supplier of milk. They were further astounded to hear that the perpetrator was simply punished and not put to death. Thus they wanted to hear more—provided the information was connected to Krsna.

Srila Prabhupada explains Saunaka Rsi’s mood in his purport to text 5: “There are many topics in the Bhagavatam about sociology, politics, economics, cultural affairs, etc., but all of them are in relation with Krsna, and therefore all of them are worth hearing. Krsna is the purifying ingredient in all matters, regardless of what they are. In the mundane world, everything is impure due to its being a product of the three mundane qualities. The purifying agent, however, is Krsna.”

Inspired, Saunaka Rsi adds: “The devotees of the Lord are accustomed to licking up the honey available from the lotus feet of the Lord. What is the use of topics which simply waste one’s valuable life?” (Bhag. [1.16.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.6)) By hearing the transcendental narration of the Lord’s pastimes, one can be freed from the grip of the cruel slaughtering process called death. In Bhagavatam [2.3.17-24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/3.17), Saunaka Rsi will speak in a similarly inspired way about hearing krsna-katha:

**Both by rising and by setting, the sun decreases the duration of life of everyone, except one who utilizes the time by discussing topics of the all-good Personality of Godhead. Do the trees not live? Do the bellows of the blacksmith not breathe? All around us, do the beasts not eat and discharge semen? Men who are like dogs, hogs, camels and asses praise those men who never listen to the transcendental pastimes of Lord Sri Krsna, the deliverer from evils. One who has not listened to the messages about the prowess and marvelous acts of the Personality of Godhead and has not sung or chanted loudly the worthy songs about the Lord is to be considered to possess earholes like the holes of snakes and a tongue like the tongue of a frog. The upper portion of the body, though crowned with a silk turban, is only a heavy burden if not bowed down before the Personality of Godhead who can award mukti \[freedom\]. And the hands, though decorated with glittering bangles, are like those of a dead man if not engaged in the service of the Personality of Godhead Hari. The eyes which do not look at the symbolic representations of the Personality of Godhead Visnu \[His forms, name, quality, etc.\] are like those printed on the plumes of the peacock, and the legs which do not move to the holy places \[where the Lord is remembered\] are considered to be like tree trunks. The person who has not at any time received the dust of the feet of the Lord’s pure devotee upon his head is certainly a dead body. And the person who has never experienced the aroma of the tulasi leaves from the lotus feet of the Lord is also a dead body, although breathing. Certainly that heart is steel-framed which, in spite of one’s chanting the holy name of the Lord with concentration, does not change when ecstasy takes place, tears fill the eyes and the hairs stand on end.**

Like Saunaka Rsi, one who thinks in this way is truly qualified to hear Srimad-Bhagavatam. Saunaka Rsi continues: If one chooses to do something other than hear about Krsna, one will simply waste his life. “Lazy human beings with paltry intelligence and a short duration of life pass the night sleeping and the day performing activities that are for naught.” (Bhag. [1.16.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.9)) In his purports to this section, Srila Prabhupada urges those wishing to escape death to hear about Krsna: “A living being is eternal by constitution. He is, so to speak, in the whirlpool of birth and death due to his contact with material energy. Freed from such material energy, a living entity is liberated and is eligible to return home, back to Godhead. Those who want to live forever without changing their material bodies should not waste valuable time with topics other than those relating to Lord Krsna and His devotees.... The surest remedy for avoiding death is to accustom oneself to hearing the nectarean pastimes of the Lord as they are systematically narrated in the text of Srimad-Bhagavatam.” (Bhag. [1.16.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.6), [8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.8), purports)

## Texts 10-24: Maharaja Pariksit Tours his Kingdom, and Dharma, Religion, Questions the Earth

In answer to Saunaka Rsi’s inquiry about Pariksit’s chastisement of Kali, Suta Gosvami states: Hearing that Kali had infiltrated his kingdom, Maharaja Pariksit armed himself with bow and arrows and sat on his chariot, decorated with the sign of a lion and drawn by black horses. He surrounded himself with his army and left his capital city.

Maharaja Pariksit found Kali’s entrance into his kingdom unpalatable, yet as a true warrior he was thrilled by the opportunity to fight, just as a sportsman feels the thrill of an upcoming contest. Thus Maharaja Pariksit, the world monarch, traveled throughout his kingdom looking for Kali. The local rulers in every province offered him tribute, and in each place “he continuously heard the glories of his great forefathers, who were all devotees of the Lord, and also of the glorious acts of Lord Krsna. He also heard how he himself had been protected by the Lord from the powerful heat of the weapon of Asvatthama. . . . Maharaja Pariksit heard that out of His causeless mercy Lord Krsna \[Visnu\], who is universally obeyed, rendered all kinds of service to the malleable sons of Pandu by accepting posts ranging from chariot driver to president to messenger, friend, night watchman, etc., according to the will of the Pandavas, obeying them like a servant and offering obeisances like one younger in years. When he heard this, Maharaja Pariksit became overwhelmed with devotion to the lotus feet of the Lord.” (Bhag. [1.16.13-16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.13))

The king appreciated hearing about Lord Krsna, his forefathers, and even about himself. Srila Prabhupada explains: “The Lord is present for the devotee by His acts and glories, and therefore Maharaja Pariksit felt the presence of the Lord when He was glorified by His acts, especially when he was saved by the Lord in the womb of his mother.” (Bhag. [1.16.13-15](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.13), purport) In his purport to text 16, Srila Prabhupada notes the depth of relationship between Krsna and the Pandavas: “Lord Krsna is everything to the unalloyed devotees like the Pandavas. The Lord was for them the Supreme Lord, the spiritual master, the worshipable Deity, the guide, the chariot driver, the friend, the servant, the messenger and everything they could conceive of. And thus the Lord also reciprocated the feelings of the Pandavas. Maharaja Pariksit, as a pure devotee of the Lord, could appreciate the Lord’s transcendental reciprocation of the feelings of His devotees, and thus he himself also was overwhelmed with the dealings of the Lord. . . . The Pandavas were so malleable to the will of the Lord that they could sacrifice any amount of energy for the service of the Lord, and by such unalloyed determination they could secure the Lord’s mercy in any shape they desired.”

Beginning in text 18 of this chapter, Srila Sukadeva Gosvami shifts the topic: Once in an area in Maharaja Pariksit’s kingdom, Dharma, the personality of religion, was wandering in the form of a bull. He met the personality of the earth, who had taken the form of a grieving cow. Text 17 describes Maharaja Pariksit as vartamanasya, “remaining absorbed in thought” of his glorious forefathers and their relationship with Krsna. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment on the text notes that the expression vartamanasya should be expanded to anuvartamanasya. Thus as Pariksit is touring, he continues his meditation on the deeds of Krsna and the Pandavas. Commenting on text 18, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains: “Right at the onset of Kali-yuga, Dharma, Prthvi, and Kali had assumed these shapes, although invisible to regular people. By this one can understand that Maharaja Pariksit is seeing through his yoga-induced vision because of his desire to see \[these things\].” Thus Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s comment indicates that the events currently being described were only visible to Pariksit Maharaja in his meditative, yogic trance.

Sukadeva Gosvami continues his narration: The earth, having assumed the form of a cow, had lost her natural beauty. Tears filled her eyes. She appeared like the mother of a lost child. Dharma, in the form of the bull, was concerned, so he questioned her about her difficulties. His questions reveal the symptoms that characterize Kali-yuga. Dharma inquired: О Madam, you appear neither hale nor hearty. Are you diseased or thinking of a distant relative? Have you noticed that I now stand on only one leg, my other three having been broken ? Has that caused you distress? Are you anxious that you may be killed by a meateater? Do you grieve for those suffering from famine or drought? Has your compassion been aroused for abandoned and forlorn women and children, or are you aggrieved to have discovered that learning has fallen into the hands of those addicted to sinful, irreligious acts? Do you lament the disordered and sorrowful conditions of government? Are you unhappy that the general population is unprincipled in their eating, sleeping, drinking, and mating? Does their lack of restriction in performing these acts cause you unhappiness?In his purports to this section, Srila Prabhupada strikingly points out the inconsistencies in the age of Kali. Here are a few extracts:

**The people of the world in this age of Kali are always full of anxieties. Everyone is diseased with some kind of ailment. From the very faces of the people of this age, one can find out the index of the mind. Everyone feels the absence of his relative who is away from home. The particular symptom of the age of Kali is that no family is now blessed to live together. (Bhag.** [**1.16.19**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.19)**, purport)**

**With the progress of the age of Kali, four things particularly, namely the duration of life, mercy, the power of recollection, and moral or religious principles will gradually diminish. Since Dharma, or the principles of religion, would be lost in the proportion of three out of four, the symbolic bull was standing on one leg only. When three fourths of the population of the whole world become irreligious, the situation is converted into hell for the animals. (Bhag.** [**1.16.20**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.20)**)**

**In the age of Kali, godless civilizations will create so many so-called religious societies in which the Personality of Godhead will be directly or indirectly defied. And thus faithless societies of men will make the world uninhabitable for the saner section of people. (Bhag.** [**1.16.20**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.20)**, purport)**

**Beef is forbidden in the scriptures, and the bulls and cows are offered special protection by followers of the Vedas. But in this age of Kali, people will exploit the body of the bull and the cow as they like, and thus they will invite sufferings of various types. (Bhag.** [**1.16.20**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.20)**, purport)**

**In the age of Kali, the women and the children, along with brdh-manas and cows, will be grossly neglected and left unprotected. In this age illicit connection with women will render many women and children uncared for. Circumstantially, the women will try to become independent of the protection of men, and marriage will be performed as a matter of formal agreement between man and woman. In most cases, the children will not be taken care of properly. (Bhag** [**1.16.21**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.21)**, purport)**

**The brahmanas are traditionally intelligent men, and thus they will be able to pick up modem education to the topmost rank, but as far as moral and religious principles are concerned, they shall be the most fallen. Education and bad character go ill together, but such things will run parallel. (Bhag.** [**1.16.21**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.21)**, purport)**

**In this age, the fathers and the guardians are not happy with the behavior of their wards. They should know that so many innocent children are victims of bad association awarded by the influence of this age of Kali. We know from Srimad-Bhagavatam that Ajamila, an innocent son of a brahmana, was walking down a road and saw a sudra pair sexually embracing. This attracted the boy, and later on the boy became a victim of all debaucheries. From a pure brahmana, he fell down to the position of a wretched urchin, and it was all due to bad association. There was but one victim like Ajamila in those days, but in this age of Kali the poor innocent students are daily victims of cinemas which attract men only for sex indulgence. (Bhag.** [**1.16.22**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.22)**, purport)**

Kali cripples the four religious principles: austerity, cleanliness, mercy, and truthfulness, which drive away the four pillars of irreligion: illicit sex, meat-eating, intoxication, and gambling. Although these four religious principles are not the final goal of religion, a society in which they are prominent is fertile for the citizens’ natural development of love for Krsna. Kali’s business, therefore, is to “beat” and break these religious legs.

In Vedic times, people valued these four principles because they bred character. Ultimately, as Srila Prabhupada notes in his purport to Bhagavatam [1.17.24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.24), “Such strong men of character were competent enough to get away from the clutches of maya.” Gradually, as Kali-yuga progresses, these basic religious principles become proportionately curtailed by pride, intoxication, and attachment to women. Thus the path of transcendental bliss disappears from human society.

The bull further inquired: Or are you suffering because you are bereft of the presence of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who appeared just to relieve your burden? Is your sadness caused by your contemplating His pastimes in their absence? Mother Earth, please tell me the cause of your tribulation, for it has reduced you to such weakness. It seems that time, the all-powerful conqueror, has forcibly stolen all your good fortune.

## Texts 25-36: The Earth’s Reply

Mother Earth in the form of a cow replied: О Dharma, I shall reply to all your questions. You once had four legs, and you increased happiness all over the world by the mercy of the Lord, in which eternally reside all auspicious and exalted qualities. “That Personality of Godhead, the reservoir of all goodness and beauty, Lord Sri Krsna, has now closed His transcendental pastimes on the face of the earth. In His absence the age of Kali has spread its influence everywhere, so I am sorry to see this condition of existence.” (Bhag. [1.16.29-30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.29)) I am lamenting for you, for all who follow the Lord’s varnasrama system, and for myself as well. Krsna bestowed the greatest fortune on me, because by His presence I was “decorated with the impressions of the flag, thunderbolt, elephant-driving rod and lotus flower, which are signs of the lotus feet of the Lord. But at the end, when I felt I was so fortunate, the Lord left me.” (Bhag. [1.16.33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.33))That the earth’s fortune vanished with the Lord’s departure is the subject of much of Srila Prabhupada’s important purport to text 33. Prabhupada compels us to remain constantly in the Lord’s presence:

**The beauty and opulence of the world can be enhanced by the grace of the Lord and not by any manmade planning. When the Lord Sri Krsna was present on this earth, the impressions of the special signs of His lotus feet were stamped on the dust, and as a result of this specific grace, the whole earth was made as perfect as possible. In other words, the rivers, the seas, the forests, the hills and the mines, which are the supplying agents for the necessities of men and animals, were folly discharging their respective duties. Therefore the riches of the world surpassed all the riches of all other planets in the three planetary systems of the universe. One should, therefore, ask that the grace of the Lord always be present on earth so that we may be favored with His causeless mercy and be happy, having all necessities of life. One may ask how we can detain the Supreme Lord on this earth after His mission is fulfilled and He has left this earth for His own abode. The answer is that there is no need to detain the Lord. The Lord, being omnipresent, can be present with us if we want Him at all. By His omnipresence, He can always be with us if we are attached to His devotional service by hearing, chanting, remembering, etc.**

**There is nothing in the world with which the Lord is disconnected. The only thing we must learn is to excavate the source of connection and thus be linked with Him by offenseless service. We can be connected with Him by the transcendental sound representation of the Lord. The holy name of the Lord and the Lord Himself are identical, and one who chants the holy name of the Lord in an offenseless manner can at once realize that the Lord is present before him. Even by the vibration of radio sound, we can partially realize sound relativity, and by resounding the sound of transcendence we can verily feel the presence of the Lord. In this age, when everything is polluted by the contamination of Kali, it is instructed in the scriptures and preached by Lord Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu that by chanting the holy name of the Lord, we can at once be free from contamination and gradually rise to the status of transcendence and go back to Godhead. The offenseless chanter of the holy name of the Lord is as auspicious as the Lord Himself, and the movement of pure devotees of the Lord all over the world can at once change the troublesome face of the world. Only by the propagation of the chanting of the holy name of the Lord can we be immune from all effects of the age of Kali.**

Aside from the final line of Srila Prabhupada’s purport being striking, Srila Krsnadasa Kaviraja Gosvami also confirms the point in two places. First: “The religious practice for the age of Kali is to broadcast the glories of the holy name. Only for this purpose has the Lord, in a yellow color, descended as Lord Caitanya.” (Cc. Adi [3.40](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/3.40)) And again, in his summary of the Caitanya-caritdmrta’s Adidila he writes: “The Third Chapter specifically describes the distribution of love of Godhead. It also describes the religion of the age, which is simply to distribute the holy name of Lord Krsna and propagate the process of loving Him.” (Cc. Adi [17.316](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/17.316))

The earth reminded Dharma how both of them had been overburdened by the excessive military strength of demoniac kings. But, she explained, the Supreme Personality of Godhead had appeared by His internal energy to offer them relief. She continued her lament: “Who, therefore, can tolerate the pangs of separation from that Supreme Personality of Godhead? He could conquer the gravity and passion' ate wrath of His sweethearts like Satyabhama by His sweet smile of love, pleasing glance and hearty appeals. When He traversed my \[earth’s\] surface, I would be immersed in the dust of His lotus feet and thus would be sumptuously covered with grass which appeared like hairs standing on me out of pleasure.” (Bhag. [1.16.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/16.35))

Srila Prabhupada’s purport to this text describes the intensity of the earth’s feelings of separation: “There were chances of separation between the Lord and His thousands of queens because of the Lord’s being absent from home, but as far as His connection with earth was concerned, the Lord would traverse the earth with His lotus feet, and therefore there was no chance of separation. When the Lord left the surface of the earth to return to His spiritual abode, the earth’s feelings of separation were therefore more acute.” One can hardly imagine the earth’s grief. For 125 years, Krsna’s lotus feet graced her soil. Then on Krsna’s leaving the planet, Kali entered just as darkness descends after sunset. Horrors followed immediately as religiosity crumbled. Cleanliness and mercy departed; meat-eating religions began.

But into this dark and miserable gloom, a great and powerful king rose like the sun, armed with krsna-sakti, Krsna’s own ruling potency. The king’s actions were perfectly decisive, potent, and balanced; he offered his rulership in devotion for Krsna’s pleasure.

## Chapter 17 - Punishment and Reward of Kali

## Texts 1-16: Maharaja Pariksit Challenges Kali, then Consoles the Cow and Bull

Near the Sarasvati River, Maharaja Pariksit saw a sudra dressed in garments of embroidered gold, as if he were a king. This sudra was beating a bull and a cow. As Srila Prabhupada comments in his purport to the chapter’s first verse, this is a “principal sign” of the age of Kali: “lower-caste sudras, i.e., men without brahminical culture and spiritual initiation, will be dressed like administrators or kings, and the principal business of such non-ksatriya rulers will be to kill the innocent animals, especially the cows and the bulls. . . .” The bull, as white as a white lotus flower, was terrified. Trembling and urinating, he stood on one leg. This symbolizes, Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 2, that in the age of Kali the spotlessly white principles of religion will be attacked by the uncultured. Some will preach boldly against these principles; others will concoct their own. What ever fragments of true principles do survive “will be embarrassed by so many obstacles as if in the trembling condition of falling down at any time.”

The cow was rendered poor and calfless, her legs being beaten by the sudra. Tears filled her eyes. Hankering for grass in the field, she felt distressed and weak. Thus the cow, the giver of liquid religiosity in the form of milk, was in a sorrowful condition. Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to text 3: “In the Kali-yuga, the calves are separated from the cows as early as possible for purposes which may not be mentioned in these pages of Srimad-Bhagavatam. The cow stands with tears in her eyes, the sudra milkman draws milk from the cow artificially, and when there is no milk the cow is sent to be slaughtered. These greatly sinful acts are responsible for all the troubles in present society. People do not know what they are doing in the name of economic development.”

Maharaja Pariksit was a true warrior-king, and Kali, the enemy, had entered. It is a cornerstone of Kali’s mission to undermine authority, for Krsna is the ultimate authority and Kali’s job is to induce irre-ligion. Kali therefore corrupts authorities and then reveals them as inept and hypocritical. Husband and wife, parent and child, priest and congregation, government leader and citizen—these natural relationships that combine authorities with their dependents prove unreliable and untrustworthy in Kali-yuga. Kali cries: See how authorities exploit their dependents! Let there be independence for every man and woman! Think for yourself. Care for yourself. Who else will care for you? Be your own authority!

Kali also propagates his pet theory of evolution, because if people think they are ever-evolving, they will come to believe that tradition and authority obstruct progress. Thus children will think of themselves as more evolved than their parents and believe that following their elders impedes humanity’s onward march. Kali also foments unbearable, continuous quarrel and dissention to break apart honored traditions and social structures, and since choosing enjoyment over duty, and mastership over submission appears more convenient, Kali found himself, even in Maharaja Pariksit’s time, preaching to the halfconverted.

Yet despite Kali’s difficult-to-deny rationales meant to drive people toward a self-oriented independence, people find themselves more and more filled with anxiety, general discontent, and loneliness. Kali, however, comes forward to offer his solution: Revolution! Break the remaining boundaries! Seek progress through science! Forever forward!

And dull the pain with intoxication, movies, computers, sports, sex, and raucous music. Enjoy instantaneously and virtually. Increase your self-esteem. After all, who but yourself is ultimately important?

As soon as one turns his back on Krsna and loses his sense of himself as God’s servant, he must develop an alternative, false sense of identity—a false ego. Kali’s assignment is to make that false ego flourish. Thus when Maharaja Pariksit, governing on Krsna’s behalf, saw that Kali was beating the personifications of religion and the earth, he picked up his bow and arrows and spoke to Kali in a voice as deep as thunder. “Oh, who are you? You appear to be strong and yet you dare kill, within my protection, those who are helpless! By your dress you pose yourself to be a godly man \[king\], but by your deeds you are opposing the principles of the twice-born ksatriyas. You rogue, do you dare beat an innocent cow because Lord Krsna and Arjuna, the carrier of the Gandiva bow, are out of sight? Since you are beating the innocent in a secluded place, you are considered a culprit and therefore deserve to be killed.” (Bhag. [1.17.5-6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.5))

Maharaja Pariksit was scarcely able to imagine a bull and a cow being mistreated. He turned to console them. Both the bull and the cow had taken birth in his kingdom, and his affection for them was the love of a father for his children. He first spoke to the bull: “Oh, who are you? Are you a bull as white as a white lotus, or are you a demigod? You have lost three of your legs and are moving on only one.... Now for the first time in a kingdom well protected by the arms of the kings of the Kuru dynasty, I see you grieving with tears in your eyes. Up till now no one on earth has ever shed tears because of royal negligence. О son of Surabhi, you need lament no longer now. There is no need to fear this low-class sudra.” (Bhag. [1.17.7-8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.7)) The king then turned to the cow: О mother, as long as I am alive and the king, there is no reason for you to cry. Everything will be auspicious for you.

Srila Prabhupada begins his purport to text 9 by explaining that cows will be protected only when a cultured and powerful executive head, a king like Pariksit, is in power: “In the material world the human society gives all protection to the human being, but there is no law to protect the descendants of Surabhi, who can give all protection to men by supplying the miracle food, milk. But Maharaja Pariksit and the Pandavas were fully conscious of the importance of the cow and bull, and they were prepared to punish the cow-killer with all chastisement, including death.” Why is cow protection so important? “For protecting the cows and brahminical culture, the Lord, who is very kind to the cow and the brahmanas (go'brahmana'hitaya), will be pleased with us and will bestow upon us real peace.”

In his purport to text 13, Srila Prabhupada writes: “The reputation of the reign of Maharaja Ramacandra and that of the kings who followed in the footsteps of Maharaja Ramacandra, like the Pandavas and their descendants, are never to be forgotten because in their kingdom offenseless and honest living beings were never in trouble. The bull and the cow are the symbols of the most offenseless living beings because even the stool and urine of these animals are utilized to benefit human society.” Srila Prabhupada explains further in his purport to text 11: “Any living being, if he terrifies other living beings, is a most wretched subject, and the king should at once kill such a disturbing element.”

Again in his purport to text 14: “Dishonest miscreants flourish because of cowardly and impotent executive heads of state. But when the executive heads are strong enough to curb all sorts of dishonest miscreants, in any part of the state, certainly they cannot flourish. When the miscreants are punished in an exemplary manner, automatically all good fortune follows. As said before, it is the prime duty of the king or the executive head to give protection in all respects to the peaceful, offenseless citizens of the state.” And in text 15: “Maharaja Pariksit challenges even such denizens of heaven if they torture the offenseless. This means that the state executive head must be as strong as Maharaja Pariksit so that he may be determined to punish the strongest offenders. It should be the principle of a state executive head that the offender of the codes of God is always punished.”

Wishing to act swiftly, the powerful and noble king repeatedly asked the bull: “O son of Surabhi, who has cut off your three legs? . . . О bull, you are offenseless and thoroughly honest; therefore I wish all good to you. Please tell me of the perpetrator of these mutilations, which blackmail the reputation of the sons of Prtha.” (Bhag. [1.17.12-13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.12)) In his commentary on texts 10-11, Srila Sridhara Svami states that Maharaja Pariksit was ready to kill the miscreant for the miscreant’s own benefit. The king therefore wanted to know, Srila Sridhara Svami comments on text 13, the identity of the perpetrator of these horrible deeds that spoil the Pandavas’ reputation. Srila Sridhara Svami also explains that the following text (14) answers the question “What good will occur if the bull informs Maharaja Pariksit of the name of the culprit who has injured his legs?”

Maharaja Pariksit continued: “Whoever causes offenseless living beings to suffer must fear me anywhere and everywhere in the world. . . . An upstart living being who commits offenses by torturing those who are offenseless shall be directly uprooted by me, even though he be a denizen of heaven with armor and decorations. The supreme duty of the ruling king is to give all protection to law-abiding persons and to chastise those who stray from the ordinances of the scriptures in ordinary times, when there is no emergency.” (Bhag. [1.17.14-16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.14)) Please inform me, the king requested, who has harmed you.

## Text 17-28: The Personality of Religion and Maharaja Pariksit Converse

Dharma, the personality of religion, said: “These words just spoken by you befit a person of the Pandava dynasty. Captivated by the devotional qualities of the Pandavas, even Lord Krsna, the Personality of Godhead, performed duties as a messenger.” (Bhag. [1.17.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.17)) Maharaja Pariksit’s bold and assuring words were not exaggerations. As Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to this text: “A devotee of the Lord is equally as powerful as the Lord or sometimes more powerful by His grace, and any promise made by a devotee, though it may be ordinarily very difficult to fulfill, is properly executed by the grace of the Lord.” Maharaja Pariksit was a great devotee. The Lord was always with him, and he was always protected by the Lord. Therefore, “the assurance of protection by Maharaja Pariksit could never be without meaning.”

After expressing his appreciation for the king, Dharma continued: You have questioned me about the identity of the one who caused my suffering. In fact, I am unable to tell you, for I have been confused by the many differing philosophical opinions about who actually is the “doer.” Some philosophers claim that due to karma, one causes his own difficulties. Others claim that suffering is caused by Brahman, the Lord’s spiritual effulgence, which is the supreme supernatural power. Still others—atheists—say that no cause exists beyond material nature. Some insist that the true cause is unknowable. О sage among kings, please therefore reach your own conclusion with your own intelligence, and decide who has caused my pain.

Generally on reflecting on the cause of one’s difficulty, one would answer with less philosophy and more accusation. By identifying someone as “the doer” and viewing that person as an enemy, one comes to seek vengeance rather than to practice introspection. While one tends to justify thoughts of retaliation and the ensuing plan of action, one may not realize that those actions will implicate him in painful exchanges for hundreds of births. In addition, by meditating on another’s bad qualities, one will develop those qualities himself. One’s mentality is formed by the object of his meditation: “A grassworm confined in a hole of a wall by a bee always thinks of the bee in fear and enmity and later becomes a bee simply because of such remembrance.” (Bhag. [7.1.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-7/1.28))

Therefore, after hearing the bull’s extraordinary and philosophical reply to his simple question, Maharaja Pariksit concluded that this bull must be religion personified. The king thus pondered Dharma’s words. “O you, who are in the form of a bull! You know the truth of religion, and you are speaking according to the principle that the destination intended for the perpetrator of irreligious acts is also intended for one who identifies the perpetrator. You are no other than the personality of religion.” (Bhag. [1.17.22](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.22)) You have understood that the Lord’s energies and actions are inconceivable. No one can estimate them.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes as follows on text 22: “Although asked by me, the king, and although you have the right to say, ‘He is the one who beats me, who am innocent,’ you did not. This is because one who points out an irreligious act attains the same destination as the perpetrator, what to say of one who expressly condemns it. Therefore you must be personified religion, Dharma himself. It cannot be otherwise. That is my conclusion.” Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura’s previous comments on text 18-20 offer further clarification. Here is a selection from those commentaries:

**Dharma, the bull: And if you say, “How can you not know your tormentor when I see him right here?” I say, “Yes, he is the tormentor (klesa-da), but there must be some seed of my torment**
