**(klesa-bija) planted by previous deeds. Otherwise I would not be suffering in this way. I do not know the identity of the person who generated that seed.”**

**Maharaja Pariksit: But aren’t you knowledgeable in sastra! How then can you not know?**

**Dharma: It is true that I am knowledgeable in sastra, but my knowledge of many sastras leaves the cause unascertained. I am bewildered by the various opinions of the different wranglers.**

From the commentary on text 20:

**Dharma: Still, it is not appropriate for the worshipers to say that the Lord is the cause of suffering. But if it is said that the Lord is irresponsibly cruel and partial, the answer is apratarkya: it is beyond our reason. Yet although He is difficult to understand, He is neither cruel nor partial. That is the meaning. It is just as Bhisma says in Bhagavatam** [**1.9.16**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.16)**: “O King, no one can know the plan of the Lord \[Krsna\]. Even though great philosophers inquire exhaustively, they are bewildered.” It could have been done to increase the humility of a pale shadow of a devotee (myself) and thus increase my remembrance of Him, or perhaps it was done to spread your glories—you, Maharaja Pariksit, the highest of devotees—by your defeating Kali. In this way my suffering brings benefit. And if none among these opinions wins your preference, then why don’t you use the power of your own intelligence to ascertain the proper conclusion? You are, after all, a rajarsi, are you not?**

**Thus by such roundabout speaking, the Vaisnava siddhanta emerges and is established. The words niscaya and kesv api indicate that it is difficult to obtain this understanding. Therefore, “deliberate on this,” for it is a worthy deliberation.**

In his commentary on text 19, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura again states the bull’s thoughts: Therefore it is only God who is the cause, and this is fixed and undeniable. But His plans and ways are hard to comprehend for all of humankind, as enunciated by Bhismadeva (Bhag. [1.9.16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/9.16)).

Who then actually causes the pain, misery, and suffering in this world? Can we name no one but God? Srila Prabhupada addresses one side of this important question in his purport to text 22: “A devotee’s conclusion is that no one is directly responsible for being a benefactor or mischief-monger without the sanction of the Lord; therefore he does not consider anyone to be directly responsible for such action. But in both the cases he takes it for granted that either benefit or loss is God-sent, and thus it is His grace. In case of benefit, no one will deny that it is God-sent, but in case of loss or reverses one becomes doubtful about how the Lord could be so unkind to His devotee as to put him in great difficulty. Jesus Christ was seemingly put into such great difficulty, being crucified by the ignorant, but he was never angry at the mischief-mongers. That is the way of accepting a thing, either favorable or unfavorable. Thus for a devotee the identifier is equally a sinner, like the mischief-monger. By God’s grace, the devotee tolerates all reverses. Maharaja Pariksit observed this, and therefore he could understand that the bull was no other than the personality of religion himself. In other words, a devotee has no suffering at all because so-called suffering is also God’s grace for a devotee who sees God in everything.”

Yet when asked by the king, Dharma did not identify Krsna or “God’s grace” as the cause of his suffering. What prevents one from seeing Krsna and His mercy in all things? Why does one turn away from this higher understanding? Srila Prabhupada answers this question in his next purport: “A question may be raised as to why a devotee should refrain from identifying an actor, although he knows definitely that the Lord is the ultimate doer of everything. Knowing the ultimate doer, one should not pose himself as ignorant of the actual performer. To answer this doubt, the reply is that the Lord is also not directly responsible, for everything is done by His deputed maya-sakti, or material energy. The material energy is always provoking doubts about the supreme authority of the Lord. The personality of religion knew perfectly well that nothing can take place without the sanction of the Supreme Lord, and still he was put into doubts by the deluding energy, and thus he refrained from mentioning the supreme cause. This doubtfulness was due to the contamination of both Kali and the material energy. The whole atmosphere of the age of Kali is magnified by the deluding energy, and the proportion of measurement is inexplicable.” (Bhag. [1.17.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.23), purport)

An accurate understanding of what occurs, therefore, exists on more than one level. If one is being unreasonably beaten by a man with a stick, he will be injured and must defend himself or suffer great pain. Despite the beating being ultimately “God’s grace,” the “beater” may not have one’s best interest in mind. Dealing on this level demands prompt and practical action. While acting practically, however, one should nevertheless remember Krsna’s ultimate control, because Krsna is the ultimate “doer.” Maintaining this awareness while acting will free one from envy, anxiety, and anger, and will carry one to Krsna’s lotus feet.

Seeing all that occurs as Krsna’s will, a devotee understands that “not a blade of grass moves without the will of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” Such a person remains free of anxiety amid even the greatest difficulties. Still, along with maintaining this vision, he must act practically while simultanously remaining detached from the results of his action.

On still another level, more than Krsna’s desire causes our circumstances. Again, as Srila Prabhupada states in his purport to text 23: “The Lord is also not directly responsible, for everything is done by His deputed mayd'sakti, or material energy.” Krsna desires that the living entities fully surrender to Him, become His devotees, and return to Him in the spiritual world: “Abandon all varieties of religion and just surrender unto Me. I shall deliver you from all sinful reactions. Do not fear.” (Bg. [18.66](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/18.66)) Each living entity has been given free will. The material energy, Krsna’s mdya-sakti, reciprocates with the living entity’s desire to be independent of Krsna by placing him under her control. She is represented by the laws of material nature. Like the living entities, these laws are also under Krsna’s ultimate jurisdiction, but they act neutrally, as does the law of the land when dispensing rewards and punishments for lawful and unlawful acts. Thus everyone finds himself in one situation or another by Krsna’s grace, and suffering or enjoying the reactions caused by his own desires and deeds.

Srila Prabhupada explains: “Although the bull, or the personality of religion, and the cow, the personality of the earth, knew perfectly well that the personality of Kali was the direct cause of their sufferings, still, as devotees of the Lord, they knew well also that without the sanction of the Lord no one could inflict trouble upon them. According to the Padma Purana, our present trouble is due to the fructifying of seedling sins, but even those seedling sins also gradually fade away by execution of pure devotional service. Thus even if the devotees see the mischief-mongers, they do not accuse them for the sufferings inflicted. They take it for granted that the mischief-monger is made to act by some indirect cause, and therefore they tolerate the sufferings, thinking them to be God-given in small doses, for otherwise the sufferings should have been greater. Maharaja Pariksit wanted to get a statement of accusation against the direct mischief-monger, but \[the victims\] declined to give it on the above-mentioned grounds.” (Bhag. [1.17.18](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.18), purport)A devotee thus sees Krsna’s merciful hand in everything; a materialist, in his attempt to avoid the Lord, sees other causes. Dharma, a devotee, wisely neglected to name a cause separate from Krsna for his difficulties, yet he was unable to directly recognize his circumstances as Krsna’s mercy. This lack was due to an atmosphere of doubt caused by Kali’s influence. If in spite of Kali one can somehow see Krsna’s merciful hand in everything that happens, he will become eligible to return to the kingdom of God. As Lord Brahma states: “My dear Lord, one who earnestly waits for You to bestow Your causeless mercy upon him, all the while patiently suffering the reactions of his past misdeeds and offering You respectful obeisances with his heart, words and body, is surely eligible for liberation, for it has become his rightful claim.” (Bhag. [10.14.8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/14.8)) Srila Prabhupada has often addressed this point. Here is a sample of his statements on this topic:

**So if we simply remember that “Krsna has put me in this condition of life; I am a sudra," that is very nice. Tat te ’nukamparh su-samiksama.no bhunjana evatma-krtam vipdkam. A devotee is satisfied always. He does not grudge that “I am put into this condition. Why I’m not put into the condition of a king or a learned brahmana7.” No. “Whatever condition Krsna has given me, that is all right.” Tat te anukampam. It is His grace. “By His grace I have got this position.” Because my only business is to remember Krsna. That we can do at any stage of life. (Lecture, Bhag.** [**1.5.36**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/5.36)**, Vrndavana, August 17, 1974)**

**Don’t think that things are taking place automatically. Therefore even in reverse condition a devotee does not see that “This thing is happening without direction of Krsna.” Even if he is in an adverse condition, he does not feel any pain, because he knows that “This adverse condition is also under the direction of Krsna. So I am fully surrendered to Krsna. Why I shall take this adverse position as not mercy of Krsna? It is also mercy of Krsna.” Tat te ’nukamparh su'samlksamano, bhunjana evatma-krtam vipdkam. A devotee is not disturbed by adverse condition. He takes that this is a gift of Krsna.**

**Tat te anukampam. “It is Krsna’s mercy. Although I am put into difficulty, it is Krsna’s mercy.” So anyone who takes in that way, mukti'pade sadaya-bhak: his going back to home, back to Godhead, is guaranteed. Because he takes everything as Krsna’s mercy. (Lecture, Bhag.** [**1.7.12**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.12)**, Vrndavana, September 11, 1976)**

**He’s always merciful. Therefore devotees never take anything as not merciful. Tat te anukampam. They take everything from Krsna as sympathy, anukampa. Tat te 'nukampam su'samiksamanam. One who can see this anukampa in reverse condition of life, the compassion of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, mukti-pade sa daya-bhak. His right to liberation becomes guaranteed. If anyone accepts the mercy of God in any circumstances, and he does not do anything wrong to anyone, such person is guaranteed to be liberated. That is the injunction of the sastra. (Lecture, Bhag.** [**1.7.49-50**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/7.49)**, Vrndavana, October 7, 1976)**

**The devotee is suffering from some reverse condition, then he is feeling very much obliged to Krsna: “O my dear Lord, it is Your great mercy that I am suffering.” This is devotee. He is suffering and he is taking it as great mercy of God. Tat te anukampam. Anukampa. Anukampa means mercy. So it is Your mercy. Tat te 'nukampam su-samiksamano bhunjana evatma ktrtam vipakam. (Lecture, Bhag.** [**6.1.9**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-6/1.9)**, Los Angeles, June 22, 1975)**

Having discussed with Dharma the actual cause of his current distress, Srila Sridhara Svami comments, Maharaja Pariksit, understanding that Dharma himself is present before him, next describes the legs of religion in texts 24-25. Maharaja Pariksit thus continued to speak to the bull. “Of your four legs (austerity, cleanliness, mercy, and truthfulness), three are broken “due to rampant irreligion in the form of pride, lust for women, and intoxication.” You now stand only on your leg of truthfulness, but “quarrel personified \[Kali\], flourishing by deceit, is also trying to destroy that leg.” (Bhag. [1.17.24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.24), [25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.25))

The king then turned to the earth in the form of a cow: The burden you felt was certainly diminished by the Personality of Godhead when He was present as an incarnation. All good was performed because of His auspicious footprints. Now with the Lord absent, you lament and fear the future with tear-filled eyes, for the earth is now ruled by low-class men posing as rulers.

Then after pacifying the bull and the cow, Maharaja Pariksit, who could fight one thousand enemies single-handedly, took up his sharp sword to kill Kali, the cause of all irreligion.

## Texts 29-45: The Surrender and Reward of Kali

“When the personality of Kali understood that the King was willing to kill him, he at once abandoned the dress of a king and, under pressure of fear, completely surrendered to him, bowing his head.” (Bhag. [1.17.29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.29)) Srila Prabhupada speaks about the significance of Kali’s abandoning his royal dress in his purport to this text: “The royal dress of the personality of Kali is artificial. The royal dress is suitable for a king or ksatriya, but when a lower-class man artificially dresses himself as a king, his real identity is disclosed by the challenge of a bona fide ksatriya like Maharaja Pariksit. A real ksatriya never surrenders. He accepts the challenge of his rival ksatriya, and he fights either to die or to win. Surrender is unknown to a real ksatriya. In the age of Kali there are so many pretenders dressed and posed like administrators or executive heads, but their real identity is disclosed when they are challenged by a real ksatriya. Therefore when the artificially dressed personality of Kali saw that to fight Maharaja Pariksit was beyond his ability, he bowed down his head like a subordinate and gave up his royal dress.”

Maharaja Pariksit was compassionate by nature, so he could not kill Kali, who had surrendered out of fear and had thus disclosed his identity as a low-class man. Rather, the king, who was kind to the poor, smiled compassionately on Kali and spoke as follows: “\[S\]ince you have surrendered yourself with folded hands you need not fear for your life. But you cannot remain in my kingdom, for you are the friend of irreligion.” (Bhag. [1.17.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.31)) If you act as a head of state, “certainly irreligious principles like greed, falsehood, robbery, incivility, treachery, misfortune, cheating, quarrel and vanity will abound.” (Bhag. [1.17.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.32)) Therefore you cannot remain, for in this kingdom no irreligious acts will be performed. Rather, sacrifices will be enacted according to religious principles for the satisfaction of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is the all-pervading Supersoul and who awards all welfare to His worshipers.

Kali, as Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 31, may have been excused because he surrendered, yet he could not have been allowed to remain in Maharaja Pariksit’s kingdom. “The friends of irre-ligiosity should be banished from the state, and that will save the state from corruption.” From the purport to text 32: “A secular state may be impartial to any particular type of faith, but the state cannot be indifferent to the principles of religion \[austerity, cleanliness, mercy, and truthfulness\] as above-mentioned.”

Srila Prabhupada speaks of sacrifice in his purport to text 33: “There are different countries in different parts of the world, and each and every country may have different types of sacrifice to please the Supreme Lord, but the central point in pleasing Him is ascertained in the Bhagavatam, and it is truthfulness. The basic principle of religion is truthfulness, and the ultimate goal of all religions is to satisfy the Lord. In this age of Kali, the greatest common formula of sacrifice is the sankirtana-yajna. That is the opinion of the experts who know how to propagate the process of yajna. Lord Caitanya preached this method of yajna, and it is understood from this verse that the sacrificial method of sankirtana'yajna may be performed anywhere and everywhere in order to drive away the personality of Kali and save human society from falling prey to the influence of the age.”

Kali saw before him the king, appearing as death, with sword in hand and prepared to kill him were he to traverse his order. Trembling in fear Kali said: О Your Majesty, you have banished me from your kingdom, but where will I go? You are the emperor of all the lands throughout the world! Everywhere I go will eventually carry me to your bows, arrows, and sword. You may as well kill me now. О king, I am surrendered unto you, and I therefore request you to find me a permanent place of residence in your kingdom.

Pariksit Maharaja then offered Kali residence “in places where gambling, drinking, prostitution and animal slaughter were performed.” (Bhag. [1.17.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.38))

In his purport to text 38, Srila Prabhupada recommends how to apply religious principles so that the degradation popularized by Kali will be minimized: “Following in the footsteps of Maharaja Pariksit, it is the duty of all executive heads of states to see that the principles of religion, namely austerity, cleanliness, mercy and truthfulness, are es-tablished in the state, and that the principles of irreligion, namely pride, illicit female association or prostitution, intoxication and fab sity, are checked by all means. And to make the best use of a bad bargain, the personality of Kali may be transferred to places of gambling, drinking, prostitution and slaughterhouses, if there are any places like that.”

On hearing Maharaja Pariksit’s order, Kali understood that the king was cheating him, for no such sinful places existed in his kingdom. He thus requested something more, as Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 39: “. . . Kali asked the King to give him something practical which could be utilized for his nefarious purposes.” Maharaja Pariksit then offered Kali a fifth place: You may also “live where there is gold because wherever there is gold there is also falsity, intoxication, lust, envy and enmity.” (Bhag. [1.17.39](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.39))

Suta Gosvami explains that because Kali was allowed to live in those five places under Maharaja Pariksit’s shelter, “whoever desires progressive well-being, especially kings, religionists, public leaders, brahmanas and sannyasls, should never come in contact with the four above-mentioned irreligious principles.” (Bhag. [1.17.41](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.41))

Gold, the fifth shelter offered to Kali, as Srila Prabhupada points out in his purport to text 42, “is certainly a generator of falsity, intoxication, prostitution, enmity and violence, but under the guidance of a proper king or public leader, or a brahmana or sannyasi, the same gold can be properly utilized to reestablish the lost legs of the bull, the personality of religion.”

In his comment on text 39, Srila Jiva Gosvami confirms that Kali resides anywhere gold is not used for religious purposes. He also comments on text 42 that Maharaja Pariksit dispelled Kali by allowing gold to be used only for religious purposes. Srila Sridhara Svami states (referring to text 41) that if one wants to be a spiritual or public leader, he should be free from attachment to women and gold. Otherwise, one cannot become a “good man,” a leader who desires everyone’s uplift -ment (udbhavitumic chuh).

Suta Gosvami continues: “Thereafter the King reestablished the lost legs of the personality of religion \[the bull\], and by encouraging activities he sufficiently improved the condition of the earth.” (Bhag. 1.17.42) That same king, Suta says, now rules the world with great success. He considers it due to Maharaja Pariksit’s expertise that the sages at Naimisaranya are able to perform their sacrifice.

Srila Prabhupada summarizes Maharaja Pariksit’s mission as king, and by recounting the king’s actions, advises all government leaders: “If we want to drive out corruption from the state, we must first of all organize society to accept the principles of religion, namely austerity, cleanliness, mercy and truthfulness, and to make the condition favorable we must close all places of gambling, drinking, prostitution and falsity. . . . The brahmanas and the sannyasis are expert in the spiritual advancement of society, whereas the ksatriyas or the administrators are expert in the material peace and prosperity of human society. Both of them are the pillars of all happiness, and therefore they are meant for full cooperation for common welfare. Maharaja Pariksit was experienced enough to drive away Kali from his field of activities and thereby make the state receptive to spiritual enlightenment. If the common people are not receptive, it is very difficult to impress upon them the necessity of spiritual enlightenment. Austerity, cleanliness, mercy and truthfulness, the basic principles of religion, prepare the ground for the reception of advancement in spiritual knowledge, and Maharaja Pariksit made this favorable condition possible.” (Bhag. [1.17.44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.44), [45](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.45), purports)

## Dialogue Eight - Maharaja Pariksit Meets Sukadeva Gosvami And Prepares for Death

## Chapter 18 - Maharaja Pariksit Cursed by a Brahmana Boy

## Texts 1-10: Suta Gosvami Glorifies Maharaja Pariksit to the Sages of Naimisaranya, and the Sages Reply Fearlessness and Surrender

The sages at Naimisaranya asked in Bhagavatam [1.4.9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/4.9): “It is said that Maharaja Pariksit is a first-class devotee of the Lord and that his birth and activities are all wonderful. Please tell us about him.” After having answered this question, Sri Suta Gosvami begins to explain why Maharaja Pariksit renounced his kingdom and began to fast until death while sitting beside the Ganges River. The sages were awestruck when they heard that the king had neutralized Kali’s ability to harm the kingdom. Now they wanted to hear more. Suta Gosvami therefore continues: “Due to the mercy of the Personality of Godhead, Sri Krsna, who acts wonderfully, Maharaja Pariksit, though struck by the weapon of the son of Drona in his mother’s womb, could not be burned. Furthermore, Maharaja Pariksit was always consciously surrendered to the Personality of Godhead, and therefore he was neither afraid nor overwhelmed by fear due to a snake-bird which was to bite him because of the fury of a brahmana boy.” (Bhag. [1.18.1-2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.1))

Suta Gosvami points out that Krsna had saved Maharaja Pariksit in the womb of his mother. The king was surrendered to Krsna and therefore fearless even when confronted by death. He understood that the snake-bird could harm him only if Krsna allowed it. All that was important to him was his continuous remembrance of the Lord. Suta’s words therefore increase the sages’ enthusiasm to hear about Pariksit because his life was related to Krsna and surrendered to His plan.

Srila Prabhupada summarizes Maharaja Pariksit’s mood in his purport to text 2: “He knew that Narayana (Lord Krsna) had saved him when he was burned in the womb of his mother, and if he were to be killed by a snake bite, it would also take place by the will of the Lord. The devotee never goes against the will of the Lord; anything sent by God is a blessing for the devotee.”

The previous two chapters in the Bhagavatam have shown Maharaja Pariksit’s opulence as a ruler. Srila Prabhupada explains: “The conclusion is, therefore, that the sufferings of the representative of religion and the representative of the earth, as present before Maharaja Pariksit, were planned to prove that Maharaja Pariksit was the ideal executive head because he knew well how to give protection to the cows (the earth) and the brahmanas (religious principles), the two pillars of spiritual advancement.” (Bhag. [1.17.20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.20), purport) Now Krsna wished to use the king to exemplify another set of qualities, including the ability to accept fate, even if that fate forces one to die untimely. When the bull and cow, religion and the earth, were in difficulty, and the bull was unable to point out that it was ultimately Krsna’s will that was causing his torment, Srila Prabhupada, in his purport to Bhagavatam [1.17.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/17.23), notes the influence of Kali and of Krsna’s illusory energy for causing his lack of spiritual acumen: “The personality of religion knew perfectly well that nothing can take place without the sanction of the Supreme Lord, and still he was put into doubts by the deluding energy, and thus he refrained from mentioning the supreme cause. This doubtfulness was due to the contamination of both Kali and the material energy.” In these chapters, Maharaja Pariksit will perfectly demonstrate the difficult principle of accepting one’s circumstances as Krsna’s grace; that is, that one must ultimately recognize and surrender to one’s destiny because it is part of Sri Krsna’s beneficent plan. Because Krsna placed Maharaja Pariksit into difficulty, the Bhagavatam was spoken—Sukadeva Gosvami Spoke the Bhagavatam to help the king prepare for death. One can observe this situation and learn to apply the principle to one’s own life, because certainly any one receiving notice of impending death would be considered unfortunate. Still, without hesitation, Maharaja Pariksit confronted the simple but existentially heavy question: How should I fill my remaining days?

Maharaja Pariksit’s example disparages a hedonistic reply, because how one leaves this world dictates one’s next birth. The next body is generated based on one’s final mood and thought flow. Maharaja Pariksit accepted the blessing of his misfortune and used it to mold his consciousness as he desired. Suta Gosvami describes Maharaja Pariksit’s behavior after the curse: The king left his associates and surrendered himself as a disciple to Sukadeva Gosvami. He was thus able to understand Krsna, the unconquerable and unknowable Lord. “This was so because those who have dedicated their lives to the transcendental topics of the Personality of Godhead, of whom the Vedic hymns sing, and who are constantly engaged in remembering the lotus feet of the Lord, do not run the risk of having misconceptions even at the last moment of their lives.” (Bhag. [1.18.4](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.4))

What is wonderful for a devotee? What can a devotee not achieve? It is possible for devotees to fearlessly remember Krsna at the time of death because the Lord gives the devotees His blessings and mercy. Maharaja Pariksit’s final words (Bhag. [12.6.2-7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-12/6.2)) to Srila Sukadeva Gosvami, his spiritual master, affirm his pure, humble, and fearless Krsna consciousness:

**I have now achieved the purpose of my life, because a great and merciful soul like you has shown such kindness to me. You have personally spoken to me this narration of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Hari, who is without beginning or end. I do not consider it at all amazing that great souls such as yourself, whose minds are always absorbed in the infallible Personality of Godhead, show mercy to the foolish conditioned souls, tormented as we are by the problems of material life. 1 have heard from you this Srimad-Bhagavatam, which is the perfect summary of all the Puranas and which perfectly describes the Supreme Lord, Uttamah-sloka. My lord, I now have no fear of Taksaka or any other living being, or even of repeated deaths, because I have absorbed myself in that purely spiritual Absolute Truth, which you have revealed and which destroys all fear. О brahmana, please give me permission to resign my speech and the functions of all my senses unto Lord Adhoksaja. Allow me to absorb my mind, purified of lusty desires, within Him and to thus give up my life. You have revealed to me that which is most auspicious, the supreme personal feature of the Lord. I am now fixed in knowledge and self-realization, and my ignorance has been eradicated.**

Placing oneself securely under Krsna’s protection is the essence of surrender. A surrendered soul’s life rests on Krsna’s mercy: if Krsna wants to protect one, who can harm him? If fate ordains harm, who can protect him? Only a surrendered soul is secure and fearless in this world. Of course, it is much easier to grasp this point theoretically than to consistently apply it, but even the theoretical understanding is a gift on which one can build.

That gift is given when one studies the Bhagavatam: “Those who have dedicated their lives to the transcendental topics of the Personality of Godhead, of whom the Vedic hymns sing, and who are constantly engaged in remembering the lotus feet of the Lord, do not run the risk of having misconceptions even at the last moment of their lives.” (Bhag. [1.18.4](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.4)) Even at death, that all-important moment, with the mind grasping for shelter and respite from pain, Maharaja Pariksit was able to fix his mind firmly on the Lord with great devotion. Maharaja Pariksit’s life, therefore, was not unfortunate but completely fortunate. Attaining fearlessness, especially at death, is the challenge of one’s existence.

**Benefits of Kali’s Presence**

We have heard how Pariksit Maharaja chastised Kali, the promoter of irreligion, and how although Kali had entered the world at the moment of Krsna’s departure, he was unable to flourish in Maharaja Pariksit’s presence. The king knew that only less intelligent people would be swayed by Kali; the self-controlled would have nothing to fear. Thus the king acted as powerfully as a tiger to protect the foolish and careless. However, as Pariksit Maharaja also understood that Kali-yuga brought advantages to conditioned souls, “he was never envious of the personality of Kali.” (Bhag. [1.18.7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.7)) Srila Prabhupada describes some of these gifts in his purport to text 7: “In this fallen age, because the living beings are in an awkward position, the Supreme Lord has given some special facilities to them. So by the will of the Lord, a living being does not become a victim of a sinful act until the act is actually performed. In other ages, simply by thinking of performing a sinful act, one used to become a victim of the act. On the contrary, a living being in this age is awarded with the results of pious acts simply by thinking of them. ... At the end of the Srimad-Bhagavatam it is said that even though all nefarious activities of the personality of Kali are present, there is a great advantage in the age of Kali. One can attain salvation simply by chanting the holy name of the Lord. Thus Maharaja Pariksit made an organized effort to propagate the chanting of the Lord’s holy name, and thus he saved the citizens from the clutches of Kali. It is for this advantage only that great sages sometimes wish all good for the age of Kali. In the Vedas also it is said that by discourse on Lord Krsna’s activities, one can get rid of all the disadvantages of the age of Kali. In the beginning of the Srimad-Bhagavatam it is also said that by the recitation of Srimad-Bhagavatam, the Supreme Lord becomes at once arrested within one’s heart. These are some of the great advantages of the age of Kali, and Maharaja Pariksit took all the advantages and did not think any ill of the age of Kali, true to his Vaisnavite cult.”

Suta Gosvami thus reminds the sages that those desiring perfection must hear about all the activities connected to the Supreme Lord and His devotees. Srila Prabhupada glorifies hearing krsna-katha in his purport to text 10:

**The systematic hearing of the transcendental activities, qualities and names of Lord Sri Krsna pushes one towards eternal life. Systematic hearing means knowing Him gradually in truth and fact, and this knowing Him in truth and fact means attaining eternal life, as stated in the Bhagavad-gita. Such transcendental, glorified activities of Lord Sri Krsna are the prescribed remedy for counteracting the process of birth, death, old age and disease, which are considered to be material awards for the conditioned living being. The culmination of such a perfectional stage of life is the goal of human life and the attainment of transcendental bliss.**

## Texts 11-16: The Sages of Naimisaranya Reply

The sages of Naimisaranya are enthusiastic about Suta’s descriptions of the king and now feel hopeful: “O grave Suta Gosvami! May you live many years and have eternal fame, for you are speaking very nicely about the activities of Lord Krsna, the Personality of Godhead. This is just like nectar for mortal beings like us. We have just begun the performance of this fruitive activity, a sacrificial fire, without certainty of its result due to the many imperfections in our action. Our bodies have become black from the smoke, but we are factually pleased by the nectar of the lotus feet of the Personality of Godhead, Govinda, which you are distributing. The value of a moment’s association with the devotee of the Lord cannot even be compared to the attainment of heavenly planets or liberation from matter, and what to speak of worldly benedictions in the form of material prosperity, which are for those who are meant for death. The Personality of Godhead, Lord Krsna \[Govinda\], is the exclusive shelter for all great living beings, and His transcendental attributes cannot even be measured by such masters of mystic powers as Lord Siva and Lord Brahma. Can anyone who is expert in relishing nectar \[rasa\] ever be fully satiated by hearing topics about Him?” (Bhag, [1.18.11-14](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.11))

Everything about Krsna is transcendental, not tinged by matter. Therefore, as Srila Prabhupada states in his purport to text 11, “the more we hear about the transcendental activities of the Lord, as they are stated in the Bhagavad-gita and Srimad-Bhagavatam, the more we can know about His transcendental nature and thus make definite progress on the path back to Godhead.” Due to their practical experience, the sages doubt the other methods of advancement, such as the smoke-producing sacrifices in which they are partaking. Hearing about Krsna from a realized person like Suta Gosvami, on the other hand, brings them satisfaction. They are experiencing Krsna, and thus they praise the incomparable effect of even a moment’s association with pure devotees. “Such association,” Srila Prabhupada writes, “is always desirable; it is worshipable, it is praiseworthy, and one may accept it as the highest goal of life.” (Bhag. [1.18.13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.13), purport) The sages therefore express their readiness to continuously hear from Suta Gosvami, for “such discourses increase the receptive mood of the purified audience.” (Bhag. [1.18.14](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.14), purport)

## Texts 17-23: Suta Gosvami Describes Himself; The Power of Hearing

Before continuing his narration (which will lead to the story of how Maharaja Pariksit was cursed to die and his subsequent hearing of the Bhagavatam from Sukadeva Gosvami), Suta Gosvami speaks of his own lower birth. Despite that birth, the great sages of Naimisaranya, who are of higher brahminical lineage, are attentively listening to him. How can one be raised from a low position to an exalted one? Suta’s message has the incredible purifying power of any association with great souls. To avail oneself of this purification, one should serve and follow the instructions of great devotees, including the instruction to chant Krsna’s holy name. One should also preach on their behalf.

In his purport to text 18, Srila Prabhupada minimizes the importance of one’s birth and emphasizes the importance of attaining purity: “Suta Gosvami learned the science of Krsna from great rsis and authorities like Sukadeva and Vyasadeva and he was so qualified that even the sages of Naimisaranya eagerly wanted to hear from him the science of Krsna in the form of Srimad-Bhagavatam. So he had the double association of great souls by hearing and preaching. Transcendental science, or the science of Krsna, has to be learned from the authorities, and when one preaches the science, he becomes still more qualified. So Suta Gosvami had both the advantages, and thus undoubtedly he was completely freed from all disqualifications of low birth and mental agonies.”

Srila Prabhupada glorifies the potency of pure association later in his purport, and this time also speaks of association as the urgent cure for the current epidemic of “mental agonies”: “As far as the great devotees of the Lord are concerned, they can purify a degraded soul even by being seen by the lowborn, and what to speak of association. Lord Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu wanted to purify the whole atmosphere of the polluted world by sending qualified preachers all over the world, and it remains with the Indians to take up this task scientifically and thus do the best kind of humanitarian work. The mental diseases of the present generation are more acute than bodily diseases; it is quite fit and proper to take up the preaching of Srimad-Bhagavatam all over the world without delay.”

In his purport to text 19, Srila Prabhupada extols the purifying potency of chanting Krsna’s holy name: “Offenseless chanting of the holy name of the Lord is transcendental, and, therefore, such chanting can at once purify one from the effects of all kinds of previous sins.

This offenseless chanting indicates that one has fully understood the transcendental nature of the holy name and has thus surrendered unto the Lord.” Kutah punah, the first phrase in text 19, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains, implies that the act of reciting Srimad-Bhagavatam removes the fault of low birth; Krsna’s holy name has the same potency.

Suta Gosvami continues: The Lord is unlimited and full of inconceivable potencies. No one is equal to Him. Who therefore is able to fully elaborate on His glories? “Who can be worthy of the name of the Supreme Lord but the Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna?” (Bhag. [1.18.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.21)) Even the greatest demigods, such as Lord Brahma and Lord Siva worship the water that has bathed His lotus feet. Those who are self-controlled and truly attached to Him can immediately renounce this world. Such persons depend on Him perfectly and worship Him in loving service. “O rsis, who are as powerfully pure as the sun, I shall try to describe to you the transcendental pastimes of Visnu as far as my knowledge is concerned. As the birds fly in the sky as far as their capacity allows, so do the learned devotees describe the Lord as far as their realization allows.” (Bhag. [1.18.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.23))

Srila Prabhupada supports Suta Gosvami’s estimation of any man’s capacity to describe the unlimited Lord in his purport to text 23: “Factually only the Lord Himself can describe Himself, and His learned devotee also can describe Him as far as the Lord gives him the power of description.”

## Texts 24-37: Suta Gosvami Tells How Maharaja Pariksit was Cursed by the Sage Samika Rsi’s Son

Suta Gosvami begins to speak about Maharaja Pariksit’s renunciation (answering the questions asked in Bhagavatam [1.4.10-12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/4.10)) and thus resumes his narration of Maharaja Pariksit’s history. “Once upon a time Maharaja Pariksit, while engaged in hunting in the forest with bow and arrows, became extremely fatigued, hungry and thirsty while following the stags. While searching for a reservoir of water, he entered the hermitage of the well-known Samika Rsi and saw the sage sitting silently with closed eyes.” (Bhag. [1.18.24-25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.24)) The sage’s limbs were covered with a deerskin and his hair was matted. King Pariksit, parched with thirst, asked the sage for water. Samika Rsi, however, remained silent, his consciousness focused on the spiritual platform. Being neither welcomed nor offered a seat, water, or even kind words in response to his simple request, King Pariksit became angry. With the end of his bow he picked up a dead snake lying nearby and hung it like a garland around the sage’s neck. He thought: You have received me coldly, and so I have reciprocated coldly.

Insulted, Maharaja Pariksit returned to his palace. Once home, however, the king began to question himself. Perhaps the sage had really been absorbed in trance, his senses pulled inward and his eyes closed. Or had he been feigning trance just to avoid receiving him, a lower-ranked ksatriya! In his purport to text 31, Srila Prabhupada reflects on the great devotee Maharaja Pariksit’s angry reaction: “The King, being a devotee of the Lord, did not approve of his own action, and thus he began to wonder whether the sage was really in a trance or was just pretending in order to avoid receiving the King, who was a ksatriya and therefore lower in rank. Repentance comes in the mind of a good soul as soon as he commits something wrong. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura and Srila Jiva Gosvami do not believe that the King’s action was due to his past misdeeds. The arrangement was so made by the Lord just to call the King back home, back to Godhead.”

Srila Prabhupada explains this situation earlier in his purport to text 24-25:

**Maharaja Pariksit was a pure devotee of the Lord, and there was no reason for him to become extremely fatigued, hungry and thirsty because a devotee of the Lord never becomes perturbed by such bodily demands. But by the desire of the Lord, even such a devotee can become apparently fatigued and thirsty just to create a situation favorable for his renunciation of worldly activities. One has to give up all attachment for worldly relations before one is able to go back to Godhead, and thus when a devotee is too much absorbed in worldly affairs, the Lord creates a situation to cause indifference. The Supreme Lord never forgets His pure devotee, even though he may be engaged in so-called worldly affairs. Sometimes He creates an awkward situation, and the devotee becomes obliged to renounce all worldly affairs. The devotee can understand by the signal of the Lord, but others take it to be unfavorable and frustrating. Maharaja Pariksit was to become the medium for the revelation of SriTnad-Bhagavatatn by Lord Sri Krsna, as his grandfather Arjuna was the medium for the Bhagavad-gita. Had Arjuna not been taken up with an illusion of family affection by the will of the Lord, the Bhagavad-gita would not have been spoken by the Lord Himself for the good of all concerned. Similarly, had Maharaja Pariksit not been fatigued, hungry and thirsty at this time, Srimad-Bhagavatam would not have been spoken by Srila Sukadeva Gosvami, the prime authority of Srimad-Bhagavatam.**

Also, from his purport to text 28: “The merciful Lord sometimes creates such awkward positions for his pure devotees in order to drag them towards Himself from the mire of material existence. But outwardly the situations appear to be frustrating to the devotees. The devotees of the Lord are always under the protection of the Lord, and in any condition, frustration or success, the Lord is the supreme guide for the devotees. The pure devotees, therefore, accept all conditions of frustration as blessings from the Lord.”

Thus we see that difficult circumstances like Maharaja Pariksit’s occur even in the lives of pure devotees, but pure devotees recognize the Lord’s hand in the situation—that He has a plan. Srila Prabhupada explained this in a letter he wrote after suffering a lifethreatening heart attack in 1968: “The answer (why Maya dealt me a near death blow) is that Hiranyakasipu the agent of Maya tried to give so many death blows to Prahlada Maharaja, but in each and every case he was saved. There is more credit for him on behalf of Krishna. This is replied in Bhagavad-gita, ‘O my dear son of Kunti, just declare it throughout the whole world that my devotee is never vanquished.’ So it will take some time to understand what Krishna’s plan is, but rest assured, a devotee of Krishna is never vanquished.”

After Maharaja Pariksit had returned to his palace, the sage’s young but powerful son heard of his father’s “snake-garland” while playing with his friends. The boy, named Srngi, said: “The descendants of the kingly orders are definitely designated as watchdogs, and they must keep themselves at the door. On what grounds can dogs enter the house and claim to dine with the master on the same plate? After the departure of Lord Sri Krsna, the Personality of Godhead and supreme ruler of everyone, these upstarts have flourished, our protector being gone. Therefore I myself shall take up this matter and punish them. Just witness my power.” (Bhag. [1.18.34-35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.34)) Srngi, his eyes red with anger, then touched the water of the river Kausika while speaking to his friends “and discharged the following thunderbolt of words: ‘On the seventh day from today a snake-bird will bite the most wretched one of that dynasty \[Maharaja Pariksit\] because of his having broken the laws of etiquette by insulting my father.’” (Bhag. [1.18.36-37](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.36))

Because of Maharaja Pariksit’s good government, even this brdh~ mana boy was as powerful as an adult brahmana, but by Kali’s influence, the boy, whose power was mixed with both immaturity and pride, could not understand the importance of both his own social order and that of the kings. Therefore a brahmana boy disrespected a virtuous king out of his own pride and allowed Kali to gain a foothold. As Srila Prabhupada states in his purport to text 33: “Thus the downfall of the brahminical powers began as they gave importance to birthright without culture. The downfall of the brahmana caste began in the age of Kali. And since brahmanas are the heads of the social order, all other orders of society also began to deteriorate.”

Srila Prabhupada makes a similar point in his purport to text 34: “This mentality of false prestige is the cause of downfall of the perfect social order, and we can see that in the beginning it was started by the inexperienced son of a brahmana.” And again: “The inexperienced brahmana, puffed up by a little brahma'tejas, became influenced by the spell of Kali-yuga. Maharaja Pariksit gave license to Kali to live in four places as mentioned hereinbefore, but by his very expert government the personality of Kali could hardly find the places allotted him. The personality of Kali-yuga, therefore, was seeking the opportunity to establish authority, and by the grace of the Lord he found a hole in the puffed-up, inexperienced son of a brahmana.” (Bhag. [1.18.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.35), purport)

The result? “Thus the beginning of the misuse of brahminical power began, and gradually the brahmanas in the age of Kali became devoid of both brahminical powers and culture. . . . The personality of Kali conquered the brahmana boy first, and gradually the other castes. Thus the whole scientific system of the orders of society in this age has assumed the form of a vitiated caste system, which is now being uprooted by another class of men similarly influenced by the age of Kali. One should see to the root cause of vitiation and not try to condemn the system as it is, without knowledge of its scientific value.” (Bhag. [1.18.37](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.37), purport)

## Texts 38-50: The Sage Regrets his Son’s Deed

After cursing the king, the boy returned to his father’s hermitage. He saw the snake around his father’s neck and began to grieve. Slowly, as Srngi’s anger began to subside, he began to think he may have committed a mistake. He had cursed the king to die! Srngi began to cry.

But there was nothing he could do to remedy the situation. He had already uttered the curse. Srngi’s loud crying gradually penetrated Samika Rsi’s trance and pulled him back to external consciousness. He saw the dead snake around his neck and threw it aside. He did not take it seriously. He asked: My son, has someone harmed you?

Srngi explained the sequence of events, and thus Samika Rsi learned how his son had cursed the pious king. “The rsi did not congratulate his son, but, on the contrary, began to repent, saying: Alas! What a great sinful act was performed by my son. He has awarded heavy punishment for an insignificant offense.” (Bhag. [1.18.41](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.41)) The sage turned to his son and said: My boy, your intelligence is immature, and therefore you do not know that the king, who is the best among people, is as good as the Personality of Godhead. He is never to be considered a common man. The citizens of the state live in prosperity, being protected by his unsurpassable prowess. “My dear boy, the Lord, who carries the wheel of a chariot, is represented by the monarchical regime, and when this regime is abolished the whole world becomes filled with thieves, who then at once vanquish the unprotected subjects like scattered lambs.” (Bhag. [1.18.43](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.43))

In his purport to text 43, Srila Prabhupada compares the results of a properly run monarchy with popular democracy: “The Battle of Kuruksetra was planned by the Lord to establish the real representative of the Lord, Maharaja Yudhisthira. An ideal king thoroughly trained by culture and devotional service with the martial spirit makes a perfect king. Such a personal monarchy is far better than the so-called democracy of no training and responsibility. The thieves and rogues of modem democracy seek election by misrepresentation of votes, and the successful rogues and thieves devour the mass of population. One trained monarch is far better than hundreds of useless ministerial rogues, and it is hinted herein that by abolition of a monarchical regime like that of Maharaja Pariksit, the mass of people become open to many attacks of the age of Kali. They are never happy in an overly advertised form of democracy.”

Srila Prabhupada also criticizes untrained democratic leaders in his purport to text 44: “The sage rightly takes the responsibility of the brah-manas as a community for killing monarchical government and thus giving an opportunity to the so-called democrats, who are generally plunderers of the wealth of the state subjects. The so-called democrats capture the administrative machine without assuming responsibility for the prosperous condition of the citizens. Everyone captures the post for personal gratification, and thus instead of one king, a number of irresponsible kings grow up to tax the citizens.”

Samika Rsi continued: Without the king people will be plundered and society disrupted. The social structure will crumble, and the citizens will neglect the purpose of life. Greed for money and lust for sense gratification will arise. We shall be responsible for all these sins!

As time has passed since the cursing of Maharaja Pariksit, Samika Rsi’s predictions have come true. Kali exerted influence over a brahmana boy, and from him, over society; the integrity of a strong spiritual culture was lost. When society is organized by qualified brahmanas, social cooperation is natural. Because the top strata of society, the brahmanas, are austere, learned in sdstra, simple-hearted, and meek, the citizens do not come to envy their superior position. Rather, they naturally offer respect. In addition, the brahmanas act as teachers, priests, counselors, and doctors, and offer these services without asking remuneration. Because people naturally appreciate these services as well as the brahmanas’ humility and other qualities, they naturally respect the brahmanas. When respect is in place, the brahmanas can effortlessly steer society toward a spiritual perspective.

But by Kali’s influence, the brahmanas, as evidenced by Srngi, became proud. Brdhmanas are qualified by their learning, which naturally engenders humility. Pride, on the other hand, is ignorance, with ignorance of one’s relationship with Krsna at its core.

In general, as Kali-yuga has progressed, brahmanas have lost their sastric knowledge, exemplary characters, humility, simplicity, and spiritual aspirations and have begun to proudly demand respect simply because of the families into which they were bom. Because the brahmanas as a class have come to think themselves superior, they have become greedy and exploitative. Throughout this age’s history,

the brahmana or priestly class has attempted to dominate the ksatriyas, who, although naturally obedient and subservient to the learned and humble, are intolerant of pride and condescension. Thus the ksatriyas have rebelled and cast off brahminical control, governing without the guidance of brahmanas and sastra. Might becomes right, and superior military force the sole foundation of power. Free from spiritual guidance, the ksatriyas have organized society around their own values and desires. In turn, they too have become oppressive, exploitative, and addicted to sense pleasure. Corrupted by power and wealth, living in extreme opulence, they have engaged in unpopular, expensive, petty wars financed by high taxes and fought not by qualified warriors but by conscripted farmers and impoverished workers. (In European history, the Middle Ages provides an example of such hedonistic ksatriyas and their subsequent exploitation of the people.)

The degradation of ksatriyas inspired the vaisya (mercantile) community to plot their overthrow. Why should they pay tribute to facilitate a corrupt king’s sense pleasure? Thus as the ksatriyas had rebelled against the control of an unqualified and proud class, so the vaisyas did the same. Capitalism as a ruling economic system was bom. The capitalistic vaisya rebellion freed the wealthy class from the ksatriyas’ rule by brute force and liberated them from strangling taxation, but it in turn subjected society to rule by financial manipulation, especially in the form of money-lending and banking. Now instead of either the brah' manas or ksatriyas being at the top of the social strata, both fell under the financial power of the vaisyas. Brahmanas then became still more corrupt and fully lost sight of religious principles. (In European history, the priestly caste sold indulgences to “free” the wealthy from sin while leaving the poor condemned to hell.) All of this caused people to lose faith in what the brahmanas represented—religion and religious principles. Subservient to vaisya wealth, ksatriyas became even weaker, allowing the vaisyas’ power to go unchecked.

To further increase their wealth, the vaisyas freely exploited the poor, industrializing society in the name of progress and changing society’s base from agrarian to industrial. As wealth became concentrated in the hands of fewer and fewer men, the middle class—the small tradesmen and farmers—disappeared and sudra labor became the only financially viable alternative to maintain a livelihood. More and more people virtually became slaves.

We have seen that the laborer class also tends to revolt, frustrated by unrelenting poverty, horrible working conditions, a lack of social mobility, and a sense of injustice at being exploited to generate wealth for others. During such revolutions, the laborers are exhorted to “throw off their chains” and to work for the collective benefit of their fellow workers. Contrasting this miserable result with true culture, which systematically engenders spiritual consciousness, Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to text 45: “The Vedic civilization’s destination is to go back to Godhead, back home, where there is no birth, no death, no old age and no disease. The Vedas direct everyone not to remain in the darkness of the material world but to go towards the light of the spiritual kingdom far beyond the material sky. The qualitative caste system and the orders of life are scientifically planned by the Lord and His representatives, the great rsis. The perfect way of life gives all sorts of instruction in things both material and spiritual. The Vedic way of life does not allow any man to be like the monkeys and dogs. A degraded civilization of sense gratification and economic development is the by-product of a godless or kingless government of the people, by the people, and for the people.” Thus in Kali-yuga, true culture is lost with a deluge of materialism, and gross sense pleasure becomes the goal of life. The citizens then become no better than “monkeys and dogs.”

Samika Rsi was a far-seeing sage and could envision the ramifications of his son’s action. Therefore he continued to lament what Srngi had so thoughtlessly done. He said: Emperor Pariksit is a pious and celebrated king as well as a first-class devotee of the Personality of Godhead. He is a saint in the dress of royalty. When such a king is fatigued and stricken with hunger and thirst, he should not be cursed but offered service.

Samika Rsi knew that Maharaja Pariksit would not counter-curse his son. If only he would, his son might be relieved of the horrendous reaction that would follow his crime of cursing a sinless person. But the king was a devotee. Samika Rsi knew he would not retaliate. “The devotees of the Lord are so forbearing that even though they are defamed, cheated, cursed, disturbed, neglected or even killed, they are never inclined to avenge themselves.” (Bhag. [1.18.48](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.48)) Regretting his son’s foolish and immature act, the rsi prayed to the all-pervading Personality of Godhead to pardon the boy.

In his purport to text 47, Srila Prabhupada explains why the brahmana’s son and indeed the entire brahmana community was held responsible for an act ultimately sanctioned by the Lord: “The answer is that the offensive act was performed by a child only so that he could be excused very easily, and thus the prayer of the father was accepted. But if the question is raised why the brahmana community as a whole was made responsible for allowing Kali into the world affairs, the answer is given in the Varaha Purana that the demons who acted inimically toward the Personality of Godhead but were not killed by the Lord were allowed to take birth in the families of brahmanas to take advantage of the age of Kali. The all-merciful Lord gave them a chance to have their births in the families of pious brahmanas so that they could progress toward salvation. But the demons, instead of utilizing the good opportunity, misused the brahminical culture due to being puffed up by vanity in becoming brahmanas. The typical example is the son of Samika Rsi, and all the foolish sons of brahmanas are warned hereby not to become as foolish as Srngi and be always on guard against the demoniac qualities which they had in their previous births. The foolish boy was, of course, excused by the Lord, but others, who may not have a father like Samika Rsi, will be put into great difficulty if they misuse the advantages obtained by birth in a brahmana family.”

Srila Prabhupada guides us in something we ourselves may one day require—to pray for forgiveness for our family members or ourselves: “Everyone is responsible for his own action, either pious or sinful. Rsi Samika could foresee that his son had committed a great sin by cursing Maharaja Pariksit, who deserved to be protected by the brahmanas, for he was a pious ruler and completely free from all sins because of his being a first-class devotee of the Lord. When an offense is done unto the devotee of the Lord, it is very difficult to overcome the reaction.... The foolish boy had done it out of sheer vanity in being a brahmana’s son, and thus he became liable to be punished by the law of God. The Lord never forgives a person who condemns His pure devotee. Therefore, by cursing a king the foolish Srngi had committed not only a sin but also the greatest offense. Therefore the rsi could foresee that only the Supreme Personality of Godhead could save his boy from his sinful act. He therefore directly prayed for pardon from the Supreme Lord, who alone can undo a thing which is impossible to change. The appeal was made in the name of a foolish boy who had developed no intelligence at all.” (Bhag. [1.18.47](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/18.47), purport)

Srila Prabhupada adds in his purport to text 49 that the foolish brahmana boy “deserved to be pardoned by the Supreme Lord, although it was not possible to get free from the sinful reaction. Maharaja Pariksit also did not mind the curse offered to him by a foolish brahmana. On the contrary, he took full advantage of the awkward situ-ation, and by the great will of the Lord, Maharaja Pariksit achieved the highest perfection of life through the grace of Srila Sukadeva Gosvami. Actually it was the desire of the Lord, and Maharaja Pariksit, Rsi Samika and his son Srngi were all instrumental in fulfilling the desire of the Lord.”

## Chapter 19 - The Appearance of Sukadeva Gosvami

## Texts 1-19: Maharaja Pariksit Renounces his Kingdom and Vows to Fast until Death

After returning to his palace, the king considered that “the act he had committed against the faultless and powerful brahmana was heinous and uncivilized. Consequently he was distressed.” (Bhag. [1.19.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.1)) He concluded that his action would bring a reaction in the near future, and he thought: “I now desire without reservation that the calamity come now, for in this way I may be freed of the sinful action and not commit such an offense again.... I wish that my king' dom, strength and riches burn up immedately by the fire of the hrahmana’s wrath so that in the future I may not be guided by such inauspicious attitudes.” (Bhag. [1.19.2-3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.2)) Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on text 3 that Maharaja Pariksit did not actually want his kingdom to bum up, for if that would happen, the brahmanas in his kingdom would also be burned. Rather, he wanted the curse to fall on himself alone so that only he would be bereft of his kingdom, strength, and riches. Thus he would learn from his mistake.

How can a soul be so humble and sincere and detached, especially a powerful king? It is difficult to understand the consciousness of a real devotee, for he is living in his relationship with Krsna even while in this world. Of the two possible viewpoints—seeing things from his relationship with Krsna or seeing things from a worldly viewpoint— a devotee allows his relationship with Krsna to dictate how he sees the world. He doesn’t independently identify with the “drama” of this world. In a drama an actor may gain an inheritance and then suddenly be stabbed. As an actor, he knows that both his gain and loss are temporary. When the curtain falls, he pulls the false knife from his back and returns the money to its owner. Only an intoxicated or crazy actor will actually identify with the part he has played.

An actor wears a costume; in the material world, each player “wears” a body. Neither the part nor the costume constitutes the real person. Aside from the part he plays, an actor has a real life outside the theater. Devotees are awake to their real, eternal life with Krsna, and they see their part in this world from that perspective. Devotees want to play their parts well, but when the director, Krsna, indicates that it’s time to leave the stage, they recognize His signs, as Pariksit did, and prepare themselves to exit. They know that as soon as the “show” is over, they will meet their dearmost friend. As devotees play their parts, they never forget this because they are awake to their relationship with Krsna. Although they take as extremely serious—as their devotional offering—the part Krsna wishes them to play in the world, they never-theless know that they possess another, eternal identity. This specific drama starring Maharaja Pariksit was staged to orchestrate the speaking of the Bhagavatam and the return of the king to Krsna’s lotus feet.

On one level, we naturally see the misfortune of a great ruler’s being forced to leave his position; on the other hand, we must acknowledge the supremacy of Krsna’s plan. As one hears this pastime, one becomes trained not only to see Krsna’s inscrutable yet merciful will in Maharaja Pariksit’s life but to accept that will in one’s own. Thus one can learn to become more malleable to Krsna’s desire. From the extreme situation forced upon Maharaja Pariksit—from kingship to death in seven days—one can learn how to focus on Krsna and gain the same perfection that Maharaja Pariksit attained by going back to Godhead.The Bhagavatam tells us: “While the King was thus repenting, he received news of his imminent death, which would be due to the bite of a snake-bird, occasioned by the curse spoken by the sage’s son. The King accepted this as good news, for it would be the cause of his indifference toward worldly things.” (Bhag. [1.19.4](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.4)) By carefully observing Maharaja Pariksit, we can learn to cope with even horrific reversals, including the approach of our own death. In his purports to the opening texts of Chapter Nineteen, Srila Prabhupada guides us in the understanding of how a devotee purifies himself and accepts Krsna’s mercy in all circumstances. Here is a sampling from those purports:

**The pious King regretted his accidental improper treatment of the powerful brahmana, who was faultless. Such repentance is natural for a good man like the King, and such repentance delivers a devotee from all kinds of sins accidentally committed. The devotees are naturally faultless. Accidental sins committed by a devotee are sincerely regretted, and by the grace of the Lord all sins unwillingly committed by a devotee are burnt in the fire of repentance. (Bhag.** [**1.19.1**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.1)**, purport)**

**A man’s personal misconduct affects all his family members. Therefore Maharaja Pariksit desired the calamity to fall on him alone. By suffering personally he would be restrained from future sins, and at the same time the sin which he had committed would be counteracted so that his descendants would not suffer. (Bhag.** [**1.19.2**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.2)**, purport)**

**As a devotee of the Lord, he could understand that the cursing of the brahmana boy, although unwise, was a blessing upon him, being the cause of detachment from worldly affairs, both political and social. Samika Muni also, after regretting the incident, conveyed the news to the King as a matter of duty so that the King would be able to prepare himself to go back to Godhead. (Bhag.** [**1.19.4**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.4)**, purport)**

**Maharaja Pariksit could have gone to the muni to beg his pardon, but the news of imminent death was conveyed to the King with so much regret by the muni that the King did not want to shame the muni further by his presence there. He decided to prepare himself for his imminent death and find out the way to go back to Godhead. (Bhag.** [**1.19.4**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.4)**, purport)**

**Pariksit Maharaja was fortunate to get a seven-day notice to meet his inevitable death. But for the common man there is no definite notice, although death is inevitable for all. Foolish men forget this sure fact of death and neglect the duty of preparing themselves for going back to Godhead. (Bhag.** [**1.19.4**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.4)**, purport)**

Thus hearing news of his imminent death, Maharaja Pariksit became fixed in determination. He knew that everything in this world is temporary and must eventually be left behind. He therefore renounced his kingdom and sat by the bank of the Ganga to concentrate his mind in Krsna consciousness and surrender himself to Lord Krsna’s lotus feet.

He rejected all other practices, for he knew that attaining Krsna’s service was the greatest achievement. Srila Sridhara Svami comments as follows on text 5: The phrase sri'krsnanghri'sevam adhimanyamana indicates that Maharaja Pariksit understood that service to Lord Krsna’s lotus feet is the goal of life. Thus it is clear that Maharaja Pariksit was a pure devotee of Krsna even before meeting Srila Sukadeva Gosvami.

Srila Prabhupada offers words for our consideration in his purport to text 7: “Maharaja Pariksit freed himself from all sorts of material association and meditated upon the lotus feet of Lord Krsna, and that is the way of liberation. To be free from all material association means to cease completely from committing any further sins. To meditate upon the lotus feet of the Lord means to become free from the effects of all previous sins. The conditions of the material world are so made that one has to commit sins willingly or unwillingly, and the best example is Maharaja Pariksit himself, who was a recognized sinless, pious king. But he also became a victim of an offense, even though he was ever unwilling to commit such a mistake. He was cursed also, but because he was a great devotee of the Lord, even such reverses of life became favorable. The principle is that one should not willingly commit any sin in his life and should constantly remember the lotus feet of the Lord without deviation. Only in such a mood will the Lord help the devotee make regular progress toward the path of liberation and thus attain the lotus feet of the Lord.”

News spread that Maharaja Pariksit was sitting on the riverbank awaiting death. Sages gathered from all directions to meet Maharaja Pariksit. They could foresee that Sukadeva Gosvami would speak the Srimad-Bhagavatam, and they desired to take advantage of the great occasion. After the rsis and sages arrived and had been welcomed and seated, the king humbly bowed his head to the ground out of respect. He stood with folded hands and expressed his gratitude that those who generally thought of royalty as contaminating had offered him their association: Of all kings, I am the most grateful. Great sages like you usually avoid royalty for fear of becoming infected with material desire. Yet out of affection for my forefathers, you are mercifully offering me your association just before my death. I have decided to fast until death.

Srila Jiva Gosvami comments that the above verse (Bhag. [1.19.13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.13)) expresses Maharaja Pariksit’s astonishment. The king thought humbly that the arrival of so many sages was due to the Lord’s special and personal mercy. He was aware that kings are generally sinful; therefore, he was astonished to see that although he had hung a dead snake around the neck of an offenseless brahmana, he was still offered such exalted association as he sat to face his death.

Maharaja Pariksit continued: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead, the controller of both the transcendental and mundane worlds, has graciously overtaken me in the form of a brahmana’s curse. Due to my being too much attached to family life, the Lord, in order to save me, has appeared before me in such a way that only out of fear I will detach myself from the world. О brahmanas, just accept me as a completely surrendered soul, and let mother Ganges, the representative of the Lord, also accept me in that way, for I have already taken the lotus feet of the Lord into my heart. Let the snake-bird— or whatever magical thing the brahmana created—bite me at once. I only desire that you all continue singing the deeds of Lord Visnu. Again, offering obeisances unto all you brahmanas, I pray that if I should again take my birth in the material world I will have complete attachment to the unlimited Lord. Krsna, association with His devotees and friendly relations with all living beings.” (Bhag. [1.19.14-16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.14))

Maharaja Pariksit, whose faith and surrender had awarded him fearlessness, sat on the southern side of the river on a mat of kusa straw and faced north. As the king sat, prepared to fast until death, he acknowledged that the sages’ presence signified Krsna’s mercy on him. His desires were focused on Krsna, and if he were not to go back to Godhead, he prayed for the association of devotees in his next life. Denizens from the higher planets scattered flowers on the earth and beat celestial drums to honor the king’s renunciation and decision to fast until death. The sages, wishing to encourage Maharaja Pariksit, responded to his words with approval, saying, “Sadhu! Sadhu!” (“Very good! Very good!”)

## Texts 20-40: Maharaja Pariksit Questions the Sages About the Duty of One About to Die, and the Great Sukadeva Gosvami Arrives

The sages said: We are not astonished that you have fearlessly renounced your throne. You are a Pandava king, unenchanted by the glare of material life and filled with the desire to achieve the eternal association of Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. We shall wait here until you, the Lord’s foremost devotee, return to the spiritual world.

Srila Prabhupada writes: “All of them consulted among themselves about the great departure of the great King, and they wanted to see him up to the last moment because they would no more be able to see such a great devotee of the Lord. When a great devotee of the Lord passes away, there is nothing to be lamented because the devotee is destined to enter into the kingdom of God. But the sorry plight is that such great devotees leave our sight, and therefore there is every reason to be sorry. As the Lord is rarely to be seen by our present eyes, so also are the great devotees. The great rsis, therefore, correctly decided to remain on the spot till the last moment.” (Bhag. [1.19.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.21), purport)

King Pariksit wished to hear about Lord Krsna, so he addressed the sages: О great souls, you have all kindly assembled here to help me, as your only interest is doing good for others. “. .. I now ask you about my immediate duty. Please, after proper deliberation, tell me of the unalloyed duty of everyone in all circumstances, and specifically of those who are just about to die.” (Bhag. [1.19.24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.24)) Srila Prabhupada explains the significance of this question in his purport to this text:

**In this verse the King has placed two questions before the learned sages. The first question is what is the duty of everyone in all circumstances, and the second question is what is the specific duty of one who is to die very shortly. Out of the two, the question relating to the dying man is most important because everyone is a dying man, either very shortly or after one hundred years. The duration of life is immaterial, but the duty of a dying man is very important. Maharaja Pariksit placed these two questions before Sukadeva Gosvami also on his arrival, and practically the whole of the Srimad'Bhagavatarn, beginning from the Second Canto up to the last Twelfth Canto, deals with these two questions. The conclusion arrived at thereof is that devotional service of the Lord Sri Krsna, as it is confirmed by the Lord Himself in the last phases of the Bhagavad-gita, is the last word in relation to everyone’s permanent duty in life. Maharaja Pariksit was already aware of this fact, but he wanted the great sages assembled there to unanimously give their verdict on his conviction so that he might be able to go on with his confirmed duty without controversy.**

According to Srila Sridhara Svami, the sages began to quarrel with one another after hearing the king’s inquiry. Some recommended he offer charity, others that he meditate. Still others spoke on behalf of austerity or sacrifice. As with doctors and astrologers, a unanimous opinion seemed distant. “At that moment there appeared the powerful son of Vyasadeva, who traveled over the earth disinterested and satisfied with himself. He did not manifest any symptoms of belonging to any social order or status of life. He was surrounded with women and children, and he dressed as if others had neglected him. This son of Vyasadeva was only sixteen years old. His legs, hands, thighs, arms, shoulders, forehead and the other parts of his body were all delicately formed. His eyes were beautifully wide, and his nose and ears were highly raised. He had a very attractive face, and his neck was well formed and beautiful like a conchshell. His collarbone was fleshy, his chest broad and thick, his navel deep and his abdomen beautifully striped. His arms were long, and curly hair was strewn over his beautiful face. He was naked, and the hue of his body reflected that of Lord Krsna. . . . the great sages present there were all expert in the art of physiognomy, and so they honored him by rising from their seats.” (Bhag. [1.19.25-28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.25))

Sukadeva Gosvami, the great devotee who excelled all, had arrived. Srila Prabhupada writes: “Everyone, except Srila Vyasadeva, Narada and a few others, stood up, and Maharaja Pariksit, who was glad to receive a great devotee of the Lord, bowed down before him with all the limbs of his body. Sukadeva Gosvami also exchanged the greetings and reception by embrace, shaking of hands, nodding and bowing down, especially before his father and Narada Muni.” (Bhag. [1.19.29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.29), purport)

Sukadeva accepted the seat for the one who would preside over the assembly, and those who had been following and mocking him were amazed to see how both the king and the sages respected this disheveled madman. They dispersed, and the atmosphere became calm, grave, and filled with anticipation. The great sage sat, “perfectly pacified, intelligent and ready to answer any question without hesitation. The great devotee, Maharaja Pariksit, approached him, offered his respects by bowing before him, and politely inquired with sweet words and folded hands.” (Bhag. [1.19.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/19.31))

In his purport to text 31, Srila Prabhupada speaks of the result that will come from the exchange between the devotee-saint and the king: “Both the spiritual master and the disciple, namely Sri Sukadeva Gosvami and Maharaja Pariksit, attained perfection through the medium of Srimad-Bhagavatam. Sukadeva Gosvami learned Srimad-Bhagavatam from his father, Vyasadeva, but he had no chance to recite it. Before Maharaja Pariksit he recited Srimad-Bhagavatam and answered the questions of Maharaja Pariksit unhesitatingly, and thus both the master and the disciple got salvation.”

The fortunate king said: You are a saintly devotee, and I am a member of the royalty. Devotees such as your good self generally keep away from both women and worldly men, for the association of either plants seeds of material desire within the heart. Yet despite my being a king, you have come here and turned this place into a place of pilgrimage. “Simply by our remembering you, our houses become instantly sanctified. And what to speak of seeing you, touching you, washing your holy feet and offering you a seat in our home?” (Bhag.
