The creation based on and using those ingredients is carried out by Lord Brahma and is called visarga. Without the guidance of Vedic literature, we will mistake visarga for sarga and thus fail to recognize the Lord as the primary creator, the cause of all causes.

The sthitir (sthanam, planetary systems) is the situation achieved by living entities in the universe. This indicates the Lord’s supreme glory, because He is the universal maintainer. Posanam, the Lord’s protection, occurs when the living entities accept the regulated path according to His instructions. The Lord provides this protection by His causeless mercy. The creative impetus (utayah) is the living entity’s desire for fruitive work, and the Manu avatdras (manvantara) instruct humankind about their occupational duties. The Lord’s activities with His devotees during His descents instruct humanity about the science of God (isa'anukathah), and the universe is annihilated when the entire cosmos, along with the living entities it contains, is again withdrawn into Maha-Visnu (nirodhah). Liberation (mukti) occurs when a living entity throws off his changeable gross and subtle material bodies and achieves his natural, permanent state of existence (muktir hitvdnyathd ruparh sva-гйрепа vyavasthitih \[Bhag. [2.10.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.6)\]).

Sri Krsna, Sukadeva Gosvami continues, is ultimately the asraya, the reservoir of everything, because He is the Supreme Being, the Supreme Soul, the source of the cosmic manifestation, the Supreme Fountainhead, and the Absolute Truth. Sukadeva Gosvami has therefore described the first nine topics to illuminate the tenth, the Absolute Truth, the asraya or shelter of all else. The asraya is Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Factual knowledge of the first nine topics will assist our understanding of Krsna. If one doesn’t understand the nine, one won’t understand the power of the tenth, because everything in existence has a relationship with the Absolute Truth. Therefore Krsna is ultimately the only topic described in Srimad-Bhagavatam, and all other topics are meant to illuminate one’s consciousness with knowledge of Him.

In a text that parallels text 1 of this chapter, Srila Suta Gosvami will later tell the sages at Naimisaranya: “O brahmana, authorities on the matter understand a Purana to contain ten characteristic topics: the creation of this universe, the subsequent creation of worlds and beings, the maintenance of all living beings, their sustenance, the rule of various Manus, the dynasties of great kings, the activities of such kings, annihilation, motivation and the supreme shelter. Other scholars state that the great Puranas deal with these ten topics, while lesser Puranas may deal with five.” (Bhag. [12.7.9-10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-12/7.9))

Sukadeva Gosvami will now begin his description of a technical subject, the three perspectives from which a person is viewed. He does this to further define the asraya. Sukadeva Gosvami explains that a person may be seen as the adhyatmic person, the person seen from the inside, the jiva or soul possessing and using his senses. He may also be seen as the adhidaivic person. The adhidaivic person refers to the demigods situated in the virat-purusa who control the subtle senses of the individual. Thus when one sees any individual, he can know that that person is ultimately dependent on the demigods for his sensory functions. Thirdly, there is the adhibhautic person, the body composed of the gross senses that others can see.

All three “persons” are interdependent; if one were not present, the other two could not exist. Without the adhidaivic person, the adhyat' mic person, housed in the gross adhibhautic body would not have access to the subtle senses. The gross senses would have nowhere to rest. Without the adhibhautic person, there would be no resting place for the other two persons. Without the adhyatmic person, that is, without the soul to identify himself with the senses, there would be no “inhabitant” to live in the world of subtle and gross senses, in the material body.

That the three are interdependent shows that none of them are the asraya, the shelter and source of everything. The asraya is the Supreme Being, the Supersoul, He who witnesses and knows these three persons. The Supreme Being alone is independent; He has no other shelter. He is the only being who is sheltered by Himself. Thus He is known as the svasraya, “one who is his own shelter.”

The Bhagavatam uses the word svasraya to describe the Supersoul in text 9. In his purport, Srila Prabhupada describes the interdependence of the three “persons” and the Lord’s independence: “Without our having eyes, the sunlight is useless, and without sunlight the eyes are useless. Thus they are interdependent, and none of them is independent. Therefore the natural question arises concerning who made them interdependent. The one who has made such a relationship of interdependence must be ultimately completely independent. As stated in the beginning of the Srimad-Bhagavatam, the ultimate source of all interdependent objectives is the complete independent subject. This ultimate source of all interdependence is the Supreme Truth or Paramatma, the Supersoul, who is not dependent on anything else. He is svasrayasrayah. He is only dependent on His self, and thus He is the supreme shelter of everything. Although Paramatma and Brahman are subordinate to Bhagavan, because Bhagavan is Purusottama or the Superperson, He is the source of the Supersoul also. In the Bhagavad-gita ([15.18](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/15.18)) Lord Krsna says that He is the Purusottama and the source of everything, and thus it is concluded that Sri Krsna is the ultimate source and shelter of all entities, including the Supersoul and Supreme Brahman.”

Srila Sridhara Svami comments that text 8 shows the asraya’s true character by dividing persons other than the asraya into subcategories. That one can be so divided shows that one is not supreme. That the jiva is not the Lord is also stated in the Hamsa-guhya prayers, particularly in Bhagavatam [6.4.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-6/4.25): “Because they are only matter, the body, the life airs, the external and internal senses, the five gross elements and the subtle sense objects \[form, taste, smell, sound and touch\] cannot know their own nature, the nature of the other senses or the nature of their controllers. But the living being, because of his spiritual nature, can know his body, the life airs, the senses, the elements and the sense objects, and he can also know the three qualities that form their roots. Nevertheless, although the living being is completely aware of them, he is unable to see the Supreme Being, who is omniscient and unlimited. I therefore offer my respectful obeisances unto Him.”

## Texts 10-31: The Dependent Jivas Should Accept the Shelter of the Independent Asraya—The Creation Begins from Lord Maha-Visnu

The conclusion implied in the previous section assures us that the Lord is always independent, even when He is in the universe as the Supersoul. The dependent jivas, therefore, should leave aside their illusion of independence and serve the independent Lord, for no one but He can be the shelter of all. Everything ultimately depends fully on Him. To demonstrate that only Krsna is the independent Lord and that everything else depends upon Him, Srila Sukadeva Gosvami now (text 10) describes Maha-Visnu’s cosmic creation: “After separating the different universes, the gigantic universal form of the Lord \[Maha-Visnu\], which came out of the causal ocean, the place of appearance for the first purusa-avatara, entered into each of the separate universes, desiring to lie on the created transcendental water \[Garbho-daka\].” Srila Prabhupada explains the purpose of this narration in his purport to Bhagavatam [2.10.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.10):

**After analysis of the living entities and the Supreme Lord, Paramatma, the independent source of all other living beings, Srila Sukadeva Gosvami is now presenting the prime necessity for devotional service to the Lord, which is the only occupational business of all living entities. The Supreme Lord Sri Krsna and all His plenary portions and extensions of plenary portions are nondif-ferent from one another, and thus the supreme independence is in each and every one of them. In order to prove this, Sukadeva Gosvami (as promised to King Pariksit) describes herein the independence of the purusa-avatara Personality of Godhead, even in the sphere of the material creation. Such activities of the Lord are also transcendental, and therefore they are also lila, or pastimes, of the absolute Lord. Such pastimes of the Lord are very conducive to the hearers for self-realization in the field of devotional service. Some may argue, why not then relish the transcendental lila of the Lord as exhibited in the land of Mathura and Vrndavana, which are sweeter than anything in the world? Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura replies that the pastimes of the Lord in Vrndavana are meant to be relished by advanced devotees of the Lord. Neophyte devotees will misunderstand such supreme transcendental activities of the Lord, and therefore the Lord’s pastimes in the material sphere related to creation, maintenance and destruction are verily relishable by the prakrta, or mundane devotees of the Lord.**

Sukadeva Gosvami continues: The Absolute Truth is clearly a person, and one should know that all the material ingredients, activities, time, the modes of nature, as well as the living entities who try to enjoy matter, exist only by His mercy. As soon as He withdraws His care, everything ceases to exist. Everything depends on Him. Thus Maha-Visnu, while lying on His bed of mystic slumber, generated the seminal symbol, golden in hue, through His external energy out of His desire to manifest varieties of living entities from Himself alone. Thus the creation begins with the Lord, and when it is time to recreate the universes, the Lord again creates. He is fully independent of the material world; everything is ultimately nondifferent from Him. Everything, including the adhyatmic, adhidaivic, and adhibhautic persons manifest from the energies He sets in motion. Srila Prabhupada states this truth clearly in his purport to text 16: “No one has independent existence, just as no electric lamp has independent effulgence. Each and every electrical instrument depends fully on the total powerhouse, the total powerhouse depends on the reservoir of water for generating electricity, water depends on the clouds, the clouds depend on the sun, the sun depends on creation, and the creation depends on the movement of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus the Supreme Personality of Godhead is the cause of all causes.”

From His energies and by His will, the virat-purusa gradually develops, just as a child develops in the womb. First, the virat-rupa’s sense energy, mental force, and bodily strength are generated. These dictate the living entity’s movements, just as a king’s movements lead his citizens. Next, because the virat-purusa possesses living force, he develops hunger and thirst and opens his mouth. Then, one after another, the palate, ears, eyes, nostrils, legs, hands, skin, genital, anus, navel, mind, abdomen, intestines, life breath, blood, fat, marrow, and bone are generated. As each of these bodily parts (the adhibhautic person) in the virat-purusa is generated, the appropriate controlling deity (adhidaivic person) is generated. For example, Varuna, the demigod controlling the tongue and sense of taste, is generated simultaneously with the virat-purusa’s tongue. The individual soul, who will experience material life through the senses by the potency of these controlling demigods, is called the adhyatmic person. Commenting on text 18, Srila Sridhara Svami remarks that in subsequent verses one should infer that any sense organs, presiding deities, or sense objects not mentioned have also been generated.

The principles described in texts 17-31 serve to reiterate how the three interdependent sense controllers (adhibhautic, adhidaivic, and adhyatmic) ultimately depend on the Supreme Lord. He alone is independent. Although a living entity thinks himself independent, he is not. His ability to see is dependent on the universal form’s vision. Yet Krsna allows each living entity the choice to use his senses either for his own pleasure or in His service.

Srila Prabhupada explains how this topic is relevant to the greater topic being discussed, the asraya: “The living entity can see only when the Lord sees, the living entity can smell when the Lord smells, and so on. The idea is that the living entity cannot do anything independently. He can simply think of doing something independently, but he cannot act independently. This independence in thinking is there by the grace of the Lord, but the thinking can be given shape by the grace of the Lord, and therefore the common saying is that man proposes and God disposes. The whole explanation is on the subject of the absolute dependence of the living entities and absolute independence of the Supreme Lord.” (Bhag. [2.10.20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.20), purport) And in his purport to text 24: “In every item we can note with profit that the sense organs of the living entity are never independent at any stage. The Lord is known as the Lord of the senses (Hrsikesa). Thus the sense organs of the living entities are manifested by the will of the Lord, and each organ is controlled by a certain type of demigod. No one, therefore, can claim any proprietorship of the senses. The living entity is controlled by the senses, the senses are controlled by the demigods, and the demigods are the servants of the Supreme Lord. That is the arrangement in the system of creation. The whole thing is controlled ultimately by the Supreme Lord, and there is no independence either of the material nature or of the living entity.”

## Texts 32-51: Beyond the Coverings Is the Lord, the Creator, Maintainer, and Destroyer of the Universe

In the opening texts of the Second Canto’s ninth chapter, Sukadeva Gosvami said that the eternal soul is pure. It is not possible to contaminate the eternal soul. Still, the soul is illusioned by maya and thus misidentifies with the gross material body. Each of the bodily parts on the universal form, as they have been described, are coverings. Now Sukadeva will continue to describe the further layers of matter that cover the living entity: “The sense organs are attached to the modes of material nature, and the modes of material nature are products of the false ego. The mind is subjected to all kinds of material experiences (happiness and distress), and the intelligence is the feature of the mind’s deliberation.” (Bhag. [2.10.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.32))

What purpose do these material coverings, which are bom of the Lord’s virat-rupa serve? Srila Prabhupada writes: “\[TJhese coverings are created by Him to cover the eyes of the conditioned souls who want to lord it over the material nature. Actually the conditioned souls are covered by the illusory creative cloud of matter, and the Lord reserves the right of not being exposed to their eyes.” (Bhag. [2.10.33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.33), purport)

The Lord’s feature just beyond the material virat-rupa manifestation is His nonmaterial, impersonal aspect. “Therefore beyond this \[gross manifestation\] is a transcendental manifestation finer than the finest form. It has no beginning, no intermediate stage and no end; therefore it is beyond the limits of expression or mental speculation and is distinct from the material conception.” (Bhag. [2.10.34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.34)) These two aspects of the Lord—the universal form (the Lord as everything material)—and the Lord’s impersonal feature (the Lord as nothing material), are the aspects to which pantheists and monists aspire. In this regard, Sukadeva Gosvami now issues an edict for devotees: “Neither of the above forms of the Lord, as just described unto you from the material angle of vision, is accepted by the pure devotees of the Lord who know Him well.” (Bhag. [2.10.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.35))

In his Paramatmd-sandarbha, anuccheda 57, commenting on this text, Sri Jiva explains why pure devotees do not accept the Lord’s universal form as an actual form of the Lord: The reason why learned devotees do not accept (na grhnanti) the universal form is given in the words maydsrste (created by maya). The universal form is not manifest by the Lord’s internal spiritual potency, and it is unlike the Lord’s other forms, which have four arms and many similar features and are transcendental. It is not above the material world of maya as the Lord’s forms always are.

Commenting on text 34, Srila Sridhara Svami states that after describing the gross form, the subtle form will now be described. Text 35, he writes, forbids both the universal form and the impersonal aspect. Text 36 describes how the Lord, by empowering Brahma, works through Brahma’s form (brahmu-rupa-dhrk) to create the world. Thus Sukadeva Gosvami states that when creation is required, the asraya, the Supreme Lord, manifests Himself for that purpose \[as Brahma\]. Srila Prabhupada clarifies this point in his purport to text 36: “The Lord as Visnu, Brahma and Siva conducts the three modes of material nature. From Visnu is bom Brahma, and from Brahma is bom Siva. Sometimes Brahma is a separated part of Visnu, and sometimes Brahma is Visnu Himself. Thus Brahma creates the different species of life all over the universe, which means that the Lord creates the whole manifestation either by Himself or through the agency of His authorized deputies.”

Thus everything is bom from the Lord and thus either directly or indirectly created by Him. Sukadeva Gosvami explains: О King, know from me that all living entities are created by the Supreme Lord according to their past deeds. This includes Brahma and his sons like Daksa, the periodical heads like Vaivasvata Manu, the demigods like Indra, Candra, and Varuna, and the great sages like Bhrgu, Vyasa, and Vasistha. Sukadeva goes on to include the inhabitants of all the planets. The Lord is the ultimate father of the forest animals, birds, domesticated animals, reptiles, mountains, moving and standing living entities, and all others whether they are in the water, on land, or in the sky. All created living beings—be they demigods, humans, or animals—are created and placed under the influence of the three modes of material nature in various proportions.

After describing how the Supreme Lord operates as Brahma, Sukadeva Gosvami next describes His function as Visnu: After the creation has commenced, the Personality of Godhead, who as Visnu maintains the universe, incarnates Himself by His own will to reclaim conditioned souls. In each incarnation, whether it be among humans, nonhumans, or demigods, He remains forever untouched by matter. And, as Siva, the Lord destroys: “Thereafter, at the end of the millennium, the Lord Himself in the form of Rudra, the destroyer, will annihilate the complete creation as the wind displaces the clouds.” (Bhag. [2.10.43](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.43))

In his purport to this text, Prabhupada calls us to seek the purpose and ultimate cause of creation, maintenance, and destruction:

**The foolish conditioned soul who has taken this temporary world as a permanent settlement has to learn intelligently why such creation and destruction take place. The fruitive actors in the material world are very enthusiastic in the creation of big enterprises, big houses, big empires, big industries and so many big, big things out of the energy and ingredients supplied by the material agent of the Supreme Lord. With such resources, and at the cost of valuable energy, the conditioned soul creates, satisfies his whims, but unwillingly has to depart from all his creations and enter into another phase of life to create again and again. To give hope to such foolish conditioned souls who waste their energy in this temporary material world, the Lord gives information that there is another nature, which is eternally existent without being occasionally created or destroyed, and that the conditioned soul can understand what he should do and how his valuable energy may be utilized. Instead of wasting his energy in matter, which is sure to be destroyed in due course by the supreme will, the conditioned soul should utilize his energy in the devotional service of the Lord so that he can be transferred to the other, eternal nature, where there is no birth, no death, no creation, no destruction, but permanent life instead, full of knowledge and unlimited bliss. The temporary creation is thus exhibited and destroyed just to give information to the conditioned soul who is attached to temporary things. It is also meant to give him a chance for self-realization, and not for sense gratification, which is the prime aim of all fruitive actors.**

Although the Lord acts through His energies and expansions in the triple function of creation, maintenance, and destruction, He has yet more wonderful features. Sukadeva Gosvami explains: “The great transcendentalists thus describe the activities of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, but the pure devotees deserve to see more glorious things in transcendence, beyond these features.” (Bhag. [2.10.44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.44)) The Lord Himself plays no direct role in the material world’s creation and destruction. What the Vedas describe as His direct interference is simply to counteract the idea that material nature is itself the creator.

Sukadeva continues: The process of creation and annihilation 1 have summarized occurs again and again. The creations by the Lord in His feature of Karanodakasayi Visnu happen over a mahd'kalpa, the creation of Brahma and dispersion of the material ingredients happen over a vikalpa, and the creation by Brahma in each day of his life (one thousand divya-yugas or cycles of four yugas) takes place over a kalpa. As these creations cycle again and again, one can glimpse the vast time frame in which creation, maintenance, and destruction occur. This temporal frame of reference (Maharaja Pariksit inquired about this in texts [2.8.13-14](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/8.13)) will be described in more detail in the eleventh chapter of the Third Canto. For now, Sukadeva will describe one of Brahma’s creations, the creation that took place during the Padma-kalpa.

After hearing so much technical information about the physical creation, Saunaka Rsi and the sages at Naimisaranya desire to hear of higher, more transcendental subjects. Therefore, they ask Suta Gosvami about Vidura, whom Suta mentioned (Canto One, Chapter Thirteen) had met Maitreya: “Let us know, please, what topics were discussed between Vidura and Maitreya, who talked on transcendental subjects, and what was inquired by Vidura and replied by Maitreya. Also please let us know the reason for Vidura’s giving up the connection of his family members, and why he again came home. Please also let us know the activities of Vidura while he was in the places of pilgrimage.” (Bhag. [2.10.49-50](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.49)) Sukadeva Gosvami accepts their desire and begins to speak on that subject.

## CANTO THREE

## Dialogue One - Vidura Meets Uddhava and They Discuss Krsna

## Chapter 1 - Questions by Vidura

## Introduction: Vidura on Pilgrimage—His Meeting with Uddhava

Vidura entered the palace in Hastinapura, once his home, to preach.

He hoped to free his half-brother, the blind, elderly, and feeble Dhrtarastra, from his complacency. Dhrtarastra was fast approaching death. Vidura wanted to awaken him to that fact and to assist him in making a spiritual end to a life based on envy. Vidura’s own life and realizations had been honed razor-sharp both by his years of austerity and pilgrimage and because he had heard the teachings of the great sage Maitreya. Vidura’s words, therefore, cut at Dhrtarastra’s heart like a blade.

Suta Gosvami had previously described Vidura’s dramatic entry into the Pandavas’ capital in the thirteenth chapter of the First Canto. He had then gone on to narrate the incidents leading up to King Pariksit meeting Sukadeva Gosvami. In the Second Canto, Suta reiterated Sukadeva’s primary instructions about preparing for death. He also explained the universal creation, the Lord’s descent as various avataras, the Bhagavatam’s original four seed texts, and how those texts had been expanded into ten topics. From the beginning of Canto Two to its end, Sukadeva focused his words on the inconceivably powerful Lord’s transcendental relationship with the material world.

At the end of Canto Two, Saunaka Rsi, on behalf of the sages, had requested that they again discuss Vidura, who had traveled the world on pilgrimage: “Let us know, please, what topics were discussed between Vidura and Maitreya, who talked on transcendental subjects, and what was inquired by Vidura and replied by Maitreya. Also please let us know the reason for Vidura’s giving up the connection of his family members, and why he again came home. Please also let us know the activities of Vidura while he was in the places of pilgrimage.” (Bhag. [2.10.49—50](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.49)) Srila Prabhupada stated in his purport to these texts that “Sri Suta Gosvami was narrating the topics of the creation and destruction of the material world, but it appears that the rsis headed by Saunaka were more inclined to hear of transcendental subjects, which are on a higher level than the physical.”

## Texts 1-24: Vidura Remains on Pilgrimage and Meets Uddhava

Suta first repeats Sukadeva’s glorification of the palace Vidura had rejected and reminds us that Sri Krsna Himself had both visited the palace and lived there as if it were His own home. Why then had Vidura renounced it, forsaking security, position, family, and friends? He left because of the actions of the blind but ambitious Dhrtarastra and his foremost son, Duryodhana.

Yudhisthira and the Pandavas had once been victims of a crooked gambling match. They were subsequently exiled but had returned to claim a share of the kingdom. Dhrtarastra, however, had refused to restore to Yudhisthira even a fragment of his rightful kingdom. Rather, Duryodhana had declared, “We cannot spare even as much land as would hold the point of a needle.” Even Krsna’s attempts at reconciliation failed to inspire a compromise. Dhrtarastra then called for Vidura’s advice. He thought of Vidura as his sagacious half-brother, a man who spoke plain truth. Vidura did not give Dhrtarastra the advice he desired. Rather, he told Dhrtarastra to appease the noble Yudhisthira, a man without enemies. Disaster would await the Kuru dynasty should it maintain enmity toward Yudhisthira, his brothers, and their Lord Krsna. Vidura assured Dhrtarastra that Bhima would kill each of his one hundred sons. Better Dhrtarastra return to Yudhisthira his legitimate share of the kingdom.

And, Vidura added, Dhrtarastra should remove the root cause of this conflict: Duryodhana, “offense personified” (Bhag. [3.1.13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/1.13)), who was even envious of Krsna and therefore could never improve. Duryodhana was present during the meeting between Dhrtarastra and Vidura, and when he heard his uncle’s words he criticized Vidura harshly: “Who asked him to come here, this son of a kept mistress? He is so crooked that he spies in the interest of the enemy against those on whose support he has grown up. Toss him out of the palace immediately and leave him with only his breath.” (Bhag. [3.1.15](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/1.15))

Srila Prabhupada describes the scene in his purport to text 15: “Duryodhana knew very well that Vidura was a great soul and well-wisher, but unfortunately he used strong words to hurt his innocent uncle. Duryodhana not only attacked Vidura’s birth, but also called him an infidel because he seemed to support the cause of Yudhisthira, whom Duryodhana considered his enemy. He desired that Vidura be immediately put out of the palace and deprived of all his possessions. If possible, he would have liked him caned until he was left with nothing but his breath. He charged that Vidura was a spy of the Pandavas because he advised King Dhrtarastra in their favor. Such is the situation of palace life and the intricacies of diplomacy that even a faultless person like Vidura could be charged with something abominable and punished. Vidura was struck with wonder at such unexpected behavior from his nephew Duryodhana, and before anything actually happened, he decided to leave the palace for good.”

Duryodhana’s harsh words pierced Vidura’s heart like an arrow. Vidura placed his bow by the palace door and departed, recognizing Krsna’s underlying desire for him. The envious Duryodhana had presented Vidura with an opportunity to increase his devotional service, and Vidura went out alone into the world as a renounced pilgrim. Srila Prabhupada explains how in one incident, the Lord’s external energy worked on Duryodhana while His internal energy worked simultaneously on Vidura: “Duryodhana was acting under such influence of the external nature, by which he would be vanquished at the ultimate end. He could not accept the sound advice of Vidura, but on the contrary he insulted that great soul, who was the well-wisher of his whole family. Vidura could understand this because he was a pure devotee. In spite of being very strongly insulted by Duryodhana’s words, Vidura could see that Duryodhana, under the influence of maya, the external energy, was making progress on the path toward his own ruination. He therefore considered the acts of the external energy to be supreme, yet he also saw how the internal energy of the Lord helped him in that particular situation. . . . Mdya, the supreme energy of the Lord, acted here both internally and externally.” (Bhag. [3.1.16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/1.16), purport)

Srila Prabhupada confirms the dual action of maya. in his purport to Bhagavatam [3.10.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/10.17): “The energy of the Lord transforms from maha'maya to yogamaya and appears to pure devotees in her real feature.”

Unseen by his relatives and understanding the shift in responsibility Krsna had arranged for him, fully dependent on and thinking of the Lord, Vidura traveled from one holy place to another for years. Text 19 uses the phrase vratani cere hari-tosanani to describe that while wandering, Vidura performed his duties to please the Supreme Lord Hari. Sridhara Svami comments that these words refer to his observing Ekadasi and other vows.

In his purport to text 17, Srila Prabhupada answers an interesting question: Why did Vidura go on pilgrimage rather than immediately seek Krsna’s association and shelter? His answer underlines the danger of bad association: “At that time, Lord Krsna was personally present in the world, and Vidura could have at once approached Him directly, but he did not do so because he was not sufficiently freed from sin. One cannot be one hundred percent devoted to the Lord unless and until he is completely free from all effects of sin. Vidura was conscious that by the association of the diplomatic Dhrtarastra and Duryodhana he had lost his piety and was therefore not fit to associate at once with the Lord.”

Instead, Vidura traveled alone. Traveling without a companion freed him from frivolous speech and allowed him to use his time to consciously cultivate fearlessness and dependence on Krsna.Srila Prabhupada, whose initiated name, Abhaya Caranaravinda, means “fearlessly situated at the Lord’s lotus feet,” once spoke of his own courage during a London morning walk conversation in 1975:

**Prabhupada: Oh, Victoria Memorial.**

**Brahmananda: That was built for the king when he was coming?**

**Prabhupada: No, it was built in memory of Victoria. It was done, imitating the Taj Mahal. It took twenty years. Sir Rajendranath Mukherjee of Martin Company, he took the contract, and after finishing he got this title “Sir.” When it was being constructed, 1 went to the top by crossing the scaffolding.**

**Brahmananda: You must have been very brave!**

**Prabhupada: Yes, I am still brave, (laughter) Otherwise how could**

**I come alone to preach Krsna consciousness? I am still brave.**

**Devotees: \]aya, Srila Prabhupada!**

**Prabhupada: Some astrologer told that “This boy, for executing his purpose, he will enter into the fire.” Yes. Recently in our Bombay affair, it was fight with the fire, is it not?**

**Brahmananda: Yes, oh, yes.**

**Prabhupada: And we have come out victorious.**

Vidura wandered fearlessly from one holy place to another, from west to east, for thirty to thirty-five years. He sanctified his mind by bathing in holy rivers and lakes, performed austerities, and neither combed his hair nor slept in a bed. His consciousness focused on Krsna, he visited the ancient cakra-topped temples established by sages and demigods. After years of constant travel, Vidura arrived at Prabhasa (in modern-day Gujarat). There he learned that Lord Krsna and the Yadu dynasty had departed from this world. Feeling great sadness, Vidura gradually made his way east until he reached the land on the bank of the Yamuna (north of present-day Delhi). Srila Prabhupada’s thought-provoking purport to text 24 describes the potency of searching for Krsna in the holy lands through which Krsna Himself has traveled: “This land is sacred because Lord Krsna traveled through it many times. From the very beginning of His appearance, He was at Mathura in the house of His maternal uncle Kamsa, and He was reared by His foster father Maharaja Nanda at Vrndavana. There are still many devotees of the Lord lingering there in ecstasy in search of Krsna and His childhood associates, the gopis. It is not that such devotees meet Krsna face to face in that tract of land, but a devotee’s eagerly searching after Krsna is as good as his seeing Him personally. How this is so cannot be explained, but it is factually realized by those who are pure devotees of the Lord. Philosophically, one can understand that Lord Krsna and His remembrance are on the absolute plane and that the very idea of searching for Him at Vrndavana in pure God consciousness gives more pleasure to the devotee than seeing Him face to face.”

Prabhupada also comments on the purpose of pilgrimage and the importance of holy pilgrimage places in his purport to text 45:

**The purpose of pilgrimages is to remember the Lord constantly, and therefore the Lord is known as arthaJarti. The purpose of going to a place of pilgrimage is to get the chance to glorify the Lord. Even today, although times have changed, there are still pilgrimage sites in India. For example, in Mathura and Vrndavana, where we had a chance to stay, people are awake from early in the morning at 4 A.M. up until nighttime and are constantly engaged, some way or other, in chanting the holy glories of the Lord. The beauty of such a pilgrimage site is that automatically one remembers the holy glories of the Lord. His name, fame, quality, form, pastimes and entourage are all identical to the Lord, and therefore chanting the glories of the Lord invokes the personal presence of the Lord. Any time or anywhere pure devotees meet and chant the glories of the Lord, the Lord is present without any doubt. It is said by the Lord Himself that He always stays where His pure devotees chant His glories.**

By the Lord’s grace, on the bank of the sanctified Yamuna river Vidura came face to face with Uddhava, Krsna’s dearmost friend. This opportunity—association with a sadhu and the chance to hear about Lord Krsna—is the true benefit of leaving everything behind for pilgrimage.

## Texts 25-45: Vidura Asks Uddhava about Krsna

On seeing Uddhava, Vidura embraced him and asked for news of the Lord and His many associates in Dvaraka (Balarama, Vasudeva, Pradyumna, Ugrasena, Samba, Yuyudhana, Akrilra, Devaki, Aniruddha, and others), even though he had already heard in Prabhasa of their “deaths.” Why did Vidura ask a question to which he already knew the answer? Srila Prabhupada writes: “Vidura asked Uddhava about the welfare of his relatives, although he already knew that they were no longer in the world. This inquiry appears to be very queer, but Srila Jiva Gosvami states that the news was shocking to Vidura, who therefore inquired again due to great curiosity. Thus his inquiry was psychological and not practical.” (Bhag. [3.1.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/1.25), purport)

Vidura did not inquire about Dhrtarastra, for whom he felt compassion. He knew “there was no chance of his well-being, only news of his gliding down to hell.” Vidura said: “I simply lament for he \[Dhrtarastra\] who rebelled against his brother after death. By him I was driven out of my own house, although I am his sincere well-wisher, because he accepted the line of action adopted by his own sons.” (Bhag. [3.1.41](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/1.41)) Note that Vidura chose not to even mention Duryodhana’s name. If one wishes to sample the pure qualities of the associates of Krsna about whom Vidura did inquire—Аkrura, for example—one can examine the texts in this section. In text 32 Vidura remembers the ecstasy Akriira experienced when he saw Krsna’s footprints in Vrndavana’s dust. Srila Jiva Gosvami describes this pastime in his comment on Bhagavatam 10.38.27 in his Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 69: “The very goal of life for all embodied beings is this ecstasy, which Akriira experienced when, upon receiving Kamsa’s order, he put aside all pride, fear and lamentation and absorbed himself in seeing, hearing and describing the things that reminded him of Lord Krsna.”

Jiva Gosvami also offers a comment from Sridhara Svami on this text: “Someone may ask, ‘Why did Akriira roll about on the ground? Is rolling on the ground something that those who have attained pure love for the Lord do?’ This text answers that doubt. The true goal of life for all embodied beings is to attain the kind of ecstasy Akriira manifest. Here it is said about Аkrura: ‘Upon receiving Kamsa’s order, he absorbed himself in seeing, hearing, and describing the things that reminded him of Lord Krsna.’” Bhagavatam [10.38.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/38.27) states that Akriira put aside all pride, fear, and lamentation. Jiva Gosvami writes: “That Akriira was not proud is seen in the words he spoke in Bhagavatam [10.38.18](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/38.18): na mayy upaisyaty ari-buddhim acyutah, ‘The infallible Lord will not consider me an enemy, even though Kamsa has sent me here as his messenger. After all, the omniscient Lord is the actual knower of the field of this material body, and with His perfect vision He witnesses both externally and internally all the endeavors of the conditioned soul’s heart.’

“Pride cannot enter a heart filled with spiritual bliss. Therefore Аkrura remained free of pride. Also, Akriira knew that Lord Krsna had descended to earth to rescue His family members from Kamsa’s harassments. Knowing this, Akrura became free of fear and lamentation. For these reasons, Akrura remained overcome with spiritual bliss, as described in Bhagavatam [10.38.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/38.26): ‘Increasingly agitated by ecstasy at seeing the Lord’s footprints, his bodily hairs standing on end because of his pure love, and his eyes filled with tears, Akrura jumped down from his chariot and began rolling about among those footprints, exclaiming, “Ah, this is the dust from my master’s feet!””’

Vidura then states that few people can understand Krsna’s actions or position as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and then concludes his questions to Uddhava with a request: “O my friend, please, therefore, chant the glories of the Lord, who is meant to be glorified in the places of pilgrimage. He is unborn, and yet He appears by His causeless mercy upon the surrendered rulers of all parts of the universe. Only for their interest did He appear in the family of His unalloyed devotees the Yadus.” (Bhag. [3.1.45](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/1.45))

## Chapter 2-4 - Remembrance of Lord Krsna, The Lord’s Pastimes Out of Vrndavana, Vidura Approaches Maitreya

## Texts 2.1-24: Uddhava Experiences Ecstasy While he Remembers Krsna

Vidura’s questions about Krsna and His associates cast Uddhava into an ocean of ecstatic longing. He wanted to again be with His Lord, that person he had worshiped since birth. Through his feelings of separation, Uddhava associated with Krsna in ecstasy. Krsna teaches how to associate with Him in separation through the message He asked Uddhava to deliver to the Vraja gopis. Uddhava now practiced the instructions the message contained and experienced deep ecstasy. Rapt in thoughts of Krsna, Uddhava fell silent, his body stunned.

He fell deeper and deeper into ecstasy as he became more and more absorbed in his remembrances, and tears flowed from his eyes and down his cheeks.

The great devotee Uddhava gradually returned to external consciousness, regained his composure, and then sorrowfully began his reply to Vidura’s questions. “My dear Vidura, the sun of the world, Lord Krsna, has set, and our house has now been swallowed by the great snake of time. What can I say to you about our welfare?” (Bhag. [3.2.7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/2.7))

Srila Prabhupada cites Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura in his purport to this text: “Vidura was struck with great sorrow when he got the hint of the annihilation of the great Yadu dynasty as well as of his own family, the Kuru dynasty. Uddhava could understand the grief of Vidura, and therefore he first of all wanted to sympathize with him by saying that after the sunset everyone is in darkness. Since the entire world was merged in darkness of grief, neither Vidura nor Uddhava nor anyone else could be happy. Uddhava was as much aggrieved as Vidura, and there was nothing further to be said about their welfare.”

He then goes on to describe Krsna’s departure from the world: “The comparison of Krsna to the sun is very appropriate. As soon as the sun sets, darkness automatically appears. But the darkness experienced by the common man does not affect the sun itself either at the time of sunrise or sunset. Lord Krsna’s appearance and disappearance are exactly like that of the sun. He appears and disappears in innumerable universes, and as long as He is present in a particular universe, there is all transcendental light in that universe, but the universe from which He passes away is put into darkness.”

Interestingly, in texts 8 and 9 Uddhava calls the Yadu dynasty unfortunate because its members had been able to recognize the Lord only as the Supersoul, not as the Supreme Bhagavan. In describing the Yadus, who had already departed, Uddhava uses the word viduh, which is in the present tense. Although both the Lord and the Yadus had already departed, Uddhava uses this tense, according to Srila Jiva Gosvami (Krsna-sandarbha, anuccheda 128), to indicate that even after their departure, the Yadavas were still intimate associates of Sri Krsna and residing eternally in His abode.

Uddhava remained absorbed in feelings of separation as he spoke to Vidura. He next addressed the Lord’s merciful purpose in appearing in the world in His all-attractive form: “The Lord appeared in the mortal world by His internal potency, yoga-maya. He came in His eternal form, which is just suitable for His pastimes. These pastimes were wonderful for everyone, even for those proud of their own opulence, including the Lord Himself in His form as the Lord of Vaikuntha. Thus His \[Sri Krsna’s\] transcendental body is the ornament of all ornaments.” (Bhag. [3.2.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/2.12))

Jiva Gosvami comments on this text in Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 80. There he states that the Lord appeared in the mortal world by His internal potency, yogamaya, and that His eternal form is just suitable for His pastimes. These pastimes were wonderful for everyone, even for those proud of their own opulence, including the Lord Himself in His other forms. Thus His transcendental body is the ornament of all ornaments.

The phrase yogamaya-balam means that Krsna appeared by His own spiritual power, His cit-sakti. Darsayata means that His appearance “manifest His glories and opulence,” and vismapanam means that those glories fill sages and philosophers with wonder because the sages and philosophers have never seen a form as wondrous as Krsna’s. When Krsna was present, the sages and philosophers were continuously won-derstruck (svasya vismapanam), as Krsna’s form is the supreme abode of glory and opulence (saubhagarddheh).

Jiva Gosvami then raises a doubt: Krsna may be glorious and opulent, but aren’t His ornaments the cause of His auspiciousness? Sri Jiva explains that Bhagavatam [3.2.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/2.12) answers this doubt: Sri Krsna’s own body is the ornament of all ornaments. In other words, ornaments are beautified by their proximity to Krsna. Someone may then ask, “What is Sri Krsna’s form like?” His spiritual form superficially resembles that of a human (martya-lilaupayikam), but actually it is so glorious that even Lord Visnu yearns to see it.

Thus with great devotion, Uddhava became absorbed in remembering Krsna and His pastimes again and again—the rajasuya sacrifice where all the demigods marveled at His beauty, the love the Vraja gopis possessed for Him, the way He had appeared in Kamsa’s prison, the affectionate exchanges He had shared with His parents, the mercy He had shown to His enemy, Sisupala, how He had liberated even the warriors opposing the Pandavas during the Battle of Kuruksetra, and how He had accepted worship from the universal controllers.

In his purport to text 14, Srila Prabhupada describes the ultimate perfection of love, which is reposed in the gopis of Vrndavana:

**Lord Krsna finally admitted His defeat before the transcendental affection of the gopis and declared that He was unable to repay them for their unalloyed affection. Although the gopis were seemingly anguished by the Lord’s teasing behavior, when Krsna would leave them they could not tolerate the separation and used to follow Him with their eyes and minds. They were so stunned by the situation that they could not finish their household duties. No one could excel Him even in the dealing of love exchanged between boys and girls. It is said in the revealed scriptures that Lord Krsna personally never goes beyond the boundary of Vrndavana. He remains there eternally because of the transcendental love of the inhabitants. Thus even though He is not visible at present, He is not away from Vrndavana for a moment.**

Krsna had once wanted Uddhava to witness the height of the gopis’ love for Him and had therefore sent him to Vrndavana with a message for them. What Uddhava speaks here in glorification of the gopis comes from his experience in Vraja. Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu embodies the same love Uddhava describes, and Srimad-Bhagavatam teaches its hearers how a soul may give him or herself fully to Krsna with the same type of love. This is the highest religious achievement.

In his love enhanced by separation, Uddhava remembered Krsna’s magnanimity and compassion: “Alas, how shall I take shelter of one more merciful than He who granted the position of mother to a she-demon \[Putana\] although she was unfaithful and she prepared deadly poison to be sucked from her breast? I consider the demons, who are inimical toward the Lord, to be more than the devotees because while fighting with the Lord, absorbed in thoughts of enmity, they are able to see the Lord carried on the shoulder of Garuda, the son of Tarksya \[Kasyapa\], and carrying the wheel weapon in His hand.” (Bhag. [3.2.23-24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/2.23))

## Texts 2.25-34 and 3.1-23: Remembering Lord Krsna In and Out of Vrndavana

Uddhava recounts Krsna’s pastimes in chronological order, beginning with His birth in the Mathura prison and how He was immediately carried to Nanda Maharaja’s pasturing grounds. Text 26 explains that Krsna lived under Nanda Maharaja’s care for eleven years. The Bhagavatam also describes that He entered Mathura during His kaisora age (Bhag. [10.45.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/45.3)), which usually falls between the ages of ten and fifteen. Yet Krsna Himself explains (Bhag. [10.45.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/45.3)) that Vasudeva and Devaki were unable to enjoy His kaisora age, which should have ended years after Krsna had entered Mathura and was living under their care. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura addresses this issue in his commentary on Bhagavatam [10.45.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/45.3): “The three years and four months that Lord Krsna stayed in Mahavana were the equivalent of five years for an ordinary child, and thus in that period He completed His kaumara stage of childhood. The period from then to the age of six years and eight months, during which He lived in Vrndavana, constitutes His pauganda stage. And the period from the age of six years and eight months through His tenth year, during which time He lived in Nandisvara \[Nandagrama\], constitutes His kaisora stage. Then, at the age of ten years and seven months, on the eleventh lunar day of the dark fortnight of the month of Caitra, He went to Mathura, and on the fourteenth day thereafter He killed Kamsa. Thus He completed His kaisora period at age ten, and He eternally remains at that age. In other words, we should understand that from this point on the Lord remains forever a kisora.” (cited in the BBT purports to Bhagavatam [10.45.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-10/45.3))

Uddhava then describes Krsna’s childhood in Vrndavana—His cowherding pastimes, charming flute playing, the killing of powerful demons, His chastisement of the snake-king Kaliya, His worship and lifting of Govardhana Hill, and His rasa-lila pastimes with His gopi girlfriends. All of these pastimes offer a full display of Krsna enjoying His internal energy.

In the third chapter, Uddhava describes the Lord’s wonderful activities outside Vrndavana, such as His killing Kamsa, studying under Sandipani Muni, kidnapping and marrying His first wife, the beautiful and fortunate Rukmini, His heroic marriage to Princess Nagnijiti, His bringing the parijata tree from heaven to please Satyabhama, His killing of Narakasura, and His expanding Himself to marry 16,100 queens, each present simultaneously with Krsna in her own individual palace.

Uddhava also describes how Krsna killed Kalayavana, the king of Magadha (Jarasandha), Salva, Sambara, Dvivida, Bana, Mura, Balvala, Dantavakra, and other demons. Then he speaks of the Battle of Kuruksetra, by which Krsna fulfilled His desire to relieve the earth from the overburdening of military forces. Regarding Krsna killing demons, many of whom were actually killed by Krsna’s associates, Prabhupada notes that Krsna Himself is the performer of His devotees’ wonderful deeds, which He performs through them as an exchange of love:

**Kalayavana and the King of Magadha were killed by Mucukunda and Bhima respectively, who acted as agents of the Lord. By such acts the Lord wanted to exhibit the prowess of His devotees, as if He were personally unable to fight but His devotees could kill them. The relationship of the Lord with His devotees is a very happy one. Actually, the Lord descended at the request of Brahma in order to kill all the undesirables of the world, but to divide the share of glory He sometimes engaged His devotees to take the credit. The Battle of Kuruksetra was designed by the Lord Himself, but just to give credit to His devotee Arjuna (nimitta^matram bhava savyasdcin), He played the part of the charioteer, while Arjuna was given the chance to play the fighter and thus become the hero of the Battle of Kuruksetra. What He wants to do Himself by His transcendental plans, He executes through His confidential devotees. That is the way of the Lord’s mercy towards His pure unalloyed devotees. (Bhag.** [**3.3.10**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/3.10)**, purport)**

This purport indirectly points to Prabhupada’s own empowered fulfilliment of the prediction that the holy name would spread throughout the world, kali-kalera dharma—krsna-nama-sankirtana, krsna-sakti vina nahe tara pravartana: “The fundamental religious system in the age of Kali is the chanting of the holy name of Krsna. Unless empowered by Krsna, one cannot propagate the sankirtana movement.” (Cc. Antya [7.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-antya/7.11))

Finally, Uddhava tells Vidura how Krsna protected Maharaja Pariksit while he was still in his mother’s womb, how He gave Yudhisthira the throne, and how the Lord enjoyed His life with His many wives in Dvaraka. Within these descriptions (Bhag. [3.3.14-19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/3.14)), Uddhava also speaks briefly how the Lord wished the Yadu dynasty to leave the world before He Himself departed.

## Texts 3.24-28: The Departure of the Yadu Dynasty from the Earth and 4.1-8: Uddhava Meets Krsna, who is Preparing for His Own Departure

Uddhava saw the Lord in His four-armed form at Prabhasa just prior to the Lord’s disappearance. Texts [3.3.24-28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/3.24) and [3.4.1-8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.1) tell briefly both how this final meeting came to pass and how Uddhava eventually arrived at Gurgaon and met Vidura.

The information is given more elaborately in the Eleventh Canto where Krsna’s departure pastime begins in the opening text of Chapter Six. Once, the demigods, headed by Brahma, visited Lord Krsna in Dvaraka to inform Him that the purpose of His incarnation—to remove the earth’s burden—had been fulfilled. It was time for Him to depart. Before long, great sages, including Visvamitra, Asita, Kanva, Durvasa, Bhrgu, Ahgira, Kasyapa, Vamadeva, Atri, Vasistha, and Narada (Bhag. [11.1.11-12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/1.11)), became angry at the Yadu princes’ youthful impudence. As the Lord desired, these sages cursed the princes in a way that would cause the destruction of the Yadu dynasty. Soon after, unfavorable omens began to appear in Dvaraka.

Seeing those omens and realizing that His dear Lord and master, Sri Krsna, would soon depart—and that he would soon be separated from his Lord—Uddhava approached Krsna in distress, begging the Lord to allow him to return to the spiritual world with Him. Krsna refused. Instead, He asked Uddhava to remain on earth to perform a specific service. The Lord ordered Uddhava to become renounced, and instructed him in detail how to attain both foil renunciation and the perfection of spiritual life. The instructions Krsna gave Uddhava are included in chapters Seven through Twenty-nine of the Eleventh Canto and are known as the Uddhava-gita. The Lord concluded these instructions with the following order: “My dear Uddhava, take My order and go to My asrama called Badarika. Purify yourself by both touching and also bathing in the holy waters there, which have emanated from My lotus feet. Rid yourself of all sinful reactions with the sight of the sacred Alakananda River. Dress yourself in bark and eat whatever is naturally available in the forest. Thus you should remain content and free from desire, tolerant of all dualities, good-natured, self-controlled, peaceful and endowed with transcendental knowledge and realization. With fixed attention, meditate constantly upon these instructions I have imparted to you and assimilate their essence. Fix your words and thoughts upon Me, and always endeavor to increase your realization of My transcendental qualities. In this way you will cross beyond the destinations of the three modes of nature and finally come back to Me.” (Bhag. [11.29.41-44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-11/29.41))

When Krsna had completed His instructions, Uddhava circumambulated the Lord and then fell at His feet, his head resting on the Lord’s foot. He knew that he would soon be bereft of the Lord’s association, and his heart cracked. From his broken heart flowed a river of tears that drenched the Lord’s lotus feet. Bowing down again and again, Uddhava placed the Lord’s shoes on his head. Then Uddhava traveled northeast toward Badarikasrama, meditating deeply on Krsna.

Following Krsna’s advice, Balarama, the other members of the Yadu dynasty, and Krsna Himself journeyed to Prabhasa-ksetra to counteract the inauspicious omens by performing an auspicious Vedic ritual. By the force of Krsna’s desire to perform His disappearance pastimes, the members of the Yadu dynasty, although aristocratic by nature, became intoxicated on the rice liquor used to complete the sacrifice. Rowdy, bewildered, and angry, they quarreled among themselves and killed one another. Krsna and Balarama also joined the melee of destruction and violence, which began at sunset and continued until all the Yadus were dead.

Previously, as He had contemplated His mission of relieving the earth of the overburdening demoniac forces (Bhag. [3.3.14](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/3.14)), Krsna Himself had referred to the strength of His Yadu dynasty as possibly “a more unbearable burden.” Srila Prabhupada explains the connotation behind Krsna’s use of the word “burden”: “There are two kinds of burdens. There is the burden of the beast and the burden of love. The burden of the beast is unbearable, but the burden of love is a source of pleasure. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti describes the burden of love very practically. He says that the burden of the husband on the young wife, the burden of the child on the lap of the mother, and the burden of wealth on the businessman, although actually burdens from the viewpoint of heaviness, are sources of pleasure, and in the absence of such burdensome objects, one may feel the burden of separation, which is heavier to bear than the actual burden of love. When Lord Krsna referred to the burden of the Yadu dynasty on the earth, He referred to something different than the burden of the beast. The large numbers of family members bom of Lord Krsna counted to some millions and were certainly a great increase in the population of the earth, but because all of them were expansions of the Lord Himself by His transcendental plenary expansions, they were a source of great pleasure for the earth. When the Lord referred to them in connection with the burden on the earth, He had in mind their imminent disappearance from the earth. All the members of the family of Lord Krsna were incarnations of different demigods, and they were to disappear from the surface of the earth along with the Lord.”

Srila Prabhupada discusses the Yadu dynasty’s dramatic departure from the world in his purport to Bhagavatam [3.4.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.3): “All the above-mentioned activities of the Yadus and Bhojas were executed by the internal potency of the Lord because He wanted them to be dispatched to their respective abodes after He had finished His mission of descent. . . . These particular pastimes of the Lord are not a manifestation of His external energy, or material nature. Such an exhibition of His internal potency is eternal, and therefore one should not conclude that the Yadus and Bhojas died in a drunken state in an ordinary fratricidal war. Sri Jiva Gosvami comments on these incidents as magical performances.”

The disappearance pastimes of Krsna and His great devotees are certainly difficult to understand, yet in these pastimes, as in all of the Lord’s pastimes, His devotees are being played as instruments of His desire. To become an instrument in the Lord’s hands is both a devotee’s aspiration and his pleasure. When a violin produces sweet music, it is the player who is applauded, not the instrument. Yet both the musician and the masterfully crafted instrument are glorious; in the performance, the true purpose of the finely-tuned instrument is fulfilled.

Similarly, in his purport to Bhagavatam [3.3.15](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/3.15), Srila Prabhupada speaks of the synergistic fulfillment of a devotee’s individuality: “The devotees and associates of the Lord are completely surrendered souls. Thus they are transcendental instruments in the hands of the Lord and can be used in any way the Lord desires. The pure devotees also enjoy such pastimes of the Lord because they want to see Him happy. Devotees of the Lord never assert independent individuality; on the contrary, they utilize their individuality in pursuit of the desires of the Lord, and this cooperation of the devotees with the Lord makes a perfect scene of the Lord’s pastimes.”

After the Yadu dynasty’s departure, Balarama sat on the ocean’s family members bom of Lord Krsna counted to some millions and were certainly a great increase in the population of the earth, but because all of them were expansions of the Lord Himself by His transcendental plenary expansions, they were a source of great pleasure for the earth. When the Lord referred to them in connection with the burden on the earth, He had in mind their imminent disappearance from the earth. All the members of the family of Lord Krsna were incarnations of different demigods, and they were to disappear from the surface of the earth along with the Lord.”

Srila Prabhupada discusses the Yadu dynasty’s dramatic departure from the world in his purport to Bhagavatam [3.4.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.3): “All the above-mentioned activities of the Yadus and Bhojas were executed by the internal potency of the Lord because He wanted them to be dispatched to their respective abodes after He had finished His mission of descent. . . . These particular pastimes of the Lord are not a manifestation of His external energy, or material nature. Such an exhibition of His internal potency is eternal, and therefore one should not conclude that the Yadus and Bhojas died in a drunken state in an ordinary fratricidal war. Sri Jiva Gosvami comments on these incidents as magical performances.”

The disappearance pastimes of Krsna and His great devotees are certainly difficult to understand, yet in these pastimes, as in all of the Lord’s pastimes, His devotees are being played as instruments of His desire. To become an instrument in the Lord’s hands is both a devotee’s aspiration and his pleasure. When a violin produces sweet music, it is the player who is applauded, not the instrument. Yet both the musician and the masterfully crafted instrument are glorious; in the performance, the true purpose of the finely-tuned instrument is fulfilled.

Similarly, in his purport to Bhagavatam [3.3.15](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/3.15), Srila Prabhupada speaks of the synergistic fulfillment of a devotee’s individuality: “The devotees and associates of the Lord are completely surrendered souls. Thus they are transcendental instruments in the hands of the Lord and can be used in any way the Lord desires. The pure devotees also enjoy such pastimes of the Lord because they want to see Him happy. Devotees of the Lord never assert independent individuality; on the contrary, they utilize their individuality in pursuit of the desires of the Lord, and this cooperation of the devotees with the Lord makes a perfect scene of the Lord’s pastimes.”

After the Yadu dynasty’s departure, Balarama sat on the ocean’s shore and, in meditation on the Supreme Personality of Godhead, left this mortal world. Krsna observed Balarama’s departure and sat silently beneath a young asvattha tree on the bank of the river Sarasvati.

Although Uddhava had already departed for Badarikasrama before the destruction of the Yadu dynasty, when on his travels he heard of Krsna’s pilgrimage to Prabhasa with His family members, he decided to go there, unable to bear separation from his Lord (Bhag. [3.4.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.5)).

Uddhava arrived at Prabhasa immediately after the Yadu dynasty’s destruction. There He saw the Lord of his life, Sri Krsna, beautiful, blackish, His reddish eyes resembling the newly risen sun. The Lord wore yellow silk garments and was resting cheerfully against a tree.

## Texts 4.9-23: Maitreya Muni Arrives, and Krsna Instructs Uddhava

Just then, by Krsna’s divine inspiration and arrangement, the great sage Maitreya, Vyasadeva’s friend and the disciple of Maharsi Parasara, arrived. Yet while Krsna was speaking, His attention remained focused on Uddhava, not Maitreya, although Maitreya was senior and, if judged by etiquette, superior. Srila Prabhupada explains the reason for this behavior: “Although both Uddhava and Maitreya were great souls, the Lord’s attention was more on Uddhava because he was a spotlessly pure devotee. A jnana'bhakta, or one whose devotion is mixed with the monistic viewpoint, is not a pure devotee. Although Maitreya was a devotee, his devotion was mixed. The Lord reciprocates with His devotees on the basis of transcendental love and not on the basis of philosophical knowledge or fruitive activities.... Herein the Lord’s attitude towards Uddhava was more intimate than with Maitreya Muni.” (Bhag. [3.4.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.10), purport)

The Lord said: “O Vasu, I know from within your mind what you desired in the days of yore when the Vasus and other demigods responsible for expanding the universal affairs performed sacrifices. You particularly desired to achieve My association. This is very difficult to obtain for others, but I award it unto you. О honest one, your present life is the last and the supermost because in this term of life you have been awarded My ultimate favor. Now you can go to My transcendental abode, Vaikuntha, by leaving this universe of conditioned living entities. Your visit to Me in this lonely place because of your pure and unflinching devotional service is a great boon for you.” (Bhag. [3.4.11-12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.11)) When Maitreya heard the Lord’s words he realized that achieving the Lord’s personal association, not merging with the Lord’s Brahman effulgence, was the highest goal of existence. He therefore renounced impersonalism and became a pure devotee.

The Lord next confirmed His identity as the Supreme Personality of Godhead by explaining that it was He who had previously revealed to Lord Brahma the concise form of Srimad-Bhagavatam in four texts. Hearing the Lord’s glories from the Lord’s own mouth, Uddhava began to cry and his body erupted in ecstasy. Uddhava lovingly expressed his mind: Although all benedictions are available to those who serve You, my only interest is loving service to Your lotus feet.

Later in the Bhagavatam ([6.17.28](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-6/17.28)), Maharaja Citraketu will express similar devotional sentiments glorifying the Lord’s service: “Devotees solely engaged in the devotional service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Narayana, never fear any condition of life. For them the heavenly planets, liberation and the hellish planets are all the same, for such devotees are interested only in the service of the Lord.”

For Maitreya’s benefit, Uddhava then expressed his wonder about the Lord’s actions, especially how the deeds performed by the Absolute Truth so closely parallel human behavior: “My Lord, even the learned sages become disturbed in their intelligence when they see that Your Greatness engages in fruitive work although You are free from all desires, that You take birth although You are unborn, that You flee out of fear of the enemy and take shelter in a fort although You are the controller of invincible time, and that You enjoy householder life surrounded by many women although You enjoy in Your Self.” (Bhag. [3.4.16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.16)) You, who are omniscient, nevertheless approached me, Uddhava said, for advice in Dvaraka! How can the Supreme Personality of Godhead perform so many activities that appear to contradict His supreme position? Uddhava then begged the Lord to please reveal the same knowledge He had long ago explained to Brahma.

Uddhava told Vidura that the Lord had then taught him the catuh' sloki Bhagavatam, and that He had additionally described His paramdm sthitim, His “transcendental situation.” Srila Prabhupada comments on the significance of the words paramdm sthitim in his purport to text 19: “The Lord’s transcendental situation was not even spoken of to Brahma when the four verses of Srimad-Bhagavatam ([2.9.33-36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/9.33)) were explained. This transcendental situation comprises His dealings with devotees engaged in transcendental loving service, as exhibited at Dvaraka and Vrndavana. When the Lord explained His specific transcendental situation, it was meant for Uddhava only, and therefore Uddhava particularly said mahyam (‘unto me’), although the great sage Maitreya was also sitting there. Such a transcendental situation is hardly understood by those whose devotion is mixed with speculative knowledge or fruitive activities. The Lord’s activities in confidential love are very rarely disclosed to the general devotees who are attracted by devotion mixed with knowledge and mysticism. Such activities are the inconceivable pastimes of the Lord.”

As He spoke to Vidura, Uddhava went almost mad with grief and separation from Lord Krsna. In anguish, Uddhava told Vidura of his attempt to alleviate his grief by following the Lord’s instructions to go to Badarikasrama. Srila Prabhupada explains this process: “A pure devotee of the Lord of the standard of Uddhava constantly associates with the Lord in the double perception of simultaneous separation and meeting. The pure devotee is not for a moment unengaged in the transcendental service of the Lord. Execution of the Lord’s service is the main occupation of the pure devotee. Uddhava’s separation from the Lord was unbearable, and therefore he started to Badarikasrama in obedience to the Lord’s order because the order of the Lord and the Lord Himself are identical. As long as one is engaged in the execution of the order of the Lord, there is no factual separation from Him.” (Bhag. [3.4.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.21), purport)After a lecture given in Montreal in August 1968, Srila Prabhupada also spoke in a wonderful way about overcoming separation:

**Rukmini: I feel so far away from you when you’re not here.**

**Srila Prabhupada: Oh, that you should not think. There are two conceptions: the physical conception and the vibration conception. So the physical conception is temporary and the vibration conception is eternal. Just like we are relishing the vibration of Krsna’s teachings. So by vibration He is present. As soon as we chant Hare Krsna or chant Bhagavad-gita or Srimad-Bhagavatam, He is present immediately by His vibration. He’s absolute. Therefore try to remember His words of instruction and you’ll not feel separation. You’ll feel that He is with you. So we should associate by the vibration, and not by the physical presence. That is real association—by sound. We are touching Krsna immediately by sound vibration. So we should give more stress on the sound vibration, either of Krsna or of the spiritual master. Then we’ll feel happy and no separation. When Krsna departed from this world, at that time Arjuna was overwhelmed with sorrow and he began to remember the instruction of Bhagavad-gita. You’ll find this in the Srimad-Bhagavatam. He immediately began to remember the teachings that were taught to him in the Battlefield of Kuruksetra. Then he was pacified. Arjuna was His constant friend, so when Krsna went to His abode he was feeling overwhelmed, but he began to remember His teaching. So whenever we shall feel separation, the best thing is to remember the teachings. Then it will be very nice. Is that clear? Yes. So you can chant Hare Krsna.**

Vidura has now heard from Uddhava the terrible answers to his inquiries—his friends and relatives have been killed in the Battle of Kuruksetra and the Yadu dynasty annihilated at Prabhasa-ksetra. All he can do now is use transcendental knowledge to pacify the grief welling up in him.

## Texts 4.24-36: Uddhava Departs Badarikasrama, and Vidura Leaves to Find Maitreya Muni

Vidura humbly yet anxiously requested Uddhava to share with him the confidential knowledge about the Lord and His pastimes that Uddhava had just heard from the Lord. Uddhava, however, declined, deferring to his senior, Maitreya Muni, who had gone to Haridwar. Still, the two spoke about Krsna throughout the night, which seemed to pass in a moment. In the morning, Uddhava, still afflicted with grief and separation, headed deep into the Himalayas toward Badarikasrama. In Priti-sandarbha, anuccheda 217, Srila Jiva Gosvami notes that Lord Krsna kept Uddhava on earth so he could preach the science of devotional service. Later, Srila Sukadeva Gosvami would be preaching the glories of the Lord’s pastimes, and Uddhava’s presence would no longer be required.

Srila Prabhupada cites Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura in his purport to text 32 to explain why Krsna wanted Uddhava to remain in the world after His own departure:

**According to Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura, that confidential message must have concerned the mystery of His departure and the annihilation of His dynasty after the end of His appearance in the mundane world for one hundred years. Everyone must have been very anxious to know about the mystery of the annihilation of the Yadu dynasty, and that message must have been explained by the Lord to Uddhava and dispatched to Badarikasrama for the information of Nara-Narayana and other pure devotees of the Lord.**

Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura speaks further on the mystery of why Krsna sent Uddhava to Badarikasrama. Why is it a mystery? Because Uddhava had never been otherwise associated with that place. Actually, Krsna had previously sent him to Vrndavana, that all-attractive holy place. In his commentary on Bhagavatam [3.4.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.32), Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura explains that Uddhava was ordered to go to Badarikasrama by the tri-loka-guruna, “the spiritual master of the three worlds.” Tri-loka-gurund implies that Krsna is also the guru, acting through the agency of Uddhava, of the devotees He was leaving behind in this world, including those at Badarikasrama.

The devotees at Badarikasrama had not had Krsna’s association during his 125 years on earth, and Krsna decided to offer them His association through His representative, Uddhava, who, as Krsna has just described in text 31, is “not inferior to Me in any way because he is never affected by the modes of material nature.”

The Personality of Godhead had visited many places on earth and elsewhere: Mithila (to meet Srutadeva and Bahulasva), heaven (to acquire the parijata tree), and the lower planets (to reclaim Sandipani Muni’s deceased sons). He had even traveled beyond the borders of the universe to reclaim the brahmana’s sons. By His presence He had perfected the lives of those who lived in all these places, all of whom saw Him and benefited from His philosophical instructions. But Krsna had never gone to Badarikasrama. Krsna sent Uddhava on His behalf in response to the eagerness of the sages to see Him.

The word sandistah in text 32 means “sent” or “being perfectly taught.” Sandistah also means “message” and therefore implies that Uddhava was given a message from Krsna and that Krsna had then told him, “Give this message to Nara-Narayana.” Text 32 also notes that Krsna is sabda-yonina, the origin of all sound and language, especially the sound of the Vedas. This implies that the Personality of Godhead, as the author of the Vedas, knows things that even the Vedas do not know.

Thus the word sandistah implies that Krsna sent Uddhava to Badarikasrama with a message, and that the message contained knowledge unknown even through the Vedas. Krsna gave this message to His most trusted and intelligent messenger, Uddhava.

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura then provides us with the message Uddhava carried on Krsna’s behalf: Greetings to Sri Nara-Narayana! The pastime of showing Myself to the world is supposed to last for a century and a quarter. I have now reached the end of that period, so I will now disappear along with My entourage, the devotees in Dvaraka. After sending back the demigods and other respective universal administrators to their respective abodes—whom I had previously caused to descend to earth—I will return to Vaikuntha in the part of Me to which Brahma prayed \[the part of Krsna known as Narayana\]. The part of Me that expanded from You, the part accompanied by Arjuna, will return unseen to Your residence. Finally, for the benefit of those who are eager to see My original, complete self, I send this most dear of My personal associates, Uddhava, to whom I have granted a physical appearance that resembles Mine. Indeed, Uddhava is not inferior to Me in any way because he is never affected by the modes of material nature. Therefore he may remain in this world in order to disseminate specific knowledge of the Personality of Godhead.”

Srila Jiva Gosvami explains in Pntisandarbha, anuccheda 217, that Uddhava, in his original spiritual form, would attain the glorious spiritual land of Vraja. This was Uddhava’s earnest desire as he himself stated it in Bhagavatam 10.47.61: “The gopis of Vrndavana have given up the association of their husbands, sons, and other family members, who are very difficult to give up, and they have forsaken the path of chastity to take shelter of the lotus feet of Mukunda, Krsna, which one should search for by Vedic knowledge. Oh, let me be fortunate enough to be one of the bushes, creepers, or herbs in Vrndavana, because the gopis trample them and bless them with the dust of their feet.”

According to Srila Sridhara Svami, commenting on earlier texts in this chapter, Krsna had inspired Maitreya Muni to hear from Him just prior to His departure from the world, and had instructed the sage to later speak the same confidential knowledge to Vidura.

As Vidura came to understand “that he was remembered by Lord Krsna \[while quitting this world\], Vidura began to cry loudly, overwhelmed by the ecstasy of love.” (Bhag. [3.4.35](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/4.35))

Srila Prabhupada explains Vidura’s tears: “Vidura was overwhelmed by the ecstasy of love when he understood that Lord Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, thought of him at the last moment. Although he thought of himself as insignificant, he was remembered by the Lord, by His causeless mercy. Vidura accepted this as a great favor, and thus he cried. This crying is the last word in the progressive path of devotional service. One who can cry for the Lord in love is certainly successful in the line of devotional service.”

Vidura remained for a few days on the bank of the Yamuna, and then, following Uddhava’s instructions, traveled north along the Ganges to meet the great sage Maitreya.

## Dialogue Two - Maitreya Describes The Beginnings of the Universe to Vidura

## Chapter 5 - Vidura’s Talk with Maitreya

## Texts 1-16: Vidura Inquires from Maitreya Muni

Vidura, a perfected soul, walked to Haridwar rapt in thoughts of Krsna. He found Maitreya Muni at a secluded place on the Ganges and began to make his inquiries.
