He is not neglectful—he is dutiful—but he does not spend too much time on the upliftment of temporary household or social life. He fully engages in the service of the Lord, and for other affairs he simply spares as much time as absolutely necessary (yathdrham upayunjatah). Such a pure devotee does not care for what is going to happen in the next life or in this life; he does not care even for family, children or society. He fully engages in the service of the Lord in Krsna consciousness.” (Bhag. [3.25.39-40](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/25.39), purport)

Srila Prabhupada often spoke from the paramahamsa platform, and from that vantage point considered the material world valuable only in the sense that it offers facility to serve Krsna. When dealing with individual devotees, however, he offered them practical advice, for he understood both their capacity and their limitations. In this purport, Srila Prabhupada presents an exalted standard of household life, a standard that would be lived by a pure devotee. One should hear the standard and accept Prabhupada’s words describing that standard with the utmost respect: The spiritual world cannot be attained while one simultaneously tries to enjoy matter. Nevertheless, one should not act artificially. According to one’s advancement and capacity, one should balance his material life with his spiritual life so that he may advance steadily toward the goal of pure Krsna consciousness. One should neither imitate exalted devotees nor pretend to be more advanced than one is; but neither should one who has material attachments deny the exalted standard of purity Srila Prabhupada presents. Rather, he should understand his own position and capacity and humbly proceed to serve Krsna under proper guidance. As Prabhupada advised Bob Cohen (Brahma-tirtha dasa) in 1972: “A devotee must work under the direction of a bona fide spiritual master, not imitate the best devotee.” (Perfect Questions, Perfect Answers, p. 56)

Pure devotees are concerned only with giving Krsna pleasure, yet despite their lack of concern for their own material and spiritual upliftment, the devotees nevertheless attain the spiritual world by the Lord’s grace because the Lord, who possesses inconceivable power, “is favorably disposed to the pure devotees.” Kapila Muni concludes His description of the glories of devotional service with His own promise of commitment: “Thus the devotee who worships Me, the allpervading Lord of the universe, in unflinching devotional service, gives up all aspirations to be promoted to heavenly planets or to become happy in this world with wealth, children, cattle, home or anything in relationship with the body. I take him to the other side of birth and death.” (Bhag. [3.25.39-40](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/25.39))

## Texts 41-44: The Lord Reveals His Reciprocation with His Devotee’s Service

In texts 32—40 Kapila sweetly described the glories of serving Him with devotion. Indeed, His concluding words were that He Himself transports His pure devotee “to the other side of birth and death.” In this next short section, texts 41-44, Kapiladeva describes His own power, which awards one confidence that His words are not hollow and that He is capable of fulfilling His promise. One can take shelter and serve Krsna with confidence: Yes, I will surrender to my Lord, for He has the potency to protect me, His servant. Kapila Muni assures us that no one can escape the fear of birth and death unless he seeks His shelter, for He is “the almighty Lord, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the original source of all creation, and also the Supreme Soul of all souls.” (Bhag. [3.25.41](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/25.41)) The wind blows out of fear of Him and by His power. The sun shines, the rain falls, fire bums, and death takes its toll out of fear of Him. Those who take shelter of His feet become fearless and can enter the kingdom of God. Kapiladeva concludes that Devahuti should fix her mind on Him, the Supreme Personality of Godhead: “That is the only means for attainment of the final perfection of life.” (Bhag. [3.25.44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/25.44))

Srila Prabhupada’s purport to this last text in the chapter emphasizes the importance of fixing the mind on Krsna: “Here the words mano mayy arpitam, which mean ‘the mind being fixed on Me,’ are significant. One should fix his mind on the lotus feet of Krsna or His incarnation. To be fixed steadily in that freedom is the way of liberation. . . . First of all, the mind should be engaged at the lotus feet of the Lord, very steadily and naturally. Because the mind is the master of the senses, when the mind is engaged, all the senses become engaged. That is bhakti-yoga. . . . The best course is to fix the mind on the lotus feet of the Lord. Mano mayy arpitam sthiram. If one seriously engages in Krsna consciousness, that is the highest perfectional stage of human life.”

## Chapter 26 - Fundamental Principles of Material Nature

## Texts 1-8: Understanding the Fundamental Categories of the Absolute Truth Frees a Soul from Material Nature

Kapila Muni next introduces Devahuti to the categories into which the Absolute Truth can be divided: “My dear mother, now I shall describe unto you the different categories of the Absolute Truth, knowing which any person can be released from the influence of the modes of material nature. Knowledge is the ultimate perfection of selfrealization. I shall explain that knowledge unto you by which the knots of attachment to the material world are cut.” (Bhag. [3.26.1-2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.1)) How does such knowledge, which is part of Sankhya-yoga, aid one’s release from the material energy? If one possesses this knowledge, one will realize himself as soul, different from everything found

in material nature. One will also realize the Lord as his source as well as the source of the entire material creation. Fixed in these realizations, one will no longer try to enjoy matter. Then, bolstered by the detachment one’s realization offers, one will be more inclined to do what Kapila Muni suggested in Bhagavatam [3.25.20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/25.20): “Every learned man knows very well that attachment for the material is the greatest entanglement of the spirit soul. But that same attachment, when applied to the self-realized devotees, opens the door of liberation.”

Clearly, material detachment is essential if one is to attain liberation. As Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to the first text in Chapter Twenty-six: “As long as one has even a slight desire to enjoy or lord it over material nature, there is no chance of his being freed from the influence of nature’s material modes.”

Sankhya-yoga equips one with knowledge. Kapila Muni first described bhakti-yoga, the heart of Sankhya-yoga, in Chapter Twenty-five. In Chapter Twenty-six, He provides through His teachings the ax of knowledge by which one can cut his material attachments and attain that heart. In the first two texts of Chapter Twenty-six, Kapila Muni has encouraged Devahuti to be attentive by describing the primal category of existence, the Absolute Truth, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the category on whom all else rests. Knowing the Absolute Truth, He explains, severs all attachment to the material world. In texts 4-8 He will describe material energy, which can be further subdivided into categories.

Text 3: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead is the Supreme Soul, and He has no beginning. He is transcendental to the material modes of nature and beyond the existence of this material world. He is perceivable everywhere because He is self-effulgent, and by His self-effulgent luster the entire creation is maintained.” The material realm is created and maintained by the Supersoul’s potency. He is present everywhere in His energies. What inspires Him to create and maintain the material realm? Kapila Muni continues: “As His pastime, that Supreme Personality of Godhead, the greatest of the great, accepted the subtle material energy, which is invested with three material modes of nature and which is related with Visnu. Divided into varieties by her threefold modes, material nature creates the forms of the living entities, and the living entities, seeing this, are illusioned by the knowledge-covering feature of the illusory energy. Because of his forgetfulness, the transcendental living entity accepts the influence of material energy as his field of activities, and thus actuated, he wrongly applies the activities to himself.” (Bhag. [3.26.4-6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.4))

Text 4 describes that the Lord accepts (abhyapadyata) the creation of the material world by His own will (yadrcchaya) as His pastime (lilaya), His self-willed activity to lift the conditioned souls back to the spiritual world. The Mayavadi impersonalists misinterpret this text to mean that He, as His pastime, for His pleasure willingly assumes the position of jiva and enters the material world to suffer in one material body after another.

Srila Prabhupada dismisses this ludicrous proposal in his purport to text 8: “The Mayavadi philosopher’s presentation is that the living entity enjoys his pastimes by accepting the body of a hog. This theory is not acceptable, however, because the word ‘pastime’ implies voluntary acceptance for enjoyment. Therefore this interpretation is most misleading. When there is enforced acceptance for suffering, it is not a pastime. The Lord’s pastimes and the conditioned living entity’s acceptance of karmic reaction are not on the same level.”

As explained in this section of the Bhagavatam, the Supreme Personality of Godhead—to reclaim the fallen jivas and to bring them back to His abode—accepts the pastime of indirectly interacting with the subtle material energy, within which are the three unmanifest modes. After the modes have manifest during the process of creation, this subtle energy will provide the forms, activities, and fields of activity for the conditioned souls. The Bhagavad-gita ([13.6-7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/13.6)) states: “The five great elements, false ego, intelligence, the unmanifested, the ten senses and the mind, the five sense objects, desire, hatred, happiness, distress, the aggregate, the life symptoms, and convictions —all these are considered, in summary, to be the field of activities and its interactions.” Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to this Bhagavad-gita text: “The unmanifested modes of material nature are called pradhana.”

Thus souls desiring enjoyment independent of the Supreme Personality of Godhead will have a field for their activities. Necessarily, that field will also provide the illusion that will cover the soul’s eternal relationship with Krsna. Once the creation is “actuated,” out of kindness the Lord descends to the material realm and performs pastimes to enlighten the conditioned souls and remind them about their relationship with Him. Srila Prabhupada further explains the need for the Lord’s creation “pastime” in his purport to text 5:

**There is a hint in the previous verse in the word lilaya, which means “for the pastimes of the Lord.” The Lord wants to rectify the enjoying temperament of the conditioned souls. It is stated in Bhagavad-gita that no one is the enjoyer but the Supreme Personality of Godhead. This material energy is created, therefore, for anyone who pretends to enjoy. An example can be cited here that there is no necessity for the government’s creation of a separate police department, but because it is a fact that some of the citizens will not accept the state laws, a department to deal with criminals is necessary. There is no necessity, but at the same time there is a necessity. Similarly, there was no necessity to create this material world for the sufferings of the conditioned souls, but at the same time there are certain living entities, known as nitya-baddha, who are eternally conditioned. We say that they have been conditioned from time immemorial because no one can trace out when the living entity, the part and parcel of the Supreme Lord, became rebellious against the supremacy of the Lord.... Without tracing out the beginning of the existence of these two classes \[the obedient and the atheists or agnostics\], we can take it for granted that some of the living entities revolted against the laws of the Lord. Such entities are called conditioned souls, for they are conditioned by the three modes of material nature.**

In his Paramatma-sandarbha, anuccheda 29, Srila Jiva Gosvami cites text 6 to describe how a soul’s rebellious independence from Krsna causes his illusion. Sri Jiva explains that when an individual soul’s blissful spiritual consciousness is reflected as a perversion in material consciousness, he thinks, “I will not act for Your benefit. I will act only for my benefit.” In this way, the soul necessarily comes under the grip of the materialistic false ego and enters the material world. Thus because a soul desires to act for his own benefit instead of Krsna’s pleasure, he comes under the grip of false ego.

Because all conditioned souls forget Krsna, their actions are controlled by the Lord’s maya. Limiting conditions are forced on them.

Thus souls in maya’s insurmountable domain identify with this world as if it were their own. In illusion they believe themselves the controllers of destiny, although their power is insignificant compared to the governing power of the material energy. Entombed by maya, the conditioned souls think they are the body. By maya’s influence their actions then invariably stem from a desire to act selfishly. The attempt to enjoy separately from Krsna forces them to assume responsibility for their own happiness and distress along with the reactions to their deeds.

But the living entity can choose to again act in Krsna’s service. As Srila Prabhupada explains: “The living entity is the cause of his own suffering, but he can also be the cause of his eternal happiness. When he wants to engage in Krsna consciousness, a suitable body is offered to him by the internal potency, the spiritual energy of the Lord, and when he wants to satisfy his senses, a material body is offered. Thus it is his free choice to accept a spiritual body or a material body, but once the body is accepted he has to enjoy or suffer the consequences.” (Bhag. [3.26.8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.8), purport)

## Text 9-72: Devahuti Inquires Further into the Workings of The Lord’s Material Energy and Kapiladeva Replies

After hearing her son’s brief description of the Lord, the conditioned souls, material nature, and the conditioned souls’ entanglement in material nature, Devahuti asks Him to explain further how the Lord interacts with His energies and causes the material creation. In response, Kapila Muni depicts the process by which God creates the material universes.

Kapiladeva first describes matter in its initial phase, when it is known as pradhana. Pradhana means “first” or “primal”. Pradhana is not Brahman, a purely spiritual substance, but is the primal, most subtle form of matter.

Matter is called prakrti, which is created after pradhana, the unmanifest material nature arising from the Lord’s potency. Thus the “condition of material nature immediately previous to its manifestation is called pradhana.” (Bhag. [3.26.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.10), purport) Pradhana is also defined as “When Brahman is mixed with the three qualities goodness, passion and ignorance, there results the material expansion, which is sometimes called saguna Brahman and which consists of these twenty-five elements.” (Bhag. [3.26.15](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.15)). Again, pradhana is that primal, most subtle manifestation of matter.

Aside from the three modes of material nature, pradhana also contains—although they are not yet manifest—the twenty-four elements necessary for creation. Kapila Muni describes them as follows in text 11: “The aggregate elements, namely the five gross elements, the five subtle elements, the four internal senses, the five senses for gathering knowledge and the five outward organs of action, are known as the pradhana.” The twenty-fifth element, the “mixing element,” the element that causes all the other elements to combine, is time.

The form of the Lord that interacts indirectly with pradhana is known as Karanadakasayi Visnu. His glance impregnates material nature with countless souls, all desiring an existence separate from the Lord. “The transcendental molecules of that glance are particles of spirit, or spiritual atoms, which appear in different species of life according to the seeds of their individual karma from the previous cosmic manifestation.” (Cc. Adi [5.69](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-adi/5.69), purport) Agitated, pradhana begins to mix, differentiate, and transform. Creation has begun.

The Sankhya philosophy analyzes and breaks down the material creation into its constituent categories of twenty-five elements. Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 18: “According to some learned philosophers, the Supersoul is included to make a total of twenty-six elements.” That particular form of the Supersoul, Ksirodakasayi Visnu, is an expansion of Karanadakasayi Visnu. He is the sanctioner and witness in each universe. By the potency of that third Visnu, as well as by His unstoppable time energy, the living entity “combines” and identifies with his karma. According to Bhagavatam [5.14.29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-5/14.29), the Lord’s “unstoppable energy of time” is His cakra:

**The personal weapon used by Lord Krsna, the disc, is called hari-cakra, the disc of Hari. This cakra is the wheel of time. It expands from the beginning of the atoms up to the time of Brahma’s death, and it controls all activities. It is always revolving and spending the lives of the living entities, from Lord Brahma down to an insignificant blade of grass.... It is impossible to check this wheel of time. This wheel is very exacting because it is the personal weapon of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.**

Srila Prabhupada speaks about the message time delivers: “The fear of death is the action of the kola, or the time factor, which represents the influence of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. In other words, time is destructive. Whatever is created is subject to destruction and dissolution, which is the action of time. Time is a representation of the Lord, and it reminds us also that we must surrender unto the Lord. The Lord speaks to every conditioned soul as time. He says in Bhagavad' gita that if someone surrenders unto Him, then there is no longer any problem of birth and death. We should therefore accept the time factor as the Supreme Personality of Godhead standing before us.” (Bhag. [3.26.16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.16), purport)

## Texts 10-25: By the Lord’s Potency, Pradhana Manifests into the Mahat'tattva—The Creation Continues

The Lord, with His incredibly potent glance, impregnated the pradhana, which is the “unmanifested eternal combination of the three modes” (Bhag. [3.26.10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.10)), and which has within it, albeit in undifferentiated form, the twenty-four elements: the “five gross elements, the five subtle elements, the four internal senses, the five senses for gathering knowledge and the five outward organs of action ...” (Bhag [3.26.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.11))

The five gross elements are earth, water, fire, air, and ether, and the five subtle elements are the five sense objects, smell, taste, color, touch, and sound (Bhag. [3.26.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.12)). “The senses for acquiring knowledge and the organs for action number ten, namely the auditory sense, the sense of taste, the tactile sense, the sense of sight, the sense of smell, the active organ for speaking, the active organs for working \[the two hands\], and those for traveling \[the two feet\], generating and evacuating.” (Bhag. [3.26.13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.13)) The four internal subtle senses, as explained in text 14, are citta (a sense of awareness or consciousness), ahankara (a false sense of self, false ego), manah (the accepting and rejecting function known as mind), and buddhih (the discriminating function known as intelligence). As the text explains, “Distinctions between them can be made only by different functions...”

Each of these internal senses is meant to worship specific expansions of the Supreme Personality of Godhead known as the catur-vyuha: Vasudeva, Sankarsana, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. To get release from ahankara (false ego), one has to worship Sankarsana through the worship of Lord Siva; to purify the mind (manah) and become free from mental disturbances, one has to worship Aniruddha through worship of the moon planet; to be fixed in buddhi (intelligence), one has to worship Pradyumna through the worship of Brahma; and to purify the citta (consciousness), one has to worship the Supersoul through his expansion Lord Vasudeva (Bhag. [3.26.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.21), purport).

Pradhana is the subtlest form of matter. Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to text 10 that pradhana is neither Brahman, time, nor the jiva. It is eternal and “the subtle, undifferentiated sum total of all material elements.” It can also be termed saguna Brahman, Brahman with qualities, as Srila Prabhupada refers to it in his purport to text 15: “When Brahman is mixed with the three qualities goodness, passion and ignorance, there results the material expansion, which is sometimes called saguna Brahman and which consists of these twenty-five elements. In the nirguna Brahman, where there is no material contamination, or in the spiritual world, the three modes—goodness, passion and ignorance—are not present. Where nirguna Brahman is found, simple unalloyed goodness prevails. Saguna Brahman is described by the Sankhya system of philosophy as consisting of twenty-five elements, including the time factor (past, present and future).”

The pradhana has received the Lord’s potent energy, which Bhag-avatam [3.26.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.19) terms viryah and Srila Prabhupada translates in that text as the Lord’s “semen (His internal potency).” Srila Jiva Gosvami defines this as the conditioned jivas (jivakhya cit-rupa sakti).

Now impregnated, the pradhana has become conscious, golden, and effulgent (hiranmayam), infused with “the sum total of the cosmic intelligence ...” It is now known as mahat-tattva (Bhag. [3.26.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.19)), and that which was unmanifest in pradhana begins to manifest. “Thus, after manifesting variegatedness, the effulgent mahat-tattva, which contains all the universes within itself, which is the root of all cosmic manifestations and which is not destroyed at the time of annihilation, swallows the darkness that covered the effulgence at the time of dissolution.” (Bhag. [3.26.20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.20))

Following Srila Sridhara Svami’s commentary, Srila Prabhupada describes the mahat-tattva in his purport to Bhagavatam [3.5.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/5.27): “The mahat-tattva is the total consciousness because a portion of it is represented in everyone as the intellect. The mahat-tattva is directly connected with the supreme consciousness of the Supreme Being, but still it appears as matter. The mahat-tattva, or shadow of pure consciousness, is the germinating place of all creation. It is pure goodness with the slight addition of the material mode of passion, and therefore activity is generated from this point.” Thus through His electrifying potencies (which also contain the jivas), the Lord impregnated and brought to life the pradhana, made it effulgent, caused it to be “cosmic intelligence,” and caused it now to be termed mahat-tattva, which Srila Prabhupada has equated in this purport with the “shadow of pure consciousness” and “the germinating place of all creation.”

In naming the elements manifesting in the mahat-tattva, text 21 first describes citta, consciousness (one of the four subtle senses), explaining that it is made primarily of sattva-guna and that it is consciousness that perceives and worships Lord Vasudeva. As this consciousness is meant to worship Vasudeva, it can also be called vasudeva. Its characteristics, prior even to the manifestation of false ego, are those of pure consciousness: “complete serenity, clarity, and freedom from distraction.” (Bhag. [3.26.22](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.22))

This consciousness, although pure, is nevertheless composed of material goodness, sattva-guna, the “shadow of pure consciousness.” Thus through it one can both perceive oneself as eternal soul and see Vasudeva, Krsna, existing everywhere through His energies. As Srila Prabhupada notes in his purport to text 22: “In pure consciousness one can perceive a slight reflection of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.”

The Bhagavatam ([3.27.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.12)) will later describe the perception of the Lord reflected in one’s own pure consciousness: “The presence of the Supreme Lord can be realized just as the sun is realized first as a reflection on water, and again as a second reflection on the wall of a room, although the sun itself is situated in the sky.” In this example, the sun is the Lord, the sun’s first reflection on water in a pot is the perception of the Lord in pure consciousness, and the reflection of the reflection—the sun’s reflection from the water pot reflected on the wall of a room—is gross matter. In his purport to this text, Srila Prabhupada explains: “The sun is situated in the sky, far, far away from the surface of the earth, but its reflection can be seen in a pot of water in the corner of a room. The room is dark, and the sun is far away in the sky, but the sun’s reflection on the water illuminates the darkness of the room. A pure devotee can realize the presence of the Supreme Personality of Godhead in everything by the reflection of His energy.” That realization on the clear water of purified consciousness is called Vasudeva, realization of the all-pervading Lord, a realization the Bhagavad-gita ([7.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/7.19)) calls vasudevah sarvam iti—the perception that the Supreme Lord is the cause of all causes and all that is.

Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 22: “As in clear, unagitated water, free from impurities, one can see everything clearly, so in pure consciousness, or Krsna consciousness, one can see things as they are. One can see the reflection of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and one can see his own existence as well. This state of consciousness is very pleasing, transparent and sober. In the beginning, consciousness is pure.”

In his commentary on text 21, Sridhara Svami states that text 21 refers to worship of the catur-vyuha, which is celebrated in the Vedic agamas. When that same substance is named as the source of the material elements it is called mahat; as personal self it is called citta, and as something to be worshiped it is called Vasudeva, whose presiding Deity is the ksetra-jna (Supersoul).

In his commentary on text 22, Sridhara Svami calls svacchatvam, clarity, a characteristic of pure citta: “Perfect transparency (svaccha-tvam) means the state of holding the reflection (or shadow) of Bhagavan.” Jiva Gosvami concurs: Consciousness can perceive a “portion or shadow” of the Lord. Both thus support Prabhupada’s statement about consciousness in material goodness: “In pure consciousness one can perceive a slight reflection of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. . . . One can see the reflection of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and one can see his own existence as well.”

Thus by pure consciousness, which allows one to see the “slight reflection” of the Lord in matter, one can gradually perceive Him still more fully as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Vasudeva: “When the mind is fixed upon the Supreme Personality of Godhead in His external feature made of the material modes of nature—the gross universal form—it is brought to the platform of pure goodness. In that transcendental position, one can understand the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Vasudeva, who in His subtler form is self-effulgent and beyond the modes of nature. О my lord, please describe vividly how that form, which covers the entire universe, is perceived.” (Bhag. [5.16.3](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-5/16.3))

**Summary Understanding of Mahat-tattva, Citta, Lord Vasudeva, Vasudeva Consciousness, and the Supersoul**

The mahat-tattva is the aggregate (samasta) of consciousness. Srila Prabhupada refers to this aggregate in his purport to Bhagavatam [3.5.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/5.27) as the “shadow of pure consciousness” and in his word-for-word translation of Bhagavatam [3.26.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.19) as “cosmic intelligence.” This same consciousness, when referring to an individual, “personal self,” is called citta. Sridhara Svami explains this in his commentary to Bhagavatam [3.26.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.21). This clear, sattva-guna consciousness, the basic consciousness of the conditioned soul, will later be vitiated with false ego and manifest in the living entities.

The Lord, whom that pure consciousness perceives, is known as Vasudeva and is the Lord as manifest in the material world “without the accompaniment of His internal energy” (Bhag. [3.26.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.21), purport), “the cause of all causes and all that is” (Bg. [7.19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/7.19)). That consciousness in which Vasudeva may be perceived may also be termed Vasudeva. Lord Vasudeva, as Prabhupada refers to Him in his purport to Bhagavatam [3.26.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.21), is the first expansion of the Supersoul, the worshipful Deity of those in Vasudeva consciousness. The Supersoul’s (ksetra-jna’s) existence neither rests on nor is fully perceived by material consciousness, even consciousness in sattva-guna. Rather, the Supersoul’s existence rests on and is perceived only by pure goodness, suddha-sattva. Fully pure consciousness that can perceive Krsna and His expansions is sometimes called vasudeva, vasudeva, vasudeva-sattva, or visuddha-sattva.

But the mahat-tattva contains far more than pure consciousness with the ability to perceive Vasudeva. Injected into the rnahat'tattva are the souls who have freely chosen to turn their backs on their identities, their position as Krsna’s servants. Forsaking their true identity, the living entities are impelled by their desires to take shelter of the illusory realm of matter. To survive there, however, they must first acquire a false identity. The essence of false ego is twofold: independence from Krsna and an enjoying spirit. Thus false ego develops immediately in the mahat-tattva, and then combines with the three already existing modes of material nature: goodness, passion, and ignorance. This combination of false ego and the three modes envelops the souls’ pure consciousness in ever-increasing coverings of darkness and also acts instrumentally to cause the remainder of the creation.

Srila Prabhupada explains why false ego can arise from pure consciousness in his purport to texts 23-24: “From the status of pure consciousness, the false ego is bom because of misuse of independence. We cannot argue about why false ego arises from pure consciousness. Factually, there is always the chance that this will happen, and therefore one has to be very careful. False ego is the basic principle for all material activities, which are executed in the modes of material nature. As soon as one deviates from pure Krsna consciousness, he increases his entanglement in material reaction. The entanglement of materialism is the material mind, and from this material mind, the senses and material organs become manifest.”

## Texts 26-49: The Creation Continues, Based on the Combination of the False Ego and the Material Modes of Nature

The mind, its transformations, and the demigods evolve from false ego influenced by the mode of goodness; both intelligence and the active and knowledge-acquiring senses manifest from false ego influenced by passion; and sound, the subtle element ether, and the sense capable of perceiving sound are produced from false ego influenced by ignorance. From ether, the next transformation formed under the impulse of time, comes air, the sensation of touch, and the organ by which touch is perceived. By the interaction of air and touch, form is generated along with fire and the eye, the organ that perceives form. By the interaction of fire with the visual sensation, taste evolves. From taste, water is produced as well as the tongue, which perceives taste. When water interacts with taste, odor evolves, followed by the earth and the olfactory sense.

Srila Prabhupada describes the significance of sound—both material and spiritual—in his purport to text 32: “It is stated also in the Vedanta-sutra that sound is the origin of all objects of material possession and that by sound one can also dissolve this material existence. Anavrttih sabdat means ‘liberation by sound.’ The entire material manifestation began from sound, and sound can also end material entanglement, if it has a particular potency. The particular sound capable of doing this is the transcendental vibration Hare Krsna. Our entanglement in material affairs has begun from material sound. Now we must purify that sound in spiritual understanding. There is sound in the spiritual world also. If we approach that sound, then our spiritual life begins, and the other requirements for spiritual advancement can be supplied.”

In a lecture given on January 10, 1968 in Los Angeles, Prabhupada compared sounds in this world to the sound produced by a gramophone: “Real sound is coming from the spiritual world. It is simply just like gramophone. The sound is coming originally from the person; the gramophone is reproducing. . . . Similarly, whatever sound is there in this material world, the original sound is produced by God.”

## Texts 50-72: The Lord Enters the Universe and Manifests His Universal Form

These newly created elements exist but remain separate in the mahat-tattva. The Lord Himself, the origin of the creation process, then expands and enters each universe as Garbhodakasayi Visnu, time, karma, the total material energy, and the three modes of material nature. Thus the universe, which was previously floating as a seed on the Garbhodaka Ocean, begins to form.

Expanding again as Ksirodakasayi Visnu, the Lord enters each living entity and each atom. Then again the Lord expands and enters further into each universe as the virat-purusa, the universal form, whose body is the fourteen planetary systems.

Many of Srila Prabhupada’s purports in Canto Two describe the virat-purusa or virat-rupa as imaginary, yet in this chapter he describes it as an incarnation of the Lord (Bhag. [3.26.52](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.52), purport). The Lord’s relationship with the universal form is similar to the soul’s relationship with his subtle body, with Garbhodakasayi Visnu being the soul, the life-giving force of each material universe, and the virat-rupa being the universal subtle body.

The demigods one after another follow the sense organs that they control and accept their respective places in the universal form. In the wake of the olfactory sense came the wind-god. A pair of eyes appeared along with the sense of sight, and the sun-god followed. Next appeared the ears, the auditory sense, and the ears’ predominating deities, who preside over the directions. The universal form’s skin, genitals, semen (faculty of procreation), anus, two hands, legs, veins, abdomen, and feelings of hunger and thirst, each followed by their respective demigods, appeared. “Then a heart became manifest, and in the wake of the heart the mind appeared. After the mind, the moon appeared. Intelligence appeared next, and after intelligence, Lord Brahma appeared. Then the false ego appeared and then Lord Siva, and after the appearance of Lord Siva came consciousness and the deity presiding over consciousness.” (Bhag. [3.26.60-61](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.60))

It is interesting to note that these appearances in the universal form are of the four subtle senses: consciousness (citta), mind (manah), intelligence (buddhi), and false ego (ahankara). Again, each is followed by its predominating deity, a demigod. The appearance here of consciousness, citta, refers specifically to the consciousness that will be apportioned to individual living beings. This consciousness, different from the consciousness that appeared as the first manifestation of the mahat-tattva and through which Vasudeva could be perceived, was not pure. This citta, already infected with false ego, possessed a spirit for self-centered enjoyment.

Srila Prabhupada describes this particular manifestation of consciousness, affected by ignorance and false ego, in his purport to text 61. There, he also describes the appearance of the three other subtle senses in the universal form:

**The moon appeared after the appearance of mind, and this indicates that the moon is the presiding deity of mind. Similarly, Lord Brahma, appearing after intelligence, is the presiding deity of intelligence, and Lord Siva, who appears after false ego, is the presiding deity of false ego. In other words, it is indicated that the moon-god is in the mode of goodness, whereas Lord Brahma is in the mode of passion and Lord Siva is in the mode of ignorance. The appearance of consciousness after the appearance of false ego indicates that, from the beginning, material consciousness is under the mode of ignorance and that one therefore has to purify himself by purifying his consciousness. This purificatory process is called Krsna consciousness. As soon as the consciousness is purified, the false ego disappears. Identification of the body with the self is called false identification, or false ego. Lord Caitanya confirms this in His Siksastaka. He states that the first result of chanting the maha-mantra, Hare Krsna, is that dirt is cleared from the consciousness, or the mirror of the mind, and then at once the blazing fire of material existence is over. The blazing fire of material existence is due to false ego, but as soon as the false ego is removed, one can understand his real identity. At that point he is actually liberated from the clutches of maya. As soon as one is freed from the clutches of false ego, his intelligence also becomes purified, and then his mind is always engaged upon the lotus feet of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.**

The manifested demigods then tried to awaken that great being to consciousness. The fire-god, sun-god, death-god, Indra, the ocean, moon, and Brahma each made an attempt. Rudra entered with ego, yet the cosmic being did not stir. Finally, the caitya-guru (Supersoul), “the deity presiding over consciousness,” entered the heart of the universal form and the gigantic being immediately arose from the causal waters. “When a man is sleeping, all his material assets—namely the vital energy, the senses for recording knowledge, the senses for working, the mind and the intelligence—cannot arouse him. He can be aroused only when the Supersoul helps him.” (Bhag. [3.26.71](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/26.71))

By describing the universal form’s awakening, Kapila Muni also indicates the essential teachings of Sankhya-yoga: Neither matter nor the intricate functions of the body cause consciousness. Rather, consciousness, including Krsna consciousness, can be aroused only with the help of the Supersoul. To make firm contact with the Supersoul is one of the main purposes of the Sankhya-yoga system. Kapila Muni concludes: “Therefore, through devotion, detachment and advancement in spiritual knowledge acquired through concentrated devotional service, one should contemplate that Supersoul as present in this very body although simultaneously apart from it.” (Bhag. [3.26.72](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/26.72))

Prabhupada’s purport to text 72 explains that we must be materially detached if we are to advance in Sankhya-yoga: “As long as the mind is distracted towards the material, there is no possibility of concentrating one’s mind and intelligence upon the Supreme Personality of Godhead or His partial representation, Supersoul. In other words, one cannot concentrate one’s mind and energy upon the Supreme unless one is detached from the material world. Following detachment from the material world, one can actually attain transcendental knowledge of the Absolute Truth. As long as one is entangled in sense enjoyment, or material enjoyment, it is not possible to understand the Absolute Truth.”

## Chapter 27 - Understanding Material Nature

## Texts 1-9: Practices to Attain Liberation

Having recommended freeing oneself from material nature by practicing devotional service, detachment, gathering transcendental knowledge, and contemplating the Supersoul, Kapila Muni now summarizes the cause of a soul’s entrapment in the cycle of transmigration: Under the spell of illusion caused by false ego, a soul considers his body himself and acts as if he were the world’s proprietor and enjoyer. His illusioned actions fail to award him the pleasure he desires; instead they entangle him in the three modes of nature. Thus he is repeatedly forced to take birth and die. The cause of his suffering is his body, his identification with matter, and the subsequent desires and choices he makes as he attempts to act as the lord of material nature.

Kapila Muni next describes the Sankhya process for attaining freedom: “It is the duty of every conditioned soul to engage his polluted consciousness, which is now attached to material enjoyment, in very serious devotional service with detachment. Thus his mind and consciousness will be under full control.” (Bhag. [3.27.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.5)) Srila Prabhupada describes that the essence of Sankhya is bhakti-yoga: “It is therefore recommended in this verse that one engage very seriously in the devotional service of the Lord. This means that one should not think that he is the proprietor, benefactor, friend or enjoyer. He should always be cognizant that the real enjoyer is Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead; that is the basic principle of bhakti-yoga. One must be firmly convinced of these three principles: one should always think that Krsna is the proprietor, Krsna is the enjoyer and Krsna is the friend. Not only should he understand these principles himself, but he should try to convince others and propagate Krsna consciousness.” (Bhag. [3.27.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.5), purport)

How can we purify our mind so that we can accomplish this order? Kapila Muni states: “One has to become faithful by practicing the controlling process of the yoga system and must elevate himself to the platform of unalloyed devotional service by chanting and hearing about Me.” (Bhag. [3.27.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.6)) Srila Prabhupada further explains the process of purifying the mind in his purports to texts 5 and 6: “Because we have been associated with material nature since time immemorial, we have become accustomed to our attachment to this temporary material nature. The mind has to be fixed at the eternal lotus feet of the Supreme Lord. Sa vai manah krsna-padaravindayoh. One has to fix the mind at the lotus feet of Krsna; then everything will be very nice.” (Bhag. [3.27.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.5), purport)

“One should be absorbed in the thought of love of Krsna. When one knows that Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, is the source of everything and that everything emanates from Him (aham sarvasya prabhavah) . . . then he can be absorbed in bhava, or the preliminary stage of love of Godhead.” (Bhag. [3.27.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.6), purport)

Kapila Muni offers further instructions to guide yoga practitioners according to the preliminary rules and regulations of yoga (yama and niyama): “In executing devotional service, one has to see every living entity equally, without enmity towards anyone yet without intimate connections with anyone. One has to observe celibacy, be grave and execute his eternal activities, offering the results to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. For his income a devotee should be satisfied with what he earns without great difficulty. He should not eat more than what is necessary. He should live in a secluded place and always be thoughtful, peaceful, friendly, compassionate and self-realized.” (Bhag. [3.27.7-8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.7)) A yogi should also differentiate between matter and spirit and neither identify himself with the body nor become attracted by bodily relationships.

Patanjali’s Yoga-sutras define the standard yamas and niyamas as follows: “Nonviolence, truthfulness, abstention from stealing, continence, and absence of greed from possessions beyond one’s need are the five pillars of yama. Yamas are the great, mighty, universal vows, unconditioned by place, time, and class. Cleanliness, contentment, religious zeal, self-study, and surrender of the self to the Supreme Self are the niyamas. Principles which run contrary to yama and niyama are to be countered with knowledge and discrimination.” (YS. 2.3O-33)

Following these preliminary rules and regulations of Sankhya-yoga further purifies the practitioner, helping him develop detachment bom of the mode of goodness. Once purified, he can advance toward transcendence by meditating on the Supersoul, a process that will be described in Chapter Twenty-eight.

In texts 6-9 Kapila Muni has described the preliminary practices that can carry us to the door of liberation through Sankhya-yoga. In his purports to these texts, Srila Prabhupada demonstrates how the basic sadhana practices of bhakti award the effects desired from the Sankhya practices. For example, text 8 prescribes that Sankhya yogis “live in a secluded place.” Srila Prabhupada explains the same principle as a bhakti-yogi would apply it: “The next item recommended is that a devotee should live in a secluded place. Generally a common man is interested in pounds, shillings and pence, or materialistic advancement in life, which is unnecessary for a devotee. A devotee should select a place of residence where everyone is interested in devotional service. Generally, therefore, a devotee goes to a sacred place of pilgrimage where devotees live. It is recommended that he live in a place where there is no large number of ordinary men. It is very important to live in a secluded place (vivikta-sarana) ”18 (Bhag. [3.27.8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.8), purport)

## Texts 10-16: The Awareness of a Liberated Soul

By practicing Sankhya-yoga, one should step through the door of liberation and enter transcendence, one’s awareness fixed beyond material consciousness. Thus situated beyond illusion, the pure souls, free from false ego, will accurately perceive themselves as eternal. They will also see the Absolute Truth, the Personality of Godhead, everywhere and in everything. Srila Prabhupada explains this vision in his purport to text 11: “A pure devotee can see the presence of the Supreme Personality of Godhead in everything materially manifested. He is present there only as a reflection, but a pure devotee can realize that in the darkness of material illusion the only light is the Supreme Lord, who is its support.”

Now Kapila Muni will offer an example: The Lord can be experienced everywhere, even in matter, just as the “sun is realized first as a reflection on water, and again as a second reflection on the wall of a room, although the sun itself is situated in the sky. The self-realized soul is thus reflected first in the threefold ego and then in the body, senses and mind.” (Bhag. [3.27.12-13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.12)) Srila Prabhupada considers text 13 more or less an elucidation of text 12: “By the understanding of the pure soul, called satya'drk, one can see everything as a reflection of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. A concrete example can be given in this connection. A conditioned soul sees a very beautiful rose, and he thinks that the nice aromatic flower should be used for his own sense gratification. This is one kind of vision. A liberated soul, however, sees the same flower as a reflection of the Supreme Lord. He thinks, ‘This beautiful flower is made possible by the superior energy of the Supreme Lord; therefore it belongs to the Supreme Lord and should be utilized in His service.’ These are two kinds of vision. The conditioned soul sees the flower for his own enjoyment, and the devotee sees the flower as an object to be used in the service of the Lord. In the same way, one can see the reflection of the Supreme Lord in one’s own senses, mind and body—in everything. With that correct vision, one can engage everything in the service of the Lord.” (Bhag. [3.27.13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.13), purport) Everything is seen as His energy: Krsna reflected in matter.

Kapila Muni now moves from a pure soul’s realization of the ultimate nature of the universe to his relationship with the material body: “Although a devotee appears to be merged in the five material elements, the objects of material enjoyment, the material senses and material mind and intelligence, he is understood to be awake and to be freed from the false ego.” (Bhag. [3.27.14](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.14)) Although superficially appearing merged in matter, a pure soul is actually free from false material identification and therefore awake to his actual eternal and individual identity.

Kapila Muni then returns to describing the soul conditioned by ignorance: The conditioned soul is quite different from the self-realized soul. A conditioned soul is, for all practical purposes, merged in matter, because he identifies with his body. In ignorance, such a conditioned soul may at times even vividly perceive his existence as a seer separate from what he sees. Nevertheless he loses that experience when he enters sleep, either dream-filled sleep (in which his physical identity is forgotten and he accepts a dream-identity) or deep sleep (when he experiences a complete sense of having lost himself). Both states indicate the illusory sense of loss he feels when he loses a dear possession, such as his money. Whether awake but illusioned, or dreaming, what has he, the soul, actually lost? The cause of his experience of loss is only his false ego. That is, he is identifying so strongly with his body, mind, and their extensions that when something he is attached to is no longer found in his possession, he feels that his life is meaningless, as if he himself has been lost. Clearly, both his sense of loss and his sense of himself being lost are illusory.

In his purport to text 15, Srila Prabhupada writes of the temporary sense of loss of individuality one may experience in deep sleep: “A living entity can never be lost. When one forgets his identity in deep sleep, he becomes absorbed in dreams, and he may think himself a different person or may think himself lost. But actually his identity is intact.”

Thus Srila Prabhupada has compared a person’s waking life to his Krsna consciousness; his dream lives, one after another, to his succession of illusory identities caused by bodily identification; and his experience of deep dreamless sleep, in which he loses his awareness of his individual identity, to merging with the Lord’s impersonal effulgence. Is it wise to advise a sleeper who is experiencing an endless series of horrible dreams to fall deeper asleep into a dreamless state? It’s better he wake up.

Indeed, despite his dream-identities or even his deep sleep experience of selflessness, he regains his actual identity on awakening. Srila Prabhupada completes the point in this purport: “This concept of being lost is due to false ego, and it continues as long as one is not awakened to the sense of his existence as an eternal servitor of the Lord.”

Kapila Muni further describes the pure soul’s liberated consciousness: “When, by mature understanding, one can realize his individuality, then the situation he accepts under false ego becomes manifest to him.” (Bhag. [3.27.16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.16)) Earlier in the Bhagavatam ([2.10.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/10.6)), Sukadeva Gosvami defined liberation as again becoming situated in our natural position—muktir hitvanyathd гйрат sva-rupena vyavasthitih: “Liberation is the permanent situation of the form of the living entity after he gives up the changeable gross and subtle material bodies.” In his purport to Bhagavatam [3.27.16](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.16), Srila Prabhupada explains that when the living entity is purified of false ego, he “takes everything in the right perspective. That is the state of liberation.” Later in the same purport he explains that a living entity’s “mature understanding” is that Krsna, not he himself, is meant to enjoy. As soon as the false ego is eliminated—the false thinking that “I am the enjoyer, the Lord” —one becomes liberated. Being fixed in one’s natural position as Krsna’s servant, one’s real constitutional position, “is called mukti, or liberation.”

## Texts 17-20: Devahuti Questions Kapila Further

Devahuti has heard her son’s description of both creation and Sankhya-yoga. She has noted that the intertwining of the soul with matter occurred at the beginning of material existence—when Maha-Visnu glanced at the pradhana. Considering the soul’s entanglement more or less ever-existent, she wonders whether or not the eternal spirit soul, whose only experience of himself is as body and mind, can truly gain release from material nature: “My dear brahmana, does material nature ever give release to the spirit soul? Since one is attracted to the other eternally, how is their separation possible? . . . even though he is the passive performer of all activities, how can there be freedom for the soul as long as material nature acts on him and binds him?” (Bhag. [3.27.17](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.17), [19](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.19)) Even if fear of material bondage is removed by mental speculation and inquiry into the fundamental principles of material existence, does illusion again appear?

In his purport to text 17, Srila Prabhupada states that Devahuti’s question is almost voidistic. Devahuti has noted the interdependence of matter and spirit, body and soul, and views their relationship to be like earth and its aroma or water and its taste: One ceases to exist without the other. She therefore wonders whether anything would remain if matter were removed from consciousness. In addition, Devahuti asks how a living entity, who is passive and under the control of the three modes, can attain freedom from the material energy. Also, because Kapila Muni has just described the fundamental principles of material existence, Devahuti asks how a living entity can extract himself from the material nature by using his intelligence, which is a product of the material nature.

She wants to know whether a living entity who has escaped the shackles of material nature by reflecting on matter’s fundamental principles can remain free without having removed the cause of his bondage. After all, his reflections on the categories of material nature have neither named nor caused that bondage. Even if he appears free for some time, will the root cause reappear and force him back into bondage?

Srila Prabhupada describes the original cause of a soul’s entrapment: “When one becomes envious of Krsna, or the Supreme Personality of Godhead, one thinks, ‘Why should Krsna be the all and all? I’m as good as Krsna.’ These two items, desire to be the Lord and envy of the Lord, are the beginning cause of material bondage.” (Bhag. [3.27.20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.20), purport) Devahuti’s questions are therefore both thoughtful and apt.

## Texts 21-30: Kapila Muni’s Replies—Fear and False Ego Can Be Engaged in Devotional Service

Kapila Muni responds to Devahuti’s first question in text 21: “One can get liberation by seriously discharging devotional service unto Me and thereby hearing for a long time about Me or from Me. By thus executing one’s prescribed duties, there will be no reaction, and one will be freed from the contamination of matter.” Srila Prabhupada explains in detail the process by which we can remain free from material contamination even while living in the material world:

**Sridhara Svami comments in this connection that by association with material nature alone one does not become conditioned. Conditional life begins only after one is infected by the modes of material nature. If someone is in contact with the police department, that does not mean that he is a criminal. As long as one does not commit criminal acts, even though there is a police department, he is not punished. Similarly, the liberated soul is not affected, although he is in the material nature.... One has to act in such a way that in spite of being in the material nature he is not affected by contamination. Although the lotus flower is in association with water, it does not mix with the water. That is how one has to live. (Bhag.** [**3.27.21**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.21)**, purport)**

If one understands oneself to be the servant of Krsna and lives without false ego—without envy of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, or without the independent desire to act as if one were the lord of material existence—one can remain untroubled by matter, as an honest man remains untroubled by the police. That is, a liberated devotee remains free of matter because he has no false ego, even if he appears to be living in the material world like everyone else. Those aspiring for liberation should think about whether their actions will please Krsna; they should act only for Krsna’s pleasure. This is how one places Krsna in the center of one’s consciousness and removes the illusion of independence that entangles one in the material world. Srila Prabhupada continues:

**If one wants to perfect his life, he should discharge his prescribed duties for the satisfaction of Krsna. One must act in Krsna consciousness, for such action will not produce any reaction (animitta-nimittena). This is also confirmed in Bhagavad-gita. Yajnarthat kar-mano ’nyatra: all activities should be performed simply for Yajna, or the satisfaction of Visnu. Anything done otherwise, without the satisfaction of Visnu, or Yajna, produces bondage, so here it is also prescribed by Kapila Muni that one can transcend material entanglement by acting in Krsna consciousness, which means seriously engaging in devotional service. This serious devotional service can develop by hearing for long periods of time. Chanting and hearing is the beginning of the process of devotional service. One should associate with devotees and hear from them about the Lord’s transcendental appearance, activities, disappearance, instructions, etc. (Bhag.** [**3.27.21**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.21)**, purport)**

Kapila Muni tells Devahuti to perform devotional service “strongly in perfect knowledge and with transcendental vision.” She must also be renounced and prepared to practice austerity. By performing mystic yoga, she can “be firmly fixed in self-absorption.” (Bhag. [3.27.22](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.22)) In this way, Devahuti will be able to free herself from her conditioning, which bums like fire. “By the process of seriously discharging devotional service, this influence can be removed, just as wooden sticks which cause a fire are themselves consumed by it. By discovering the faultiness of his desiring to lord it over material nature and by therefore giving it up, the living entity becomes independent and stands in his own glory.” (Bhag. [3.27.23-24](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.23))

Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to text 23 that the enjoying spirit caused by false ego manifests in two ways: one wishes either to exploit matter or to merge into the Lord’s impersonal effulgence. Both of these contaminations can be “consumed by the careful discharge of devotional service in Krsna consciousness.”

Srila Prabhupada next discusses how this instruction may be applied in a practical way: “A devotee in full Krsna consciousness appears superficially to be a great karmi, always working, but the inner significance of the devotee’s activities is that they are meant for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord. This is called bhakti, or devotional service. Arjuna was apparently a fighter, but when by his fighting he satisfied the senses of Lord Krsna, he became a devotee. Since a devotee also engages in philosophical research to understand the Supreme Person as He is, his activities may thus appear to be like those of a mental speculator, but actually he is trying to understand the spiritual nature and transcendental activities. Thus although the tendency for philosophical speculation exists, the material effects of fruitive activities and empiric speculation do not, because this activity is meant for the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” (Bhag. [3.27.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.23), purport)

Thus through serious devotional practice, one frees oneself from false ego, the root of material existence, and steps into one’s true glory as Krsna’s eternal servant. In his purport to text 24 Srila Prabhupada notes: “To be the servant of the Lord is the greatest position. If one can understand this and can thus revive one’s original nature of eternal servitorship of the Lord, one stands fully independent.” Such a pure soul remains undisturbed even in the tumultuous material world.

A person’s perception of reality is colored by his own level of consciousness. It is therefore difficult to describe a liberated soul’s activities, for each person will interpret the description according to the limitations of his own consciousness. In text 25, Kapila Muni offers an example to help us understand how liberated souls interact with matter: “In the dreaming state one’s consciousness is almost covered, and one sees many inauspicious things, but when he is awakened and fully conscious, such inauspicious things cannot bewilder him.” Srila Prabhupada completes the analogy by contrasting contaminated, “sleeping” consciousness with pure consciousness: “In contaminated consciousness one sees everything to be for his own enjoyment, but in pure consciousness, or Krsna consciousness, he sees that everything exists for the enjoyment of the supreme enjoyer. That is the difference between the dream state and wakefulness. The state of contaminated consciousness is compared to dream consciousness, and Krsna consciousness is compared to the awakened stage of life.” (Bhag. [3.27.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.25), purport)

Kapila Muni then repeats an important point: Material nature cannot harm an enlightened soul, even if that pure soul appears to be engaged in material activities, because the mind of such a soul is fixed only on the Supreme Lord: “When a person thus engages in devotional service and self-realization for many, many years and births, he becomes completely reluctant to enjoy any one of the material planets, even up to the highest planet, which is known as Brahmaloka; he becomes fully developed in consciousness.” (Bhag. [3.27.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.27)) Possessing neither false ego nor material consciousness, reluctant to take part in material enjoyment on any planet, a pure soul expects neither relief from material miseries nor material gain. What is his interest? Prabhupada explains that a pure devotee’s only interest is to express his love for the Supreme Personality of Godhead. He wants only to satisfy Him. “The highest example of pure devotional service is that of the gopis in Vrndavana. They are not interested in understanding Krsna, but only in loving Him. That platform of love is the pure state of devotional service. Unless one is advanced to this pure state of devotional service, there is a tendency to desire elevation to a higher material position.” (Bhag. [3.27.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.27), purport)

“My devotee actually becomes self-realized,” Kapila Muni explains, “by My unlimited causeless mercy, and thus, when freed from all doubts, he steadily progresses towards his destined abode, which is directly under the protection of My spiritual energy of unadulterated bliss. That is the ultimate perfectional goal of the living entity. After giving up the present material body, the mystic devotee goes to that transcendental abode and never comes back.” (Bhag. [3.27.28-29](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/27.28)) Progress toward the spiritual world under the protection of the spiritual energy is mat'prasadena, by the Lord’s special grace. In his purport to texts 28-29 Prabhupada explains how to attract the Lord’s causeless mercy: “Devotional service is revealed to the pure devotee by the unlimited causeless mercy of the Lord. . . . This is also confirmed in Bhagavad-gita. Only those who engage in devotional service with love and faith receive the necessary intelligence from the Supreme Personality of Godhead so that gradually and progressively they can advance to the abode of the Personality of Godhead.”

Kapila Muni concludes this set of instructions by glorifying the perfect yogi: The progress of a perfect yogi, a bhakti-yogi, who is attracted by neither the material world nor mystic powers, is unlimited. He cannot be overcome by death. Srila Prabhupada explains: “A devotee’s attention is concentrated only upon the eternal loving service of the Lord, and therefore the power of death has no influence over him. In such a devotional state, a perfect yogi can attain the status of immortal knowledge and bliss.”

## Chapter 28 - Kapila’s Instructions on the Execution of Devotional Service

## Texts 1-12: Astanga-Yoga—Preliminary Yogic Practices for Attaining Devotional Service

To practice uninterrupted, pure devotional service without hindrance, focusing one’s consciousness on the Supreme Personality of Godhead as Kapila Muni recommends, one must bring the mind fully under control. Kapila Muni therefore next describes how to practice astdnga-yoga, “the object of which is to concentrate the mind.” (Bhag. [3.28.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.1)) When one practices mental control, one should do so with the desire to focus the mind fully on Krsna.

Among his first yoga-sutras, Patanjali has presented citta-vrtti niro-dha and isvara pranidahnat va. That is, that the purpose of yoga is “the cessation of movements in the consciousness” (YS [1.2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/ysop/1.2)), and that “One’s consciousness may be controlled through profound meditation on the Supreme Lord and total surrender to Him.” (YS [1.23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/ysop/1.23)) Thus in Bhagavatam [3.28.1-7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.1), Kapila Muni describes the yoga practices that allow us to achieve the goal of yoga: separating the soul from matter and dependence on the Supersoul.

Texts 2-4 describe the yamas (injunctions) and niyamas (prohibitions), the first two steps on the eightfold path. The next six steps are asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, and samadhi.

While practicing the first two steps on this path (yama and niyama), Kapila Muni explains, one needs to observe celibacy and silence, and to attain mental steadiness, practice the various asanas (sitting postures). After mastering the asanas and practicing pranayama and pratyahara (withdrawing the mind from sense objects), one can fix one’s mind on the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

Practicing yama and niyama will uplift one to the mode of goodness. One can then practice asanas. Mastery of each asana is called jaya. When performing the mastered asana, the yogi will have to become fully conscious of every part of his body, having banished unconsciousness—ignorance—from that asana. Thus body and mind are harmonized in that specific posture. This creates steadiness.

After mastering each of the many asanas, the yogi can then begin the breathing exercises known as pranayama. These exercises move prana, the life energy, through the six cakras or “energy stations.” Wherever the yogi encounters tamas or rajas, he moves prana to that place, shifting his consciousness. Gradually, the yogi’s body and mind become purified and peaceful. At that point, he can begin pratyahara, withdrawing the mind from the sense objects. Pratyahara is a precursor to increased concentration on the Lord. Dharana (concentration), intensifies to the stage of dhyana (meditation). When meditation is completely fixed on Krsna, the yogi attains samadhi.

The yogi who has focused his mind on Krsna has achieved the goal of yoga, as Krsna Himself confirms in Bhagavad-gita ([6.47](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/6.47)): “And of all yogis, the one with great faith who always abides in Me, thinks of Me within himself, and renders transcendental loving service to Me— he is the most intimately united with Me in yoga and is the highest of all. That is My opinion.”Prabhupada repeats Kapila Muni’s criticism of those who think that the goal of yoga is to focus the mind on the impersonal or void: “It is never mentioned that one should concentrate on the impersonal or void. It is clearly stated, vaikuntha-lila. Lila means ‘pastimes.’ Unless the Absolute Truth, the Personality of Godhead, has transcendental activities, where is the scope for thinking of these pastimes? It is through the processes of devotional service, chanting and hearing of the pastimes of the Supreme Personality of Godhead, that one can achieve this concentration. As described in the Srimad-Bhagavatam, the Lord appears and disappears according to His relationships with different devotees.” (Bhag. [3.28.6](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.6), purport) He offers further parallels between the two yogas, astanga and bhakti, in his purports to texts 9-11:

**Practicing the yoga system of exercise and breath control is very difficult for a person in this age, and therefore Lord Caitanya recommended, kirtaniyah soda harih: one should always chant the holy name of the Supreme Lord, Krsna, because Krsna is the most suitable name of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. The name Krsna and the Supreme Person Krsna are nondifferent. Therefore, if one concentrates his mind on hearing and chanting Hare Krsna, the same result is achieved. (Bhag.** [**3.28.9**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.9)**, purport)**

**This process of purifying the mind is also recommended by Lord Caitanya; He says that one should chant Hare Krsna. He says further, param vijayate: “All glories to Sri Krsna sanklrtana!” All glories are given to the chanting of the holy names of Krsna because as soon as one begins this process of chanting, the mind becomes purified. Ceto-darpana-marjanam: by chanting the holy name of Krsna one is cleansed of the dirt that accumulates in the mind. One can purify the mind either by the breathing process or by the chanting process, just as one can purify gold by putting it in a fire and fanning it with a bellows. (Bhag.** [**3.28.10**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.10)**, purport)**

**For every item in the yoga system there is a parallel activity in bhakti-yoga, but the practice of bhakti-yoga is easier for this age. What was introduced by Lord Caitanya is not a new interpretation. Bhakti-yoga is a feasible process that begins with chanting and hearing. Bhakti-yoga and other yogas have as their ultimate goal the same Personality of Godhead, but one is practical, and the others are difficult. One has to purify his physiological condition by concentration and by restraint of the senses; then he can fix his mind upon the Supreme Personality of Godhead. That is called samadhi. (Bhag.** [**3.28.11**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.11)**, purport)**

Lord Kapila continues: “When the mind is perfectly purified by this practice of yoga, one should concentrate on the tip of the nose with half-closed eyes and see the form of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” (Bhag. [3.28.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.12))

## Texts 13-19: The Vision of the Perfected Yogi

The Supreme Personality of Godhead is not impersonal. Lord Kapila describes the Lord on whom the yogi meditates as follows: One who has perfected his yoga can see -with concentrated attention the beautiful Lord, who has a swarthy body resembling the petals of a blue lotus. That Lord carries a conch, disc, and mace and is marked with srivatsa, a curl of white hair on His breast. He wears the brilliant kaustubha gem suspended from His neck. His cloth shines saffronyellow like the effulgent pollen of a lotus, and a fragrant garland and pearl necklace further adorn His body. Devotees always see their Lord, whose inclination is to offer benedictions to all those engaged in His service.

Srila Prabhupada’s purports in this section accomplish three purposes: they denigrate impersonalism, direct the devotees to the Lord’s deity form, and describe the Lord’s beauty. In his purport to text 19, Srila Prabhupada refers to chanting and hearing about Krsna as meditation: “The process of meditating on the form of the Supreme Personality of Godhead within oneself and the process of chanting the glories and pastimes of the Lord are the same. The only difference is that hearing and fixing the mind on the pastimes of the Lord is easier than visualizing the form of the Lord within one’s heart because as soon as one begins to think of the Lord, especially in this age, the mind becomes disturbed, and due to so much agitation, the process of seeing the Lord within the mind is interrupted. When there is sound vibrated praising the transcendental pastimes of the Lord, however, one is forced to hear. ... In this age of Kali-yuga, Lord Caitanya has recommended that one should always engage in chanting and hearing Bhagavad-gita. The Lord also says that the mahatmas, or great souls, always engage in the process of chanting the glories of the Lord, and just by hearing, others derive the same benefit.”

## Texts 20-33: Meditating on the Lord

Kapila Muni continues: “In fixing his mind on the eternal form of the Lord, the yogi should not take a collective view of all His limbs, but should fix the mind on each individual limb of the Lord.” (Bhag. [3.28.20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.20)) One should begin his meditation on the Lord’s form by seeing His feet and gradually looking upward in meditation, limb by limb, until he reaches the Lord’s face. This method combats the tendency for impersonalism and ensures that one’s meditation on the Lord is based on a proper understanding of His position—that He is the all-powerful Supreme Lord. Kapila thus advises yogis to “meditate on the lotus feet of the Lord for a long time.” (Bhag. [3.28.22](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.22))

Srila Prabhupada notes in his purport to text 16 that “the Lord is so beautiful that the devotee-yogi does not wish to see anything else. His desire to see beautiful objects is completely satisfied by the sight of the Lord.”

Srila Prabhupada later describes the importance of meditating on the Lord’s lotus feet:

**Another significant point of this verse is that the mind of the conditioned soul, on account of its association with the material energy from time immemorial, contains heaps of dirt in the form of desires to lord it over material nature. This dirt is like a mountain, but a mountain can be shattered when hit, by a thunderbolt. Meditating on the lotus feet of the Lord acts like a thunderbolt on the mountain of dirt in the mind of the yogi. If a yogi wants to shatter the mountain of dirt in his mind, he should concentrate on the lotus feet of the Lord and not imagine something void or impersonal. Because the dirt has accumulated like a solid mountain, one must meditate on the lotus feet of the Lord for quite a long time. For one who is accustomed to thinking of the lotus feet of the Lord constantly, however, it is a different matter. The devotees are so fixed on the lotus feet of the Lord that they do not think of anything else. (Bhag.** [**3.28.22**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.22)**, purport)**

Later, Srila Prabhupada states: “Yogis take advantage of the process of smaranam, whereas bhakti-yogis take special advantage of the process of hearing and chanting.” (Bhag. [3.28.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.26), purport)

Kapila continues: Step by step, the devotee meditates on the Lord’s feet, on Laksmidevi, who serves the Lord’s legs and thighs, and on the Lord’s moonlike navel, the nipples on His chest, His forearms, and His club, disc, conch, and lotus. The devotee also meditates on the Lord’s lotuslike face with its prominent nose, crystal-clear cheeks, glittering earrings, and curling hair. The devotee sees the Lord’s lotus eyes, dancing eyebrows, and compassionate glance, which “frequently cast by the Lord’s eyes . . . soothe the most fearful agonies of His devotees.” (Bhag. [3.28.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.31)) Those glances, accompanied by loving smiles, are full of abundant grace. A devotee should also meditate on the Lord’s charmingly arched eyebrows.

“Agonies and anxieties” can be mitigated, Srila Prabhupada assures us in his purport to text 31: “As long as one is in conditional life, in the material body, it is natural that he will suffer from anxieties and agonies. One cannot avoid the influence of material energy, even when one is on the transcendental plane. Sometimes disturbances come, but the agonies and anxieties of the devotees are at once mitigated when they think of the Supreme Personality of Godhead in His beautiful form or the smiling face of the Lord. The Lord bestows innumerable favors upon His devotee, and the greatest manifestation of His grace is His smiling face, which is full of compassion for His pure devotees.”

Srila Prabhupada repeats this instruction on how to remove misery in his purport to text 32: “The entire universe is full of miseries, and therefore the inhabitants of this material universe are always shedding tears out of intense grief. There is a great ocean of water made from such tears, but for one who surrenders unto the Supreme Personality of Godhead, the ocean of tears is at once dried up. One need only see the charming smile of the Supreme Lord. In other words, the bereavement of material existence immediately subsides when one sees the charming smile of the Lord.”

Kapila Muni continues: “With devotion steeped in love and affection, the yogi should meditate within the core of his heart upon the laughter of Lord Visnu. . . . When the Supreme Lord is laughing, one can see His small teeth, which resemble jasmine buds rendered rosy by the splendor of His lips. Once devoting his mind to this, the yogi should no longer desire to see anything else.” (Bhag. [3.28.33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/28.33))
