But the apparently substantial difference between the two options is actually insignificant because both are temporary. Is it worth working even to become the president of a country when we know that the term of office is nothing in relation to eternity? From the perspective of eternity (liberation), nothing in this world—whether good or bad—is significant. Thus Srimad-Bhagavatam ([3.11.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/11.38)) regards even the incalculable length of Brahma’s life as “equal to one nimesa \[less than a second\] for the Supreme Personality of Godhead, who is unchanging and unlimited and is the cause of all causes of the universe.”

Srila Prabhupada expands convincingly on these points in his purport to text 36. He stresses leaving the world of matter to attain the spiritual world: “We should try to get out of the material cosmic manifestation, go to the spiritual world and take shelter of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. That is our highest achievement. We should not be attracted by anything material, higher or lower, but should consider them all on the same level. Our real engagement should be in inquiring about the real purpose of life and rendering devotional service to the Lord. Thus we will be eternally blessed in our spiritual activities, full of knowledge and bliss.” He concludes the purport with a contrast: “At the present moment human civilization is too much attached to economic development and sense gratification and is therefore nearing the path of ruination.”

Sanat-kumara then told Maharaja Prthu that one should try to understand the Supersoul, Bhagavan, because it is He who lives in every being’s heart no matter what body that being inhabits. One should understand the Supersoul, the Lord in the heart, who is awaiting each soul’s turning toward Him. One should try to understand Him because without knowledge it will be difficult to foster surrender. Therefore, Sanat-kumara next described the Supersoul’s power and position: He is the cause and effect of everything, including everything in the body. He is one with everything, yet simultaneously different from it. One should know the Lord’s all-pervading, all-powerful position, and one should know that He “is eternally transcendental to the material creation and situated in pure internal energy. Thus the Lord is transcendental to all material contamination. Unto Him only must one surrender.” (Bhag. [4.22.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.38))

Everything rests on Him. He is nondifferent from everything in existence, yet purely transcendental, living in His own abode, Goloka Vrndavana, and engaging in the pastimes conducted by His eternal, non-changing, internal energy. It is to that Lord that we should surrender. Yet we become afraid in the face of Sanat-kumara’s strong request that we surrender. When we look at everything we stand to lose, ephemeral as it may be, we become afraid. But by the force of time and the destructive nature of the material energy, we are guaranteed to lose everything we possess.

Later in the Bhagavatam, Prahlada Maharaja’s instructions offer both solace and encouragement: “One who is sufficiently intelligent should use the human form of body from the very beginning of life—in other words, from the tender age of childhood—to practice the activities of devotional service, giving up all other engagements. The human body is most rarely achieved, and although temporary like other bodies, it is meaningful because in human life one can perform devotional service. Even a slight amount of sincere devotional service can give one complete perfection.” (Bhag. [7.6.1](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-7/6.1))

Commenting on text 37 of this chapter, Srila Sridhara Svami states that Sanat-kumara is asking Prthu Maharaja to please try to understand the truth he will speak in texts 39 and 40. These two texts, then, contain the essence of Sanat-kumara’s instructions to Prthu Maharaja:

**The devotees, who are always engaged in the service of the toes of the lotus feet of the Lord, can very easily overcome hard-knotted desires for fruitive activities. Because this is very difficult, the nondevotees—the jndnis and yogis—although trying to stop the waves of sense gratification, cannot do so. Therefore you are advised to engage in the devotional service of Krsna, the son of Vasudeva. (Bhag.** [**4.22.39**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.39)**)**

The purport of the above text is reminiscent of the purport to Bhagavatam [1.2.7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.7). That verse states, vasudeve bhagavati bhakti-yogah prayojitah, janayaty asu vairagyam jnanam ca yad ahaitukam: “By rendering devotional service unto the Personality of Godhead, Sri Krsna, one immediately acquires causeless knowledge and detachment from the world.” Both the Fourth Canto text and the First Canto text describe the practical superiority of devotional service over all other methods of spiritual advancement. While encouraging his readers to cross the dangerous ocean of matter by taking shelter of the Lord’s soft, pinkish feet, in his purport Srila Prabhupada expands the meaning of Bhagavatam [4.22.39](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.39) as follows: “One can give up inferior desires when engaged in superior desires. To try to stop desires is impossible. One has to desire the Supreme in order not to be entangled in inferior desires. jnanis maintain a desire to become one with the Supreme, but such desire is also considered to be kama, lust. Similarly, the yogis desire mystic power, and that is also kama. And the bhaktas, not being desirous of any sort of material enjoyment, become purified. There is no artificial attempt to stop desire. Desire becomes a source of spiritual enjoyment under the protection of the toes of the lotus feet of the Lord. It is stated herein by the Kumaras that the lotus feet of Lord Krsna are the ultimate reservoir of all pleasure. One should therefore take shelter of the lotus feet of the Lord instead of trying unsuccessfully to stop desires for material enjoyment. As long as one is unable to stop the desire for material enjoyment, there is no possibility of becoming liberated from the entanglement of material existence. It may be argued that the waves of a river are incessantly flowing and that they cannot be stopped, but the waves of the river flow toward the sea. When the tide comes over the river, it overwhelms the flowing of the river, and the river itself becomes overflooded, and the waves from the sea become more prominent than the waves from the river. Similarly, a devotee with intelligence plans so many things for the service of the Lord in Krsna consciousness that stagnant material desires become overflooded by the desire to serve the Lord.”

Thus, as Srila Prabhupada explains, we must substantially increase our desire for devotional service if we wish to avoid having waves of material desires overpower the river of our Krsna consciousness. If we wish to increase spiritual desire, Srila Prabhupada recommends hearing about Krsna. He spoke about this in a lecture on Bhagavatam [1.2.8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/2.8), given in New Vrindavan in 1972:

**So you can have your churches, temple or mosque, but if you do not develop your tendency to hear about God, then it will not be successful.Sramaevahikevalam. . . . Dharmahsvanusthitahpumsam visvaksena'kathasu yah notpadayed yadi ratim, by going daily to the temple, or to the church, or to the mosque, or anywhere, any religious building or institution, if you do not develop your propensity to hear about God, then you have wasted your time. Srama eva hi kevalam. Going and coming, it is simply labor, that’s all. So that is the test. Therefore either in temple or in church or in mosque there must be regular recitation on the talks of God. Otherwise people will lose interest and the churches and temples have to be closed. So talks of God are here in Krsna consciousness, because our God is not impersonal, void. No. He is the Supreme Person, Krsna. You can see personally how He’s standing, how He’s enjoying with His eternal consort, lover, Srimati Radharani. Here is God. Actually God is not engaged in punishing somebody. Here is the original God. God is engaged in enjoying with His eternal consort, Srimati Radharani, and Srimati Radharani is enchanting Krsna. And Krsna is enchanting Radharani. This is the business of God. ... By becoming servant of God, you’ll eternally enjoy, same as the master. By becoming a friend of God, you’ll enjoy eternal friendship. By becoming father or mother of God, you’ll enjoy the parental affection exchanged between father and son. And by becoming lover of God, you become eternally happy. So unless you hear about these things, then how you can be intensified to go to God?**

The four Kumaras, headed by Sanat-kumara, are the gurus of all jndnis. They offered Prthu Maharaja their final, weighty words of instruction:

**The ocean of nescience is very difficult to cross because it is infested with many dangerous sharks. Although those who are nondevotees undergo severe austerities and penances to cross that ocean, we recommend that you simply take shelter of the lotus feet of the Lord, which are like boats for crossing the ocean. Although the ocean is difficult to cross, by taking shelter of His lotus feet you will overcome all dangers.” (Bhag.** [**4.22.40**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.40)**)**

In establishing that bhakti-yoga—not jnana-yoga, which sees the Lord as impersonal—is the actual process by which one can attain the Absolute Truth, Srila Jiva Gosvami comments on texts 39 and 40 in Bhakti-sandarbha, anuccheda 48. There he explains that Sanat-kumara has established bhakti after having explained the path of philosophical knowledge (jnana).

Sri Jiva goes on to say that the two paths (devotional service and impersonal speculation) have the same goal: to cross the ocean of nescience. But the jnana-marga is difficult, whereas the bhakti-marga carries its adherents to the destination by its own accord. That is, although the impersonalists desire to cross the ocean of nescience (titirsanti), they are factually unable to do so.

Srila Sridhara Svami also discusses text 40 in his Bhagavatam commentaries. There he raises a doubt: Someone may object that the sruti'sastras, such as the Taittiriya Upanisad ([2.1.2](https://vedarama.com/en/books/taittiriya/2.1.2)), say that one who understands Brahman attains the Supreme. How is it possible, then, that jnanis and yogis cannot actually overcome their hard-knotted desires for fruitive activity?

Srila Sridhara Svami responds that the Lord speaks text 40 to specifically answer this objection. In text 40, aplava'isam refers to those who have not taken shelter of the boat (the Supreme Personality of Godhead) to cross the ocean of nescience. Such persons find it difficult to cross on their own, although they had hoped that their difficult yoga practices would suffice to carry them across the shark-filled ocean. One should therefore take the boat (udupam) of the Lord’s feet to cross that difficult ocean (dustararnam).

Srila Prabhupada writes: “Although there are many methods or boats by which one can cross the ocean, the Kumaras recommend that the King take shelter of the lotus feet of the Lord, just as one would take shelter of a good boat. Nondevotees, who do not take shelter of the Lord’s lotus feet, try to cross the ocean of nescience by other methods (karma, jnana and yoga), but they have a great deal of trouble. ... On the other hand, anyone who takes to the process of devotional service and has faith that the lotus feet of the Lord are safe boats to cross that ocean is certain to cross very easily and comfortably. Prthu Maharaja is therefore advised to take the boat of the lotus feet of the Lord to easily cross over all dangers. Dangerous elements in the universe are compared to sharks in the ocean. Even though one may be a very expert swimmer, he cannot possibly survive if he is attacked by sharks.” (Bhag. [4.22.40](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.40), purport)

## Texts 41-48: Prthu Maharaja Responds, and the Four Kumaras Depart

After hearing from Sanat-kumara, the King told the four sages that the Lord had predicted that they would give him their association. Now that you have come, he said, you have awarded me with the Lord’s causeless mercy.

In his purport to text 42 Srila Prabhupada discusses how devotees fulfill the Lord’s prediction: “When Lord Visnu appeared in the great arena of sacrifice at the time when King Prthu was performing a great sacrifice (asvamedha), He predicted that the Kumaras would very soon come and advise the King. Therefore Prthu Maharaja remembered the causeless mercy of the Lord and thus welcomed the arrival of the Kumaras, who were fulfilling the Lord’s prediction. In other words, when the Lord makes a prediction, He fulfills that prediction through some of His devotees. Similarly, Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu predicted that both His glorious names and the Hare Krsna maha-mantra would be broadcast in all the towns and villages of the world. Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakura and Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Prabhupada desired to fulfill this great prediction, and we are following in their footsteps.”

Wishing to reciprocate with the compassionate gift of knowledge offered by the four Kumaras, Prthu Maharaja felt awkward. The saintly persons who had cursed and killed his father had granted him the kingdom he now ruled, and he continued to rule it on their behalf. Prthu Maharaja thus considered that He possessed nothing but his kingdom, which was actually the property of Bhrgu Muni and the other sages. How, then, could he reciprocate with the gift of knowledge the four Kumaras had given him? Thus Prthu Maharaja felt he possessed no suitable gift to offer the four Kumaras. The King said: “Therefore, My dear brahmanas, my life, wife, children, home, furniture and household paraphernalia, my kingdom, strength, land and especially my treasury are all offered unto you.” (Bhag. [4.22.44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.44))

In his purport to this text Srila Prabhupada discusses Prthu Maharaja’s mood in offering his treasury to the Kumaras: “The ratna-bhanda was a special treasury room which contained special jewelries, such as bangles, necklaces and so on, which were presented to the king by the citizens. This jewelry was kept separate from the regular treasury house where all the collected revenues were kept. Thus Prthu Maharaja offered his stock of private jewelry to the lotus feet of the Kumaras. It has already been admitted that all the King’s property belonged to the brahmanas and that Prthu Maharaja was simply using it for the welfare of the state. If it were actually the property of the brahmanas, how could it be offered again to them? In this regard, Sripada Sridhara Svami has explained that this offering is just like the servant’s offering of food to his master. The food already belongs to the master, for the master has purchased it, but the servant, by preparing food, makes it acceptable to the master and thus offers it to him. In this way, everything belonging to Prthu Maharaja was offered to the Kumaras.”

Feeling that his gifts of perishable matter were an insufficient reciprocation with the four youthful sages who had awarded him, by their instructions, eternal benefit, Prthu Maharaja then asked that they kindly be satisfied with their own actions, which were full of mercy.

Srila Prabhupada speaks of the gift of transcendental knowledge in his purport to text 47: “Knowledge of Krsna is such a great gift that it is impossible to repay the benefactor. Therefore Prthu Maharaja requested the Kumaras to be satisfied by their own benevolent activities in delivering souls from the clutches of maya. The King saw that there was no other way to satisfy them for their exalted activities. The word vinoda-patram can be divided into two words, vina and uda-patram, or can be understood as one word, vinoda-patram, which means ‘joker.’ A joker’s activities simply arouse laughter, and a person who tries to repay the spiritual master or teacher of the transcendental message of Krsna becomes a laughingstock just like a joker because it is not possible to repay such a debt. The best friend and benefactor of all people is one who awakens humanity to its original Krsna consciousness.”

The great sages listened, satisfied with the King’s expressions, and then departed.

## Texts 49-63: Prthu Maharaja’s Actions as King

Thereafter, being self-satisfied and peaceful, Prthu Maharaja practiced bhakti by performing his duties solely for Krsna’s pleasure. Prabhupada explains how to become peaceful, like Prthu: “Remaining fixed in devotional service gives one the utmost in self-satisfaction. Actually self-satisfaction can be achieved only by pure devotees, who have no desire other than to serve the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Since the Supreme Personality of Godhead has nothing to desire, He is fully satisfied with Himself. Similarly, a devotee who has no desire other than to serve the Supreme Personality of Godhead is as selfsatisfied as the Supreme Lord. Everyone is hankering after peace of mind and self-satisfaction, but these can only be achieved by becoming a pure devotee of the Lord.” (Bhag. [4.22.49](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.49), purport)

In his purport to text 50, Prabhupada describes Maharaja Prthu’s extraordinary activities: “Srila Rupa Gosvami has advised that things which are favorable to devotional service should not be rejected, nor should activity favorable for devotional service be considered ordinary work or fruitive activity. For example, an ordinary worker conducts business in order to earn money for his sense gratification. A devotee may perform the same work in exactly the same way, but his aim is to satisfy the Supreme Lord. Consequently his activities are not ordinary.”

Prthu Maharaja’s activities were not ordinary but spiritual and transcendental because he wanted only to satisfy the Lord by performing them. Just as warrior Arjuna had to fight to satisfy Krsna, Prthu Maharaja had to perform his kingly duties for the Lord’s satisfaction. He did nothing while he was world emperor that was not befitting a pure devotee. Not everyone may recognize Maharaja Prthu’s activities as exemplary devotional service. That is, vaisnavera kriya-mudra, vijne nd bujhaya: no one can understand the activities of a pure devotee.

Prthu had instructed his subjects how to turn their work—their karma—into bhakti. And the four Kumaras had described how to actively apply the principle of jndna—the understanding that all living beings are eternal souls—in the Lord’s service. Thus they also preached bhakti. Now after all the instructions had been given and received, Prthu Maharaja himself acted in bhakti and through his actions dedicated himself fully to the Lord’s service. He practiced what he preached.

In his purport to text 51 Srila Prabhupada explains how to practically apply the principle of acting only for Krsna’s pleasure:

**In this material world a person is always thinking of the proprietorship of everything he accumulates or works for. When the fruits of one’s activities are rendered to the service of the Lord, one is actually practicing karma-yoga. Anyone can practice karma-yoga, but it is especially easy for the householder, who can install the Deity of the Lord in the home and worship Him according to the methods of bhakti-yoga. This method includes nine items: hearing, chanting, remembering, serving, worshiping the Deity, praying, carrying out orders, serving Krsna as friend and sacrificing everything for Him.**

**Sravanam klrtanam visnoh smaranam pada-sevanam, arcanam vandanam dasyam sakhyam atma-nivedanam (Bhag.** [**7.5.23**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-7/5.23)**). These methods of karma-yoga and bhakti-yoga are being broadcast all over the world by the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. Anyone can learn these methods simply by following the examples of the members of the Society.**

Prthu Maharaja remained at home and used his opulence for Krsna’s pleasure, and his citizens became fully satisfied by their King’s words, mentality, work, and gentle behavior. Commenting on text 54, Srila Jiva Gosvami explains, “Maharaja Prthu has now displayed all the glories the vandis praised in him.”

Srila Prabhupada describes the duties of a king in fulfilling the Lord’s purpose: “Although this material world is condemned when it is compared to the spiritual world, there is still some purpose behind it. Modem scientists and philosophers cannot understand that purpose, nor do they believe in the existence of a creator. They try to establish everything by their so-called scientific research, but they do not center anything around the supreme creator. A devotee, however, can understand the purpose of creation, which is to give facilities to the individual living entities who want to lord it over material nature. The ruler of this planet should therefore know that all the inhabitants, especially human beings, have come to this material world for sense enjoyment. It is therefore the duty of the ruler to satisfy them in their sense enjoyment as well as to elevate them to Krsna consciousness so that they all can ultimately return home, back to Godhead. With this idea in mind, the king or government head should rule the world. In this way, everyone will be satisfied.” (Bhag. [4.22.55](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.55), purport)

One could no more understand Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, by studying the material world than the personality and family of a wheat farmer by studying a capatt. Prthu Maharaja was a devotee king and therefore understood both the Lord and the purpose of the material world. He ruled accordingly: “One can understand Me as I am, as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, only by devotional service.” (Bg. [18.55](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/18.55)) Prthu Maharaja ruled with power and unconquerable strength, and his kingdom became like heaven itself. His words were as unstoppable as Indra’s thunderbolts, and his discretion as fine as Yamaraja’s. His strength resembled the power of the wind, and his physical beauty resembled Cupid’s. He faultlessly followed the devotees who were attached to cow protection and serving the guru and brahmanas. He was shy, gentle, and charitable. He always worked as if he were working for his own interest, but his mind was always absorbed in devotional service. Thus his reputation spread throughout the universe.

## Chapter 23 - Prthu Maharaja Goes Back to Godhead

## Texts 1-12: Prthu Maharaja Renounces His Kingdom to Go to the Forest

The brahmanas had caused Prthu Maharaja to be bom by churning Vena’s body. He appeared to perform a specific mission: to exemplify perfect kingship and to reestablish the sacrificial performances for bidden by his father. After completing his mission, King Prthu realized he was growing old. He distributed whatever wealth he had accumulated and arranged pensions for his citizens according to religious principles. By the Lord’s desire he then dedicated his sons to the earth, whom he considered his daughter. Leaving his citizens, who cried in separation from him, he and his wife Arci journeyed to the forest to practice yoga and to prepare for death.

To cast off attachment to the comforts of household life, Prthu Maharaja performed the eightfold mystic yoga system, practicing austerities with the same determination he had used to rule the kingdom. Sometimes he ate tree bark or roots. Eating only whatever nature provided, he conquered his senses and became completely tolerant. For some weeks he fasted on water alone. Finally he was able to maintain his life simply on air. “All this he did for the satisfaction of Krsna. He had no other purpose.” (Bhag. [4.23.7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.7))

In his purport to text 8 Srila Prabhupada explains the actual purpose behind pranayama: “As far as pranayama is concerned, chanting of the holy name of the Lord and dancing in ecstasy are also considered pranayama. In a previous verse, Sanat-kumara instructed Maharaja Prthu to engage constantly in the service of the Supreme Lord, Vasudeva: yat pada-pankaja-palasa-vilasa-bhaktya, karmasayam grathitam udgrathayanti santah: Only by worshiping Vasudeva can one become free from the desires of fruitive activities. Outside of worshiping Vasudeva, the yogis and jndnis cannot attain freedom from such desires. Tadvan na rikta-matayo yatayo ’pi ruddha-sroto-ganas tarn aranam bhaja vasudevam (Bhag. [4.22.39](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.39)). Here the word pranayama does not refer to any ulterior motive. The actual aim is to strengthen the mind and senses in order to engage them in devotional service. In the present age this determination can be very easily acquired simply by chanting the holy names— Hare Krsna, Hare Krsna, Krsna Krsna, Hare Hare / Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.”

In his purports to texts 5 and 7, Srila Prabhupada brings Prthu Maharaja’s practices in line with the capacity of contemporary people: “Srila Rupa Gosvami, after retiring from his minister’s seat in the government, went to Vrndavana and lived beneath a tree, like Maharaja Prthu. Since then, many people have gone to Vrndavana to imitate Rupa Gosvami’s behavior. Instead of advancing in spiritual life, many have fallen into material habits and even in Vrndavana have become victims of illicit sex, gambling and intoxication. The Krsna consciousness movement has been introduced in the Western countries, but it is not possible for Westerners to go to the forest and practice the severe austerities which were ideally practiced by Prthu Maharaja or Rupa Gosvami. However, Westerners or anyone else can follow in the footsteps of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura by living in a temple, which is transcendental to residence in a forest, and to vow to accept krsna-prasada and nothing else, follow the regulative principles and chant sixteen rounds daily of the Hare Krsna mantra. In this way, one’s spiritual life will never be disturbed.” (Bhag. [4.23.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.5), purport)From the purport to text 7:

**In Kali-yuga the following is recommended: harer nama harer nama harer namaiva kevalam, kalau nasty eva nasty eva nasty eva gatir anyatha (Brhan-naradiya Purana). In order to be recognized by Krsna, the Supreme Personality of Godhead, one should chant the holy name of the Lord continuously, twenty-four hours a day. Unfortunate persons who cannot accept this formula prefer to execute some type of pseudomeditation, without accepting the other processes of austerity. The fact is, however, that one must accept either the severe method of austerity described above to become purified or take to the process of devotional service recommended for pleasing the Supreme Lord, Krsna. The person who is Krsna conscious is most intelligent because in Kali-yuga it is not at all possible to undergo such severe austerities. We need only follow great personalities like Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu. In His Siksastaka, Lord Caitanya Mahaprabhu wrote, param vijay-ate sri-krsna-sankirtanam: all glories to the holy names of Lord Krsna, which from the very beginning purify the heart and immediately liberate one. Bhava-maha-davagni-nirvapanam. If the real purpose of all yoga is to please Lord Krsna, then this simple bhakti-yoga system recommended for this age is sufficient. It is necessary, however, to engage constantly in the service of the Lord. Although Prthu Maharaja executed his austerities long before the appearance of Lord Krsna on this planet, his purpose was still to please Krsna.**

**. . . We should therefore not be discouraged just because we cannot go to the forest and practice severe austerities. Our life is so short that we must strictly adhere to the principles laid down by the Vaisnava acaryas and peacefully execute Krsna consciousness. There is no need to become despondent. Narottama dasa Thakura recommends: anande bala hari, bhaja vrndavana, sri-guru-vaisnava-pade majaiya mana. For a transcendental, blissful life, chant the Hare Krsna mantra, come worship the holy place of Vrndavana, and always engage in the service of the Lord, of the spiritual master and of the Vaisnavas. This Krsna consciousness movement is therefore very safe and easy. We have only to execute the order of the Lord and fully surrender unto Him. We have only to execute the order of the spiritual master, preach Krsna consciousness and follow in the path of the Vaisnavas. The spiritual master represents both Lord Krsna and the Vaisnavas; therefore by following the instructions of the spiritual master and by chanting Hare Krsna, everything will be all right.**

Thus through yoga Prthu Maharaja followed the path of bhakti (not jndna) as Sanat-kumara had advised. By engaging fully in the Lord’s service, his loving devotion to the Supreme Lord gradually developed and became unflinching. His powerful devotional practices allowed Prthu Maharaja to become fully detached from matter and completely free from false ego, which is the heart of the material concept. He could then think constantly of the Lord’s lotus feet.

If one examines Prthu Maharaja’s life, one can see demonstrated the purpose of each of the main rungs of the yoga ladder. Prthu Maharaja preached to his subjects about karma—the purpose of which is to work, think of the Lord, offer Him the fruits of one’s work, and serve His devotees (Bhag. [4.21.33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/21.33)). Thus karma bears its ultimate fruit, bhakti. When the Kumaras taught the King, they described bhakti, the soul’s surrender to the Supersoul, as the ultimate fruit of jndna (Bhag. [4.22.38](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/22.38)). Here in the forest, Prthu Maharaja performed austerities for the Lord’s pleasure (Bhag. [4.23.7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.7)), which is bhakti performed through yoga practice (Bhag. [4.23.8-9](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.8)). Therefore not only is bhakti the true goal of the other processes, whether one practices the other processes or not, bhakti can award the fruit of karma and jndna. Srila Prabhupada writes: “In the Narada-pancaratra, devotional service to the Lord is likened unto a queen. When a queen gives an audience, many maidservants follow her. The maidservants of devotional service are material opulence, liberation and mystic powers. The karmis are very much attached to material enjoyment, the jndnis are very anxious

to become freed from material clutches, and the yogis are very fond of attaining the eight kinds of mystic perfection. From the Narada' pancaratra we understand that if one attains the stage of pure devo-tional service, he also attains all the opulences derived from fruitive activities, empiric philosophical speculation and mystic yogic practice. Srila Bilvamangala Thakura therefore prayed in his Krsna'karnamrta: ‘My dear Lord, if I have unflinching devotion to You, You become manifest before me personally, and the results of fruitive activity and empiric philosophical speculation—namely religion, economic development, sense gratification and liberation—become like personal attendants and remain standing before me as if awaiting my order.’” (Bhag. [4.23.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.11), purport)

“Maharaja Prthu thus engaged completely in devotional service, executing the rules and regulations strictly according to principles, twenty-four hours daily. Thus his love and devotion unto the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Krsna, developed and became unflinching and fixed. By regularly discharging devotional service, Prthu Maharaja became transcendental in mind and could therefore constantly think of the lotus feet of the Lord. Because of this, he became completely detached and attained perfect knowledge by which he could transcend all doubt. Thus he was freed from the clutches of false ego and the material conception of life.” (Bhag. [4.23.10-11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.10))

Thus freed from bodily identification through his yogic practice, he renounced lesser systems (yoga and jnana) and took shelter of the Supersoul in his heart. Srila Prabhupada indicates that practices other than direct bhakti are unnecessary: “Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura gives the following example: If one has strong digestive power, after eating he automatically lights a fire within his stomach to digest everything and does not need to take medicine to aid his digestion. Similarly, the fire of devotional service is so strong that a devotee does not need to act separately to attain perfect knowledge or detachment from material attractions. A jnani may become detached from material attractions by prolonged discussions on subjects of knowledge and may in this way finally come to the brahma-bhuta stage, but a devotee does not have to undergo so much trouble. By virtue of his devotional service, he attains the brahma-bhuta stage without a doubt.” (Bhag. [4.23.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.11), purport)

Sukadeva Gosvami has already glorified the bhakti process as paramount: “For those who are wandering in the material universe, there is no more auspicious means of deliverance than what is aimed at in the direct devotional service of Lord Krsna. The great personality Brahma, with great attention and concentration of the mind, studied the Vedas three times, and after scrutinizingly examining them, he ascertained that attraction for the Supreme Personality of Godhead Sri Krsna is the highest perfection of religion.” (Bhag. [2.2.33-34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-2/2.33))

## Texts 13-18: Prthu Maharaja Goes Back to Godhead

As Prthu Maharaja was about to give up his body, he fixed his mind firmly on Krsna’s lotus feet and fully situated himself in spiritual consciousness. Srila Prabhupada notes the importance of maintaining pure consciousness at the time of death: “Those who are practicing Krsna consciousness know that their examination will be held at the time of death. If one can remember Krsna at death, he is immediately transferred to Goloka Vrndavana, or Krsnaloka, and thus his life becomes successful. Prthu Maharaja, by the grace of Krsna, could understand that the end of his life was near, and thus he became very jubilant and proceeded to completely give up his body on the brahma'bhuta stage by practicing the yogic process. It is thoroughly described in the following verses how one can voluntarily give up this body and return home, back to Godhead. The yogic process practiced by Prthu Maharaja at the time of death accelerates the giving up of this body while one is in sound health physically and mentally. Every devotee desires to give up the body while it is sound physically and mentally. This desire was also expressed by King Kulasekhara in his Mukunda-mala-stotra. . . . King Kulasekhara wanted to give up his body while in a healthy state, and he thus prayed to Krsna to let him die immediately while he was in good health and while his mind was sound.” (Bhag. [4.23.13](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.13), purport)

Prthu Maharaja gradually raised his life air to the top of his skull and merged each of his body’s created elements back into the element from which it had come. “In this way, being situated in his original constitutional position of Krsna consciousness, he gave up this body as a prabhu, or controller of the senses.” (Bhag. [4.23.18](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.18))

In his purport to text 18 Srila Prabhupada explains the meaning of the title “Prabhupada”: “In this verse the word prabhu is also significant. As stated before, when one is completely self-realized and acts according to that position, he can be called prabhu. The spiritual master is addressed as ‘Prabhupada’ because he is a completely selfrealized soul. The word pada means ‘position,’ and Prabhupada indicates that he is given the position of prabhu, or the Supreme Personality of Godhead, for he acts on behalf of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Unless one is a prabhu, or controller of the senses, he cannot act as spiritual master, who is authorized by the supreme prabhu, or Lord Krsna. In his verses praising the spiritual master, Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura writes: saksad-dharitvena samasta-sastrair uktas tatha bhavyata eva sadbhih: ‘The spiritual master is honored as much as the Supreme Lord because he is the most confidential servitor of the Lord.’ Thus Prthu Maharaja can also be called Prabhupada, or, as described herein, prabhu."

## Texts 19-29: Queen Arci Attains Her Husband’s Planet

Prior to accompanying Prthu Maharaja, chaste Queen Arci had always remained in the palace. Her lotus feet had therefore never touched the earth. But in following her husband to the forest she had touched her feet to the ground and had accepted all the same difficulties her husband had endured. Although she was delicate and unaccustomed to austerity, because she served her husband with great affection, she did not consider the difficulty. Still, she became frail.

When Arci realized that her husband had left his body, she first lamented, then built a fire atop a hill and placed her husband’s body on it. Queen Arci performed the funeral ceremony. She circumambulated the fire and, thinking of her husband’s lotus feet, entered the flames.

Satisfied by Arci’s bravery, the wives of the demigods, accompanied by their husbands, offered prayers to Arci and spoke of her glory. They also noted that she had obtained the same spiritual destination as her husband, and that both were developing spiritual bodies. The wives of the demigods, as direct observers, marveled at the power of devotional service, for it had empowered Arci to go back home, back to Godhead.

The standard of a wife’s chastity was set by Rukminidevi, Krsna’s first wife, who served her Lord personally even though she had unlimited servants. There was no question of divorce in Vedic culture.

Both husband and wife therefore lived together dutifully, and families remained intact. Srila Prabhupada takes a strong stand as he discusses this point in his purport to text 25: “We should understand the neces-sity for maintaining family life in human society and should thus abolish this artificial law known as divorce. The husband and wife should live in Krsna consciousness and follow in the footsteps of Laksmi-Narayana or Krsna-Rukmini. In this way peace and harmony can be possible within this world.”

In his purport to text 27, he expands on the thoughts of some of the demigods’ wives: “Generally the processes of jndna, yoga and karma are executed life after life before one gets a chance to render pure devotional service to the Lord. This chance is given by the grace of a pure devotee, and it is in this way only that one can actually attain liberation. In the context of this narration, the wives of the demigods repented because although they had the opportunity of a birth in a higher planetary system, a lifetime spanning millions of years and all material comforts, they were not as fortunate as Prthu Maharaja and his wife, who were actually surpassing them. In other words, Prthu Maharaja and his wife scorned promotion to the higher planetary systems and even to Brahmaloka because the position which they were attaining was incomparable.”

Witnessing the wonderful effect of devotional service, the wives of the demigods lamented for those in the material world who, although possessing human bodies, neglected to practice bhakti-yoga. They considered the materialists both “cheated” and “envious” of the self. They thought that people should strive for liberation from material misery and think of returning to the spiritual world as one’s only goal.

Queen Arci reached the same planet attained by her husband. This means that like her husband, Arci attained eternal perfection and liberation in the Vaikuntha planets and did not gain perfection in impersonal Brahman realization. In his purport to text 29, Srila Prabhupada explains the glory of a proper husband-and-wife relationship: “According to Bhaktivinoda Thakura also, a husband and wife can turn the home into a place as good as Vaikuntha, even while in this material world. Being absorbed in Krsna consciousness, even in this world husband and wife can live in Vaikuntha simply by installing the Deity of the Lord within the home and serving the Deity according to the directions of the sastras. In this way, they will never feel the sex urge. That is the test of advancement in devotional

service. One who is advanced in devotional service is never attracted by sex life, and as soon as one becomes detached from sex life and proportionately attached to the service of the Lord, he actually experiences living in the Vaikuntha planets. In the ultimate issue, there is actually no material world, but when one forgets the service of the Lord and engages himself in the service of his senses, he is said to be living in the material world.”

## Texts 30-39: The Glories of Hearing and Chanting about Prthu Maharaja

Maitreya Muni ends his description of Prthu Maharaja by explaining the incredible results one accrues by hearing and describing these activities: One who describes King Prthu’s activities and characteristics with faith and determination attains the same planet as Prthu Maharaja. One hearing of Prthu Maharaja’s characteristics becomes perfect in his occupation as either a brahmana, ksatriya, vaisya, or sudra. One who with great respect hears about Prthu Maharaja “will become the father of many children if he is without children and will become the richest of men if he is without money. Also, one who hears this narration three times will become very reputable if he is not recognized in society, and he will become a great scholar if he is illiterate. In other words, hearing of the narrations of Prthu Maharaja is so auspicious that it drives away all bad luck.” (Bhag. [4.23.33-34](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.33)) Hearing of Prthu Maharaja allows one to become great, increases one’s life duration, awards one promotion to the heavenly planets, and counteracts the contamination of Kali-yuga. If before battle a king thrice chants the narration of Prthu Maharaja, subordinate kings will automatically render all taxes to him.

But these are all fulfillments of material desires. “A pure devotee who is executing the different processes of devotional service may be situated in the transcendental position, being completely absorbed in Krsna consciousness, but even he, while discharging devotional service, must hear, read and induce others to hear about the character and life of Prthu Maharaja.” (Bhag. [4.23.37](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.37))

Maitreya Muni then offers the ultimate benedictions: “The narrations about Prthu Maharaja . . . enrich one’s devotional attitude. Whoever takes advantage of these benefits also goes back home, back to Godhead, like Maharaja Prthu. Whoever, with great reverence and adoration, regularly reads, chants and describes the history of Maharaja Prthu’s activities will certainly increase unflinching faith and attraction for the lotus feet of the Lord. The Lord’s lotus feet are the boat by which one can cross the ocean of nescience.” (Bhag. [4.23.38-39](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.38))

Srila Prabhupada adds: “One who has taken shelter of the lotus feet of the Lord need not cross over the ocean, for he has already crossed it by virtue of his position at the Lord’s lotus feet. By hearing and chanting of the glories of the Lord or the Lord’s devotee, one can become firmly fixed in the service of the lotus feet of the Lord. This position can also be achieved very easily by narrating the history of the life of Prthu Maharaja.” (Bhag. [4.23.39](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/23.39))

## Dialogue Six - Narada’s Instructions to King Pracinabarhisat

## A Glimpse of Chapter Twenty-four

After narrating Prthu Maharaja’s return to the spiritual world (Chapter Twenty-three), Maitreya Muni outlines Prthu Maharaja’s descendants (Chapter Twenty-four). Prthu Maharaja had several sons, but Vijitasva (Antardhana) was prominent among them. Vijitasva’s son was Havirdhana, whose son was Barhisat (Pracinabarhisat). Maitreya then tells Vidura that Lord Siva instructed the Pracetas, Pracinabarhisat’s sons, when they set out to perform austerities on their father’s order.

Vidura wants to hear Lord Siva’s instructions, which in the Bhag' avatarn are known as the Rudra^ta, the “Song Sung by Lord Siva.” Maitreya recites the Rudra'gita, which takes up most of Chapter Twenty-four of the Fourth Canto. In that chapter’s remaining texts he delineates the glorious results one achieves when one chants or reads Lord Siva’s prayers with attention and reverence.

The first two texts of Chapter Twenty-five describe how the Pracetas adopted Lord Siva’s instructions and their subsequent meditation on the Lord by chanting his prayers. The third text, however, carries the narration in a new direction by describing Narada Muni’s compassion for Maharaja Pracinabarhisat. Maitreya Muni will pick up the thread of the Pracetas’ life again at the end of the Fourth Canto, Chapters Thirty and Thirty-one. We will explore the Puranjana allegory with King Pracinabarhisat first, and then return to the Pracetas, including the chapter, “The Song Sung by Lord Siva,” afterwards.

## Chapter 25 - The Characteristics of \<span class="footnote" data-footnote-content="Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura defines puranjana as follows: purmetat sariram svakarmana janayattti tasya purnjanasya, “One whose actions (karma) generate (janayati) the city (puram) of the body.”" data-footnote-number="313" role="footnote"\>King Puranjana\</span\>

## Texts 3-6: Narada Muni Shows Mercy to Pracinabarhisat, the Father of the Pracetas

Maharaja Pracinabarhisat performed constant fruitive sacrifices (Bhag. [4.24.9-10](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/24.9)) to both increase his piety and ensure a future of pleasure. Narada Muni decided to undermine his plans, for Pracinabarhisat was a descendant of Narada’s disciple Dhruva Maharaja and Narada did not like to see him sunk in material life. Also, the King had forgotten the true purpose of performing Vedic sacrifices. Narada therefore challenged the King: “My dear King, what do you desire to achieve by performing these fruitive activities? The chief aim of life is to get rid of all miseries and enjoy happiness, but these two things cannot be realized by fruitive activity.” (Bhag. [4.25.4](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.4)) Narada reminded the King that even the positive results of fruitive actions are temporary and thus illusory.In his purport to text 4, Srila Prabhupada exposes the fundamental flaw in Maharaja Pracinabarhisat’s attempt to find happiness through fruitive work:

**In this material world there is a great illusion which covers real intelligence. A man in the mode of passion wants to work very hard to derive some benefit, but he does not know that time will never allow him to enjoy anything permanently. . . . On the whole, suffering is the nature of this material world, and whatever enjoyment we are trying to achieve is simply illusion. After all, we have to suffer the miseries of birth, old age, disease and death. We may discover many fine medicines, but it is not possible to stop the sufferings of disease or death. Actually, medicine is not the counteracting agent for either disease or death. On the whole there is no happiness in this material world, but an illusioned person works very hard for so-called happiness. Indeed, this process of working hard is actually taken for happiness. This is called illusion.**

**Therefore Narada Muni asked King Pracinabarhisat what he desired to attain by performing so many costly sacrifices. Even if one attains a heavenly planet, he cannot avoid the distresses of birth, old age, disease and death.**

Maharaja Pracinabarhisat considered the sage’s question and admitted that he was correct. Although he was performing rituals, he did not know the goal of either the sacrifices or of life. He also agreed with Narada’s statement that no material situation is completely free of misery. Thus by Narada Muni’s influence the King began to think that fruitive activities, even if pious, do not solve anything. Living a self-centered life necessarily means suffering.

Those aspiring to make spiritual advancement must reach this same conclusion. Sri Prahlada Maharaja confirms this truth: “Because of their uncontrolled senses, persons too addicted to materialistic life make progress toward hellish conditions and repeatedly chew that which has already been chewed. Their inclinations toward Krsna are never aroused, either by the instructions of others, by their own efforts, or by a combination of both.” (Bhag. [7.5.30](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-7/5.30)) Narada Muni planted the seeds of detachment in the King’s heart, along with a new seed, a spiritual seed in the form of the desire to make spiritual progress. Maharaja Pracinabarhisat then accepted Narada Muni as his guru: “Kindly instruct me in pure knowledge so that I can get out of the entanglement of fruitive activities.” (Bhag. [4.25.5](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.5))

## Texts 7-24: Narada Narrates the History of King Puranjana

Narada Muni thought that before instructing the King in transcendence, it would be helpful to draw him away from his attachment to fruitive activities and inspire him with vairagya. He used fear as a tool: “O ruler of the citizens, my dear King, please see in the sky those animals which you have sacrificed without compassion and without mercy in the sacrificial arena. All these animals are awaiting your death so that they can avenge the injuries you have inflicted upon them. After you die, they will angrily pierce your body with iron horns.” (Bhag. [4.25.7-8](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.7))

In his purports to these texts, Prabhupada explains that animal sacrifices, even those prescribed in sastra, are risky. Sacrificed animals are said to attain a human birth, but if there is a discrepancy in the performance of the ritual, the animal may not ascend to a higher birth. Narada warned the King that such animals would seek revenge for the violence committed against them.

To teach Pracinabarhisat about the futility of material life, Narada Muni narrated what he called “an old history,” the story of a king named Puranjana. Puranjana’s story was simply Pracinabarhisat’s own story couched in allegory—the word puranjana means “a soul who attempts to enjoy in a material body.”

Narada called his story old because each soul has been transmigrating through countless bodies since the beginning of time, each body serving only as a temporary dwelling place for the eternally conditioned soul. Thus Narada wanted to warn the King about his own possibly dark future.

In his comment on text 9, Srila Jiva Gosvami states that Narada Muni, not perceiving eligibility for pure bhakti in the king, instructed Pracinabarhisat in jnana'misra'bhakti, which is the means to liberation. Thus Narada began by telling a suitable story that paralleled the King’s life and which might prove helpful to him.

King Puranjana was always accompanied by Avijnata, an unknown friend whose activities no one could understand. This unknown friend never left Puranjana’s side. Later verses will reveal that Avijnata is the Supersoul. The Supersoul is truly our unknown friend. As the Supersoul, the Lord accompanies the living entity, remaining always near him, by residing along with the soul in his heart, regardless of which body the living entity is placed in by his own karma. The Supersoul also acts as a friend by reminding the living entity of his previous desires as well as giving his directions to fulfill those desires.

Narada said: “King Puranjana began to search for a suitable place to live, and thus he traveled all over the world. Even after a great deal of traveling, he could not find a place just to his liking. Finally he became morose and disappointed.” (Bhag. [4.25.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.11)) No place was to Puranjana’s liking because he possessed unlimited desires, and it was impossible to satisfy them all in any one place. Ultimately, there is no suitable residence for the living entity in the material world.

Every place from the greatest to the most humble simply leaves the living entity frustrated and unfulfilled; the eternal soul is out of place here, like a fish out of water. In his purport to text 11 Prabhupada explains the root of Puranjana’s frustration: “As stated in this verse, the living entity wants to become a prabhu or master. The word pra-bhu means ‘master,’ but actually the living entity is not a master; he is the eternal servant of God. When the living entity abandons the shelter of God, Krsna, and tries to become a prabhu independently, he travels all over the creation. There are 8,400,000 species of life and millions and millions and trillions of planets within the creation. The living entity wanders throughout these various types of bodies and throughout different planets, and thus he is like King Puranjana, who traveled all over the world looking for a suitable place to live.”

During his travels, Puranjana approached an auspicious nine-gated city in Bharata-varsa (India). In his purport to text 13 Srila Prabhupada describes the allegorical meaning of this city:

**The tract of land south of the Himalaya Mountains is the land of India . . . When a living entity takes birth in Bharata-varsa he is considered to be most fortunate. Indeed, Caitanya Mahaprabhu has stated: bharata-bhumite haila manusya-janma yara, janma sarthaka kari’ kara para-upakara.... whoever takes birth in the land of Bharata-varsa attains all the facilities of life. He may take advantage of all these facilities for both material and spiritual advancement and thus make his life successful. After attaining the goal of life, one may distribute his knowledge and experience all over the world for humanitarian purposes.... one who takes birth in the land of Bharata-varsa by virtue of his past pious activities gets full facility to develop the human form of life.... At the present moment, India may be compared to the lame man and the Western countries to the blind man. For the past two thousand years India has been subjugated by the rule of foreigners, and the legs of progress have been broken. In the Western countries the eyes of the people have become blind due to the dazzling glitter of material opulence. The blind man of the Western countries and the lame man of India should combine together in this Krsna consciousness movement. Then the lame man of India can walk with the help of the Westerner, and the blind Westerner can see with the help of the lame man. In short, the material advancement of the Western countries and the spiritual assets of India should combine for the elevation of all human society.**

Narada said: The city was surrounded by walls and parks, and within it were towers, canals, windows, and outlets. The houses were domed in gold, silver, and iron, and their floors were made of sapphire, crystal, diamonds, pearls, emeralds, and rubies. On the outskirts were many beautiful trees and creepers and a nice lake. Birds and bees chanted and hummed. The air was misted with water carried by the spring air from the falls coming down from the icy mountain. In such an atmosphere even the forest animals became as nonviolent as great sages and did not attack anyone. Above everything rose the cooing of cuckoos. Travelers and city residents passing along that path were invited by the atmosphere to rest in the nice garden.

As a city’s walls keep out intruders, the body’s walls (skin) keep out invading germs. The city’s windows are the eyes, and the gold, silver, and iron domes are the three modes of material nature. Gold, being goodness, is most rare. As a king lives in his capital, the soul lives in the heart. In his purport to text 15 Srila Prabhupada further explains the allegory: “In the city of the body, the heart is considered to be the capital. Just as the capital of a state is especially gorgeously filled with various high buildings and lustrous palaces, the heart of the body is filled with various desires and plans for material enjoyment. Such plans are sometimes compared to valuable jewels such as sapphires, rubies, pearls and emeralds. The heart becomes the center for all planning for material enjoyment.”

While wandering in the lush city gardens King Puranjana suddenly saw a beautiful young woman wandering with ten servants (the ten senses), each of whom possessed one hundred wives (desires). She was protected by a five-hooded snake. By her shy movements she attempted to cover her body. “The woman’s nose, teeth and forehead were all very beautiful. Her ears were equally very beautiful and were bedecked with dazzling earrings. The waist and hips of the woman were very beautiful. She was dressed in a yellow san with a golden belt. While she walked, her ankle bells rang. She appeared exactly like a denizen of the heavens.” (Bhag. [4.25.22-23](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.22)) She also seemed to be anxiously seeking a husband.

In his comment on text 20, Sridhara Svami writes: “The word yadrcchaya, ‘all of a sudden, on its own,’ indicates that it is extremely difficult to explain the union of these two \[the King and the woman\].”

Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura comments that “King Puranjana has seen a beautiful woman (intelligence covered by ignorance), who came ‘on her own’ or ‘somehow or other’ (yadrcchaya). This means the first contact between the two is nirhetutvam, causeless.”

Srila Prabhupada writes: “The word niguhantim (‘trying to cover’) indicates that even if one is tainted by kama, lobha, krodha, etc., they can be transfigured by Krsna consciousness. In other words, one can utilize kama (lust) for serving Krsna. Being impelled by lust, an ordinary worker will work hard day and night; similarly a devotee can work hard day and night to satisfy Krsna. Just as karmis are working hard to satisfy kdma'krodha, a devotee should work in the same way to satisfy Krsna. Similarly, krodha (anger) can also be used in the service of Krsna when it is applied to the nondevotee demons. Hanumanji applied his anger in this way. He was a great devotee of Lord Ramacandra, and he utilized his anger to set fire to the kingdom of Ravana, a nondevotee demon. Thus kama (lust) can be utilized to satisfy Krsna, and krodha (anger) can be utilized to punish the demons. When both are used for Krsna’s service, they lose their material significance and become spiritually important.” (Bhag. 4.25.24, purport)

Most of the elements in the Puranjana story are allegorical, and their meanings will be disclosed in later Bhagavatam texts or in Srila Prabhupada purports. The five-hooded serpent protecting the woman, for example, represents the vital life force that, with its five airs, works inside the body and fully protects it. Srila Prabhupada notes: “The woman, who represents intelligence, was searching after a husband. This indicates that intelligence cannot act without consciousness. A beautiful woman is useless unless protected by the proper husband. Intelligence must always be very fresh; therefore the word apraudham (‘very young’) is used here. Material enjoyment means utilizing the intelligence for the sake of rupa, rasa, gandha, sabda and sparsa, or form, taste, smell, sound and touch.” (Bhag. [4.25.21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.21), purport)

## Texts 25-43: The Beautiful Woman Becomes King Puranjana’s Queen

Puranjana, the hero, was attracted by the eyebrows and smiling face of the beautiful girl, and was pierced by the arrows of her lust. She was beautiful when she smiled so shyly, and the King was struck with desire. If one stares at a bright light he will lose the ability to see. Similarly, if a soul stares at possible sense pleasure, it loses its ability to see itself. Soon the soul is surrounded by the blazing fire of illusion and is blinded. The soul thus loses its capacity to see its own eternal nature and the body’s inevitable march toward death. Srila Prabhupada offers a relevant quote in his purport to text 25: “Krsna-bahirmukha hand bhoga-vancha kare, nikata-stha maya tare japatiya dhare. It is said in the Prema-vivarta that when a living entity wants to enjoy material nature, he is immediately victimized by the material energy.”

Unable to refrain from addressing the beautiful girl, Puranjana inquired: “My dear lotus-eyed, kindly explain to me where you are coming from, who you are, and whose daughter you are. You appear very chaste. What is the purpose of your coming here? What are you trying to do? Please explain all these things to me.” (Bhag. [4.25.26](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.26))

Attraction to material enjoyment, as Srila Prabhupada writes in his purport to text 25, is freely chosen: “Every living entity has the freedom to be attracted by material nature or to stand as a hero and resist that attraction. It is simply a question of the living entity’s being attracted or not being attracted. There is no question of his being forced to come into contact with material energy. One who can keep himself steady and resist the attraction of material nature is certainly a hero and deserves to be called a gosvami. Unless one is master of the senses, he cannot become a gosvami. The living entity can take one of two positions in this world. He may become a servant of his senses, or he may become master of them. By becoming a servant of the senses, one becomes a great material hero, and by becoming master of the senses, he becomes a gosvami, or spiritual hero.”

All conditioned souls have turned away from Krsna. On awakening to their danger in this world they should turn back toward Him. This is difficult for those habituated to self-centered enjoyment. Therefore they must gain knowledge. Knowledge can help the conditioned souls curb the mind’s tendency to grasp at sense pleasure. Such knowledge includes an understanding of the essentially miserable nature of material existence. The mind’s tendency to grasp should be turned to grasping for Krsna’s service. This requires that the mind experience a higher taste. The conditioned souls should then sincerely ask Krsna to grant them the sweet shelter of His service, a request that is the essence of chanting the Hare Krsna maha-mantra. Srila Prabhupada therefore once compared the chanting to a child crying for its mother. Our chanting needs to be invested with a realization of our need for shelter and a desire for service.

Still pursuing material enjoyment, however, Puranjana inquired further from the girl: “My dear lotus-eyed, who are those eleven strong bodyguards with you, and who are those ten specific servants? Who are those women following the ten servants, and who is the snake that is preceding you?” (Bhag. [4.25.27](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.27))

Animals cannot inquire about their true identity. The inquiries of animals—and they do make inquiries—are limited to the physical necessities of eating, sleeping, mating, and defending. Humans should use their intelligence differently. They should inquire about the nature of the self, as Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 26: “In the animal form the living entity is completely forgetful of his relationship with God. This is called apohanam, or forgetfulness. In the human form of life, however, consciousness is more greatly developed, and consequently the human being has a chance to understand his relationship with God. In the human form one should utilize his intelligence by asking all these questions, just as Puranjana, the living entity, is asking the unknown girl where she has come from, what her business is, why she is present, etc. These are inquiries about atma'tattva—selfrealization. The conclusion is that unless a living entity is inquisitive about self-realization he is nothing but an animal.” In the next purport Srila Prabhupada describes the identity of the servants (the ten senses and the mind, who acts as the eleventh servant), the serpent bodyguard (the life force), and the hundreds of women following the ten servants (the desires that accompany the senses and cause anxiety by their constant demands).

Puranjana continued, speaking sweetly: My dear beautiful girl, you are exactly like the goddess of fortune or Parvati or Sarasvati. Though you must be a goddess, you are loitering in this forest, as silent as a great sage. Are you searching for your husband? But if you are not a goddess but a woman of this planet, you can, like the goddess of fortune who increases the beauty of the Vaikuntha planets, increase the beauty of this city by associating with me. I am a great hero and a powerful king here. Certainly your glancing at me today has attracted my mind. “Your smile, which is full of shyness but at the same time lusty, is agitating the most powerful cupid within me. Therefore, О most beautiful, I ask you to be merciful upon me. My dear girl, your face is so beautiful with your nice eyebrows and eyes and with your bluish hair scattered about. In addition, very sweet sounds are coming from your mouth. Nonetheless, you are so covered with shyness that you do not see me face to face. I therefore request you, my dear girl, to smile and kindly raise your head to see me.” (Bhag. [4.25.30-31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.30))

Puranjana was attracted to the young girl’s beauty—her eyebrows, lips, and hair. Flattering her, he compared her beauty to the beauty of Laksmidevi. He then promised her happiness by speaking of his own heroism.

Practically speaking, however, one whose desires are aroused is incapable of distinguishing between beauty and beastliness. Often those who were attracted from a distance become aware that they simply imagined the beauty they saw, because as they approached, they may have even found themselves repulsed by what now appears to be ugliness. If the beauty was imagined, where, then, was the hoped-for pleasure? It too was imagined, illusory. The eternal soul, starving for pleasure, continuously superimposes mental constructs of pleasure on the stark truth of the material energy. These constructs have only the capacity to deliver a hope of pleasure. And of course, frustration is bom from the disappointment that follows a dashed hope. Srila Prabhupada summarizes this point in his purport to text 31: “When thus attracted by the beauty of the material energy, one becomes very eager to enjoy. This is elaborately described in this instance of Puranjana’s becoming attracted by the beautiful woman. In conditional life the living entity is attracted by a face, eyebrows or eyes, a voice or anything. In short, everything becomes attractive. When a man or a woman is attracted by the opposite sex, it does not matter whether the opposite sex is beautiful or not. The lover sees everything beautiful in the face of the beloved and thus becomes attracted. This attraction causes the living entity to fall down in this material world.”

The girl, who was also attracted to Puranjana, then admitted her ignorance as she attempted to answer his inquiries: “O best of human beings, I do not know who has begotten me. I cannot speak to you perfectly about this. Nor do I know the names or the origin of the associates with me.” (Bhag. [4.25.33](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.33))

Prabhupada clarifies more of the allegory: “The living entity is ignorant of his origin. He does not know why this material world was created, why others are working in this material world and what the ultimate source of this manifestation is. No one knows the answers to these questions, and this is called ignorance. By researching into the origin of life, important scientists are finding some chemical compositions or cellular combinations, but actually no one knows the original source of life within this material world.”

The girl continued: I know that I exist, but I don’t know what will come next. I am so foolish that I do not even care to understand who created this beautiful place in which I live. This snake (the life force) and my friends are always awake—even while 1 sleep—and they protect me. I know nothing beyond this.

The young girl’s desires paralleled Puranjana’s, so she agreed to marry the King. She said: “I wish all auspicious things for you. You have a great desire to satisfy your senses, and all my friends and I shall try our best in all respects to fulfill your desires.” (Bhag. [4.25.36](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.36))

Representing material intelligence, the young girl was unable to perceive her origins; her awareness was limited to the mind and senses and their objects. Material intelligence also tends to neglect inquiry into its own source. The intelligence is meant to help the soul gain knowledge, but when it is materially contaminated it remains itself in ignorance. In his purport to text 36 Srila Prabhupada underscores Narada Muni’s point, that intelligence corrupted by material desire entangles the living entity further in the material world: “The living entity comes down into this material world for sense gratification, and his intelligence, represented by the woman, gives him the proper direction by which he can satisfy his senses to their best capacity. In actuality, however, intelligence comes from the Supersoul, or the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and He gives full facility to the living entity who has come down to this material world.... When a devotee is advancing toward spiritual realization, his only aim is the service of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. He does not care for any other material or spiritual activity. King Puranjana represents the ordinary living entity, and the woman represents the ordinary living entity’s intelligence. Combined, the living entity enjoys his material senses, and the intelligence supplies all paraphernalia for his enjoyment.”

Glorifying Puranjana’s qualities and thereby strongly establishing their relationship, the beautiful woman expressed her attraction to Puranjana: “O my dear hero, who in this world will not accept a husband like you? You are so famous, so magnanimous, so beautiful and so easily gotten.” (Bhag. [4.25.41](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.41))

In his purport to this text Prabhupada states that a husband’s duty is to satisfy his wife. Toward the end of this purport, he writes: “A man is always famous for his aggression toward a beautiful woman, and such aggression is sometimes considered rape. Although rape is not legally allowed, it is a fact that a woman likes a man who is very expert at rape.”

Is Prabhupada proposing that a woman appreciates the violence of rape? Certainly not. The perpetrator of such a brutish act could hardly be considered “expert.” It is more likely that Prabhupada is referring here to seduction, an aggressive alluring and attempt to lead a woman astray. One who is expert at seduction is, in that sense, “expert at rape,” for the expert seducer “forcibly” induces women to have sexual intercourse by subverting their will and better judgment. One definition of rape is “to enrapture; transport with the strength of an emotion.” Prabhupada states: “By this incident we can understand that when a man is aggressive and begins to woo a woman, the woman becomes attracted to the man.” (Bhag. [4.25.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.32)) And again, as his purport to this text states, “Although rape is not legally allowed, it is a fact that a woman likes a man who is very expert at rape.”

Thus the beautiful woman (the intelligence) vowed to arrange the city of nine gates (the body, which has nine “gates”: two eyes, two ears, two nostrils, a mouth, genital, and anus) to facilitate King Puranjana’s (the illusioned soul living in the body) experience of sense pleasures as he interacts with the world’s sense objects. “The great sage Narada continued: My dear King, those two—the man and the woman—supporting one another through mutual understanding, entered that city and enjoyed life for one hundred years.” (Bhag. [4.25.43](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.43))

Husband and wife—the contaminated soul and his material intelligence—conspire in their common desire to achieve as much self-centered pleasure as possible. In his purport to text 51 Srila Prabhupada suggests that a conditioned soul’s tendency to seek material pleasure over spiritual life is indicated by the nature of one’s two ears. The right ear, which is meant to experience materially pleasing sounds, is stronger than the left, which is meant to hear spiritual topics.

## Texts 44-62: Puranjana Becomes Captivated by His Wife

In that city, Narada continued, Puranjana and his wife achieved great happiness. “Many professional singers used to sing about the glories of King Puranjana and his glorious activities. When it was too hot in the summer, he used to enter a reservoir of water. He would surround himself with many women and enjoy their company.” (Bhag. [4.25.44](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.44)) At times, Puranjana left through one or another of the city’s gates, accompanied by specific friends, to visit distant cities to taste particular types of pleasure. At other times, “Although King Puranjana was the ruler of citizens who possessed eyes, he unfortunately used to associate with ... blind men. Accompanied by them, he used to go here and there and perform various activities.” (Bhag. [4.25.54](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.54))

The gates through which Puranjana traveled are the nine gateways leading into and out of the body. Each gate afforded him enjoyment of a particular type of sense object. Puranjana’s blind associates were his arms and legs. Although we depend on our arms and legs, they are blind—without holes through which to experience the outside world. Because they are blind, they must be directed by the intelligence.

Narada then told Pracinabarhisat of the trap into which Maharaja Puranjana fell: “Sometimes he used to go to his private home with one of his chief servants \[the mind\], who was named Visucina. At that time, illusion, satisfaction and happiness used to be produced from his wife and children. Being thus entangled in different types of mental concoction and engaged in fruitive activities, King Puranjana came completely under the control of material intelligence and was thus cheated. Indeed, he used to fulfill all the desires of his wife, the Queen. When the Queen drank liquor, King Puranjana also engaged in drinking. When the Queen dined, he used to dine with her, and when she chewed, King Puranjana used to chew along with her. When the Queen sang, he also sang. Similarly, when the Queen cried, he also cried, and when the Queen laughed, he also laughed. When the Queen talked loosely, he also talked loosely, and when the Queen walked, the King walked behind her. ... In this way, King Puranjana was captivated by his nice wife and was thus cheated. Indeed, he became cheated in his whole existence in the material world. Even against that poor foolish King’s desire, he remained under the control of his wife, just like a pet animal that dances according to the order of its master.” (Bhag. [4.25.55-59](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.55), [62](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.62))

In his purport to texts 57-61, Srila Prabhupada clarifies the meaning of Puranjana’s surrender to his queen: “The mind is the place where the self is situated, and the mind is conducted by the intelligence. The living entity, situated within the heart, follows the intelligence. The intelligence is herein depicted as the Queen, and the soul, under mental control, follows the material intelligence just as the King follows his wife. The conclusion is that material intelligence is the cause of bondage for the living entity. The point is that one has to take to spiritual intelligence to come out of this entanglement.”

The purport continues as Srila Prabhupada explains the means by which the spiritual intelligence directs the self from material entanglement: “In the life of Maharaja Ambarisa, we find that the great Maharaja first engaged his mind on the lotus feet of Krsna. In this way his intelligence became purified. Maharaja Ambarisa also used his other senses in the service of the Lord. He engaged his eyes in seeing the Deity in the temple nicely decorated with flowers. He engaged his sense of smell by smelling the flowers, and he engaged his legs by walking to the temple. His hands were engaged in cleansing the temple, and his ears were engaged in hearing about Krsna. His tongue was engaged in two ways: in speaking about Krsna and in tasting prasada offered to the Deity. Materialistic persons, who are under the full control of material intelligence, cannot perform all these activities. Thus, consciously or unconsciously, they become entangled by the dictations of material intelligence.” (Bhag. [4.25.57-61](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/25.57), purport) And from the purport to text 55: “Everyone who is not in Krsna consciousness must be considered to be in illusion. One’s so-called feelings of happiness and satisfaction resulting from material things are also illusions.”

Srila Prabhupada adds in his purport to text 62: “Just to satisfy his desires, the King got the Queen, and thus he became cheated by material existence. Although he was not willing to do so, he remained a pet animal under the control of material intelligence. Just as a pet monkey dances according to the desires of its master, the King danced according to the desires of the Queen.”

## Chapter 26 - King Puranjana Goes to the Forest to Hunt and His Queen Becomes \<span class="footnote" data-footnote-content="Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura mentions that the twenty-sixth chapter of the Fourth Canto demonstrates the results of becoming overcome by ignorance and attracted to impious sense gratification." data-footnote-number="319" role="footnote"\>Angry\</span\>

## Texts 1-12: Puranjana Goes to the Forest to Hunt

Narada Muni continued: Once, King Puranjana mounted his chariot and, armed with his bow and arrows, headed for a nearby forest to hunt. Although Puranjana was usually unable to leave his Queen even for a moment, filled with pride he forgot her, entered the forest, and remained unconcerned about the pain he caused as he mercilessly killed the innocent animals with his sharp arrows.

Maharaja Puranjana went hunting with his mind and senses but without his intelligence. It is unfortunate if one possesses only material intelligence, but if one possesses no intelligence, that is worse. Without his intelligence, Puranjana acted in the deepest ignorance.

Narada explained this to King Pracinabarhisat because he too was killing animals in his many sacrifices. Narada considered such killing ignorance even when performed in the guise of religiosity.

The forest as well as each part of Puranjana’s chariot contains parallels that illustrate how the living entity is controlled by the three modes of material nature. Narada Muni used these analogies to again point out that even though King Pracinabarhisat thought himself pious, he was actually under the influence of the lowest of the three modes.
