To spread the Krsna consciousness movement throughout the world, the devotees should be satisfied in all conditions. . . . narayana-parah sarve, na kutascana bibhyati/ svargapavarga-narakesv, api tulyartha-darsinah (Bhag.** [**6.17.28**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-6/17.28)**). It does not matter to the pure devotee if he has to go to hell to preach. The Supreme Lord lives in the heart of a hog, although the Lord is in Vaikuntha. Even while preaching in hell, a pure devotee remains a pure devotee by his constant association with the Supreme Personality of Godhead. To attain this state, one has to control his senses. The senses are automatically controlled when one’s mind is engaged in the service of the Lord.**

What is the result of such service? One’s heart becomes purified. Devotees “can always think of the Lord constantly and address Him very feelingly. The Supreme Personality of Godhead, knowing Himself to be controlled by His devotees, does not leave them for a second, just as the sky overhead never becomes invisible. The Supreme Personality of Godhead becomes very dear to those devotees who have no material possessions but are fully happy in possessing the devotional service of the Lord. Indeed, the Lord relishes the devotional activities of such devotees. Those who are puffed up with material education, wealth, aristocracy and fruitive activity are very proud of possessing material things, and they often deride the devotees. Even if such people offer the Lord worship, the Lord never accepts them.” (Bhag. [4.31.20-21](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/31.20))

The essence of all sadhana is to constantly think of the Lord (Padma Purana, quoted in Cc., Madhya [22.113](https://vedarama.com/en/books/cc-madhya/22.113)). In his purport to text 20 Srila Prabhupada describes the cleansed heart of a pure devotee rapt in thinking of Krsna: “It is clear from the previous text that the Supreme Personality of Godhead, Janardana, is very quickly satisfied by the activities of His devotees. The pure devotee is always absorbed in the thought of the Supreme Personality of Godhead. As stated, srnvatdm sva-kathah. krsnah. By always thinking of Krsna, the pure devotee’s heart is freed from all kinds of desires. In the material world, the heart of the living entity is filled with material desires. When the living entity is cleansed, he does not think of anything material. As the mind is completely cleansed, one attains the perfectional stage of mystic yoga, for then the yogi always sees the Supreme Personality of Godhead within his heart (dhyanavasthita-tad-gatena manasa pasyanti yam yoginah). As soon as the Lord is seated within the heart of the devotee, the devotee cannot be contaminated by the material modes of nature. As long as one is under the control of the material modes, he desires so many things and makes so many plans for material sense enjoyment, but as soon as the Lord is perceived in the heart, all material desires vanish. When the mind is completely free from material desire, the devotee can think of the Lord constantly. In this way he becomes completely dependent upon the lotus feet of the Lord. Caitanya Mahaprabhu prays . . . ‘My dear Lord, I am Your eternal servant, but somehow or other I have fallen into the ocean of this material world. Kindly pick me up and fix me as a speck of dust at Your lotus feet.’ (Siksastaka 5)”

In his purport to text 21 Srila Prabhupada describes the characteristics of a pure devotee as well as the danger of offending him: “The Supreme Personality of Godhead is dependent on His pure devotees. He does not even accept the offerings of those who are not devotees. A pure devotee is one who feels He does not possess anything material. A devotee is always happy in possessing the devotional service of the Lord. Devotees may sometimes appear materially poor, but because they are spiritually advanced and enriched, they are most dear to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Such devotees are free from attachment to family, society, friendship, children and so on. They abandon affection for all these material possessions and are always happy in possessing the shelter of the lotus feet of the Lord. The Supreme Personality of Godhead understands the position of His devotee. If a person derides a pure devotee, he is never recognized by the Supreme Personality of Godhead. In other words, the Supreme Lord never excuses one who offends a pure devotee. There are many examples of this in history. A great mystic yogi, Durvasa Muni, offended the great devotee Ambarisa Maharaja. The great sage Durvasa was to be chastised by the Sudarsana cakra of the Lord. Even though the great mystic directly approached the Supreme Personality of Godhead, he was never excused. Those on the path of liberation should be very careful not to offend a pure devotee.”

Narada Muni sweetly concluded his instructions to the Pracetas: “Although the Supreme Personality of Godhead is self-sufficient, He becomes dependent on His devotees. He does not care for the goddess of fortune, nor for the kings and demigods who are after the favors of the goddess of fortune. Where is that person who is actually grateful and will not worship the Personality of Godhead?” (Bhag. [4.31.22](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/31.22))

There were three parts to Narada Muni’s instructions: First, he explained that devotional service is the goal of all spiritual practices (texts 8-14). Second, he explained that everything emanates from the Lord and that the Lord is therefore worshipable (texts 15-18). Third, Narada concluded that everyone should satisfy the all-powerful Lord by performing devotional service (texts 19-22).

In his purport to text 22 Srila Prabhupada describes the reciprocal love between the Lord and His devotees: “A devotee cannot forget his obligation to the Supreme Personality of Godhead even for a single moment. Srila Visvanatha Cakravarti Thakura says that both the Supreme Lord and His devotee are rasa-jna, full of transcendental humor. . .. Those who are unaware of the position of the living entity and the Supreme Person, Krsna, think that the mutual attachment between the Lord and His devotees is a creation of the material energy. Factually such attachment is natural both for the Supreme Lord and for the devotee, and it cannot be accepted as material.”

## Texts 23-31: Narada Returns to Brahmaloka, Maitreya Concludes His Discourse, and Sukadeva Gosvami Offers Benedictions

Narada Muni returned to Brahmaloka, and the Pracetas, by Narada’s mercy, regained their attachment to the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Thus they began to constantly meditate on serving His lotus feet. Hearing about the Lord from a pure devotee and then thinking about Him, as Srila Prabhupada explains in his purport to text 24, takes one back to Godhead: “Here it is seen that by hearing the glories of the Lord from a realized devotee the Pracetas easily attained strong attachment for the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Then, meditating on the lotus feet of the Supreme Lord at the end of their lives, they advanced to the ultimate goal, Visnuloka. It is sure and certain that anyone who always hears the glories of the Lord and thinks of His lotus feet will reach that supreme destination. As Krsna says in Bhagavad-gita ([18.65](https://vedarama.com/en/books/bg/18.65))... ‘Always think of Me and become My devotee. Worship Me and offer your homage unto Me. Thus you will come to Me without fail. I promise you this because you are My very dear friend.’”

The Bhagavatam’s Fourth Canto concludes by returning to Sukadeva Gosvami’s discussion with Maharaja Pariksit. Sukadeva has completed his description of Uttanapada’s descendants—a topic that has taken the entirety of the Fourth Canto. In the Fifth Canto Sukadeva will narrate the activities of Priyavrata, Svayambhuva Manu’s elder son. Although Priyavrata became a renunciant after receiving Narada’s instructions, he later married and ruled the earth. Then he divided his property among his sons and returned to the spiritual world.

Sukadeva Gosvami says: Hearing about Uttanapada’s descendants from Maitreya Muni, Vidura was overwhelmed with ecstasy. With tears in his eyes, he fell down at the lotus feet of his spiritual master. He fixed the Supreme Personality of Godhead in his heart, offered his obeisances, and taking permission from Maitreya Muni, departed for Hastinapura, his home and the Pandavas’ capital.

Srila Prabhupada explains something we have seen and heard again and again in the Srimad-Bhagavatam: our devotion increases when we hear from and associate with pure devotees. In his purport to text 28 he writes: “This is a sign of associating with great devotees. A devotee takes instructions from a liberated soul and is thus overwhelmed by ecstasy from transcendental pleasure. As stated by Prahlada Maharaja: naisam matis tavad urukramanghrim sprsaty anarthapagamo yad-arthah, mahiyasam pada-rajo-’bhisekam niskincananam na vanita yavat—One cannot become a perfect devotee of the Lord without having touched the lotus feet of a great devotee. (Bhag. [7.5.32](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-7/5.32))”

In his purport to text 30 Srila Prabhupada explains Vidura’s selfless motive for returning to Hastinapura: “When a saintly person wants to see his kinsmen, he has no material desire to see them. He simply wants to give them some instructions so that they can benefit. Vidura belonged to the royal family of the Kauravas, and although he knew that all the family members were destroyed at the Battle of Kuruksetra, he nonetheless wanted to see his elder brother, Dhrtarastra, to see if he could deliver Dhrtarastra from the clutches of maya. When a great saintly person like Vidura sees his relatives, he desires only to deliver them from the clutches of maya. Vidura thus offered his respectful obeisances to his spiritual master and departed for the city of Hastinapura, the kingdom of the Kauravas.”

What happened when Vidura returned to see Dhrtarastra has already been described in the thirteenth chapter of Canto One. By Vidura’s strong, cutting words, old Dhrtarastra, who was languishing in the palace, was pulled out of his home and guided to use the few remaining days of his life for spiritual elevation. This inspiration to return to Hastinapura and help Dhrtarastra came to Vidura, of course, from Krsna, but he was also inspired after having heard Maitreya’s narration of one king after another retiring to the forest to make spiritual advancement at the end of his life. In Canto Four, a number of prominent kings followed this path of renunciation, among them Dhruva Maharaja, Prthu Maharaja, Pracinabarhisat Maharaja, and the Pracetas. Thus after hearing these narrations, Vidura wanted to offer the same opportunity to Dhrtarastra.

Sukadeva Gosvami ends Canto Four by blessing all those who have heard the instructions the Fourth Canto contains. Such hearers will attain “without difficulty a long life, wealth, good reputation, good fortune and, ultimately, the opportunity to return home, back to Godhead.” (Bhag. [4.31.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-4/31.31))

## Appendix

## Appendix I - Sruti and Smrti-Vedic Literature

*What follows is a brief, simplified synopsis of what constitutes Vedic literature.*

Veda means knowledge, and Vedic knowledge is apauruseya, originating from a transcendental source. The Vedas deal with both mundane and spiritual knowledge, but especially contain specific directions for spiritual realization, the highest spiritual realization being defined as knowledge of the Personality of Godhead. There are three sources (prasthana-traya) of Vedic knowledge: sruti-prasthana (Upanisads and Vedic mantras), smrti-prasthana (Bhagavad-gita, Mahabharata, Puranas, etc.), and nyaya-prasthana (Vedanta philosophy). All scientific knowledge of transcendence must be supported by sruti, smrti, and a sound logical basis (nyaya). Smrti and nyaya always confirm what is said in the sruti.

Material life is based on sense gratification. To cater to this aim, the Vedas mention three paths:

1. The karma-kanda path, or the path of fruitive activities meant to gain one promotion to higher planets. Using the method from the first five Vedangas, the Kalpa-sutras explain this path.
2. The upasana-kanda involves worshiping different controllers for promotion to their planets. The Agamas explain this path.
3. The jnana-kanda path involves reaizing the Absolute Truth in His impersonal feature in order to become one with Him. The Upanisads explain this path.

Although these three paths all come from the Vedas, the ultimate purpose of the Vedas is to gradually push one toward surrender in devotional service to Sri Krsna. Srila Prabhupada states, “But the best upasana is Visnupasana. Visnor aradhanam sarvesam. Visnor aradhanam param. От tad visnum paramam padam. There are different types of upasana recommendation, but the visnor aradhanam, worshiping Lord Visnu, that is the Supreme.” (Answers to questionnaire from Bhavan’s journal, June 28, 1976, Vrndavana)

**Sruti—“That Which Is Heard” The Four Vedas and Their Corollaries**

**Rg**—book of 1,028 divine hymns in ten mandalas, praising the gods, mainly Indra and Agni, but mentioning thirty-one other gods, and asking benedictions for wealth, health, longevity, protection, and victory. Considered the oldest of the four Vedas, it is the Veda from which the other three are derived.

**Sama**—over 1,500 songs and chants with metrical instructions, derived mainly from the Rg Veda and rearranged to facilitate singing the hymns during sacrifices.

**Yajur**—sacrificial mantras along with ritual formulae and instructions for the construction of sacrificial arenas and other aspects of sacrificial performances for priests.

**Atharva**—1,200 of the 6,000 verses have been derived from the Rg Veda. Considered the last of the Vedas to be composed, it contains magical incantations and mantras not for sacrificial performance but for everyday life.

Vyasadeva compiled and then divided the Vedas between various philosophers “so that they may be practically followed by less intelligent persons in the modes of passion and ignorance.” (Bhag. 1.4.24, purport) The Bhagavatam states that he gave charge of each Veda to a different “professor,” as follows:

**After the Vedas were divided into four divisions, Paila Rsi became the professor of the Rg Veda, Jaimini the professor of the Sama Veda, and Vaisampayana alone became glorified by the Yajur Veda. The Sumantu Muni Ahgira, who was very devotedly engaged, was entrusted with the Atharva Veda. And my father, Romaharsana, was entrusted with the Puraruis and historical record. (Bhag.** [**1.4.21-22**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/4.21)**)**

These scholars developed and preserved their respective Veda, offering their understanding of the meaning of sacrifice, the hymns, and the prayers the Vedas contained, creating the Brahmanas. The Brahmanas were mainly for city-dwelling householders, containing all the rituals and sacrifices prescribed for such persons. From the Rg Veda came the Aitarya and Kaushitaki Brahmanas; from the Sama Veda came the Tandya, Shadvimsa, Chandogya, and Jaiminya Brahmanas; from the Yajur Veda came the Taittiriya and Satapatha Brahmanas. The Brahmanas were followed by the “forest books,” the Aranyakas, which contained instructions for rituals and regulations to be practiced by renunciants, and which were then developed into the Upanisads.

The Upanisads supply the basis of philosophy and were available to all, whereas the four original Vedas remained mainly with the priests and scholars. Upanisad means “to receive knowledge while sitting near one’s teacher,” and these books contain conversations on the Absolute Truth between gurus and their disciples. The Upanisads basically negate the material conception and philosophically establish the transcendental understanding of the universe, and especially, the supremacy of the personal aspect of the Absolute Truth.

About the Upanisads, Srila Prabhupada said: “Upanisads are the headlines of the Vedas. Just like in a chapter there is a headline, similarly these Upanisads are the headlines of the Vedas. There are 108 Upanisads, principal. Out of that, nine Upanisads are very important. Out of those nine Upanisads, Svetasvatara Upanisad, Taittireya UpanT sad, Aitareya Upanisad, Isopanisad, Mundaka Upanisad, Mandukya Upanisad, Kathopanisad . . . are very important. And whenever there is argument on some point, one has to give reference from these Upani-sads. If one can give reference from the Upanisads, then his argument is very strong. Sahda-pramana.” (Lecture, November 27, 1968)Samhita, literally “joined” or “collected,” is another name for the four Vedas after they were divided. The term samhita was originally used to refer to the style of recitation of the hymns and mantras. The Brahmanas and Upanisads, as explained above, provide commentaries on the Samhitds. The Bhagavatam further explains the division of the Vedas and their relation to the Samhitds as follows:

**Srila Vyasadeva separated the mantras of the Rg, Atharva, Yajur and Sama Vedas into four divisions, just as one sorts out a mixed collection of jewels into piles. Thus he composed four distinct Vedic literatures. When Lord Brahma first spoke the four Vedas with his four mouths, the mantras were mixed together like an unsorted collection of various types of jewels. Srila Vyasadeva sorted the Vedic mantras into four divisions (samhitas), which thus became the recognizable Rg, Atharva, Yajur and Sama Vedas. (Bhag.** [**12.6.50**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-12/6.50)**)**

**The most powerful and intelligent Vyasadeva called four of his disciples, О brahmana, and entrusted to each of them one of these four samhitas. (Bhag.** [**12.6.51**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-12/6.51)**)**

Gopiparanadhana Prabhu, in a commentary on Sri Jiva’s Tattva' sandarbha, writes: “Casual readers of the Samhitas of the four Vedas usually see in them an unorganized assortment of praise and appeals offered to a large number of demigods. Many of these incompletely individualized deities seem nothing more than convenient personifications of forces of nature. Their personalities often overlap to the extent that it is difficult to clearly separate their identities. The Upanisads of each Veda correct this misunderstanding by elucidating the underlying reference throughout the Vedas to the one Absolute Truth, Brahman. The various deities of the Vedas and the energies of nature are shown in the Upanisads to be all integrally related to Brahman as its expansions, borrowing its own names, forms, and functions.”

**Smrti—“That Which Is Remembered (Or Understood) from What One Has Heard”**

The smrti is rooted in the sruti, and as such, is considered, along with the Upanisads and the Brdhmanas, to be a commentary on the original four Vedas.

As commentaries on the Upanisads, various sages developed the “Six Darsanas” or “six philosophical views.” All of the Darsanas consider the same philosophical problems central and share many basic ideas with one another and with Buddhism. The “Six Darsanas” are:

**Karma- (or Piirva-) mimamsa** (“Ritual” or “Former” Investigation)

**Main proponent:** Jaimini

**Main text:** Jaimini’s Purva'Mimdmsa'Sutra

**Basic philosophy:** Karma—the law of action and reaction—is an automatic and independent universal force. If one does his duty and perfectly performs sacrifices according to Vedic prescription, then God is obliged to follow His own law of action and reaction and give one the results. Any separate worship of or devotion to God, therefore, is purposeless.

**Uttara-mimamsa** (“Later Investigation”)

**Main proponent:** Vyasadeva

**Main text:** Vyasadeva’s Vedanta-sutra

**Basic philosophy:** Spiritual life begins with inquiry into the Absolute Truth. “Brahman is, in a nutshell, described: ‘Brahman means the origin of everything.’ Janmady asya yatah. And in Bhagavad-gita it is said, vedais ca sarvair aham eva vedyam. All the Vedas, all books of knowledge, their business is how to search out God. . . . the whole Vedanta is description of the Supreme Personality of Godhead.” (Answers to a questionnaire from Bhavan’s journal, June 28, 1976, Vrndavana)

**Sankhya-yoga** (yoga of “counting” or “analysis of elements”)

**Main proponent:** Kapila, Devahuti’s son, taught Sankhya, but it was later co-opted by the atheist Kapila.

**Basic philosophy:** Uses three types of evidence, perception, inference, and sruti. Divides the universe into two main categories, purusa and prakrti, and then further divides it into the gunas, the elements, etc. Devahuti’s son states that the purpose of analyzing the elements is to discern spirit from matter, understanding that spirit is the source of matter, and “bhakti-vitana-yogam, how bhakti, devotional service to the Lord, is expanded.” (Lecture, December 1, 1974, on Bhagavatam [3.25.31](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/25.31), Bombay) The atheist Kapila used the same system with the understanding that matter was the source of spirit. Srila Prabhupada writes, “\[The atheist Kapila\] concluded that the material world consists of twenty-four material elements, . . . and the unmanifested state of the three modes of nature (pradhana). When Kapila was unable to perceive the unmanifested soul after analyzing the twenty-four elements, he concluded that God does not exist.” (Renunciation through Wisdom, p. 53)

**Yoga** (linking with the Supreme)

**Main proponent:** Patanjali.

**Main text:** Yoga-sutras written by Patanjali.

**Basic philosophy:** The Yoga'sutras focus on Krsna as Paramatma and the means to attain Him. Patanjali systemized yoga into eight steps (aspinga-yoga): yama, niyama, asana, pranayama, pratyahara, dharana, dhyana, and samadhi.

**Vaisesika** (specialized logic)

**Main proponent:** Kanada Rsi

**Main text:** Vaisesika-sutra

**Basic philosophy:** “The Vaisesikas say that the visible universe is created from an original stock of atoms (janim asatah). As Kanada Rsi’s Vaisesika-sutras ([7.1.20](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-7/1.20)) state, nityam parimandalam: ‘That which is of the smallest size, the atom, is eternal.’ Kanada and his followers also postulate etemality for other, nonatomic entities, including the souls who become embodied, and even a Supreme Soul. But in Vaisesika cosmology the souls and the Supersoul play only token roles in the atomic production of the universe.” (Bhag. 10.87.25, purport) They therefore do not worship a single supreme being, but worship many gods as part of the “infinity of souls.”

**Nyaya** (logic)

**Main proponent:** Gautama Rsi

**Main text:** Nydya-sastra

**Basic philosophy:** A systemized process meant to teach the correct method by which to engage in philosophical inquiry, the process of reasoning, and the laws of thought.

**Other Smrti Literature**

**Agamas**—lit., “handed down, approaching, emanating” as in a tradition being handed down or one scripture emanating from another. Srila Prabhupada defines the agamas as, “coming from a higher plane; not from here.” (Lecture, Hyderbad, August 17, 1976) The agamas are theological treatises containing practical instructions on how to worship the Lord, specifically in His deity form, through mantra, tantra, and у antra, and include instructions on festivals, home worship, temple-building, how to make deities, etc. There are three divisions of agamas: Vaisnava, Saivite, and Sakta. The Vaisnava agamas are divided into four groups: Vijnanalalitas, Pancaratras, Vaikhdnasas, and Pratisthasaras. The Pancaratras, which are accepted by Vaisnavas as the most authoritative, are further divided into seven groups: Naradiya, Gautamiya, Brahma, Saiva, Kaumara, Vasistha, and Kapila. The Pancaratras state that Krsna is the source of everything.

Under the Vedic rules (vidhi), a student is required to be the son of a brahmana or otherwise twicebom before receiving knowledge; the Pancaratrika-vidhi, however, bases its acceptance on quality, not birth, and therefore even a siidra can be elevated to the status of a brahmana to receive transcendental knowledge. The Pahcaratrika system initiates candidates into devotional service, engaging them fully in serving the Lord’s deity. As human society has become more and more degraded, no one is fit any longer for the Vedic system (kalau sudra-sambhavah), and the Pahcaratrika system therefore provides an avenue for deliverance for the people of Kali-yuga.

Acaryas in the four authorized Vaisnava sampraddyas have compiled deity worship manuals based on the Pahcaratras. Sri Caitanya Mahaprabhu instructed Srila Sanatana Gosvami to do the same. The Haribhakti'Vildsa is the result. Srila Rupa Gosvami also included much information especially from the Narada-Pancaratra in his book, Bhakti-rasamrta'sindhu.

There are twenty-eight Saivite agamas and twenty-seven Sakta agamas. The agamas cater to an individual’s consciousness by providing instructions on how to worship a controller in order to reach a certain standard of material or spiritual fulfillment. The agamas are therefore divided into concentration on five separate controllers:

1. Sakti, or the energy of God—Sakta-agamas
2. Surya or the visible source of energy in this world—Soura-agamas
3. Ganapati or master of the ganas, the multitudes and remover of obstacles in one’s endeavors—Ganapatya'dgamas
4. Siva or the destroyer—Saiva-dgamas
5. Visnu or the ultimate source—Vaikhanasa-agamas

**Dharma-sastras**—smrti commentation on sruti, related directly to the Brdhmanas, and containing approximately 100,000 texts. Among them is the famous Manu-samhita. Srila Prabhupada writes, “For karmadcanda there are eighty authorized scriptures, such as Manu-samhita, which are known as dharmaAdstras. In these scriptures one is advised to counteract his sinful acts by performing other types of fruitive action. This was the path first recommended by Sukadeva Gosvami to Maharaja Pariksit, and actually it is a fact that one who does not take to devotional service must follow the decision of these scriptures by performing pious acts to counteract his impious acts. This is known as atonement.” (Bhag. [6.1.7](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-6/1.7), purport)

Elsewhere (Bhag. [6.2.11](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-6/2.11), purport) Srila Prabhupada says there are twenty types of dharma-sastras, “beginning with the Manu-samhita and Pardsarasamhita. ”

**Mahabharata and Ramayana**—texts that use narrative to teach philosophy. The history of “Greater India,” particularly the Kuru dynasty, and the story of Lord Ramacandra respectively. “As stated in Bhagavatam ([1.4.25](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-1/4.25)), Srila Vyasadeva compiled the Mahabharata for the less intelligent class of men, who take more interest in mundane topics than in the philosophy of life.” (Bhag. [3.5.12](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-3/5.12), purport) These books fall in the category of itihasas, “histories.”

**Puranas** (pura-nava = “old-new”—“things that are as good as new but which have existed since ancient times”):

While the Upanisads are mainly philosophical texts, the Puranas form a compendium of social, cultural, religious, and political thought. According to the Amara-kosa dictionary (and cited in Srimad-Bhagavatam), a Purana is defined as containing the following topics:

*sargo ’syatha visargas ca vrtti'raknantarani ca*  
*vamso vamsanucaritam samstha hetur apdsrayah*

**“O brahmana, authorities on the matter understand a Purana to contain ten characteristic topics: the creation of this universe, the subsequent creation of worlds and beings, the maintenance of all living beings, their sustenance, the rule of various Manus, the dynasties of great kings, the activities of such kings, annihilation, motivation and the supreme shelter. Other scholars state that the great Puranas \[Maha-Purdnas\] deal with these ten topics, while lesser Puranas \[Upa-Puranas\] may deal with five.” (Bhag.** [**12.7.9-10**](https://vedarama.com/en/books/sb-12/7.9)**)**

There are eighteen major Puranas and eighteen minor Puranas. The major Puranas are divided into three groups based on the three modes of nature and therefore the deity by whom they are influenced:

**Visnu-based Puranas:** Visnu, Bhagavata, Ndradiya, Garuda, Padma, Varaha

**Brahma-based Puranas:** Brahma, Brahmanda, Brahma-vaivarta, Markandeya, Bhavisya, Vamana

**Siva-based Puranas:** Vdyu, Linga, Skanda, Agni, Matsya, Kurma Upa-Puranas: Sanatkumdra, Ndrasimha, Naradiya, Siva, Durvasa, Kapila, Manava, Usanas, Varuna, Kalika, Samba, Saura, Aditya, Mdhesvara, Devi' bhagavata, Vasistha, Visnudharmottara, Nilamata

**Tantras:** texts considered “left-hand” or unorthodox, containing information on yoga techniques, goddess worship, black magic, and the use of yan-tras, mandalas, mantras, and certain sacrifices.

**Summary by Bhaktisiddhanta Sarasvati Thakura in Sri Krsna Caitanya**

The method of divine worship was elaborated in the Agama consisting of its twenty-four Samhitas. The Vedas are in old Sanskrit and were for that reason called the Nigama. The Agama was so named as having been written in the then new language to distinguish it from the Nigama. The Vaisnava Agama bears the name Pancaratra. The Pancaratra contains the rules for the regulation of the spiritual life of the Vaisnavas. These are the sattvika Tantras. . . . The term Pancaratra means “that which contains knowledge about the five subjects, viz., tapa, pundra \[tilaka markings\], ndma, mantram, and worship. . . . The term tantra, which means “that which elaborates,” is ordinarily applied to the rajasic and tamasic Tantras. The Pancaratra instructs regarding the application of those theistic principles that are declared in the spiritual portion of the Vedas, illustrated concretely in the narratives of the Puranas, and collated in the Sutras.

All those are the extensions of the real Veda. If the Veda is conceived as a person, the Upanisads may be regarded as his intellect and the Vedangas as his different functional organs (karmanga). The Vedangas are six in number, viz, (1) Siksd (intonation), (2) Kalpa (procedure), (3) Nirukta (dictionary), (4) Vyakarana (science of sound), (5) Jyotisa (astronomy, including astrology, dealing with space, time, and direction), and (6) Chhandas (poetic meters). These furnished the starting point of the various physical sciences of the subsequent rationalistic age in which there was a great advance in practical facilities of all kinds.

The aphoristic literature, which took upon itself the collation of the Vedangas, led to the Grkya- and Srauta-sutras, family and community sacrifices or rituals, the forerunners of the Pancaratra or the Tantra literature. The Dharma-sastras or smrtis belong to a later period.

The twenty Dharma-sastras are also divided into sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic, and are concerned with the regulation of an individual’s whole life. The sattvic smrtis . . . are distinguished from the rest. . . . The Dharma-sastras were made by royal authority and are of a miscellaneous and secular character. They had no jurisdiction over the intellectual communities. The Dharma-sastras do not belong to the class of revealed literature.

The Pancaratras bear the names of persons to whom they were spoken by Narayana and are in the form of conversations between Siva and Parvati.

The Pancaratras are thus an authoritative expansion and supplement of the Veda (Truth or Absolute knowledge) in the same way as the Puranas. There are early statements in the body of the technical Vedic literature to the effect that the Puranas are an integral part of the revealed literature. Those passages have been pointed out by the later Vaisnava acaryas. It is specifically stated in the Mahabharata and by Manu that the Veda should be supplemented by the Itihasa (histories) and the Puranas. Because the Veda is supplemented by the Purana, the latter is called purana \[bringing together old and new\]. The Madhyandin smrti classes itihasas and Purana, with the Vedic Samhitas to form the body of the revealed literature.

\[The\] sattvic Puranas are said to lead to emancipation, the rajasic to paradise, and the tamasic to hell. This principle holds in regard to the Tantras. The distinction between sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic sastras is also defined in another way. The sattvic sastras are those that establish that Godhead is full of all the qualities and is the highest of all. Those sastras that declare the superiority of Brahma, Agni, and Sarasvati, are rajasic. Those that state the superiority of Siva and recommend the Siva-lihgam as the object of worship are tamasic Tantras. Sattvic persons worship Visnu, rajasic persons Brahma, and tamasic persons Rudra. . . . The superiority of the sattvic Purana is nowhere explicitly challenged.

**Points Regarding the Nature of the Vedas, by Gopiparanadhana Dasa, While Discussing Sri Jiva Gosvami’s Tattva-sandarbha**

Because the Vedic sound directly emanates from the intelligence of the Supreme Being, all the Vedas and their numerous supplements form a unified whole. They are expressions of one and the same consciousness. The intelligence of the Supreme is infinite, and communicates with the variously limited intelligences of His countless creatures in an unlimited number of ways. . . . Thus the Vedic literature appears as many separate books in a number of categories of texts that seem to have been written at different times, for different purposes, in different styles of language, and by authors with different convictions and different levels of knowledge. The Vedas explain themselves in another way, however, and if we are willing to look at the entire Vedic literature from its own point of view instead of with the attitude of critical analysis, then with some scrutiny we can see the true picture: the apparent diversity of the texts is in fact due not to their being written by different authors but to their being spoken for several different audiences.

Vedic literature is divided into two main kinds of texts, sruti and smrti. Sruti ... is eternal, revealed scripture received in this world by rsis in their meditation and repeated unchanged through disciplic chains of teachers and disciples. Smrti ... is literature composed by the sages in their own words and reflecting the message of sruti without having to maintain the same exact wording in the same order perpetually. ... To ordinary perception, the language and contents of the Samhitas, especially of the Rg Veda Samhita, seem the most archaic. The Brahmanas, Aranyakas, and Upanisads appear to be afterthoughts, speculations by later generations about the meaning and purpose of the Samhitas; they were written in a variety of successively “newer” dialects, gradually approaching “classical” Sanskrit.

The Upanisads seem an altogether different sort of work, discussing as they do otherworldly concerns hardly touched on in the “older” ritual sruti. There are many superficial reasons, therefore, for critical scholars to disregard the Vedas’ own claim to being a single, coherent whole. Not understanding the methods of sabda-pramana, the unfortunate Indologists can only try to dissect the separate organs of the Vedic corpus, unaware that the organism is actually alive.

From one viewpoint, a particular plant’s stages of growth—its seed, sprout, flower, and fruit—are quite distinct events that occur at different times. Viewed another way, however, the plant’s stages of growth are part of a timeless cycle: there have been many earlier generations of plants of the same kind, and there will be many more in the future. Each new instance of the plant simply copies the permanent genetic plan. In essence, the seed of the species is no older than its fruit. Similarly, we can understand that the eternal Vedas temporarily display parts of themselves to human perception at various historical

points in the cycle of ages. Srimad-Bhagavatam calls Sri Krsna svayam bhagavan, the “original Personality of Godhead,” or in other words, the oldest person; but the Bhagavatam also describes Lord Krsna’s appearance on earth as an avatara in the dynasty of the moon god fifty-six generations after its founder. The Vedas, being co-etemal with the Supreme Lord, also descend to earth at specific times. Thus the language of the Rg Veda can appear to be an ancestor of “later” Sanskrit, though in reality the two are simultaneously existing dialects of the same language, one liturgical and the other vernacular .. .

Especially important for the spiritual education of the general public are the itihasas and the Puranas. These works are written in simple, spoken Sanskrit and aim at explaining all aspects of Vedic knowledge to nonspecialists, often through entertaining historical narrations. Although both the itihasas and the Puranas describe the ancient history of the universe, the itihasas generally concentrate on single heroes or events, while the Puranas deal with an assortment of topics. ... As many authoritative sources attest, the itihasas and Puranas are faithful to sruti, so much so that the Upanisads call them the fifth Veda. They are available and not difficult to understand. They give us access to ways of ancient wisdom that would otherwise be closed off.

## Appendix II - Names in the Bhagavatam

What follows is not a complete listing of all names found in the first four cantos of Srimad-Bhagavatam, but a partial list of names that appear in this book, with their literal definitions (in most cases) and a note on who the person is and his or her family connections.

Devotees often comment that the names of the persons described in scripture are extremely suitable to their personalities and activities. It is interesting to note that certain names are actually titles and not personal names at all. The name Janaka, for example, means “father of the people,” and is a generic name for “king.” In other cases, names were chosen by astrologers, who made accurate predictions of a child’s future activities, and thus the accuracy of the names. And in Vedic culture, people often had more than one name beyond their “birth” name, names gathered throughout life based on their qualities and deeds. The Bhagavatam often uses these names when telling the various pastimes.

**A**

Abhimanyu—“fearless (abhi),” “capable of powerful anger (many и)”; son of Arjuna and Subhadra.

Adhoksaja—“he who cannot be seen by direct sense perception”; Krsna or Visnu.

Agastya Muni—“mountain-thrower”; bom from a water jar as the son of Mitra-Varuna and Urvasi, he once swallowed the ocean and forced the Vindhya mountain range to prostrate itself before him and thus curbed the Vindhyas’ pride.

Akrura—“not cruel, gentle”; Krsna’s maternal uncle.

Akuti—“one who accomplishes the wishes of; the fulfillment of a desire”; daughter of Svayambhuva Manu and Satariipa.

Anasiiya—“free from envy”; daughter of Daksa, wife of Atri Muni, and mother of Soma, Dattatreya, and Durvasa. She was a powerful ascetic in her own right, and according to the Ramayana, was once able to cause trees to bear fruit and the Ganga to flow again after a ten-year drought.

Angira—son of Brahma, father of Brhaspati, and the sage to whom the hymns of the Atharva Veda were entrusted and author of some writings on astronomy.

Aniruddha—“unobstructed, self-willed”; the director of the mind; Krsna’s grandson.

Antardhana—“invisibility”; name for Vijitasva, eldest son of King Prthu. He received the gift of invisibility from Indra when, out of respect, he did not stop Indra, who himself was invisible at the time, from stealing Maharaja Prthu’s one hundredth horse.

Arjuna—“one of pure deeds,” “pure, unsullied”; from arjava, “uncomplicated mind, speech, and behavior”; one of the five Pandavas.

Asvatthama—asvasya eva sthama balam yasya: “he whose strength is like that of a horse”—the Mahabharata states that because Asvatthama cried like a horse at birth, he received this name; son of Dronacarya and Krpi, and friend of Duryodhana. He lived through the Kuruksetra war but was cursed by Krsna for killing Draupadi’s five sons in their sleep and attempting to kill Pariksit in Uttara’s womb.

Atri—“devourer” (after Lord Siva); one of Brahma’s mental sons, husband of Anasuya, and father of Soma, Dattatreya, and Durvasa. Also, one of the seven sages (saptarsis).

**В**

Bahuka—“dwarflike”; churned from Vena’s body, Bahuka was considered the extirpation of Vena’s sins.

Baladeva—“divinely powerful”; Krsna’s elder brother and first plenary expansion.

Barhisat—related to “grasses used in sacrifices”; son of Havirdhana. He was so expert in performing sacrifices that he became known as a Prajapati.

Bharata—“to maintain”; a number of kings in the Bhagavatam had this name—Bharata, son of Dusyanta and Sakuntala, after whom the world is purported to have been named; Bharata, son of Dasaratha and Kaikeyi; and Bharata, the son of Rsabhadeva, whose three lives are described in the Fifth Canto.

Bhima(sena)—“formidable”; one of the five Pandavas.

Bhisma—“terrible, dreadful”; he received this name because he renounced his claim to his father’s throne so his father could remarry. Son of Santanu and Gahgadevi, “grandfather” of the Kuru dynasty, and one of the twelve mahajanas, he was given a boon to leave his body at will. He died while lying on a bed of arrows in Sri Krsna’s presence.

Bhrgu—“the shining one”; son of Brahma, a great sage, and the founder of the Bhrgu vamsa, whose members are known as the Bhargavas.

Brahma—vamhati vardhate yah: “he who becomes greater,” “the greatest one”; first created being.

Brhaspati—“lord of prayer or devotion”; priest of the demigods.

Buddha—“enlightened”; one of the dasavataras, who appeared to bewilder atheists and dissuade them from unnecessary animal sacrifices.

**C**

Candavega—“he whose impulse is fierce”; time personified.

Citraketu—“amazing”; a king who was enlightened by Narada and Ahgira Muni and later cursed by Parvati to become the demon, Vrtrasura. He was a devotee of Lord Sankarsana.

**D**

Daksa—“expert”; a mind-bom son of Brahma and a Prajapati. Father of Lord Siva’s wife, Sati.

Daksina—“she who is meant to be offered to Yajna”; partial incarnation of the goddess of fortune and daughter of Prajapati Ruci and his wife, Akuti.

Dattatreya—data, “gift,” atreya, “son of Atri”; the gift to Atri Muni (and his wife, Anasiiya). A partial incarnation of Lord Visnu, who taught the philosophy of the spirit soul.

Devahuti—“she who calls God”; daughter of Svayambhuva Manu and Satarupa, wife of Kardama Muni, and mother of Kapiladeva.

Devaki—“divine”; wife of Vasudeva and mother of Krsna.

Dhanvantari—“moving in a curve”; a partial incarnation of Lord Visnu, who carried the jug containing the nectar churned from the milk ocean.

Dhrtarastra—dhrtam rastram yena: “he by whom the kingdom is held”; son of Vyasadeva, blind older brother of Pandu and Vidura, and father of Duryodhana.

Diti—“to cut or divide”; daughter of Daksa, wife of Kasyapa Muni, and mother of the daityas, Hiranyaksa and Hiranyakasipu.

Drona—“he who was bom in a bucket”; military guru of the Kurus and Pandavas.

Dhruva—“fixed in purpose”; son of Uttanapada and Suniti.

Draupadi—“daughter of Drupada”; fire-bom sister of Dhrstadyumna and wife of all five Pandava brothers.

Durga—“one who brings pain or difficulty”; wife of Lord Siva and goddess presiding over material nature, bewildering souls there to accept the body as themselves and to try to enjoy matter. Her power is superseded only by Lord Visnu’s power.

Durvasa—“he who is ill-dressed”; son of Atri Muni and Anasuya. A partial incarnation of Lord Siva, Durvasa is famous for his bad temper.

Duryodhana—“one who gives pain or hardship”; firstborn son of Dhrtarastra and Gandhari and chief rival of the Pandavas. Killed by Bhima at the end of the Kuruksetra war.

**G**

Gajendra—“lord of elephants”; he was saved from a crocodile by Lord Visnu and awarded liberation.

Gandhari—“of the kingdom of Gandhara,” thought to be located in the eastern-Afghanistan-northwest-Pakistan region; wife of Dhrtarastra and mother of Duryodhana, she embraced voluntary blindness as an act of chastity to her husband.

Garuda—“devourer”; son of Kasyapa and Vinata and devoted eagle carrier of Visnu. The emblem of Garuda is always on Krsna’s chariot.

Govinda—“one who pleases and protects the cows, senses, and the earth (land)”; a name for Lord Krsna.

**H**

Hanuman—“large-jawed”; named because as a child he thought to swallow the sun. Vanara son of Vayu and Anjana, an eleventh portion of Rudra, halfbrother of Bhima, and great devotee of Lord Ramacandra, assisting Him to defeat Ravana.

Hari—“one who steals away what is inauspicious”; a name for Lord Krsna.

Hayagriva—“horse-necked”; an incarnation of Lord Visnu who rescued the Vedas from the daityas and presented them to Brahma.

Hiranyakasipu—“one who likes gold and soft beds”; son of Kasyapa and Diti, brother of Hiranyaksa, father of Prahlada Maharaja, and ultimately killed by Nrsimhadeva.

Hiranyaksa—hiranyavat pite aksini yasya: “he whose eyes are yellow like gold”; son of Kasyapa and Diti, brother of Hiranyakasipu, he was killed by Varahadeva after causing the earth to be submerged in the Garbhodaka Ocean.

**I**

Indra—“conqueror”; chief of the demigods.

J

Janardana—“one who by His nature protects His devotees and removes obstacles on the devotional path”; a name for Lord Krsna.

Jara—“old age, withering”; daughter of Candavega (time) and wife of Bhaya (fear).

Jarasandha—“he whose body was reunited by the witch, Jara”; son of Brhadratha, king of Magadha, and enemy of Lord Krsna.

Jaya—“victory”; one of the Vaikuntha doorkeepers cursed by the Kumaras to take birth in the material world.

**К**

Kalakanya—“daughter of time,” she is the invalidity of old age; another name for Jara.

Kali—“quarrel”; the personification of the Iron Age.

Kalki—kalkar papam haryyataya asti asya: “he whose duty is to remove the sins (kalka)”; the tenth incarnation of Visnu, He comes at the end of Kali-yuga.

Kamsa—“bell metal”; son of Ugrasena, cousin-brother of Devaki, and enemy of Krsna.

Kapila—“he whose complexion is tawny”; an incarnation of Krsna, son of Kardama and Devahuti, and teacher of Sankhya-yoga.

Kardama—“shadow”; son of Pulaha and Ksama, husband of Devahuti, and father of Kapiladeva.

Kama—“of the ear”; son of the sun god and Kuntidevi before she was married. Kunti abandoned the child and he was raised by the charioteer Adhirata and his wife, Radha. He was bom with earrings and natural body armor—a gift from his divine father. A friend of Duryodhana, he was killed by Arjuna during the Kuruksetra war.

Kasyapa—kasyam somarasam adijanitarh madyam pibatid: “he who drinks beverages such as soma'rasa, etc.”; grandson of Brahma, a Prajapati, father of Vamanadeva, and husband to thirteen of Daksa’s daughters. He fathered a number of races.

Kesava—“killer of the Kesi demon,” “one with fine black hair,” “supreme controller”; a name for Lord Krsna.

Khatvanga—“one who is on his deathbed”; another name for King Dilipa of the Iksvaku dynasty. After pleasing Krsna, he was given the benediction to know when he would die and surrendered himself fully to the Lord.

Krsna—“he who attracts the minds and hearts of everyone”; the Supreme Personality of Godhead.

Kumaras—four sons of Brahma who have chosen to remain eternally as children (kumaras); they are Sanaka, Sanatana, Sananda, and Sanat-kumara.

Kumbhakarna—“pot-eared”; younger brother of Ravana, who while trying to secure the boon, nirdevatam (“no demigods”), asked for nirdravatvam (“sleep”) when the demigods encouraged Sarasvati to trip up his tongue. He was killed in the battle to regain Sita by Lord Ramacandra.

Kunti—“daughter of Kuntibhoja”; wife of Pandu, mother of the Pandavas, and aunt of Lord Krsna.

Kuru—the ancient king from which the Kauravas and the Pandavas trace their lineage.

Kuvera—lord of the Yaksas and god of wealth and treasure.

**L**

Laksmi(devi)—“success, happiness, fortune, grace”; consort of Lord Narayana in Vaikuntha and the goddess of fortune.

**M**

Maitreya—“the son of Mitra,” “the friendly one”; guru of Vidura after Krsna returned to the spiritual world. He spoke Srimad-Bhagavatam to Vidura during Vidura’s voluntary exile from the Kaurava kingdom.

Malayadhvaja—“ firm as the Malaya Hills”; a king in the Pandu country to whom Vaidarbhi was married after her life as Pracinabarhisat.

Marisa—“worthy” or “respectable”; wife of the Pracetas and mother of Daksa in his incarnation after having insulted Lord Siva.

**N**

Naimisaranya—yas tu nimisenadam nihatam danavam balam/ aranye smith tatas tena naimisaranyasas'jnitam: “Because an army of demons was destroyed in a second (nimisa) at this place, this forest is called naimisa"; the forest chosen by the sages at the beginning of Kali-yuga for the performance of their thousand-year sacrifice.

Nakula—nasti kulam yasya: “he who is homeless”; one of the five Pandavas, along with his twin brother, Sahadeva.

Narada—naram paramatmdjnanam dadati yah sah naradah: “he who gives the essence, knowledge about God”; son of Lord Brahma and transcendental preacher of the holy name.

Narakasura—“hell-demon”; son of the earth goddess, but under Banasura’s influence, he became a demon and was later killed by Krsna.

Narayana—nara jalam ayanam sthanam yasya: “he whose abode is the water called nara”; the Supreme Lord.

**P**

Pandu—“pale”; son of Vyasadeva, brother to Dhrtarastra and Vidura, and father to the five Pandavas, Pandu was king of Hastinapura.

Parasurama—“the Rama who holds an ax”; son of Jamadagni and Renuka, he destroyed twenty-one generations of lawless ksatriyas. The sixth incarnation of Krsna.

Pariksit—“one who seeks with the eyes,” “examiner.” Also, “one who is beheld with the eyes”; son of Abhimanyu and Uttara, grandson of Arjuna and Subhadra, and king after the Pandavas left for the north.

Pracetas—“those who are highly conscious, clever, wise, and observant”; the ten sons of Pracinabarhi.

Pracinabarhi—“because he carpeted the ground with darbha grass, with its heads turned east, this was his name—praci = east; barhis = bed of kusa grass”; the king to whom Narada told the analogy of Puranjana.

Pradyumna—“the mightiest one”; Lord of intelligence; son of Krsna and Rukmini.

Prasuti—“fruitful”; daughter of Svayambhuva Manu and Satarupa; wife of Daksa, and mother of sixteen daughters, including Sati, her youngest.

Priyavrata—“blessed vow,” “one who is beloved because of his vow”; son of Svayambhuva Manu and Satarupa.

Prthu—“broad, magnanimous” (the earth is named Prthvi after him); an incarnation of the Lord, son of Vena, and husband of Arci.

Puranjana—puram dehaksetram janayatiti: “he who causes the production of a body”; an allegorical king representing Maharaja Pracinabarhi.

Pusa—“to nourish, increase”; a sage who smiled when Daksa insulted Lord Siva and who subsequently had his teeth knocked out by Virabhadra.

**R**

Rama—“reservoir of pleasure,” “charming,” “bringing rest”; can refer to Krsna’s brother, Balarama, or Lord Ramacandra, or, as in the Hare Krsna mantra, to Krsna Himself.

Ravana—“loud wailing or lamentation”; son of Visravas and great-grandson of Brahma, Ravana was the ten-headed demon king of Lanka and Rama’s enemy.

Romaharsana—“he who causes the hairs to stand on end”; a famous disciple of Vyasadeva, killed by Lord Balarama because of his pride.

Rsabhadeva—“the Lord of the best ones”; an incarnation of the Lord and father of King Nabhi.

Ruci—“resplendent”; husband of Akuti and father to the Lord’s incarnation, Yajna, Prajapati Ruci gave his son to his father-in-law Svayambhuva Manu to raise, as per the marriage agreement.

Rudra—“one who cries,” also, “ruddy or reddish”; the form of Lord Siva that personifies Lord Brahma’s anger and who destroys the universe during devastation.

Rukmini—“radiant”; daughter of King Bhismaka, sister of Rukmi, wife of Krsna, and mother of Pradyumna.

**S**

Sahadeva—“he who is accompanied by God”; one of the younger of the five Pandava brothers, along with Nakula.

Sankarsana—“completely attractive”; incarnation of the total ego. Also, another name for Lord Balarama (who was attracted from Devaki’s womb to Rohini’s womb).

Satarupa—“she who has hundreds of forms or who expands herself into hundreds (by producing descendants)”; wife of Svayambhuva Manu and mother of Devahuti, grandmother of Kapiladeva and Yajna.

Saunaka—“son of sage Sunaka”; a famous acarya and head of the sages at Naimisaranya who asked questions of Suta Gosvami.

Siva—“auspicious”; the guna-avatara for the mode of ignorance.

Subhadra—“beautiful and auspicious”; sister of Krsna and Balarama, wife of Arjuna, and mother of Abhimanyu.

Sukadeva—“parrot”; son of Vyasa, he spoke the Srimad-Bhagavatam to Maharaja Pariksit on the bank of the Ganga.

Suniti—“righteous or with good conduct”; wife of Uttanapada and mother of Dhruva Maharaja.

Suta—“the son of a ksatriya and a brahmana”; a sage who was present when Sukadeva Gosvami spoke the Bhagavatam to Maharaja Pariksit and who later repeated it to the sages at Naimisaranya.

Svayambhuva—“the son of Svayambhu (Brahma)”; a Manu, husband of Satarupa, father of Uttanapada, Priyavrata, Devahuti, and others, and grandfather of two incarnations, Kapiladeva and Yajna.

**U**

Uddhava—uddhnoti durham iti: “he who removes miseries.” Krsna’s friend and advisor in Mathura.

Uttama—“best, highest”; son of Uttanapada and Suruci and brother of Dhruva Maharaja.

Uttanapada—“he who has spread his feet” (and therefore owns a vast tract of land); son of Svayambhuva Manu, husband to Suniti and Suruci, and father of Dhruva Maharaja.

**V**

Vadarayana—vadarayane vadarikasrame mivasatiti: “he who dwells in Badarikasrama”; another name for Vyasadeva.

Vamana—vamayati vamati va madam iti: “he who gives up pride or makes one throw out his pride”; Krsna’s dwarf incarnation, appearing as the son of Kasyapa and Aditi, and the brother of Indra.

Vasudeva—vasuna dhanena dlvyatiti: “he who enjoys or shines with wealth”; Krsna’s father in Mathura and the husband of Devaki.

Vibhisana—grandson of Pulastya Muni, brother of Ravana, and devotee of Lord Rama. Rama gave him Sri Lanka to rule for four yugas. He is one of eight personalities who lives for more than one cycle of four yugas.

Vidura—“the wise one”; son of Vyasadeva by the maidservant Ambalika, halfbrother of Dhrtarastra and Pandu, and incarnation of Yamaraja. A great devotee of Krsna, he constantly tried to restrain Dhrtarastra from mistreating the Pandavas. Later, he encouraged Dhrtarastra to embrace the path of self-realization.

Visnu—“all-pervading”; the Supreme Lord.

Vyasa—“he who splits or compiles, an editor”; son of Parasara Muni and Satyavati, father of Sukadeva Gosvami, and disciple of Narada Muni. Vyasadeva split the Vedas into sections and was responsible for writing them down.

**Y**

Yadu—yajate iti: “he who sacrifices”; son of Yayati and Devayani and founder of the Yadu dynasty, of which Krsna was a member.

Yajna—“he to whom everything is to be offered”; son of Ruci and Akuti, grandson of Svayambhuva Manu, an incarnation of the Lord.

Yudhisthira—yudhi sangrame sthirah: “one who is firm in battle”; eldest of the five Pandava brothers.
